Re: 
Berklee College of Music – Submittal of IMPNF for Renewal and Extension of 2022-
2024 Institutional Master Plan 
Mr. Carter: 
On behalf of Berklee College of Music, Inc. (Berklee), please find enclosed for submittal a 
request to renew and extend Berklee’s 2022-2024 Institutional Master Plan (IMP) with the City 
of Boston Planning Department (formerly known as the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency) for an additional two years. The proposed Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
(IMPNF) would renew and extend Berklee’s current IMP for two years, until November 2026, to 
allow Berklee to complete a campus-wide master planning evaluation. The results of that 
evaluation will help Berklee develop a comprehensive 10-year Institutional Master Plan for the 
City’s review, to be submitted in Fall 2026. Further details are included in the attached IMPNF. 
No substantive changes to Berklee’s IMP are proposed. 
If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me at (617) 621-6562. 
Very truly yours,

6420/Berklee College of Music 
1-1 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
1.0 
INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL INFORMATION 
1.1 
Introduction 
Berklee College of Music, Inc. is pleased to submit this Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
(IMPNF) to the Boston Redevelopment Authority (d/b/a Boston Planning and Development 
Agency and referred to herein as the BRA or BPDA depending upon context). As described further 
below in Section 1.2, Berklee College of Music merged with the Boston Conservatory of Music on 
June 1, 2016. This IMPNF presents a description of the merged institution, referred to herein as 
Berklee or the Proponent unless noted otherwise. 
With this submission, Berklee is initiating the process for approval of a new Institutional Master 
Plan (IMP) pursuant to Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code (the Code). Berklee is currently in 
the early planning stages of several potential future developments that have not yet been defined 
and is seeking an IMP for a two-year term. 
The purposes of the proposed IMP are threefold, including: 
♦ To describe the purpose and effects of the merger of Berklee College of Music, Inc. and 
The Boston Conservatory of Music, Inc. (i.e. Berklee) that became effective on June 1, 
2016, as well as to incorporate the former Conservatory properties in the description of 
the Berklee campus within the Berklee IMP; 
♦ To provide information on the status of the IMP projects included in the College’s IMP 
approved by the Boston Zoning Commission effective June 15, 2011, as well as those 
included in the Conservatory’s IMP approved by the Boston Zoning Commission effective 
October 19, 2011, and in Amendment #1 thereto approved by the then Boston 
Redevelopment Authority (BRA) on May 15, 2012; 
♦ To describe a new IMP project at 12 Hemenway Street, an existing building, which Berklee 
intends to use for student housing. Berklee’s goal is to be able to house 50% of students 
on campus to meet the City of Boston’s request to the higher education community in 
2013. Currently, the college only has around 25% of its students residing on campus. The 
additional beds at 12 Hemenway will contribute towards helping Berklee reach its goal; 
and 
♦ To describe potential future projects beyond the term of this two-year IMP which will also 
contribute towards Berklee’s goal of housing more students on campus. 
Berklee is the world’s largest independent music college and the premier institution for the study 
of contemporary music. Berklee College of Music (the College) was founded by pianist/arranger 
and MIT-trained engineer Lawrence Berk in 1945 as Schillinger House of Music. Berk changed the 
name to Berklee School of Music in 1954, and the school granted its first bachelor of music 
degrees in 1966. In 1973, the College obtained accreditation and changed its name to Berklee 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
1-2 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
College of Music. In 2004, the College inaugurated Roger Brown as its third president and 
announced a new vision for its future focused on the student experience. In July 2021, Dr. Erica 
Muhl was inaugurated as Berklee's fourth president. She has worked steadily to catalyze higher 
education toward change, in particular as a staunch public advocate for multidisciplinary and 
integrative programs that nurture innovative thought through an emphasis on creativity as fueled 
by technology and entrepreneurship. 
The College was founded on two revolutionary ideas: that musicianship could be taught through 
the music of the time; and that the College’s students need practical, professional skills for 
successful, sustainable music careers. While that bedrock philosophy has not changed, the music 
around the College has and requires that the College evolve with it. 
For more than half a century, the College has demonstrated its commitment to its philosophy by 
wholeheartedly embracing change. The College continually updates its curriculum and technology 
to make them more relevant, and to attract diverse students who reflect the multiplicity of 
influences in today's music. To assure that the College continually attracts an ever-widening 
audience, the College strives to develop new initiatives that reflect the contemporary music 
component of its curriculum. 
The Boston Conservatory of Music (the Conservatory) was founded in 1867 by Julius Eichberg, a 
German-born violinist. In 1920, Agide Jacchia, the Italian-born Boston Pops Orchestra conductor, 
took over leadership of the school and worked to revitalize its legacy by establishing the first grand 
opera department in the nation. Since that time, the Conservatory has grown to become the first 
conservatory to offer undergraduate degrees in dance, music, and theater – all three major arts 
disciplines – and solidified its place as the leading performing arts institution in the area. 
The Conservatory was founded on the principal that building strong connections with students 
and providing opportunities for all students to excel, regardless of gender or race, is essential to 
achieve superior music education. Throughout the Conservatory’s history, this founding idea has 
remained a guiding force. In 2007, it began offering private music lessons to students on the 
autism spectrum, the first conservatory to create this type of program. A few years later, it 
presented the college’s first performance that was autism friendly. Most recently in 2015, it 
became the first conservatory to offer graduate degrees in music education and autism. While 
much has changed since the Conservatory’s founding in 1867, it remains committed to offering 
all individuals a superior performance arts education. 
1.2 
Overview of the Merger 
Following a nearly two year-long period of informal discussions, consultations, and exploration; 
the trustees of the College and The Boston Conservatory authorized entering into a Memorandum 
of Understanding in June, 2015 to formally explore a possible merger. Following a six-month 
period of detailed due diligence, the trustees of both institutions unanimously approved an 
agreement to merge the two institutions, which was executed on January 20, 2016. Thereafter, 
 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
1-3 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
the necessary regulatory and accreditation review and approval processes were successfully 
completed, culminating in a merger of these two preeminent performing arts institutions on June 
1, 2016. Formal notice of the then-pending merger was provided to the then BRA on April 29, 
2016. 
At Berklee, students explore interdisciplinary approaches to music, dance, theater, film, business, 
healthcare, education, technology, and more. Pioneering youth programs reach underserved 
classrooms throughout the U.S. and beyond. With students and alumni from more than 100 
nations and educational partners across the world, new connections are being forged among art 
forms, musical traditions, and technologies to build a dynamic, diverse, and collaborative global 
arts community. 
The purpose and the aspiration of the merged institution are best described by the adopted Vision 
for 2025: 
“As the preeminent institute of contemporary music and the performing arts, Berklee will 
transform arts education and empower artists to better our world. Building an inclusive 
culture that promotes diversity in all its forms, we will nurture the growth of the world’s 
most inspired artists in music, theater, and dance so they may fully realize their creative 
and career potential. Berklee will forge new connections among art forms, musical 
traditions, technologies, and institutions, creating a dynamic global network that fosters 
innovation, collaboration, and community.” 
The objectives of the combined institution as summarized in the January 2016 Memorandum of 
Understanding include: 
♦ To jointly raise the global profile of Music, Theater, and Dance through leveraging the 
strengths of the combined organization 
♦ To elevate the quality of respective student populations 
♦ To enhance career opportunities for all students 
♦ To elevate the worldwide visibility of the combined entity and programs 
♦ To provide synergistic opportunities and reinvest net savings in Music, Theater, and Dance 
programs and scholarships while assuring a world-class education 
♦ To give all students a better overall experience through the breadth of offerings not 
currently available to students at either institution 
♦ To fully realize all identified programmatic opportunities with Berklee Online and Valencia 
♦ To explore and create opportunities across disciplines and art forms 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
1-4 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
The merger allows Berklee to leverage the individual strengths of both institutions in co-designing 
new courses and hybrid programs not possible elsewhere. These new offerings afford 
Conservatory students enhanced access to the College’s leading studies in improvisation and 
contemporary music, technology, music business, music therapy, sound design, production, film 
scoring, and online education. Likewise, the College’s students now benefit from access to the 
Conservatory’s expertise in classical music, opera, dance, movement, acting, and musical theater. 
The merger also allows for the creation of new summer and study abroad programs at the Berklee 
campus in Valencia, Spain that is housed in the Palau de les Arts Reina Sofia, the city’s iconic opera 
house. In addition, Conservatory faculty have begun to develop courses for Berklee On Line, the 
largest nonprofit online music school in the world. Students of the College and the Conservatory 
likewise will benefit from Berklee’s most recent endeavor, the Power Station recording studio and 
teaching facility located in the Hell’s Kitchen section of New York City, which opened for students 
in the Fall of 2021. Berklee is also committed to expanding online education as a component of 
addressing college affordability for students enrolled at the College and the Conservatory. 
1.3 
Berklee College Mission and Objectives 
The mission of Berklee is to educate, train, and develop students to excel in music as a career. 
Developing the musicianship of students is the foundation of Berklee’s curriculum. Berklee 
believes that the lessons and qualities derived from that work—the self-discipline needed for 
excellence, the empathy required for music making and the openness and inquisitiveness 
essential to creativity—are critical to achievement in any pursuit, musical or otherwise; and that 
music is a powerful catalyst for personal growth, which is central to any collegiate experience. 
Founded on jazz and popular music rooted in the African cultural diaspora, Berklee’s 
comprehensive curriculum is distinctly contemporary in its content and approach and embraces 
the principal musical movements of our time. Through a course of scholarly and practical learning 
experiences integrating performance and writing, the curriculum covers the variety of influential 
styles, relevant technologies, and career opportunities open to today's music professional. 
Berklee’s objectives are to: 
1. Adjust the curriculum to help students successfully progress through programs and 
graduate on time. 
2. Promote and support innovation and excellence in teaching and learning. 
3. Develop a global ecosystem of centers and partnerships that establishes Berklee as the 
world leader in creative and artistic education. 
4. Develop innovative programs that redefine creative education, broaden the type of 
students Berklee attracts, and reflect current industry and career trends. 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
1-5 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
5. Refine marketing, admissions, and financial aid–awarding strategies to attract, nurture, 
and enroll students with exceptional promise to succeed at Berklee. 
6. Improve student retention through meaningful and personalized engagement. 
7. Better prepare students to apply their skills, talents, and relationships to achieve their full 
potential in their chosen careers. 
8. Deepen sense of community by defining shared values and creating an institution-wide 
mission statement. 
9. Upgrade operational systems and processes to support a personalized student experience 
and excellent financial stewardship. 
10. Consistently achieve strong operational performance and ensure long-term financial 
sustainability. 
11. Use a data-driven approach to measure progress toward these goals. 
1.4 
History of IMP Process to Date/Zoning 
1.4.1 
Berklee IMP 
The College worked with the staff of the then BRA and the appointed Berklee Institutional Master 
Plan Task Force over the course of seventeen public meetings held over two years in which elected 
officials, area residents and community group representatives also participated. The College then 
prepared and filed an IMPNF on January 30, 2009, in accordance with Article 80D of the Boston 
Zoning Code in which two institutional projects were proposed. These included: 
♦ The Berklee Crossroads project, a proposed 295,000 gross floor area (gfa), 330-foot-tall 
mixed-use development that would include a new 1,200–1,600 seat Berklee Performance 
Center, a 425-450 bed residence hall and additional academic and student life space. 
♦ 161-171 Massachusetts Avenue, the proposed substantial rehabilitation of and addition 
to two existing structures to accommodate new classrooms and other academic space. 
The then BRA issued its Scoping Determination on April 6, 2009. In that Scoping Determination, 
concerns were expressed about the impacts associated with proposed height of the Berklee 
Crossroads project, and the College was encouraged to make a cogent case for the proposed 
height of that project, or to otherwise respond to the concerns expressed. 
Subsequently, the College was able to acquire two parcels of land totaling approximately 13,350 
square feet (sf) on the east side of Massachusetts Avenue one block south of Boylston Street from 
an affiliate of the First Church of Christ, Scientist. A planning process for redevelopment of that 
combined parcel ensued, resulting in a plan for a new building of 170,000 sf of gross floor area 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
1-6 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
(gfa) containing a 379-bed residence hall, a 400-seat central campus dining facility and evening 
performance venue, three recording studios and other music technology space and ground floor 
retail space. 
The College then filed a Notice of Project Change on December 7, 2010, effectively adding this 
third proposed institutional project at 168 Massachusetts Avenue to its IMPNF. An amended 
Scoping Determination was issued December 24, 2010, requiring study of the additional impacts 
of this proposed project. 
On February 18, 2011, the College filed its combined Institutional Master Plan/Project Notification 
Form (IMP/PNF) for the proposed 168 Massachusetts Avenue mixed-use development. Following 
additional public meetings, the receipt of comments on the IMP/PNF and review by the Boston 
Civic Design Commission, the then BRA recommended approval of the College’s IMP to the Boston 
Zoning Commission, and also authorized issuance of an Adequacy Determination approving 
Berklee’s IMP, a Scoping Determination Waiving Further Review for the 168 Massachusetts 
Avenue project, and associated actions on May 12, 2011. Effective June 15, 2011, the Boston 
Zoning Commission approved the College’s IMP for a 10-year term. As described in Section 3.1.1, 
construction of 168 Massachusetts Avenue was completed in December 2013. 
1.4.2 
The Boston Conservatory IMP 
Following the successful completion of The Hemenway Theater and Studios project located at 
27-31 Hemenway Street in the East Fens, the Conservatory prepared and filed an IMPNF on June 
22, 2011. 
The IMPNF identified the substantial rehabilitation of an approximately 17,000 sf former 
manufacturing building located at 132 Ipswich Street as a proposed institutional project. The 
project would result in the creation of dance, music and theater studios and related support 
spaces, and would enable the Conservatory to relocate academic uses then housed in leased 
space into the building the Conservatory was in the process of acquiring. 
The Scoping Determination was issued on July 7, 2011, and the Conservatory subsequently filed 
its Institutional Master Plan on July 15, 2011. The IMP was revised and submitted on September 
12, 2011. Revisions to the IMP included changes to the height and FAR of renovations to the 
existing building at 132 Ipswich Street, and to introduce a potential future project at the 132 
Ipswich Street site that would be the subject of either an IMP Amendment or new IMP. The then 
BRA recommended approval of the revised IMP to the Boston Zoning Commission on September 
15, 2011. Effective October 19, 2011, the Boston Zoning Commission approved the Conservatory’s 
IMP for a ten-year term. 
Following further due diligence and study of the Ipswich Street existing structure, the 
Conservatory determined that the substantial rehabilitation of the building was financially 
infeasible. As a newly constructed, approximately 20,000 sf building was then proposed, the 
Conservatory filed an IMPNF for the First Amendment to the IMP on March 9, 2012, reflecting

1.5 
Existing Campus Description 
The heart of Berklee’s campus is in the vicinity of the corner of Massachusetts Avenue and 
Boylston Street and the intersection of Fenway and Boylston Street, between two neighborhoods 
within the City of Boston, the Fenway and the Back Bay, and adjacent to a mixed-use district 
surrounding the Prudential Center. Each neighborhood sustains a variety of uses, a strong sense 
of history, and is home to many of Boston’s finest cultural, entertainment and sports venues. 
Berklee is located within an area rich with public resources and private institutions that have a 
public mission. Resources contributing to the public realm that are located within a ten-minute 
walk of campus include the green space at Charlesgate, the Back Bay Fens portion of the Emerald 
Necklace, the Charles River Esplanade, the Commonwealth Avenue Mall, Hynes Convention 
Center, and the Boston Public Library. Private institutions with a public mission include The First 
Church of Christ, Scientist, the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Northeastern University, New 
England Conservatory of Music, the Massachusetts Historical Society, the Museum of Fine Arts, 
Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, and Fenway Park.

owned by Berklee by operation of law. Upon approval of this IMP and a related zoning map

in the description of properties included in the Berklee IMP and IMP area. 
Including the Boston Conservatory properties, Berklee owns 25 buildings totaling approximately

Below is a summary of sustainability initiatives at Berklee. With all these initiatives, Berklee has

Waste 
♦ Physical Plant and Housing departments teamed up with Waste Management to create a 
Drop, Shop and Donate shop for May 2018’s move-out, helping eliminate waste during 
the clean-out process. Berklee collected almost 1,000 pounds and saved approximately 
920 pounds from going to landfill. 
♦ Food waste from Berklee dining is diverted from landfills where it doesn’t decompose, to 
an anaerobic digestion plant. The food is put through a Somat machine, which acts like a 
giant garbage disposal. Here water is added to make a slurry, the solid pulp is strained 
out. This pulp is what is sent out to the treatment plant. The water that is separated gets 
recycled back and is used to continue the process of making the slurry.

processed through the Somat machine pulper instead of plastic. 
♦ In 2019 Berklee diverted approximately 208 tons from landfill between single stream 
recycling and organics recycling from the Somat pulper.

2.0 
COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
Berklee remains deeply committed to making meaningful community contributions in its surrounding 
neighborhoods of Fenway and Back Bay and throughout the City of Boston. The institution will continue 
its work with neighborhood organizations to understand and adequately address the localized impact of 
Berklee. More broadly, Berklee maintains support for its programs that provide Boston residents, 
particularly youth, with the opportunity to experience the transformative nature of the performing arts. 
The arts and culture sector of Boston is not only a critical component to the economic recovery of the city 
but is also a powerful tool in helping residents heal from the emotional trauma caused by the Covid-19 
pandemic. Berklee is eager to find new opportunities to support the City of Boston and its partners in 
these recovery efforts as well as continuing the programs outlined below. 
2.1 
Berklee City Music Program 
Founded over 25 years ago by Berklee College of Music, Berklee City Music reaches more than 
65,000 students annually through a variety of programs and initiatives including the Berklee City 
Music Network®, Berklee City Music Boston, and the innovative online Berklee PULSE® Music 
Method. By using culturally relevant music as a vehicle for holistic youth development, City Music 
helps young people flourish as students, musicians, performing artists, and—perhaps most 
importantly—confident and well-rounded individuals ready to shape the world. Whether 
students decide to pursue a career in music or another field, they receive benefits that last a 
lifetime. 
Berklee City Music programs are based around Berklee College of Music curricula and teaching 
methods, and use popular music as a vehicle for holistic child development. By using culturally 
relevant music, the programs encourage a greater level of interest and commitment from 
students, and help them to develop discipline, communication, teamwork, leadership skills, and 
a broader perspective of the world. Participating students receive valuable guidance and support 
from positive mentors, including dedicated instructors, and are exposed to unique experiences 
that can make an impact on their lives—all at little cost to their families. Additionally, students 
have the opportunity to obtain full scholarships to Berklee College of Music, with dozens of full-
tuition City Music College Scholars attending the school every year. 
2.1.1 
City Music Boston 
City Music Boston—the founding site of the City Music Network—provides music education 
programs and scholarship opportunities to 1,200 underserved students annually throughout the 
Greater Boston area. For over 25 years, City Music Boston has utilized a holistic approach to train 
musicians, build leaders, and foster community development. Program participants receive music 
theory, instrumental and ensemble instruction, individualized mentoring, and the Berklee PULSE® 
online curriculum. Students also have access to performance opportunities, workshops with 
visiting artists, master classes, and other valuable resources on the Berklee campus.

2.1.6 
Berklee PULSE® Music Method 
The Berklee PULSE® Music Method is a unique and innovative online music education portal that 
enables students to study, jam, and practice using interactive modules and an ever-expanding 
collection of popular music. Using a Berklee-designed curriculum, students learn instrumental 
technique, theoretical understanding, ensemble playing, historical context, and more through 
self-guided learning modules and video lessons with world-renowned musicians and 
professionally trained instructors. PULSE features lesson plans and arrangements that teachers 
can utilize in classes and ensembles. PULSE is open to anyone, with exclusive resources available 
through Berklee City Music and select public school partners. PULSE gives students and teachers 
the benefits of a Berklee education—no matter where they live. 
2.1.7 
Berklee City Music Scholarships 
Since its inception, Berklee City Music has awarded scholarships to more than 2,000 students to 
attend the Berklee’s Aspire: Five-Week Music Performance Intensive as well as hundreds of full- 
and partial-tuition scholarships to attend Berklee College of Music. 
City Music Summer Scholarship 
Students in City Music have the opportunity to receive a full-tuition scholarship to Berklee’s 
Aspire: Five-Week Music Performance Intensive. This program allows students to immerse 
themselves in their chosen style and study with world-class faculty in a college setting. Five-Week 
is the largest, most comprehensive summer music program available anywhere. With its variety 
of study and performance options, world-class Berklee faculty, visiting artists, and state-of-the-
art facilities, Five-Week has become the premiere contemporary summer music program for 
aspiring musicians. Students study performance, theory, musicianship, and ensemble playing, 
which is highlighted in an end-of-program blowout concert. Five-Week scholarships are awarded 
in the spring based on availability, an online application with supplemental forms, and an audition. 
City Music College Scholarship 
Berklee City Music students have an opportunity to receive a full scholarship to attend Berklee 
College of Music via the City Music College Scholarship (CMCS), which is a partial- or full-tuition 
scholarship award to attend Berklee. The scholarship allows students to pursue their dreams of 
excelling in music as a career.

Boston Arts Academy/Pro Arts Consortium 
The Boston Arts Academy (BAA) located at 174 Ipswich Street, within walking proximity to 
Berklee's campus, is a collaborative project of the Boston Public Schools and the Professional Arts 
(Pro Arts) Consortium. The Pro Arts Consortium is a group of six Boston institutions committed to 
advancing arts education in the public schools. Among its members are Berklee College of Music 
and five other arts- related institutions of higher education. 
The Boston Arts Academy, the only public school of its kind in the Boston metropolitan area, offers 
high- level training in visual and performing arts. Since opening its doors in August 1998, the 
Academy and its faculty have received numerous awards and accolades. Berklee College of Music 
provides on-going programmatic support by hosting the BAA Winter Festival at the Berklee 
Performance Center, providing instrument and equipment donations, scholarships and cross-
registration to BAA students, advising, faculty, and work-study employees. In addition, Berklee's 
City Music Saturday Preparatory School for grades four through eight has been housed at the 
Academy since its inception in the year 2000. Berklee is proud to be one of the founding 
institutions of this high-profile educational jewel. 
Since its establishment in 1990, the President's Office of Education Outreach has awarded $7.9 
million in student scholarships to Boston resident musicians. It is proud to have played a role in 
the lives of this select group of talented youth and will continue helping them fulfill their dreams. 
This entails not only providing them with an education in their passion, but also demonstrating 
how this passion can fuel a career. With each new year, the office is able to help growing numbers 
of young and talented musicians attain successful careers in the music industry. And once 
scholarship recipients take the first step—a college education—they can take off and soar.

classroom learning. Examples of CSE positions include music mentors, literacy tutors, and arts

bring large groups of children and adults to professional-level performances. Following a gap in 
the program due to Covid-19 in-person event restrictions, Berklee reintroduced both components 
for the spring and summer of 2022. 
Through the second component, made possible through partnerships with the City of Boston 
Parks & Recreation Department and a number of neighborhood agencies, Berklee presents 
concerts of contemporary music in the City’s public parks. 
Annual projects during the last five years have included: 
♦ Tito Puente Latin Music Series at various Boston parks in the South End, Mission Hill, East 
Boston and Jamaica Plain; 
♦ Jazz at the Fort at Roxbury's Highland Park; 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
2-8 
Community Benefits 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
♦ Swingin' in the Fens at Ramler Park in the Fens; 
♦ Sunset Concerts at Symphony Park; and 
♦ Berklee Summer in the City presents more than 200 concerts each summer throughout 
Boston neighborhoods. 
2.5 
Berklee Police and Public Safety 
The Berklee Police and Public Safety Department employs fully sworn police officers and 
contracted corporate security professionals to monitor and patrol the entire campus which is 
nestled in the Back Bay and Fenway neighborhoods. Department personnel conduct several 
proactive patrols of the campus property throughout the three dedicated shifts, which provide 
for 24/7/365 coverage regardless of whether the college is in session or on break. This translates 
to one or two marked police vehicles on patrol in the neighborhood and any number of police 
officers and/or security officers on foot patrol or mountain bike patrol in warmer weather. The 
Department takes pride in Berklee’s community and addresses concerns of the community that 
may be of a lesser concern to the Boston Police Department such as vandalism and tagging. The 
Department investigates these matters and, in some instances, works in partnership with the 
Physical Plant team to address these types of concerns. With many of Berklee’s students residing 
in the immediate area, the Department responds to calls for service, ongoing and active 
emergencies, and varying types of crises. Department personnel are trained to the same level as 
a Boston Police Officer, and have access to the same kinds of resources and services to assist the 
Berklee community and its neighbors. 
One of the biggest benefits to the surrounding community is Berklee’s collaboration with the 
Neighborhood Improvement Committee (NIC), where the Department's Command Staff meets 
with stakeholders from the surrounding community to address specific concerns and to discuss 
ideas on how to best deliver police services to make the most lasting and positive impact. The 
Department has been successful in obtaining court orders for individuals suffering from addiction, 
has provided transportation services to area shelters for those in need, has rendered aid for 
medical emergencies and has partnered with Boston EMS. The Neighborhood Improvement 
Committee has been a huge benefit to the Berklee Police Department by keeping them aware of 
community concerns and providing ideas and suggestions so that Berklee may direct patrol 
services to those areas that need it the most. The Berklee Police Department’s collaboration with 
the NIC is a constant stream of information sharing that is instrumental in helping the Department 
address neighborhood concerns as well as helping the Department ensure those in the 
community are linked to the resources available to address their needs.

PROPOSED PROJECTS 
3.1 
IMP Project Status 
This section describes the status of the projects included in both the 2011 Berklee IMP and the 
2011 Conservatory IMP. As described previously, the institutions have since merged, and any 
projects that continue to be proposed will be incorporated into the Berklee IMP for the merged 
institutions. 
3.1.1 
168 Massachusetts Avenue 
Construction of the project identified in the 2011 Berklee IMP as the 168 Massachusetts Avenue 
project was initiated in October 2012 and was completed in December 2013. The address of this 
building is now 160 Massachusetts Avenue and will be referred to as that throughout the rest of 
the document. 
The LEED Gold-certified building includes 369 beds of student housing, a 475 -seat central campus 
dining facility that also serves as a performance venue in the late evenings, approximately 4,200 
sf of gfa of ground floor retail/restaurant space and two levels of below grade recording studios 
and other music technology space. 
The project has added to Berklee’s inventory of student housing, created an exciting new 
performance venue, state-of-the-art recording studios and other music technology spaces, and 
has been very well received by the campus community. Designed by the Boston architectural firm 
of William Rawn Associates, Architects and constructed by Lee Kennedy Company; the 160 
Massachusetts Avenue development also garnered a number of design awards, including the 
American Institute of Architects’ 2015 AIA Housing Award for Specialized Housing and the 2015 
AIA Educational Facility Design Award for Excellence. 
3.1.2 
161-171 Massachusetts Avenue 
This project as proposed in the 2011 Berklee IMP envisioned the substantial rehabilitation of the 
existing four story, concrete frame 161 Massachusetts Avenue building, as well as the substantial 
rehabilitation of the adjacent, three story, wood frame and masonry bearing walls structure 
located at 171 Massachusetts Avenue. The building is currently used for staff and faculty offices, 
private instruction, classroom, and practice rooms. In the course of preliminary engineering 
analysis of the latter building, it was revealed that any significant investment in that building 
would require substantial modifications to meet current seismic codes, e.g., installation of shear 
walls. The structure is not well suited to Berklee’s distinctive programmatic needs, including, for 
example, sound insulation, and therefore the substantial expense and disruption associated with 
bringing the building up to contemporary codes and standards is not currently proposed. Several 
alternative development scenarios are currently being considered for this site.

3.1.3 
Berklee Crossroads 
The 2011 Berklee IMP included the proposed Berklee Crossroads project, a planned mixed-use 
development consisting of ground floor retail space, a new Berklee Performance Center, student 
housing, and academic/student life space. Since the adoption of the IMP, Berklee has done further 
planning and conceptual design of the performance venue element of the project. 
Further study of the performance center component of this planned mixed-use development was 
undertaken by Wilson Butler Architects, a Boston-based architectural firm specializing in 
performance venue design, and Fisher Dachs Associates, a specialty performing arts programming 
and design consultancy based in New York, NY. 
As a result of the merger, planning of the performance center considered not only performance 
of amplified music, but also classical music, musical theater and dance. More detailed study for 
this proposed performance venue confirms the ability of the site to accommodate the program, 
though doing so would require acquiring a property interest in the present Cambria Street right-
of-way and adjusting the alignment of the Cambria Street roadway to include a portion of Air 
Rights Parcel 14 owned by the Massachusetts Department of Transportation (formerly the 
Massachusetts Highway Department) as described in the approved IMP. 
Berklee continues to pursue this project; however, in view of the need to relocate the functions 
presently on the Berklee Crossroads site and certain utilities in the Cambria Street right-of-way 
before beginning the development of the proposed Berklee Crossroads project, there will be 
significant lead time associated with delivering this project. Rather than defer the creation of 
additional student housing, Berklee plans to sequence this previously approved IMP project after 
the development of the 134 Ipswich Street project described in Section 3.4.2 below. The 134 
Ipswich Street site is improved as a surface parking lot, and is therefore “shovel ready,” and will 
enable the creation of additional student housing significantly sooner than the site of the Berklee 
Crossroads development. 
3.1.4 
Renovation of The Boston Conservatory Theater Building 
The approved 2011 Conservatory IMP included one project, the renovation and expansion of the 
Conservatory’s Theater building located at 31 Hemenway Street in the East Fens. The original 
theater, constructed in 1948 and added onto in 1958, was not accessible to people with 
disabilities. The Conservatory undertook to address that deficiency, as well as to improve the 
performer and audience experience with a comprehensive facility improvement project 
completed in 2010. This project was made possible by expanding the footprint of the theater 
facility on an adjacent parcel of land acquired from Berklee College of Music. 
The renovated and expanded facility now includes the 325 seat Boston Conservatory Theater, the 
100 seat Studio 401 concert venue, dance studios and rehearsal rooms, classrooms and the Dance 
and Theater Division offices.

3.1.5 
Richard Ortner Studio Building 
The subject of the approved Amendment #1 to the Conservatory’s IMP, this 20,000 sf dance and 
music rehearsal facility located at 132 Ipswich Street was completed in 2014. It includes 
classrooms, dance studios, multipurpose studios, a performance library, a large rehearsal hall and 
teaching studios. The building occupies roughly a 10,000 sf parcel of land, leaving an 
approximately 8,000 sf development site. During public meetings on the proposed IMP 
Amendment of the 2011 Conservatory IMP, the Conservatory indicated the site was intended for 
a future building, likely a dormitory. This is described in Section 3.4.2 below. 
3.1.6 
Other Improvement Projects 
In addition to the specific proposed projects listed in the approved IMPs of the two legacy 
institutions, other capital improvement projects have been accomplished subsequent to the 
approval of the IMPs. Following design review and approval of the Urban Design staff of the BPDA, 
the following projects were completed: 
150 Massachusetts Avenue 
As discussed with Berklee’s IMP task force members and as described in the approved Berklee 
IMP, Berklee completed a $23 million building improvement project to this existing, 240,000 sf 
academic and student residence building. 
Originally built in two phases beginning in 1900-1902, the former Massachusetts Chambers 
apartment hotel was converted to the Embassy Apartments in the 1930’s, and later substantially 
remodeled and reopened in 1955 as the Sherry Biltmore Hotel. At some point, a porte cochere 
was developed for the hotel along Belvidere Street that later was enclosed as a single-story 
addition to the building, resulting in a reduced sidewalk width of 6.5 feet. 
Following the College’s acquisition of the building in 1972 and subsequent conversion into a 
residence hall, student dining facility and academic space; red granite panels were installed on 
the ground floor of the Massachusetts Avenue and Belvidere Street elevations. These large stone 
panels, with the exception of three arched window openings, created a virtually opaque 
appearance to pedestrian passersby. 
Consistent with the description of the planned 150 Massachusetts Avenue project in the Berklee 
IMP, the College undertook a substantial rehabilitation project on the ground floor and the two 
below grade levels of the building in two phases beginning in 2013 and concluding in 2016. In 
order to create additional open space along Belvidere Street and to restore the building’s 
southerly facade to its original footprint along Belvidere Street, the single-story addition was 
removed, thereby widening the Belvidere sidewalk from 6.5 feet to 15 feet. This has afforded 
improved views from Massachusetts Avenue to nearby St. Cecilia Church’s recently renovated 
structure, as well as enabled the creation of additional bicycle storage capacity.

accessible entrance was created by constructing a new lobby floor at street level allowing access 
to the residential elevators. A new elevator was also added to serve all the academic floors of the 
building allowing all members of the community to easily navigate through the building. 
The solid red brick panels along the base of the building on Massachusetts Avenue and Belvidere 
Street were replaced by large glass windows, affording views into two music teaching and 
rehearsal spaces and student gathering and lobby spaces, thereby enlivening the pedestrian 
experience along Massachusetts Avenue. This more transparent appearance recalls large plate 
glass windows of the several retail storefronts that formerly were located along Massachusetts 
Avenue.

3.2 
Program Need 
Approximately 25% of Berklee students are currently able to live on campus. Berklee’s long-term 
goal is to provide on-campus housing for approximately 50% of its student population. Berklee 
believes that locating a higher percentage of its students in on campus housing will not only 
benefit the surrounding neighborhoods, but help foster a sense of campus community and enrich 
the student experience. The proposed project described below will create approximately 100 new 
student beds, bringing Berklee closer to achieving this goal. 
3.3 
Proposed Project 
Berklee proposes to renovate an existing, four-story, approximately 30,400 square foot building 
located at 12 Hemenway Street to accommodate approximately 110 student beds in 63 units (the 
Project). There are four existing parking spaces that will remain. 12 Hemenway Street (shown in 
Figure 1-1) is an ideal location for student housing as it is across the street from one of Berklee’s 
main buildings at 1140 Boylston Street, and next door to the new practice facility on Boylston 
Street. 

6420/Berklee College of Music 
3-5 
Proposed Projects 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
The building is currently permitted for lodging house use and is being operated as private housing 
for students, with the ability to operate as a hostel, pursuant to a 1-year lease back agreement to 
the prior owner until December 31, 2022. No major changes to the facade, massing or structure 
are anticipated with the exception of some facade restoration, roof repairs, accessibility 
improvements and minor interior renovations. Berklee is also exploring the possibility of adding 
an elevator to the building and replacing the heating and cooling system with a more sustainable 
option. There will also be minor interior renovations improving the accessibility and creating 
student engagement space. 
Like all other student housing on campus, Berklee will provide 24-hour on-site security at the 
Project, as well as Resident Directors who live in the resident halls, and resident assistants. In 
addition, there will be security cameras that feed into the Berklee Command Center and 
electronic building access to ensure safety and on call housing 24/7. 
3.4 
Potential Future Projects 
The below projects are in early planning stages, and are being considered for after the term of 
this proposed two-year IMP. 
3.4.1 
161-171 Massachusetts Avenue 
As an alternative to the substantial rehabilitation of the 161-171 Massachusetts Avenue building 
described in Section 3.1.2, Berklee is exploring several alternatives for this site that would contain 
academic space and some performance space. In addition, Berklee has determined that a suitable 
use for the ground floor of the existing building at 167 Massachusetts Avenue would be a student 
health clinic. The facility is currently used to test for COVID-19 as part of Berklee’s efforts to 
combat the pandemic and limit community spread. Long term, Berklee envisions expanding the 
services offered at the facility to include treatment for other common illnesses or minor health 
concerns. This will promote the health and safety of the student population and the surrounding 
community by reducing the need to send ill students to health services providers off campus. This 
model will also proactively and permanently allow Berklee to manage future increases in COVID-
19 infections. 
3.4.2 
134 Ipswich Street 
Berklee is exploring a potential project at 134 Ipswich Street that will connect to the existing 
building at 132 Ipswich Street. The development program for the proposed project has not yet 
been defined but is currently anticipated to consist of a mixed-use building, including student 
housing. This project will assist Berklee in continuing their goal of creating more on-campus 
student housing.

Included here are Boston Public Works Department comments for the Boston Children’s Hospital IMPNF.
Project Specific Scope Considerations:
The developer should coordinate with BPDA, BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for
all modes of transportation in the area.
Site Plan:
The developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb
functionality on both sides of all streets that abut the property.
Construction Within The Public Right-of- Way (ROW):
All proposed design and construction within the Public ROW shall conform to PWD Design Standards
(https://www.boston.gov/departments/public-works/public-works-design-standards). Any non-standard materials
(i.e. pavers, landscaping, bike racks, etc.) proposed within the Public ROW will require approval through the Public
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification (LM&I)
Agreement with the PIC. Please note that the comments below are specific to proposed work within the Public
ROW.
Sidewalks:
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet
current Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)/Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines,
including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections
abutting the project site if not already constructed to ADA/AAB compliance per Code of Massachusetts Regulations
Title 521, Section 21 (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/521-CMR-21-curb-cuts). This includes converting apex
ramps to perpendicular ramps at intersection corners and constructing or reconstructing reciprocal pedestrian
ramps where applicable. Plans showing the extents of the proposed sidewalk improvements associated with this
project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb geometry
will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC.
Please note that at signalized intersections, any alteration to pedestrian ramps may also require upgrading the
traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and
Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) requirements. Any changes to the traffic signal system must
be coordinated and approved by BTD.
All proposed sidewalk widths and cross-slopes must comply to both City of Boston and ADA/AAB standards.
The developer is encouraged to contact the City’s Disabilities Commission to confirm compliant accessibility within
the Public ROW.
Driveway Curb Cuts:
Any proposed driveway curb cuts within the Public ROW will need to be reviewed and approved by the PIC. All
existing curb cuts that will no longer be utilized shall be closed.

Roadway:
Based on the extent of construction activity, including utility connections and taps, the developer will be responsible

Green Infrastructure:
The developer shall work with PWD, the Green Infrastructure Division, and the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission (BWSC) to determine appropriate methods of green infrastructure and/or stormwater management
systems within the Public ROW. The ongoing maintenance of such systems shall require an LM&I Agreement with
the PIC. Effects of water infiltration with respect to the adjacent underpass structure and underground MBTA

considered. Coordination with PWD and MBTA will be required.

Proposed designs should follow the Boston Public Works Climate Resilient Design Guidelines
(https://www.boston.gov/environment-and-energy/climate-resilient-design-guidelines) where applicable.

I.
Introduction 
The Children’s Hospital Corporation d/b/a Boston Children’s Hospital (“BCH”) submits this 
Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) to the Boston Redevelopment Authority d/b/a 
Boston Planning & Development Agency (the “BPDA”) in compliance with Section 80D-8 of the Boston 
Zoning Code (the “Code”) to renew the existing BCH Institutional Master Plan (as amended from time to 
time, the “IMP”) without change prior to such IMP otherwise expiring on December 20, 2023 (as further 
described below). At this time, BCH has no new proposed projects within the IMP area beyond those listed 
in the existing IMP, and proposes no substantive changes to the uses, dimensions, parking or loading of 
existing facilities. This IMPNF requests a two-year renewal period extending the IMP term to December 
20, 2025. 
II.
Background and Description of IMP Area
Founded in 1869 as a 20-bed hospital for children, BCH has since grown into one of the largest 
pediatric medical centers in the United States, with more than 40 clinical departments and 258 specialized 
clinical programs. BCH is New England’s regional referral pediatric center and a safety net hospital for 
critically ill children and those from low-income families. BCH also is one of Boston’s largest employers, 
consistently ranked by U.S. News & World Report among the top pediatric hospitals nationwide. 
The IMP Area consists of three separate areas as follows: 
(i)
the Core Campus within in the Longwood Medical and Academic Area, which 
includes 300 Longwood Avenue, 333 Longwood Avenue, 340 Brookline Avenue, 
the Karp Research Building, the Patient-Family Garage, and a portion of 
Longwood Avenue under the Pedestrian Connector; 
(ii)
1 and 21 Autumn Street; and 
(iii)
819 Beacon Street. 
III.
Summary of IMP Process 
The BPDA approved the original IMP on April 29, 2008, followed by Zoning Commission 
approval on May 28, 2008, effective May 29, 2008. BCH amended the original IMP several times over the 
course of the last 15 years, which amendments included an extension of the term to December 20, 2023, by 
an amendment approved by the BPDA on November 14, 2013, and the Zoning Commission on December 
11, 2013, effective December 20, 2013. 
The most recent IMP amendment (Fourth Amendment) authorized Patient-Family Housing at 819 
Beacon Street, as approved by the BPDA on November 17, 2022, and the Zoning Commission on December 
14, 2022, effective January 23, 2023. This recent amendment did not change the IMP expiration date.

1. PURPOSE OF SUBMISSION 
Boston College submits this Institutional Master Plan Notification Form to renew without 
change its Institutional Master Plan, under Section 80D-5 .2 (e) of the Boston Zoning Code 
(“Waiver of Further Review of Unchanged Plans”) for an additional two-year period, ending 
on October 14, 2025. 
2. OVERVIEW OF BOSTON COLLEGE INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
In the spring of 2004, Boston College ("the University") embarked on a comprehensive 
strategic planning initiative to assess its academic program and to set institutional goals for 
the next decade and beyond. After several years of planning, a strategic plan was adopted by 
the Board of Trustees in February of 2006. Following two years of consultation with the 
surrounding neighborhood, Boston College submitted an Institutional Master Plan 
Notification Form (“IMPNF”) outlining the institutional needs of the University in December 
of 2007. In response to a Scoping Determination issued by the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority (“BRA”) (doing business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
since 2016), Boston College submitted an Institutional Master Plan (IMP) in June of 2008. The 
IMP was ultimately approved by the BRA on June 10, 2009, and renewed in 2013 for a four-
year period. The BPDA subsequently renewed the IMP in 2017 for a four-year period through 
June 20, 2021, and renewed in 2021 for a two-year period through October 14, 2023. 
Since the IMP was approved in 2009, four amendments have been approved by the BRA. 
The First Amendment to the IMP reflected de minimus dimensional changes to the Thomas 
More Apartments located at 2150 Commonwealth Avenue. The First Amendment went into 
effect in October 2013. The Second Amendment to the IMP reflected a proposed change for 
the renovation of 2101 Commonwealth Avenue (formerly known as the Cardinal's Residence) 
for a University Conference Center and the McMullen Museum of Art. The Second 
Amendment went into effect in May 2014. The Third Amendment to the IMP reflected de 
minimus dimensional changes to the Margot Connell Recreation Center project located at 
200 St. Thomas More Road. The Third Amendment went into effect in July 2016. The Fourth 
Amendment to the IMP added the Fish Field House located at 12 Chestnut Hill Driveway as 
a Proposed Institutional Project. The Fourth Amendment went into effect in March 2017. A 
modest expansion and renovation of the Conte Forum was permitted as an Exempt Project 
and was completed in August, 2023. 
As outlined below, the University is currently preparing to submit a new Institutional Master 
Plan for community and BPDA review in the first quarter of 2024.

roadway. 
 
The Project is located on the interior of the University’s Brighton Campus, to the 
west of the “Spine Road,” in the Brighton neighborhood of Boston, Massachusetts. 
The Project Site is bordered land along Lake Street to the west, the Lake Street 
entrance to the Brighton Campus to the north, the “Spine Road” to the east, and the

DESCRIPTION OF THE FIFTH AMENDMENT TO THE BC IMP 
 
Originally described in the 2009 Boston College IMP as an approximately 14,000 
square foot addition to the Theological and Ministry Library, the Fifth Amendment 
to the BC IMP seeks to change the originally described project to an approximately 
45,000 square foot building attached to the Theological and Ministry Library. No 
other changes are contemplated. 
 
PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
The Library Storage Project, originally described in the 2009 IMP as an 
approximately 40-foot high, 14,000 square foot addition to the Theology and 
Ministry Library on the Brighton Campus. The Library Storage Project was located 
immediately to the North of the Library and east of Lake Street (the “Project Site”). 
 
The amended Library Storage Project, referred to as the Catholic Religious Archives 
Project, will be in the same location as the Library Storage project, but enlarged to 
comprise less than 45,000 sf Gross Floor Area (“GFA”) with an overall height less 
than 55 feet.

When complete, the Project will primarily store collections, as well as limited 
artwork and cultural artifacts. The two floors of the building will have a mixture of 
fixed and compact shelving, map cases, and art racks. The consistent internal 
climate of the collection and processing spaces will be serviced from climate control 
mechanical equipment in a partial basement. The building will have a loading dock, 
internal receiving area, and a holding room for collection of objects. The Project will 
utilize space in the Library for processing and a research reading room that will be 
accessed by a one-story connector between the two buildings. 
 
Transportation access for the building’s visitors and staff in accordance with the 
University’s overall parking and transportation plan, which includes a campus 
shuttle serving the Brighton Campus with a stop at Commonwealth Avenue at 
Greycliff Road. Sufficient parking is available to meet anticipated demand in the 
existing surface parking lots located directly east of the Library. The Project will also 
incorporate two service parking spaces along the building and two accessible 
parking spaces to the west of the building.

ARTICLE 80 AND PUBLIC REVIEW 
 
The IMPNF for Amendment, filed on July 12, 2024, is being reviewed under the 
Expedited Review Procedure of Section 80D-9.2 of the Code. Pursuant to Section 
80D-9.2 of the Code, a proposed amendment to an IMP may be submitted under an 
expedited review procedure if: (1) such amendment proposes no changes to the 
IMP other that the addition of one of more Proposed Projects; and (2) each of such 
Proposed Projects meets the requirements of Section 80D-9.2(b) (i) or (ii) and does 
not meet the size thresholds of Large Project Review. The Proposed Project does 
not meet the threshold for Large Project Review and complies with the 
requirements of 80D-9.2(b)(ii). No other changes are proposed. There was a joint, 
BC Task Force and public meeting on August 6, 2024. The comment period for the 
IMPNF closed on August 11, 2024. 
 
Planning and Zoning Context 
 
Boston College seeks to build a new Catholic archives facility, as an addition to an 
existing theology library. The Proposed Project is located in the Brighton Campus of 
the school, governed by Boston College Institutional Master Plan (IMP) zoning. The

existing IMP was approved by the BRA in 2009. In 2013 the IMP was renewed for 
four years, and then again was renewed in 2017 for four years. In 2021 it was 
renewed for two years, and most recently in 2023 it was renewed for another two 
year period through October 14, 2025. 
 
The existing IMP identifies the location of the Proposed Project as a site for future 
library storage. Staff have determined that the proposed use is well aligned with 
the intended use described by the site’s existing IMP zoning. The existing IMP 
describes the storage facility on this site as a 40 foot, 14,000 square foot addition to 
an existing library. The Proposed Project’s dimensions have increased to 55 feet 
and 44,000 square feet. The proposed dimensions would facilitate new storage 
demands of the library and achieve program goals of the school outlined in the 
purpose of the IMP, while having minimal impact on the surrounding context. 
 
Parking requirements will be satisfied by two accessible parking spaces, two service 
parking spaces and a loading area in front of the entrance to the Proposed Project.

Lake Street and take any other actions and execute any other agreements and 
documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection with 
the Proposed Project. An appropriate vote follows:

CHAPTER 1: 
INTRODUCTION 
 
INTRODUCTION 
Boston University (“BU” or the “University”) is a world-leading private research university 
spanning three campuses in the City of Boston. BU’s flagship campus, the Charles River 
Campus (“BU Charles River Campus”), consists of over 113 acres of land centered on 
Commonwealth Avenue between Massachusetts Avenue and Packard’s Corner. The BU 
Charles River Campus is currently guided by an Institutional Master Plan (“IMP”) approved 
by the Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) in 2013 (the “2013 – 2023 
IMP”). With this IMP set to expire in February 2023, the Trustees of Boston University (the 
“Proponent”) is pleased to submit this Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) 
to initiate the BPDA Article 80D IMP review process for the upcoming BU Charles River 
Campus 2023 – 2033 Institutional Master Plan (the “2023 – 2033 IMP”). 
This IMPNF provides updates on the progress of the 2013 – 2023 IMP, describes existing 
property and uses, and identifies BU’s strategic priorities and development objectives for 
the BU Charles River Campus over the upcoming decade. 
 
BOSTON UNIVERSITY HISTORY AND BACKGROUND 
BU is the fourth-largest private nonprofit university in the nation, home to more than 
35,000 students each year, and one of the oldest institutions of higher education in the 
Boston area. The University was founded in 1839 as the Newbury Biblical Institute in 
Vermont by a group of laymen and ministers committed to social equality and 
inclusiveness. The school relocated to Boston in 1867, and in 1869 the Massachusetts 
legislature granted a charter for BU, formally establishing the University as it is currently 
known. Originally scattered throughout Beacon Hill, downtown Boston, and the South End, 
the University has undergone dramatic physical and academic transformations since 1869. 
Today, more than 10,000 staff and faculty support 17 schools and colleges on three distinct 
campuses: the BU Charles River Campus, the Medical Campus in the South End, and the 
Fenway Campus in the Longwood Medical Area. 
The BU Charles River Campus, which serves as the core campus, began to take shape in 
1920 when the University purchased 15 acres of land between Commonwealth Avenue 
and the Charles River. Now spanning 113 acres, the BU Charles River Campus houses all of 
the University’s undergraduate and most graduate programs in a diverse stock of buildings 
that varies substantially in height, age, and style. The University has actively pursued both 
restoration of historic buildings and construction of purpose-built facilities to provide a 
world-class educational environment. 
Located two miles southeast of the BU Charles River Campus is the Medical Campus, which 
is composed of three of the University’s health science schools: the School of Medicine, the 
Henry M. Goldman School of Dental Medicine, and the School of Public Health. The 
Medical Campus has a rich history dating back to 1848, when its School of Medicine began 
as the New England Female Medical College, the first institution in the world to offer 
medical education to women and to graduate a black woman physician. The University 

Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
 
Introduction 
 
1-2 
 
acquired the Medical College in 1873, creating the first coeducational medical school in 
the nation. Together, the three schools of the Medical Campus educate a diverse group of 
3,500 students a year, with a focus on underserved populations. The Medical Campus is 
currently guided by the BU Medical Campus 2021 – 2031 IMP, approved in February 
2022. 
The Fenway Campus was formed in 2018 after a merger between the University and 
Wheelock College. The property holdings of Wheelock College in the Longwood Medical 
Area of Boston and Brookline were assumed by the University and the area is now known 
as the BU Fenway Campus. Founded in 1888, Wheelock College was characterized by its 
focus on training future educators and social workers to improve the lives of children and 
families. The merger allows the University to again use its resources to strengthen and build 
upon the historic legacy of a Boston institution committed to bettering the lives of others. 
The buildings on the Fenway Campus are used for a variety of programs, research institutes, 
and housing options that serve the entire BU community. The Fenway Campus is currently 
guided by the BU Fenway Campus 2021 – 2031 IMP, approved in January 2022. 
 
BOSTON UNIVERSITY MISSION AND OBJECTIVES 
BU is an international, comprehensive, private research university committed to educating 
students to be reflective and resourceful individuals ready to live, adapt, and lead in an 
interconnected world. The University is committed to generating new knowledge to benefit 
society. 
The University remains dedicated to its founding principles: that higher education should 
be accessible to all and that research, scholarship, artistic creation, and professional practice 
should be conducted in the service of the wider community on a local and international 
scale. These principles endure in the University’s insistence on the value of diversity, in its 
tradition and standards of excellence, and in its dynamic engagement with the City of 
Boston and the world. 
BU is composed of a remarkable range of undergraduate, graduate, and professional 
programs built on a strong foundation of the liberal arts and sciences. With the support and 
oversight of the Board of Trustees, the University continually innovates in education and 
research to ensure that it meets the needs of its students and an ever-changing world. 
1.3.1 BU STRATEGIC PLAN 
In 2020, the Board of Trustees approved a new, University-wide Strategic Plan 
outlining a vision statement and five strategic priorities to guide BU through 2030. 
The Strategic Plan is the culmination of two years of listening and planning by a 
Strategic Planning Task Force, consisting of a diverse group of faculty and staff from 
across the University. 
The University’s Mission Statement and feedback from the BU community helped to 
articulate the University’s Strategic Vision Statement for the decade ahead: 
• 
Continue the ascent of BU as a leading private research university focused on 
research excellence and outstanding, innovative residential undergraduate and 

Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
 
Introduction 
 
1-3 
 
graduate education that prepares students for the evolving, global world of 
work. 
• 
Strengthen interconnectedness across disciplines to create novel approaches in 
research and teaching, leading to bold discoveries and research impact. 
• 
Be a leader in the utilization of state-of-the-art remote, digital, and online 
technologies to enhance our in-person programs and expand our educational 
outreach. 
• 
Become an even more diverse and inclusive institution in which individuals can 
find their communities and thrive, and lead in social and racial justice scholarly 
work. 
Part of, and integral to, this Strategic Vision are the five strategic priorities that will 
be emphasized in order to achieve the University’s Strategic Vision: 
1. A Vibrant Academic Experience: BU will provide all students a high-quality, 
residential educational experience, including academic offerings that address 
the world’s complex challenges, keep pace with rapidly advancing pedagogy, 
and prepare students for global citizenship. 
2. Research that Matters: BU will continue its trajectory of excellence and grow 
the eminence of its collective research portfolio by hiring and supporting world-
class, diverse faculty and enabling research across interconnecting disciplines to 
address society’s biggest challenges. 
3. Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: BU will be a more diverse institution with 
equitable access, inclusive practices, and opportunities for all faculty, staff, and 
students while also contributing to leading research and programs on social 
justice. 
4. Community, Big Yet Small: BU will be an institution that empowers students, 
staff, and faculty to cultivate diverse communities where individuals can learn, 
grow, and engage across a large, urban campus and around the world. 
5. Global Engagement: BU will build and grow its presence in global hubs that 
support continued excellence in research that transcends national boundaries, 
offer compelling academic programs, and strengthen partnerships with alumni 
and other institutions for global impact. 
1.3.2 DIVERSITY & INCLUSION INITATIVES 
From its beginnings, BU has strived to open its doors to all. Today, we aim for 
greater diversity, equity, and inclusion because we know that diversity—of people, 
ideas, experiences, and approaches to problem-solving—leads to excellence. This 
pledge is one of five pillars in the University’s Strategic Plan. 

Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
 
Introduction 
 
1-4 
 
Building and sustaining a vibrant community of scholars, students, and staff remains 
essential to our mission of contributing to, and preparing students to thrive in, an 
increasingly interconnected world. 
We strive to create environments for learning, working, and living that are enriched 
by racial, ethnic, and cultural diversity. We seek to cultivate an atmosphere of 
respect for individual differences in life experience, sexual orientation, and religious 
belief, and we aspire to be free of intellectual parochialism, barriers to access, and 
ethnocentrism. 
Success in a competitive, global milieu depends upon our ongoing commitment to 
welcome and engage the wisdom, creativity, and aspirations of all peoples. The 
excellence we seek emerges from the contributions and talents of every member of 
the BU community. 
We are creating space on campus for students, faculty, and staff to gather and 
connect in small, like-minded groups within the larger University and greater 
Boston community to build a sense of belonging for all. 
By becoming a more diverse, equitable, and inclusive institution, BU strives to live 
up to its historical roots as an institution founded by abolitionists that later became 
the home of Martin Luther King, Jr. and Howard Thurman. We will also become a 
stronger university and a better place for all members of our community to learn, 
work, and live. This strategic priority is a foundational element within each of the 
four other priorities; it is both distinctly important and necessarily embedded in all 
we do. Objectives of this effort include: 
• 
Recruit and Retain Diverse, World-Class Faculty, Students, and Staff: Cultivate 
a campus community that is welcoming and inclusive to all. 
• 
Inclusive Pedagogy that Engages All Students: Ensure course materials feature 
diverse voices and perspectives and teaching techniques reach a wider variety 
of students. 
• 
Ensure that Those with Financial Need have Access to BU: Build upon our 
commitment to ensure access for students of all socioeconomic backgrounds 
and provide support and programming to ensure they graduate and move on to 
productive lives. 
• 
A University-Wide Research Program that Advances Diversity: Bring together 
scholars, students, and practitioners around diversity issues and initiatives in the 
social sciences and humanities. 
• 
Educational Opportunities for Faculty, Staff, and Students to Engage with 
Issues of Diversity: By becoming more knowledgeable individuals, we can 
become a more equitable and inclusive institution. 
• 
Support Diverse Business, especially within out Surrounding Boston 
Community: The University’s Sourcing and Procurement organization has 

Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
 
Introduction 
 
1-5 
 
developed a Supplier Diversity Program to align with goals and objectives 
outlined in the University’s Strategic Plan. The primary goal of this effort is to 
create a more diverse and inclusive supplier base and provide increased access 
and opportunity to underrepresented diverse businesses, both locally and 
nationally, to provide products and service to the BU community. The vision of 
this initiative is to be the leader amongst peer urban research universities in 
providing increased access and opportunity to certified diverse businesses. 
 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN HISTORY 
BU was the first university in the City of Boston to prepare an IMP. The first BU Charles 
River Campus IMP was approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”), now 
BPDA, in 1986. Subsequent IMPs were approved in 1997, 2003, and 2013. 
Since the 2013 – 2023 IMP was approved, the University has sought and received approval 
for six amendments to the IMP in order to modify or add to the list of Proposed Institutional 
Projects (“PIPs”) identified in the 2013 – 2023 IMP. A brief description of each of these 
amendments is found in Chapter 2. 
 
NEW INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
The current 2013 – 2023 IMP will expire on February 15, 2023. The University has begun 
the process of compiling information related to the upcoming 2023 – 2033 IMP and 
identifying its needs over the next decade to achieve the vision outlined in the Strategic 
Plan. The University is committed to taking the time necessary to thoroughly evaluate the 
future needs of the BU Charles River Campus and to develop a creative and thoughtful plan 
to realize the University’s overall goals and objectives. The University will continue to work 
with faculty, staff, students, and the surrounding community to define its next steps. This 
document is a framework to setting forth those goals and working with the City of Boston 
and the community to define the 2023 – 2033 IMP. 
 
IMPACT OF COVID-19 ON THE UNIVERSITY 
Like many colleges and universities, BU continues to navigate challenges to campus life 
because of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. When the virus first appeared in early 2020, 
the University was able to quickly put in place comprehensive health and safety protocols, 
thanks to the excellence of its faculty, staff, and researchers and extraordinary cooperation 
from the entire University community. These protocols included a clinical testing lab, a 
dedicated healthcare team, and later, immunization clinics and mandatory vaccination and 
booster shots. 
For the 2020 – 2021 academic year, the University offered students a choice of attending 
in-person classes or taking classes remotely under a new hybrid teaching format called 
Learn from Anywhere (“LfA”). The flexibility of LfA was designed to accommodate safety 
requirements that were imposed by public health authorities to control the spread of 
COVID-19, as well as by travel and other challenges faced by students. The aim was to 
present the same academic content to all students, whether they were in a classroom, in a 

Boston University Charles River Campus Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
 
Introduction 
 
1-6 
 
BU residence, or in an off-campus location, and to allow all students to take part in the 
same classroom discussions. 
The impacts of the LfA format and other disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic are 
reflected in much of the data included in this IMPNF. Data from the past two years 
concerning enrollment, housing, and transportation are indicative of the extraordinary 
effects of the pandemic on campus operations. As the University transitioned back to more 
typical campus life during the 2021 – 2022 school year and is no longer offering the LfA 
format, these enrollment, housing, and transportation numbers are returning to pre-
pandemic levels. 
 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLANNING PROCESS 
In recognition of the impact of institutional developments on the community, colleges and 
universities in Boston are required under Article 80D of the Zoning Code to submit a 
comprehensive development plan to the BPDA every ten years, at a minimum. While many 
PIPs are subject to further review under Article 80B, the IMP allows the BPDA to assess the 
impact and suitability of the institution’s development programs. The purpose of this IMPNF 
is to initiate the BPDA Article 80D IMP review process for the creation of the BU Charles 
River Campus 2023 – 2033 IMP. 
The University welcomes the City’s participation in its development planning, viewing it as 
a chance to optimize its own plans and initiatives with the expertise of public agencies and 
to create a positive impact in the community. The forthcoming BU Charles River Campus 
2023 – 2033 IMP will represent the collaborative efforts of the community, government 
agencies, elected officials, and the University. 
1.7.1 BOSTON UNIVERSITY CHARLES RIVER CAMPUS TASK FORCE 
In 2021, the BU Task Force celebrated its 35th anniversary. In 1986, BU was the first 
institution in Boston to establish such a committee, and it has benefited from the 
diverse experience and perspectives of the committee’s constituent members. The 
Task Force advises the City and University on the implementation of the IMP. 
Concurrent with the submission of the IMPNF to the BPDA, the University will meet 
with BPDA staff to present the planned IMP to the Task Force and to members of the 
public.

INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The University has made significant progress in implementing many of the objectives 
described in the 2013-2023 IMP. This chapter details the progress made in the areas of 
enrollment and student housing, provides updates on the PIPs included in the 2013 – 2023 
IMP and the First through Sixth Amendments, as well as describes improvements to the public 
realm and other facilities. 
 
UNDERGRADUATE ENROLLMENT 
The strategic management of enrollment at BU is a top priority of University leadership. 
Enrollment is carefully managed with a strategic vision to maintain a full-time undergraduate 
population of approximately 16,000 students. The University’s domestic undergraduate 
students come from all 50 states with over half hailing from Massachusetts, New York, 
California, and New Jersey. BU’s international undergraduate students come from 133 
different countries, with the majority coming from China, India, and South Korea. 
Full-time undergraduate enrollment at the BU Charles River Campus increased from 15,419 to 
16,997 between 2012 and 2021, which is a 10% increase over a decade. (See Table 2-1: 
Historical Full-time Undergraduate Enrollment). Over this period of time two major occurrences 
had an impact on enrollment: 
• 
In the summer of 2018, BU merged with Wheelock College and enrolled 311 
undergraduate students. 
• 
In 2020, the University’s undergraduate enrollment reflects the impact of the COVID-19 
pandemic. Implementing the LfA program allowed enrollment to hold steady, but the 
rebound effect raised enrollment to 16,997 students. Similar to other institutions, this 
increase is likely attributed to the students who deferred attending their freshman year 
remotely.
