Telehealth 
Clinical Services 
The COVID-19 pandemic pushed 
most face-to-face interaction online, 
forcing the Robbins Speech, Lan­
guage, and Hearing Center, the 
clinical training facility for Emerson’s 
Department of Communication 
Sciences and Disorders (CSD), to 
orchestrate telehealth sessions instead 
of in-person, one-on-one therapy. 
Sessions took place in clients’ homes, 
so graduate student clinicians could 
see their clients’ daily environments 
and what they had to work with. By 
utilizing an interactive computer 
program instead of showing physical 
pictures, as done in a clinic setting, 
student clinicians worked with clients 
to use appropriate syntax in multiple 
word utterances. The telehealth 
sessions have provided a valuable 
new learning experience for Emerson 
students, as telehealth is expected to 
become more common in the industry. 
The Robbins Speech, Language, and Hearing 
Center worked with about 100 clients before the 
pandemic and retained 71 percent of them. Being 
able to interact with both parent and child in their 
own home setting has advantages when it comes 
to testing treatment and theories. Before the 
telehealth sessions, student clinicians would have 
to wait a week for a parent to tell them that some­
thing didn’t work at home. Now, they can problem 
solve with their client immediately and change the 
approach. The students learned to adjust their 
expectations, be flexible, and know that through­
out their career, they’re going to experience 
unexpected outcomes.

_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Planning & Development 
Agency (“BPDA”): waive further review of the Institutional Master Plan 
Notification Form for the Renewal of the Emerson College Institutional 
Master Plan (“IMPNF for Renewal”), dated October 16, 2023, and 
approve the renewal of the Emerson College Institutional Master Plan 
(the “Emerson College IMP”) pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 
80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the Code; and (2) authorize the Director to 
take all actions and execute any and all documents deemed necessary 
and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The Emerson College (“Emerson”) Institutional Master Plan (“IMP”) was 
approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) Board on December 5, 
2002 and approved by the Boston Zoning Commission on December 11, 2002. The 
Original IMP was subsequently amended on July 19, 2006; September 26, 2007; 
January 8, 2014; May 20, 2015; March 8, 2017; September 12, 2018; and renewed on 
November 18, 2021. 
 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
16 
DOC No. 8085 
 
 
 
On October 16, 2023, Emerson submitted an IMPNF for Renewal to the Boston 
Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”), signaling its intention to renew the 
Emerson IMP for a period of two years. Emerson is not proposing a “Proposed 
Institutional Project”, as that term is understood in the Code; is not adding new land 
area to the Emerson IMP; is not proposing any changes to the Emerson IMP which 
would constitute a change in use, dimensional, parking or loading elements thereof 
(other than de minimus dimensional changes), and BPDA staff do not anticipate any 
greater impacts from the continuation of the implementation of the Emerson IMP 
than that which were originally evaluated. 
 
 
INSTITUTIONAL TEAM 
 
Proponent: 
Emerson College 
Margaret A. Ings 
Mary Higgins 
 
 
 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 
The IMPNF for Renewal is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review and qualifies 
for a waiver of further review in accordance with Sections 80D-5.2(e) and 80D-6 of 
the Code in that: (i) no new Proposed Institutional Projects are planned; (ii) no 
changes in the Institutional Master Plan are proposed that would constitute a 
change in the use, dimensional, parking or loading elements of the Institutional 
Master Plan (other than de minimus dimensional changes); and (iii) no significantly 
greater impacts would result from continued implementation of the approved 
Institutional Master Plan than were originally projected. The IMPNF for Renewal 
seeks approval of the IMPNF and the Emerson IMP together, as the renewed IMP, 
for a period of two years, until November 16, 2025. 
 
The submission of the IMPNF for Renewal on October 16, 2023, initiated a 30-day 
comment period that ended on November 15, 2023. Notice of submission was 
published in the Boston Herald on October 16, 2023. 
 
CONTINUED COMMUNITY BENEFITS

All community benefits currently offered pursuant to the existing Emerson IMP will 
continue through the length of the renewed IMP. 
 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, staff recommends that the BPDA Board: (1) waive further 
review of the IMPNF for Renewal and approve the Emerson College Institutional 
Master Plan pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the 
Code; and (2) authorize the Director to take all actions and execute any and all 
documents deemed necessary and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That in connection with the Emerson College Institutional Master Plan 
Notification Form for Renewal, dated October 16, 2023, (the “IMPNF for 
Renewal”), and after consideration of the Emerson College Institutional 
Master Plan (the “Emerson College IMP”), the BRA hereby finds that: (a) 
the Emerson College IMP, now amended by the IMPNF for Renewal, 
conforms to the provisions of Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code 
(“the Code”); (b) the Emerson College IMP, now amended by the IMPNF 
for Renewal conforms to the general plan for the City as a whole; and 
(c) on balance, nothing in the Emerson College IMP, now amended by 
the IMPNF for Renewal, will be injurious to the neighborhood or 
otherwise detrimental to the public welfare, weighing all the benefits 
and burdens; and 
 
FURTHER

That pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e) of the Code, the BRA has

elements of the Emerson College IMP, and (iii) no significantly greater 
impacts would result from continued implementation of the approved 
Emerson IMP than were originally projected; and

INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL INFORMATION 
1.1 
Introduction 
Franciscan Hospital for Children (FC or Proponent) is pleased to submit this Institutional Master 
Plan Notification Form/Project Notification Form (IMPNF/PNF) to the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority, doing business as Boston Planning & Development Agency (herein, the BPDA). With 
this submission, FC is initiating the process for approval of an Institutional Master Plan (IMP) 
pursuant to Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code (the Code) for a 10-year term and initiating 
Large Project Review under Article 80B of the Code to enable the development of the projects 
outlined below. 
Since its founding in 1949, FC has become a premier, nationally recognized pediatric specialty care 
provider offering services critical to families in Boston and throughout the region. FC is a 
Massachusetts public charity dedicated to serving (i) the most medically complex children, 
including newborn babies on ventilators, (ii) children with behavioral health conditions requiring 
inpatient services, short-term residential, school-based, ambulatory and/or community-based 
services, (iii) children who need specialized dental services, including dental surgeries under 
general anesthesia, and (iv) children with specialized educational needs due to their physical 
and/or cognitive condition.1 FC is the only pediatric chronic disease and rehabilitation hospital in 
Massachusetts and one of the largest providers of pediatric behavioral health services in the state. 
It also operates the Kennedy Day School, a special education school for children with complex

While FC has grown programmatically over the last seven decades to meet the evolving needs of

well as initiate Large Project Review under Article 80B) process because the campus has not been 
significantly developed through the years. 
Through its IMP, FC seeks to modernize its campus to better meet the current needs of patients 
and families. The organization hopes to build a state-of-the-art, family-friendly facility which 
matches its reputation for providing high quality care. 
FC proposes three projects, collectively referred to in this document as the “2022 IMP Projects” 
or “Projects.” The Projects include: (1) the construction of a new, approximately 289,500 square 
foot (sf) inpatient building for both behavioral health and medical services (Inpatient Building); 
(2) a new gymnasium with a connector to the existing Kennedy Day School (Gym and Connector); 
and (3) a new parking garage with approximately 475 parking spaces.

scale and nature of the surrounding facilities on Warren Street. They also meet environmental 
goals and considerations set forth by the City of Boston, including the maintenance of the 
Kennedy Rock Conservation Protection Subdistrict situated on FC’s campus. 
In addition to seeking approval from the City of Boston for its proposed campus modernization, 
FC will also need approval from the Department of Public Health (DPH) prior to significant 
construction or any expansion of licensed capacity. If approved by the City, the proposed IMP 
would establish a reasonable set of parameters for its campus, within which FC would seek 
approval for hospital construction from DPH. 
The need to modernize FC’s campus and expand is both long overdue and urgent, particularly 
since the need for the hospital’s services is greater than ever before. After decades of stigma, 
continued and growing workforce shortfalls, institutional and system under-investment, and a 
lack of systems integration—all of which have only been further exacerbated by the current 
COVID-19 pandemic—pediatric behavioral health has reached a crisis point in Massachusetts and 
beyond.2 The National Institute of Mental Health estimates that nearly half of U.S. adolescents 
ages 13-18 years now have at least one behavioral health condition with nearly a quarter having

PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
2.1 
Program Need 
This IMPNF urgently addresses the need to modernize FC’s aging infrastructure and expand 
access to desperately needed services. 
FC’s current facilities face a variety of limitations and challenges. Today mental health programs 
that serve similar patient populations are inefficiently located on opposite ends of FC’s campus. 
Due to space constraints, most patients are in multiple occupancy rooms, which is not ideal for 
patients and families. This also limits FC’s ability to admit children because clinical teams must 
match prospective patients by age, gender identity, acuity, diagnosis, and other factors. With an 
increased need for social distancing, COVID-19 has exacerbated these space challenges for FC, as 
it has for hospitals nationwide. Furthermore, while FC has tried to maximize its existing 
footprint, there is limited space that can be devoted to patients and families outside of hospital 
rooms. 
Current space constraints also hinder FC’s ability to expand programs at a time when the need 
for its services is greater than ever before. The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in exponentially 
greater need for access to pediatric inpatient psychiatric services.1 There is also growing need to 
expand services for children with complex medical needs, a population that is increasing 
because of improved technology and treatment options. 
Within the parameters set by the IMP, FC will work directly, and through its proposed affiliation 
with BCH, to redevelop and modernize FC’s campus into a state-of-the art center for pediatric 
behavioral health and medical rehabilitative excellence through a new building to be 
constructed. 
The proposed new Inpatient Building described in section 2.3, if approved, will significantly 
address the most pressing needs by: i) relocating and reconfiguring hospital capacity into single 
occupancy patient rooms, ii) increasing and improving family and visitor spaces, iii) providing 
caregivers with the latest technology, and iv) relocating programs to share expertise, resources, 
and staff to improve efficiency. Additionally, upon receiving approval from the Department of 
Public Health, the new building will expand capacity by increasing the number of beds for FC’s 
pediatric post-acute care, inpatient behavioral health, and Community Based Acute Treatment 
(CBAT) programs, as well as allow space for the development of new programs to meet the 
rising need.

2.2 
Planning Efforts to Date 
A longstanding goal of FC’s has been to update the organization’s aging campus and expand 
access to the hospital’s behavioral health and rehabilitation programs. These goals were 
approved by FC’s Board of Directors and leadership team in the 2016 five-year organizational 
plan and were reaffirmed in 2021. The 2021 strategic plan was a result of a comprehensive 
strategic planning process informed by an examination of FC, state, and national data, 
consultation with medical and behavioral health experts, and external assessments of the 
market and critical need for increased services. FC’s 2018 and 2021 community health needs 
assessments of the Allston/Brighton community – informed by city and state data and 
interviews with Allston/Brighton community organizations and residents – further reiterated the 
need for expansion of FC’s services. 
Over the last five years, FC engaged in campus planning efforts through a multi-disciplinary team 
of behavioral health and medical leaders and experts in facilities, information technology, and 
other areas of hospital operations. FC visited hospitals with state-of-the-art pediatric post-acute 
care and behavioral health units and worked with teams of consultants with architectural, 
sustainability, traffic and parking, mechanical and geotechnical engineering, and environmental 
expertise, among others. Prior to the proposed affiliation with BCH, FC worked with architects to 
develop the concept of a building on the front of its campus on Warren Street that would 
feature an expansion of FC’s inpatient behavioral health and post-acute care programs. Current 
plans have built upon that vision while also becoming more transformative given the nature of 
the proposed BCH affiliation. Multi-disciplinary clinical teams at BCH and FC have been working 
together to develop a clinical vision for the future and a corresponding campus plan that will 
meet the needs of children and adolescents requiring behavioral health and/or rehabilitative 
services. 
Beyond the term of the IMP, the 20-year plan envisions replacing the rest of the FC buildings. As 
part of the feasibility and concept design, an overall long-term site strategy concept was 
developed, illustrating the development of future buildings along Warren Street with outdoor 
fields and playgrounds situated toward the back of the property.

Inpatient Building 
The Inpatient Building will be situated on the location of parking spaces and Building 7, which is 
proposed to be demolished. Building 7 was constructed in 1949 and has since outlived its useful

face for FC. It will include both pediatric post-acute care and psychiatric inpatient care on

as well as a new main entrance and lobby for the campus, among other services to be defined.

The new building will feature single rooms for these new programs instead of the multiple

and connections to existing buildings. From a branding and visibility perspective, having such a 
significant new building along Warren Street will enhance FC’s presence in the community.

Campus Circulation 
The main entry to the Inpatient Building will occur at ground level, at grade. The upper levels 
will overhang the access driveway and form a covered drop-off area. Pedestrians from the 
street, those being dropped off, and those using the accessible surface parking spots in front of 
the building, will enter the building under this overhang, providing additional accessibility to 
many of those FC serves who have mobility impairments. Vehicles entering the building through 
the front U-shaped main entry drive to use the parking garage will descend to a ground plane 
lower than the walk-in access level. The vehicular exit from the garage will be via side alley on 
the west side of the campus. Patients may also enter/exit the facility by ambulance transfer at 
ground level, at the southwest corner of the Inpatient Building. To enable a suitable rear drive 
aisle, Building 6 will be demolished, a 1954 structure with a 3,500-square-foot footprint not 
visible from the street that currently houses the campus communications servers, and offices. 
These will be replaced with up-to-date and suitable spaces elsewhere on the campus. 
Visitors approaching from ground level will ascend using steps, a ramp, or an elevator to Level 2 
(see Appendix A). This level will be on the same elevation as Level 2 of the main campus and the 
Kennedy Day School. The primary connection spine through the existing campus is on this level, 
and this connection to the campus will be the most direct indoor pedestrian route for staff to 
access other areas and for visitors who will park in the proposed East Parking Garage.

Existing Zoning 
The FC campus, which is comprised of City of Boston Assessing Parcel Nos. 2101272000 (80-30 
Warren Street) (“80 Warren”) and 2101271000 (100-98 Warren Street) (“98 Warren”), is located 
entirely within the Allston-Brighton Neighborhood District as indicated on City of Boston Zoning 
Map 7A/7B/7C/7D (the “Zoning Map”). As such, Article 51 of the City of Boston Zoning Code2 
currently provides the relevant zoning controls for the campus. As noted on the Zoning Map, a 
portion of 80 Warren is located in two zoning Subdistricts: the Kennedy Rock Conservation 
Protection Subdistrict (the “CPS”) and the Franciscan Children's Hospital Institutional Subdistrict 
(the “IS”). Given the split zoning lot nature of 80 Warren, the transition zoning rules contained in 
Section 12-1 extend the more restrictive zoning controls of the CPS a distance of thirty (30) feet 
into the IS. 98 Warren is located entirely within the Multifamily Residential (the “MFR-1 
Subdistrict”) Subdistrict. The campus is not situated in any Overlay Districts. 
In the IS, Hospital and Open Space uses are allowed as-of-right. The IS also allows the following 
uses by Conditional Use Permit: clinic, clinical laboratory, agency or professional office, research 
laboratory, and product development/prototype manufacturing. 
The CPS, which is intended to protect and enhance natural and scenic resources, generally limits 
the uses allowed therein to certain community, cultural, educational and residential uses, as 
well as open space. In addition, the CPS allows clinics, clinical laboratories, general offices, 
agency or professional offices, and research laboratories as Conditional Uses. 
 
Allowed or conditional uses under MFR-1 Subdistrict generally are limited to certain residential 
uses and open space.

3.1 
Transportation 
This section of the IMPNF presents an overview of FC’s existing transportation infrastructure and 
a summary of the 2022 IMP Projects from a transportation perspective. 
The first section includes a description of FC’s existing transportation infrastructure and a 
discussion of parking, passenger pick-up/drop-off, and loading activities. The second section 
provides a brief discussion of transportation infrastructure surrounding the campus. The third 
section provides preliminary trip generation estimates and an overview of the parking supply with 
the completion of the proposed Projects. 
3.1.1 
Proposed 2022 IMP Projects Overview 
FC is located at 30 Warren Street in the Brighton neighborhood of Boston. Figure 3.1-1 shows the 
general campus location, between Cambridge Street and Commonwealth Avenue. FC provides a 
wide range of medical services for children and adolescents, including inpatient and outpatient 
care. The Kennedy Day School, a special education school with a current enrollment of 57 students 
is also located on the premises. The school operates for 200 days a year; typical school hours are 
8:15 a.m. to 3:20 p.m. 
As described previously in Chapter 2, FC is currently proposing three Projects. The Projects are 
described in more detail in Chapter 2 and include construction of a new Inpatient Building with 
ground-floor parking, construction of a Gymnasium and Connector building, and construction of 
a parking garage on an existing parking lot. In addition, the existing Buildings 6 and 7 will be 
demolished to allow for construction of the Projects. The Projects will continue to be primarily 
accessed from Warren Street, with secondary access to Cambridge Street. A new drop-off area is 
proposed on-campus, which will connect to both the existing and proposed building main 
entrances and portions of on-site parking. A new campus loop roadway is proposed to provide a 
drop-off area for school vans, along with loading and emergency vehicle access, for improved 
traffic flow.

FC will develop a detailed evaluation of potential short-term construction-related transportation 
impacts during the course of the Projects, including construction vehicle traffic, parking supply 
and demand, and pedestrian access to the campus. A detailed Construction Management Plan 
will be developed and submitted to BTD for its approval.

Construction vehicles will be necessary to move construction materials to and from the 
construction site. FC recognizes that construction traffic is a concern to area residents, other 
institutions, and to the hospital itself. Every effort will be made to reduce the noise, control

anticipated that Cambridge Street and Warren Street will serve as the principal construction 
traffic routes to the campus, and that trucks will be routed to avoid nearby residential areas. Truck 
staging and lay-down areas for the Projects will be carefully planned. The need for street 
occupancy along roadways adjacent to the campus is not known at this time.

3.8.1 
Hazardous Waste Conditions 
Prior to commencement of the work, an investigation will be performed at the Project sites and 
within the existing buildings to determine if contaminated soils, groundwater, asbestos, lead 
paint, or other hazardous materials are present. If such materials are present, they will be 
characterized based on the type, composition, and level of the contaminants. 
Remedial work plans for soil or groundwater contaminants will be prepared by a Licensed Site 
Professional (LSP) in accordance with the requirements of the Massachusetts Contingency Plan 
(MCP) to outline procedures for safe removal and legal disposal during construction. 
Contaminated soils will be categorized for acceptance at the appropriate facilities prior to 
excavation to minimize the need for temporary stockpiling of soils on-site. Excavated soils will be 
observed for evidence of contamination and screened with real-time instrumentation to 
determine the presence of volatile vapors. Perimeter dust monitoring will be conducted during 
active excavation of contaminated soils. Dust suppression methods will be employed if visible dust 
is observed.

3.9 
Geotechnical and Groundwater Impacts 
Subsurface conditions are based on review of historic test boring information and a recently 
completed preliminary test boring program. Subsurface conditions in the general consist of Fill 
soils overlying Glacial Till Deposits and/or weathered Bedrock. Depth to weathered Bedrock varies 
and was identified by sampler refusal, encountering weathered Bedrock, or bedrock refusal. The 
elevation for top of naturally occurring Bedrock is generally between El. 82 and El. 87 (Boston City 
Base Datum) near the south and east limits of the campus. In the area of the western portion of 
the campus, test borings encountered Bedrock at approximately El. 67 to 75. Bedrock was also 
encountered between El. 83 and 89 near the southwest corner of the campus. 
Groundwater levels are anticipated to vary from 15 to 22 feet below existing ground surface, 
corresponding to approximately El. 77 to El. 81. 
Development will require excavation in close proximity to existing buildings to remain and 
generally in the location of existing parking areas of the campus. The type and design of both the 
temporary earth support system for the excavation and the permanent foundation wall system 
will provide for adequate support of the structures and utilities, be compatible with the 
subsurface conditions, and be capable of maintaining groundwater levels outside the campus at 
or near pre-construction levels. 
Investigations will be performed to review existing foundation conditions for the campus buildings 
to remain as well as proposed new construction. Given the existing structures are three to four 
stories above grade, it is assumed that foundations for the existing structures derive support in 
the natural underlying Glacial Till deposits or Bedrock.

3.14.2 
Carbon Neutral Building Assessment 
In support of the City of Boston's Greenhouse Gas (GHG) reduction goals including Carbon Free 
Boston, a Carbon Neutral Building Assessment (CNBA) has been performed. 
The Project team has examined all practical measures to minimize the Project’s energy use and 
GHG emissions to the maximum extent feasible, while still incorporating essential design 
elements vital to the Project’s viability. Building design decisions have been informed through 
careful modeling and cost analysis. The Project team will continue to evaluate ways to minimize 
energy use and improve efficiency as the Project advances. 
3.14.2.1 
Proposed Project Description 
To meet the needs described in Section 2.1, FC proposes three projects: a new 265,500 sf inpatient 
building (Inpatient Building), a 5,500 sf gymnasium and connector (Gym and Connector), and a 
new 475-space parking garage (East Garage). This assessment focuses on the Inpatient Building. 
Additionally, the modeling includes the energy consumption of the East Garage. 
3.14.2.2 
Building Envelope 
A high-performing building envelope is essential to any emissions reduction strategy. Through an 
iterative, collaborative process, the design team has developed a proposed building envelope 
design that exceeds code envelope requirements, while still allowing the Inpatient Building to 
meet its objectives. 
The vertical wall assemblies for the Inpatient Building are proposed to consist of a combination of 
framed opaque wall and thermally-broken high-performance unitized curtain wall systems. Please 
refer to Appendix C for detailed envelope calculations. 
Basis of design assumptions include: 
♦ Steel frame construction with 33% vision, 22% opaque spandrel, and 45% 
framed/insulated wall. 
♦ Overall UA of 0.10, which is a 15.6% improvement vs Mass. Code (IECC 2018) 
♦ Fenestration will be Triple Glazed, Double Low-E glass with U-factor of 0.24 
♦ Steel stud framed wall with 4” of continuous insulation on thermally broken cladding 
supports and a minimum of 3 ½” mineral wool insulation in the stud cavity for a total U = 
0.041 (R-24.4) 
♦ Roof will be R-55.6 continuous insulation 
♦ Per MA Energy Code, air infiltration will meet C406.1 #8, which requires 0.25 cfm/sf at 75 
Pa confirmed with field testing.

3.14.2.3 
HVAC and Mechanical Design 
The HVAC and mechanical systems design have been evaluated for opportunities to reduce GHG 
emissions. The evaluation includes a review of options to maximize the use of electricity as an 
energy source, based on the expectation that the electric grid will continue its downward GHG 
emissions trend due to a greater reliance on renewable sources, and that electrification of HVAC 
systems would allow the Project’s GHG emissions to mirror that downward trend. The design 
team has considered available incentives and operational savings in evaluating these alternatives. 
Proposed Case 
The primary HVAC system for the laboratory spaces will be a 30 percent outside air system 
providing air to most hospital spaces. Any specialty program areas such Pharmacies, Operating 
Rooms to have dedicated AHU's. Dedicated Outdoor Air Handling Unit (DOAS) to treat ventilation 
air to the main air handling units. The DOAS units will have energy recovery wheels to transfer 
heat from the building exhaust to the outside air for energy efficiency. 
The primary heating for the building will be a combination of 2-pipe modular air-to-water heat 
pumps, gas-fired high-efficiency condensing boilers, and a heat recovery chiller. The heat recovery 
chiller is sequenced as the first stage of heating to satisfy simultaneous heating and cooling loads. 
The air-to-water heat pumps operate as the next stage of heating, capable of delivering the design 
hot water supply temperature down to 12.4°F ambient. The pumps will also offset condensing 
boiler gas consumption in the summer months. The building will also have a gas-fired condensing 
boiler plant, sized for the full heating load, to operate as a backup and supplement the base load 
heat pump during peak heating demand. This combination of heat recovery chillers, heat pumps, 
and gas boilers constitutes hybrid electrification of space heating. 
The primary cooling for the building will be a combination of 2-pipe modular air-to-water heat 
pumps, water cooled chillers with associated cooling towers, and a heat recovery chiller. The heat 
recovery chiller is sequenced as the first stage of cooling to satisfy simultaneous heating and 
cooling loads. The heat recovery chiller is supplemented by a water cooled chiller plant. The 
cooling towers and chiller are sized for the complete cooling load of the building for redundancy. 
The air-to-water heat pumps operate as the redundant stage of cooling to supplement the water 
cooled chillers in the case of a failure. 
The enhanced air-side energy recovery systems and tightly controlled air change rates will 
dramatically reduce the required operating capacity of the building’s heating and cooling plant 
compared to a typical hospital facility. The building will have a modular heat recovery chiller to 
satisfy simultaneous heating and cooling loads, and air source heat pumps which can also provide 
full heating and backup cooling (water cooled chillers are prioritized for higher energy efficiency). 
As such, the majority of the building’s heating load will be satisfied with electricity. 
Domestic hot water will be provided by electric water heaters.

3.14.2.6 
Off‐Site Renewable Energy 
To achieve carbon neutrality, projects can purchase renewable energy certificates (RECs), which 
represent one megawatt‐hour (MWh) of electricity that is generated and delivered to the electric 
grid from a renewable energy source. The cost of RECs can vary widely. Green‐e Certified 
Massachusetts RECs are currently priced at approximately $30 per REC. 
The Inpatient Building and East Garage are estimated to consume approximately 7,730 MWh of 
electricity. To offset the carbon emitted by the Inpatient Building’s and East Garage’s electrical 
consumption, approximately 7,730 RECs would need to be purchased. This could cost 
approximately $231,900 annually (based on current rates). Future technologies may allow the 
Inpatient Building’s natural gas use to switch to electricity.

3.14.3 
Climate Change Resilience 
The Project's design address resiliency against extreme heat, precipitation, and high wind. The 
design of the Projects will significantly decrease stormwater run-off at the site by installing 
infiltration chambers for each of the three proposed Projects. The proposed site plan also 
converts approximately 3,000 sf of existing impervious surfaces to pervious surfaces by replacing 
existing parking lot area and built structures with green space. Providing additional pervious area 
will also mitigate heat island effect at the campus. 
To further mitigate urban heat island effect, the Inpatient, Connector and Gym buildings will 
utilize white roofs, triple glazing with low SHGC, and will incorporate photovoltaics as is feasible. 
A photovoltaic canopy will be installed over the parking structure to reduce extreme heat and 
provide shade for the uppermost level of parking. In addition, the chiller plant is sized for ASHRAE 
0.4% summer design condition. Chiller plant will also feature n+1 capacity giving the further 
cooling above peak conditions. 
The Inpatient Building also includes emergency power systems and standby power systems that 
include power supply to the full chilled water plant for 48 hours of operation. Heat is currently 
provided by natural gas boilers with an N+1 configuration with portions of the plant also running 
on electricity for additional resilience. Provisions will also be made for medical gas resilience. 
A Climate Resiliency Checklist for each Project is provided in Appendix D.

3.15.1 
Land Use 
Existing land uses surrounding the FC campus are primarily institutional and residential. As with 
FC’s campus, the large multi-acre institutional land uses in this area were historically owned by 
the Catholic Archdiocese / Vatican. Along with its topography, the immediate neighborhood gains 
its unique character from this legacy of ecclesiastical and service orientation. 
Adjacent educational campuses include Brighton High School across the street to the south, 
nestled into a broadly terraced hill ascending prominently above the campus, and the three-story 
Boston Green Academy / William Howard Taft School building next door that directly abuts the 
proposed new Inpatient Building on the west. The St. Joseph Preparatory High School campus is 
located across Cambridge Street to the north of the conservation area. 
There are several major health care campuses nearby including the Steward St. Elizabeth’s 
Medical Center; its main entrance parking access drive is from Warren Street. In addition, Brighton 
Marine Health Center is directly across the street from FC. Its campus, also sited up the hill, 
features a mix of uses including health care and supported and priority housing for veterans.

The campus consists of two adjacent parcels of land totaling approximately 10.5 acres in the 
Allston-Brighton Neighborhood District. The campus is bounded by Warren Street to the south, 
taller residential buildings to the east, Cambridge Street and residential buildings to the north, 
and the William Howard Taft School at 20 Warren Street to the west. The northern portion of the 
parcel is comprised of a wooded area known as Kennedy Rock, which has been classified by the 
City of Boston as an “urban wild” but is owned by the Proponent and is not affiliated with the 
City’s public park system or under any protections. 
Building 7, proposed for removal, is a four-story institutional building on a raised basement with 
a flat roof. Located at the southwestern corner of the parcel, the L-shaped, yellow-brick building 
has two main entryways fronting on Warren Street. Within its inner corner is a two-story 
extension. Built as a medical campus, construction on Building 7 and the other three original 
campus buildings began in 1947. The original owner was the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of 
Boston. On a 1948 permit to amend the original campus building plans John Edmund Kelley of 
Boston is listed as the architect. 
The other three original campus buildings (Buildings 1, 2, and 3) are in succession to the east. They 
also front on Warren Street and feature the same muted yellow brick and varying hipped and 
gable roofs. The original administrative headquarters—the central, H-shaped building—is 1–2.5 
stories and is flanked by identical double-E-shaped, 1.5 story buildings. 
The campus expansion occurred between the 1950s and 2010. Building 6 was constructed in the 
late 1950s and is the second building proposed for removal. It is a two-story, muted yellow brick 
building with punched window openings and a flat roof. On a 1957 document, Whelan and 
Westman Architects are listed as the architect. 
In the early 1960s, Building 5 was added. Building 4 was built in the mid-1970s. In the early 1990s, 
a one-story addition was constructed at the inner corner of Building 5. The most recent campus 
expansion effort took place in 2010 with the construction of Building 8. 
The medical campus was known by its original name for much of its history; it was named the 
Joseph P. Kennedy Memorial Hospital because of the financial support the project received from 
the Kennedy family. In the early 1960s, FC converted parts of the original campus buildings into 
classrooms to found and operate a school for children with special needs known as the Kennedy 
Day School. The building added to FC’s campus in 2010 functions as additional educational space 
for children with special needs as part of the Kennedy Day School.

District to the southwest, listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

3.17.1 
Introduction 
This section describes the existing infrastructure systems used by FC, as well as future demands 
and proposed system modifications. The infrastructure systems addressed include sanitary sewer, 
water supply, stormwater drainage, electrical service, natural gas, and telecommunications. 
Future demands are based on projects proposed during the term of the IMP. As described in 
previous sections, there are three IMP Projects: the Inpatient Building, the East Garage and the 
Gymnasium and Connector. In the following sections, these Projects are evaluated for potential 
impacts to infrastructure systems. 
3.17.2 
Sanitary Sewer 
3.17.2.1 
Existing System Conditions 
The Boston Water and Sewer Commission (BWSC) owns and maintains the sewer lines in the 
public ways that service FC. Existing sewer lines within the campus are maintained by FC. 
Sanitary sewer systems in the nearby public streets and campus service roads are separate from 
stormwater collection systems. FC is serviced by an existing 12-inch sanitary sewer in Cambridge 
Street and two sewers in Warren Street ranging in size from 10-15 inches. There is also a 
Massachusetts Water Resources Authority (MWRA) sewer in Warren Street that does not directly 
service FC. Wastewater flows from FC are ultimately conveyed to the MWRA Deer Island 
Wastewater Treatment Plant for treatment and disposal. 
3.17.2.2 
Future Wastewater Generation & System Modifications 
Based on wastewater generation rates established by the Massachusetts Department of 
Environmental Protection (310 CMR 15.203) of 200 gallons per day per bed, the Inpatient Building 
is expected to generate approximately 31,600 gallons per day of sewage. Sewage generation has 
been calculated on the current Basis of Design and will be refined as the program is refined1. The 
Inpatient Building is expected to discharge to the sanitary sewer in Warren Street. The East Garage 
is not expected to contain occupiable space. The covered portions of the Garage will have floor 
drains directed to an oil/gas separator which is expected to discharge to the existing sanitary 
sewer in Warren Street. The Gymnasium and Connector discharge location will be either Warren 
Street or Cambridge Street. The Gymnasium is accessory to the other programs on campus and 
thus is not expected to generate sanitary sewage as an independently functioning gymnasium. All 
proposed connections will be submitted to BWSC for review and approval.

the design progresses.

INTRODUCTION 
Franciscan Hospital for Children is a 7 story 265,500 SF1 inpatient hospital building located in Boston, MA. It is connected to 
a 24,000 SF parking garage which is located on the first level. 
The design has been optimized to target best in class energy performance, including ultra-low fossil fuel consumption and 
an overall Energy Use Intensity (EUI) of 121 kBtu/sf-yr. This is considered best in class performance for hospital buildings, 
targeting approximately 97% reduction in fossil fuel consumption. 
Based on current assumptions and preliminary concept design document information for Franciscan Hospital for Children, 
the energy results demonstrate compliance with: 
1. The current (2020 adopted) MA Stretch Energy Code 
2. The proposed (October 2021 draft) Boston Zero Net Carbon Zoning 
3. The MEPA DOER expectations for hybrid electrification of healthcare 
4. LEED NC Minimum Energy Performance Prerequisite and Optimize Energy Performance Credit, targeting 10 
Points 
Compliance with the requirements above is outlined in more detail below.

• 
A minimum of 10% site energy savings. The Proposed design shows a 29% site energy savings relative to the MA 
2020 Stretch Energy Code baseline. 
•

MEPA / DOER Expectations for Healthcare: COMPLIES 
The energy analysis results indicate compliance with MEPA / DOER expectations, as follows: 
1. 25% heat pump capacity. The air-to-water heat pump [or other heat pump] capacity at ASHRAE 99% design 
condition (12.7°F) is equal to 25% of the boiler plant capacity. 
2. A minimum of 90% fossil fuel reduction. The Proposed design currently shows at least 90% fossil fuel reduction 
compared to the Stretch Code baseline, including the combination of both heating and domestic hot water. 
3. Optimized on-site solar PV array. The Proposed design will be PV ready, with approximately 3,000 SF of PV 
available on the roof. Parking garage roof area is being evaluated for solar. This is about 45 kW, which produces 
about 54,000 kWh per year.

The energy analysis results indicate compliance with the proposed (October 2021 draft) Boston Zero Net Carbon Zoning

TARGETING CARBON NEUTRAL 
Greenhouse Gas Emissions 
Boston has set a goal to become carbon neutral by 2050 and has outlined a path to decarbonize buildings in the Carbon 
Free Boston action plan. In addition, the Massachusetts Climate Bill enacted in 2021 requires the entire Commonwealth to 
be carbon neutral by 2050. Anticipated carbon emissions from new buildings are reviewed by the BPDA in comparison to 
the energy code baseline to ensure that developments are meeting the states carbon neutrality goal. 
 
Franciscan Hospital for Children’s carbon reduction strategy prioritizes electrification of space heating, positioning the 
building to trend towards carbon neutrality in lock step with the electrical grid’s ratcheting renewable electricity thresholds 
mandated by the State Legislature. In contrast, buildings relying primarily on fossil fuels will see smaller incremental carbon 
reductions because fossil fuel emissions factors are static. Because the electric emission factor is a moving target, it is 
useful to consider emissions today (2022) and the projected emissions in 2035, halfway between now and the 2050 carbon 
neutrality goal.

BENCHMARKING 
The purpose of benchmarking is to compare the proposed design energy use intensity to other similar existing buildings. 
While the Stretch Code baseline is useful for determining code compliance, it should be considered a theoretical design for 
comparison purposed only, more than it represents a building that would actually be built. Therefore, it is useful to compare 
the energy analysis results to measured data from existing buildings. We have identified hospitals in Boston and nearby 
Cambridge data gathered from 2018-2019 Boston BERDO data and 2020 Cambridge BUEDO data for hospitals. 
 
 
These buildings have an average Site Energy Use Intensity (EUI) of 280 kBtu/sf-yr and an average gas EUI of 191 kBtu/sf-yr. 
This benchmark data is represented in the chart below, in comparison to Franciscan Hospital for Children. The modeled 
result for the proposed design achieves a 57% reduction in site EUI compared to the benchmark data.

APPENDIX E: POST-PROCESSING SUMMARY 
For the proposed deign, the simulation software (eQUEST) was used to model the building loads and air-side systems. 
However, because the software is not able to accurately model the intended sequences for the specified air-source heat 
pumps and heat recovery chillers, this equipment has been modeled in a custom spreadsheet using the hourly hot water 
and chilled water loop flow from the energy model. 
 
The post processing tool calculates the following on an hourly basis: 
 
The primary heating for the buildings will be heat recovery chillers and 2-pipe modular air-to-water heat pumps. The 
heat recovery chiller provides simultaneous heating and cooling to satisfy the base loads. The air-to-water heat pumps 
are the next stage of heating. A gas-fired condensing boiler plant, sized for the full heating load, will operate for peak 
heating loads as a backup if heating if it is not satisfied by the heat recover chillers and air source heat pumps. This 
combination of heat recovery chillers, heat pumps, and gas boilers constitutes hybrid electrification of space heating. 
 
The heat recovery chiller and the air-source heat pump load are determined by the hourly heating and cooling loads. 
These hourly load profiles are distributed to the equipment. The loads are applied to the heat recovery chillers until the 
base loads are satisfied. If there is a remaining heating load, the air-to-water heat pump operates to meet the load. If 
there is still a heating load, the condensing boilers operate to meet the remaining load. The condensing boilers also 
serve as a backup. For remaining cooling loads, the remaining load is applied to the centrifugal chillers. The primary 
pumps for each piece of equipment is also included in these post processing calculations. The spreadsheet includes the 
impact on the efficiency of the equipment at part load, and ambient conditions as well as the peak capacity at ambient 
conditions. 
 
The spreadsheet determines the number of air-source heat pump modules and heat recovering chillers operating to 
satisfy the load and calculates the electricity consumption of the chillers, pumps, and the natural gas consumption of the 
boilers at the given operating condition. The spreadsheet includes the impact on the efficiency of the equipment at part 
load, and ambient conditions as well as the peak capacity at ambient conditions. 
 
The simultaneous heating and cooling loads are then subtracted from the total building load to give the net heating and 
cooling loads for the next step. 
 
The net heating and cooling loads are factored into the final energy analysis results for the buildings.

The City of Boston is working to cultivate a broadband ecosystem that serves the current 
and future connectivity needs of residents, businesses, and institutions.  The real estate 
development process offers a unique opportunity to create a building stock in Boston that 
enables this vision.  In partnership with the development community, the Boston Planning 
and Development Authority and the City of Boston will begin to leverage this opportunity 
by adding a broadband readiness component to the Article 80 Design Review.  This 
component will take the form of a set of questions to be completed as part of the Project

process will contribute to progress towards the following goals:

technologies

Part 7 - Smart Utility Standards
The Smart Utility Standards set forth guidelines for planning and integration of SUTs with
existing utility infrastructure in existing or new streets, including cross-section, lateral, and
intersection diagrams. The Smart Utility Standards are intended to serve as guidelines for
developers, architects, engineers, and utility providers for planning, designing, and locating
utilities. The Smart Utility Standards will serve as the baseline for discussions on any
deviations from the standards needed/proposed for any given utility infrastructure.

infrastructure in the proposed development area (including infrastructure related to the
applicable SUTs).

I. 
INTRODUCTION 
 
This Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) is submitted to the City of Boston 
Planning Department (the “Planning Department”), supporting the Boston Planning & 
Development Agency Board (the “BPDA Board”) in compliance with Section 80D-8 of the Boston 
Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), for purposes of renewing with no changes the current 
Institutional Master Plan for the Harvard University Longwood Campus (the “Harvard Longwood 
IMP” or the “IMP”). 
 
At this time, Harvard has no new Proposed Institutional Projects planned for the Longwood 
Campus beyond those described in the current IMP, as amended in 2004, 2010, and 2024. 
 
 
 
II. 
CONTEXT 
 
The Harvard Longwood Campus is located within Boston’s Longwood Medical and Academic Area 
(LMA) and consists of five parcels of land containing approximately 21 acres and 25 buildings. A 
map of the Harvard Longwood Campus is included as “Figure A.” 
 
Three of Harvard’s graduate and professional schools are based at the Harvard Longwood Campus: 
the Harvard Medical School (HMS), the Harvard School of Dental Medicine (HSDM), and the 
Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health (HSPH). Information on the mission and objectives 
of each of these schools is included in Section 1.4 of the original IMP. 
 
 
 
III. IMP BACKGROUND and STATUS 
 
2003 IMP: The Harvard Longwood IMP was approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) on February 27, 2003 and by the Boston Zoning Commission on March 26, 2003. 
Consistent with the requirements of Article 80D of the Zoning Code, the IMP described the 
existing uses, structures, and activities on the Harvard Longwood Campus, along with future needs, 
master planning objectives, and proposed construction projects over the five-year term of the IMP. 
The IMP described five proposed IMP projects (one new building and four additions to existing 
Harvard Medical School buildings) and ten campus improvement projects. The status of each of 
these projects is indicated in Table 1, attached. Project locations are shown in IMP Figures 4-1 and 
4-3, attached. 
 
IMP Amendment #1: The First Amendment to the Harvard Longwood IMP (the “First IMP 
Amendment”) was approved by the BRA on April 1, 2004 and by the Boston Zoning Commission 
on May 5, 2004. The First IMP Amendment described Harvard’s proposed use of an approximately 
140,000 square-foot component of the Fenway Mixed-Use Project (now known as Trilogy) 
consisting of rental residential apartments for Harvard affiliates, rental residential apartments for 
income-certified local residents, and associated parking rights. 
 

Harvard University Longwood Campus • Institutional Master Plan Notification Form • 2024 Renewal 
2 
IMP Amendment #2: The Second Amendment to the Harvard Longwood IMP (the “Second 
IMP Amendment”) was approved by the BRA on January 12, 2010. The Second IMP Amendment 
described Harvard’s proposed lease and use, for office purposes, of approximately 38,852 square 
feet of space at 90 Smith Street in Mission Hill, along with 40 adjacent surface parking spaces. 
 
IMP Amendment #3: The Third Amendment to the Harvard Longwood IMP (the “Third IMP 
Amendment”) was approved by the BPDA Board on March 14, 2024. The Third IMP Amendment 
modified the proposed square footage and certain other dimensional characteristics of the Harvard 
Medical School Building “C” courtyard addition project, a project included in the original 2003 IMP. 
 
IMP Renewal Status: The most-recent IMP renewal was approved by the BPDA on August 16, 
2018, for a five-year period. Pursuant to Chapter 53 of the Acts of 2020, which tolled the expiration 
date of local permits and approvals during the Commonwealth’s Covid State of Emergency, the 
term of the renewed Harvard Longwood IMP runs until November 20, 2024. 
 
 
 
IV. PROJECT UPDATES 
 
A. Activities Completed or Underway: The following projects include activities undertaken 
since the previous (2018) IMP renewal and the subsequent biannual updates (2020 and 
2022). While these activities do not constitute “Proposed Institutional Projects” that meet 
IMP review thresholds under the provisions of the Zoning Code, they are included here for 
informational purposes. 
 
HSDM/Harvard Dental Center Entrance Upgrade: The HSDM completed 
minor modifications and improvements to the patient entrance at the Harvard 
Dental Center, 188 Longwood Avenue, in late 2022. 
 
HMS/Countway Library LL1 Program Initiative: This renovation focused on 
conversion of library stack space on level L1 in support of the campus community 
need for space to facilitate individual and group study, foster collaboration, promote 
exchange of ideas, address the space and technological needs associated with the new 
curriculum, and inspire an appreciation for the history of medicine. The renovation 
was completed in 2023. 
 
HSPH/Francois Xavier Bagnoud (FXB) Roof Replacement: A roof 
replacement project at the FXB Building, 651 Huntington Avenue, was completed in 
2023. 
 
HMS/West Quad Science Program Renewal and Infrastructure Upgrades: As 
reported in our 2022 biannual update, HMS is in the process of modernizing 
research programs in Building C, the Seeley G. Mudd Building, and the Laboratory 
for Human Reproduction and Reproductive Biology (LHRRB). The multi-phased 
project is intended to improve density, create a collaborative environment, improve 
adjacencies and workflows, and upgrade infrastructure. The project is anticipated to 
be complete in late 2024. 

Harvard University Longwood Campus • Institutional Master Plan Notification Form • 2024 Renewal 
3 
 
HMS/Gordon Hall Flexspace and Infrastructure: HMS is implementing space 
alignment and efficiency improvements in support of new work models and hybrid 
staff populations. The project scope includes relocation of an existing server room 
data center, fitout of a flexspace program targeting floors 03, 04, and 05, integration 
of a second building elevator, and coordination of building infrastructure upgrades 
and improvements. Project completion is anticipated in early 2025. 
 
HMS/180 Longwood Avenue Façade and Roof Balustrade Repairs: A project 
is currently underway to address deterioration of the upper-roof balustrade and 
north entry portico roof and façade of the HMS building at 180 Longwood Avenue. 
The project scope includes in-kind replacement of the upper-roof balustrade, piers, 
and base stone at street-visible locations; replacement of the rear balustrade with 
steel guardrail (rear balustrade is not visible from the public way); repair of the north 
portico façade and roof, and removal of two rooftop headhouses (also not visible 
from the public way). The project is targeting completion in early 2025. 
 
CAMPUS-WIDE/Energy Conservation Measures: All three Harvard 
Longwood schools continue to implement multiple energy conservation initiatives to 
reduce energy consumption and lower carbon emissions. Examples of measures 
implemented or continued over the past two years include the retrofit of existing 
interior and exterior lighting with new energy-efficient LED fixtures, installation of 
variable speed drives on hydraulic heating and cooling loops in select buildings, and 
installation of heat-recovery and automated HVAC control systems. 
 
 
 
B. Upcoming Activities: The following projects include activities that are currently expected 
to commence within the upcoming renewal term of the IMP. Except as otherwise noted, 
these activities do not constitute “Proposed Institutional Projects” that meet IMP review 
thresholds under the definitions of the Zoning Code. They are included here for 
informational purposes. 
 
HMS/ West Commons / Building C Courtyard Addition: A proposed addition 
within the courtyard of HMS Building C was first described and approved as part of 
the 2003 Harvard Longwood IMP (identified as “Site 5” in IMP Figure 4-1, 
attached). Dimensional modifications to the original proposal were subsequently 
approved by the BPDA Board in March 2024 as part of the Third IMP Amendment. 
The proposed addition will be approximately 19,800 gross square feet in size and will 
create community, meeting, collaborative, and gathering space for HMS academic 
departments and affiliated research initiatives that are housed in adjacent buildings. 
The new addition will be contained within the existing courtyard, surrounded on all 
sides by other Harvard budlings, and will not be visible at street level from the HMS 
Quadrangle or from the public way along Longwood Avenue. Construction is 
expected to begin in late 2024, with substantial completion targeted for 2026. 
 
HSPH/Building #1 Roof Replacement: HSPH will undertake a roof 
replacement project at SPH Building 1, 665 Huntington Avenue, over the coming

months. Work is set to begin in late summer 2024 and be completed by the end of 
2024. 
 
HSPH/ Building #1 HVAC Maintenance and Upgrades: A project to improve 
the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning system in SPH Building 1, 665 
Huntington, is slated to begin this fall. Work may be implemented in phases over 
the coming years in order to limit disruptions to research programs and building 
occupants. 
 
HSPH/ Banner Signage: As a result of an updated branding effort, the HSPH will 
be seeking to replace current façade banners facing Huntington Avenue and the 
campus plaza, on the Kresge Building and the FXB Building. In addition, working 
with the Longwood Collective, the HSPH will be seeking to replace 8-10 existing 
streetlight banners situated along Huntington Avenue. This work is expected to 
occur in the fall of 2024. 
 
HMS/Goldenson Building Façade and Exterior Envelope 
Repairs/Restoration: The exterior restoration of Goldenson Hall at HMS will 
include masonry restoration, cast iron restoration, copper roofing and flashing, and 
window replacement. Design and details used for previous façade restoration 
projects at Building C, Gordon Hall, and the Tosteson Medical Education Center 
(TMEC) will be continued in this effort. An earlier proposal for the Goldenson 
project was reviewed and approved by the Boston Landmarks Commission in 2018. 
HMS anticipates returning to the Landmarks Commission for an updated 
determination later this year. Work is expected to begin in early 2025 and be 
completed by late 2025.

VI. POTENTIAL FUTURE PROJECTS 
 
As described in the 2018 IMP renewal, all three Harvard Longwood schools face ongoing challenges 
for how best to accommodate their changing programmatic needs and provide state-of-the-art 
teaching and research facilities within the confines of their aging buildings. The Kresge Building at 
HSPH was raised as one example of these challenges. 
 
Since that time, the COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath prompted new questions and 
considerations about how Harvard schools should best deploy their physical facilities in support of 
teaching, research, and scholarship. The emergence and expanded acceptance of hybrid work 
culture has created further opportunities to rethink office environments and potentially achieve 
greater efficiency in how space is used. 
 
The leadership of all three Harvard Longwood schools are currently collaborating to examine the 
campus holistically and explore how existing facilities might be reconfigured, repurposed, or 
redeveloped to better meet the evolving needs of all stakeholders within the larger campus 
community. If and when specific proposals emerge from these discussions, Harvard may seek to 
pursue an IMP amendment or a new IMP, as necessary, to support such proposals.

This Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) is being submitted by Harvard 
University (“Harvard”) to the Boston Planning and Development Agency (“BPDA”) in 
accordance with Section 80D-9(2) of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), for

2.0 Campus Context 
 
The Harvard Longwood Campus is located within Boston’s Longwood Medical and Academic 
Area (LMA) and consists of five parcels of land containing approximately 21 acres and 25 
buildings. A map of the Harvard Longwood Campus is included as Attachment A. 
 
Three of Harvard’s graduate and professional schools are based at the Harvard Longwood 
Campus: the Harvard Medical School (HMS), the Harvard School of Dental Medicine 
(HSDM), and the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health (HCSPH). Information on the 
mission and objectives of each of these schools is included in Section 1.4 of the original IMP. 
 
3.0 Status and History of the Harvard Longwood Campus IMP 
 
The Harvard Longwood IMP was approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) 
on February 27, 2003 and by the Boston Zoning Commission on March 26, 2003. The IMP 
described five proposed IMP projects, consisting of one new building (the Harvard School of 
Dental Medicine Research and Education Building, completed in 2004) and four additions to 
existing Harvard Medical School buildings. 
 
The First Amendment to the Harvard Longwood IMP (the “First IMP Amendment”) occurred 
in 2004 and described Harvard’s proposed use of an approximately 140,000 square-foot 
component of the Fenway Mixed-Use Project (now known as Trilogy) consisting of rental 
residential apartments for Harvard affiliates, rental residential apartments for income-
certified local residents, and associated parking rights. The First IMP Amendment was 
approved by the BRA on April 1, 2004 and by the Boston Zoning Commission on May 5, 2004. 
 
The Second Amendment to the Harvard Longwood IMP (the “Second IMP Amendment”) 
occurred in 2009-2010 and described Harvard’s plan to lease and use, for institutional office 
purposes, the former Mission School building at 90 Smith Street in the Mission Hill 
neighborhood, along with parking spaces in the adjacent surface parking lot. The Second IMP

5.0 Program Need and Project Description 
The proposed addition supports a shift in Harvard Medical School’s approach from the 
typically closed research model to one that is more collaborative and engaging with other 
disciplines, focused on discovery, and developing the therapeutic pipeline. It will provide 
program offices for the Biological Chemistry & Molecular Pharmacology Department and 
the Harvard Blavatnik Life Lab, and will also foster connections by providing community, 
meeting, collaborative, and gathering space. 
 
The project is located in the courtyard of Building C, one of the five original Shepley, Rutan, 
and Coolidge-designed buildings from 1906 facing the main Harvard Medical School 
Quadrangle. The site is bordered to the west by two modernist HMS buildings built in the 
1970s, Seeley G Mudd (SGM) and the Laboratory for Human Reproduction and 
Reproductive Biology (LHRRB). The project will enclose the courtyard surrounded by 
Building C, LHRRB, and SGM; provide office, meeting, and collaboration spaces; connect the 
three buildings at street level; provide an accessible entrance; create an improved entryway 
to the West Quad; and undertake associated site enhancements. The project continues a 
pattern of infilling building courtyards to capture program space while maintaining the

6.0 Zoning Code Requirements 
 
This IMPNF seeks to amend the Harvard Longwood Campus IMP in accordance with the 
provisions of Section 80D-9.2 of the Zoning Code (“Expedited Review for Certain Small 
Projects”). 
 
Criteria for Expedited Review: Section 80D-9.2(b) of the Zoning Code states that a Proposed 
Institutional Project shall qualify for an expedited IMP amendment procedure if the project 
does not meet the size thresholds for Large Project Review and: 
(i) the Proposed Institutional Project is an exempt project, as provided in subsection 2 
of Section 80D-2, and the Institution elects to make such project subject to the provisions of 
its Institutional Master Plan pursuant to subsection 5 of Section 80D-2; or 
(ii) the Proposed Institutional Project is not an exempt project, pursuant to Section 80D-2, 
and the project meets all of the following requirements: 
(1) the project is located within an Institutional District or Subdistrict or, if it is located 
outside an Institutional District or Subdistrict, the use category that most closely 
describes such project is designated in the underlying zoning as an allowed use; and 
(2) if the project is located outside an Institutional District or Subdistrict, its 
dimensions and parking and loading spaces meet all the requirements of the 
underlying zoning applicable to the use category that most closely describes the 
project; and 
(3) the project is not for one or more of the High Impact Subuses of an Institutional

Overview 
This Institutional Master Plan Project Notification Form/Project Notification Form (“IMPNF/PNF”) 
is being submitted by The President and Fellows of Harvard College (“Harvard” or the 
“Proponent”), on behalf of Harvard University Housing (“HUH”) and the American Repertory 
Theater at Harvard University (the “A.R.T.”), to the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”), 
doing business as Boston Planning & Development Agency (herein, the “BPDA” except when 
referring to activities prior to 2016). 
Through this IMPNF/PNF, Harvard is pleased to propose a mixed-use institutional project that will 
transform the property at 175 North Harvard Street in Allston (the “Project Site”) into a 
performing arts center that will be the new home for the A.R.T., and which will deliver much-
needed housing for Harvard affiliates (the “Project”). 
Under Article 80B of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), this submission will initiate 
Large Project Review of the Project. 
Under Article 80D of the Zoning Code, this submission will initiate the process for approval of a 
Sixth Amendment to Harvard’s Institutional Master Plan. Harvard’s Ten-Year Institutional Master 
Plan for the Allston Campus (also referred to as the “IMP Area”), approved in 2013 (as 
subsequently amended, herein referred to as the “IMP”), included seven new construction 
projects, including the proposed construction of a new housing building and a new basketball 
venue identified in the IMP as the “Mixed Use Facility & Basketball Venue,” located at 175 North 
Harvard Street. As discussed in more detail in Section 2.1, subsequent to the approval of the 
original 2013 IMP, Harvard decided to update and modernize the existing Lavietes Basketball 
Pavilion instead of building a new arena. 
As such, this IMPNF/PNF serves two purposes: 
1. The Project proposes changes to the Mixed-Use Facility & Basketball Venue project as it was 
described in the approved IMP. 
2. In order to accommodate the relocation of institutional uses from the existing 175 North 
Harvard Street building, the University proposes to add the existing building at 1120 Soldiers 
Field Road to the IMP Area and the IMP, and remove an institutional building at 1230 Soldiers 
Field Road from the IMP Area and the IMP. 
The locations of the Project Site, 1120 Soldiers Field Road, and 1230 Soldiers Field Road are all 
depicted on Figure 1-1, later in this chapter. Figure 1-2 shows the Project Site.

1.1.2 
Project Overview 
Understanding the importance of providing a variety of experiences in Allston to Harvard students 
and staff, as well as the community, and the need for a new home for the A.R.T., Harvard 
announced in 2019 that the A.R.T. would move to the Allston campus. As a mixed-use 
development, the new performance center building will be joined with a new housing building as 
contemplated in the IMP. 
The Project includes two components (each a “Project Component”): 
♦ Performance Center Component: An approximately 68,000 square foot (“sf”)1 building to 
be occupied by the A.R.T. with two theaters, rehearsal spaces, and building support and 
office space. 
♦ Affiliate Housing Component: An approximately 276,000 sf residential building with 
approximately 264 housing units for Harvard graduate students, faculty, staff, and their 
families, amenity space for building residents, and approximately 75 parking spaces in a 
below grade garage. 
The Project will also include site improvements along the streetscapes, activating and improving 
the pedestrian experience on the streets circling the Project Site and improving the edge along 
Smith Field, as well as new open space. 
American Repertory Theatre 
The American Repertory Theater at Harvard University is a leading force in American theater. The 
A.R.T. was founded in 1980 by Robert Brustein and seeks to expand the boundaries of theater by 
programming transformative theatrical experiences. The A.R.T.’s club theater, OBERON, has been 
recognized annually as a top performance venue in the Boston area, and has attracted national 
attention for its innovative programming and business models. 
As the professional theater on the campus of Harvard University, the A.R.T. is committed to 
playing a central role in interdisciplinary collaboration and creative exchange among a wide range 
of academic departments, institutions, students, and faculty members. The A.R.T. is engaged in a 
number of multi-year initiatives with partners at Harvard that explore some of the most pressing 
issues of our day, including collaborations with the Harvard University Center for the Environment 
to develop new work that addresses climate change and with the Healthy Buildings Program at 
the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health to develop a Roadmap for Recovery and Resilience 
for Theater that prioritizes a commitment to ethics, equity, and anti-racism as a guiding principle.

The A.R.T. also plays a central role in Harvard’s undergraduate Theater, Dance & Media 
concentration, teaching courses in directing, dramatic literature, acting, voice, design, and 
dramaturgy. Staff also mentor students in the Harvard Radcliffe Dramatic Club working at the 
Loeb Drama Center. 
Dedicated to making great theater accessible, the A.R.T. actively engages more than 5,000 
community members and local students annually in project-based partnerships, workshops, 
conversations with artists, and other enrichment activities both at the theater and across the 
Greater Boston area. 
Harvard University Housing Portfolio 
Harvard University Housing is a department of Harvard Campus Services, a multi-department 
organization within Harvard’s Central Administration providing a wide range of non-academic 
services to the Harvard community. HUH’s role is to support Harvard’s educational and research 
efforts by offering Harvard affiliates (graduate students, faculty, staff, and their families) a wide 
array of housing choices in Harvard-owned and managed properties. HUH offers community-
building activities to all HUH residents through the Graduate Commons Program (“GCP”), a unique 
interdisciplinary community-building program for all Harvard affiliates and their families living in 
HUH properties. 
The HUH portfolio of Harvard-owned affiliate housing consists of approximately 2,900 apartment 
units and approximately 120 dormitory rooms, located in Cambridge, Boston, and Somerville, of 
which almost 700 are located within Allston. This portfolio is exclusive of those beds/units 
operated by Harvard College and Harvard’s graduate and professional schools. The HUH portfolio 
is physically varied, with properties ranging from single family homes to 500-unit apartment 
complexes, and an apartment unit mix that includes studios through four-bedroom apartment 
units. Portfolio-wide turnover averages approximately 50% annually and demand typically 
exceeds supply on a four to one ratio. All full-time Harvard graduate students, faculty and staff 
are eligible to live with HUH and housing is typically allocated via an annual spring lottery.

Harvard has been filing Institutional Master Plans for its Allston campus since 1989. Most recently, 
Harvard’s IMP for its campus in Allston was approved by the BRA Board in October 2013 and by 
the Boston Zoning Commission in November 2013. 
Since that time, the City has approved four amendments to Harvard’s original IMP from 2013. In 
addition, a proposed Fifth Amendment is currently under review: 
1. The First Amendment described changes to Harvard’s Allston Science Complex, now referred 
to as the Science and Engineering Complex (“SEC”). This First Amendment and the revised SEC 
project were approved at the BPDA Board Meeting on April 14, 2016, and the Boston Zoning 
Commission on May 18, 2016 (effective on May 25, 2016).

PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
2.1 
Description of the Project in 2013 IMP 
The IMP included a project referred to as the “Mixed Use Facility & Basketball Venue” to be 
located at 175 North Harvard Street. As presented in the IMP, Harvard envisioned that the project 
would include demolition of the existing building at 175 North Harvard Street and the 
redevelopment of the site with a new project of between 270,000 sf and 340,000 sf that would 
include a basketball venue, with the balance of the site accommodating institutional/mixed uses. 
The new basketball venue was envisioned to be approximately 60,000 sf and would include 
approximately 3,000 seats, locker rooms, athletics offices, and concession areas. The remainder 
of the site was to be developed for a mixed‐use institutional development largely focused on 
institutional affiliate/graduate student housing. 
As presented in the IMP, the non‐basketball portion of the project was to include between 
approximately 200,000 and 250,000 sf of residential space and approximately 10,000‐30,000 sf of 
ground floor retail. 
Since the approval of the original 2013 IMP, and after further study, Harvard undertook a 
significant renovation to revitalize and improve the existing Lavietes Basketball Pavilion rather 
than building a new basketball facility at 175 North Harvard Street. The Lavietes Pavilion project 
provided the unique opportunity to improve support spaces and spectator amenities, and to 
renew mechanical and life safety systems of the building. While the uses of the building remained 
the same, the project updated, modernized, and relocated existing uses and included a small 
addition at the front of the building. The renovation of the Lavietes Pavilion was completed prior 
to the start of the 2017-2018 basketball season. 
In mid‐2019, Harvard announced its intention to develop a new home in Allston for the American 
Repertory Theater in order to create a state‐of‐the‐art community, research and performance 
center in Allston where it could fulfill its mission to expand the boundaries of theater through 
innovation explored in collaboration with the tech sector, local businesses, non-profits, and other 
cultural partners. A.R.T.’s approach to research is related to its relationship to a research 
university and rooted in its value of inquiry. Consistent with earlier planning, the remainder of the 
site will be developed with a housing component for Harvard affiliates. 
2.2 
Purpose and Need 
The needed improvements to and expansion of the A.R.T.’s theater facilities, and the construction 
of Harvard-affiliate housing, represent one of the Harvard’s strategic building blocks focused on 
implementing changes and growth for Harvard to ensure its vitality and its future. The proposed 
Project described in this chapter will unite updated facilities with existing academic and 
administrative facilities and will balance the benefit of a comprehensive and predictable plan with 
the long-term flexibility needed by a dynamic, rapidly evolving academic enterprise. The two 
Project Components included in this filing include:

Performance Center 
Since its founding, the A.R.T. has been in residence at the Loeb Drama Center, a building originally 
constructed for undergraduate use in 1960, on Brattle Street in Cambridge. The Loeb Drama 
Center is a Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences building. Though it was a state-of-the-art building 
when it was designed, it currently lacks access for patrons and artists and no longer meets the 
standards of excellence for theater practice, and by extension, the overall vision for the future of 
the A.R.T. 
Housing 
Although Harvard has an extensive and diverse housing portfolio, the need for housing for 
Harvard affiliates – graduate students, faculty, staff, and their families – continues to exceed 
demand. Despite approximately 50% annual turnover, the HUH portfolio-wide occupancy is 
consistently at or near 100%. During the annual spring housing lottery, the number of applicants 
is typically four times that of available units. Given the robust demand, Harvard seeks to provide 
affiliate housing that offers a diverse mix of unit types that supports the varied needs of individual 
affiliates, groups of affiliates, and families. In addition, Harvard seeks to offer opportunity to 
expand the GCP, furthering support for Harvard initiatives and programmatic offerings in Allston.

2.3.2.1 
Performance Center Component 
The mission of the Performance Center Component is to create a new center for research and 
performance that will allow the A.R.T. to continue to expand the boundaries of theater and 
reaffirm the theater as a vital public space. Based on the model of a teaching hospital, it will 
combine student learning and professional practice. 
The Performance Center Component will be located on the eastern side of the Project Site along 
North Harvard Street. The proposed program involves the construction of an approximately 
68,000 sf theater building consisting of two flexible performance spaces including a large 
auditorium to the west and smaller theater to the east, lobby space that extends into the 
Performance Yard, as well as rehearsal and classroom and other education spaces, ticket sales, 
food and beverage sales, scenic assembly and costume shops, dressing rooms, additional support 
spaces, and administrative offices for the A.R.T. staff. The west stage will provide flexibility to 
accommodate up to approximately 700 seated patrons or up to approximately 1,000 standing 
patrons, and the east stage will have the flexibility for up to approximately 300 seated patrons or 
up to approximately 400 standing patrons. The Performance Center Component will provide bike 
parking for approximately 32 bicycles outside of the building and another approximately 42 
bicycles inside a storage space in the building, entered off Ivy Lane. 
The main entrance will be on North Harvard Street with accessible sloped walkways that will 
connect the entrance to the sidewalk (the building will be raised for resiliency purposes). On the 
northeast corner will be the Performance Yard, an outdoor room that can be used for a variety of 
functions throughout the year. The south side of the building will include a secondary entry as 
well as the loading and trash area. 
The A.R.T. seeks to expand the boundaries of theater by programming events that immerse 
audiences in transformative theatrical experiences. The Performance Center Component is 
anticipated to provide a highly flexible building that would be suitable for modification as theater 
production evolves over the coming decades. 
The Performance Center Component will create a state-of-the-art theater that fosters innovation 
in programming and pedagogy. The facility will build upon Allston’s broad and longstanding 
commitment to the arts, and deepen the theater’s impact on the cognitive life of Harvard. The 
Project will provide a space that will accommodate activities that engage and serve as a gateway 
for the Allston community.
