2.3.2.2 
Affiliate Housing Component 
The Affiliate Housing Component will join a tradition of Harvard housing distinctive for its quality 
and permanence. The Affiliate Housing Component, which will provide much-needed residential 
space for Harvard graduate students, faculty, staff, and their families will complement a growing 
cultural, institutional and residential campus interfacing with the existing Allston neighborhood 
to contribute to a thriving community. 
The Affiliate Housing Component will provide much‐needed new housing for graduate students, 
faculty, staff, and their families in a new building that promotes sustainability and healthy living. 
The Affiliate Housing Component will pursue Living Building Challenge Core, along with of Living 
Building Challenge Materials Petal accreditation, the intent of which is to foster a materials 
economy that is non‐toxic, ecologically restorative, transparent, and socially equitable. Passive 
House certification will also be pursued, resulting in a high‐performance building envelope that 
seeks to minimize energy consumption. The building will be connected to the Harvard District 
Energy Facility for optimized energy efficiency. In addition, the Affiliate Housing Component will 
be designed to meet LEED Gold certification requirements and will feature rooftop photovoltaics 
and will have selective areas of green roof for stormwater attenuation and reduced heat-island 
effect. 
The necessary service functions including loading dock and waste management area will be 
located on the southern side of the building at Ivy Lane between the package room and the 
entrance to the below-grade, approximately 75 space parking garage. In addition to 
approximately 60 bicycle spaces inside the building, a freestanding, at grade, daylit bike pavilion 
consistent with BTD guidelines with spaces for up to 180 bikes will be located at the southern end 
of the residential courtyard and will hold the street wall along Ivy Lane. 
To foster a sense of community and support, formal and casual meeting areas will be accessible 
from multiple points along common paths of travel within the Project Site and Affiliate Housing 
Component. Resident amenity areas to support Harvard’s GCP will be primarily aggregated on the 
ground floor and second floor, and include wellness and fitness rooms; study, recreation, and 
social leisure lounges; and adaptable meeting spaces. Larger meeting areas will take advantage 
of adjacency to the courtyard to permit larger indoor/outdoor gatherings of up to approximately 
300 of the building’s residents and their guests with curated programming coordinated by GCP. 
The faculty director’s suite on the twelfth floor will have direct access to the landscaped rooftop. 
From the exterior, the thirteenth floor will feature a “Beacon Effect”, a spatial reference point 
intended to beckon the community to Barry’s Corner. The thirteenth and fourteenth floors include 
additional duplex units with window detailing accentuating the high point of the Project.

1120 Soldiers Field Road and 1230 Soldiers Field Road 
The IMPNF also seeks to amend the IMP to reflect changes in two Harvard-owned properties. In 
order to accommodate the relocation of institutional uses from the existing 175 North Harvard 
Street building, Harvard proposes to add the existing building at 1120 Soldiers Field Road to the 
IMP Area. The University also proposes to remove an institutional building at 1230 Soldiers Field 
Road from the IMP Area. 
1120 Soldiers Field Road 
The building at 1120 Soldiers Field Road is a one-story office building of approximately 8,800 sf. It 
was constructed in 1955 and was acquired by Harvard in 1993. The building has been used for 
non-institutional uses; past uses have included a Ground Round Restaurant and a television studio 
for PAX TV, and currently a portion of the building is occupied by offices of Head of the Charles 
Regatta, Inc. 
As part of this IMP Amendment process, Harvard proposes to add the building to the IMP Area 
and the IMP, and utilize a portion of it for College and University uses, including athletic program 
uses. Harvard plans to relocate the operations of the Harvard Ski team to an approximately 2,800 
sf space within the building. The Ski team would use its portion of the building for office space for 
coaches, meeting space, ski preparation and maintenance, and lockers and other storage areas. 
Student athletes and the coaching staff will visit the building consistent with their current use at 
175 North Harvard Street. While most will walk or bike to the facility, this is the location where 
team vans heading to area mountains for races will depart during winter months. 
1230 Soldiers Field Road 
The building at 1230 Soldiers Field Road is a one-story office building of approximately 16,000 sf. 
It was constructed in 1960 and was acquired by Harvard and added to Harvard’s IMP in 2002. 
There are currently two commercial tenants in the building: stemexpress and Amplify Fitness. As 
part of the zoning approvals for these tenants, Harvard agreed to remove the building from the 
Harvard IMP Area.

3.1.12 
Transit Capacity Analysis 
Understanding the impact that Project Site-generated transit trips will have on existing and future 
MBTA public transportation services, Harvard shuttle services, and potential future other private 
shuttle services will help determine current and future capacity constraints and identify 
opportunities for potential transit improvements. 
3.1.12.1 
Transit Analysis Scenarios 
Transit capacity will be analyzed under Fall 2022 conditions (the most recent ridership data that 
is anticipated to be available for MBTA buses and Harvard shuttles at the time the analysis is 
completed), and in 2030 under both a No-Build and a Build Condition. To examine future 
scenarios, the existing Fall 2022 ridership may be expanded with an annual growth rate (derived 
from the City’s population projections) and new trips generated by other projects in the area, and 
by the Project in the Build condition, will be added and distributed according to relevant 
transportation impact studies. This methodology will be confirmed with the City of Boston and be 
based on current methodology practices accepted by the MBTA at the time it is completed. 
3.1.12.2 
Transit Analysis Method 
The transit analysis in the DPIR will examine the impact of Project trips (transit riders) assigned to 
the MBTA local bus and Harvard shuttle services identified earlier in the chapter, that provide 
service within one-half mile of the Project Site. Baseline ridership data will be derived from the 
most recently available data sets (anticipated to be Fall 2022) at the time the analysis is 
completed. 
The transit capacity analyses will be performed in a manner consistent with MassDOT Office of 
Performance Management and Innovation methods that are used to evaluate MBTA service and 
will be applied in a similar manner to evaluate the Harvard shuttle service. The capacity analysis 
includes a comparison of the expected demand for transit to the existing and planned capacity of 
the service. The capacity threshold of the bus routes is based on the MBTA’s Service Delivery

175 North Harvard Street 
Policy, which is based on the design of the vehicle, the number of riders aboard, and the time 
period during the service day. During peak periods, the passenger comfort standard has a higher 
capacity threshold than off-peak periods. Average peak passenger loads are compared against the 
policy capacity. 
For each route and each direction, the approximate time buses/shuttles arrive at the Project Site 
will be computed by adding running time to the start time of each trip. Travel time applied will be 
uniform across all trips on a given route in the same direction during service periods. The 
passenger load will be determined for each bus/shuttle trip as buses/shuttles reach the first stop 
serving the Project Site. 
Ridership demand by the Project will be assigned by bus/shuttle route and direction. The 
distribution patterns will mirror those applied in the traffic study, and route assignment will be 
informed service frequency, anticipated travel time (factoring in the number of stops between 
origin and destination), and fee (Harvard shuttles are free to Harvard affiliates). The daily transit 
trips generated by the Project are distributed by time of day to each of the scheduled bus/shuttle 
trips, generally matching the existing ridership patterns observed on the area routes and 
considering future route changes by the Bus Network Redesign. Per MBTA’s analysis method, the 
Project-generated transit trips are assumed to travel via the peak load point for each analysis 
segment: the connection between the Project Site and the next rapid transit station or end/start-
of-line. The peak passenger load (which includes future growth in riders added to the existing 
levels, plus the Project-generated transit riders) for each trip is compared against the policy 
capacity for the bus service. 
3.1.13 
Bicycle Level of Traffic Stress Analysis 
A bicycle level of comfort study will be conducted to assess area bicycle infrastructure conditions 
and the effectiveness of significant improvements that are slated for the area roadways. 
3.1.13.1 
Bicycle Level of Traffic Stress Methodology 
Bicyclists have varying levels of comfort when traveling on/along streets depending on the type 
of bicycle facility provided, vehicle volumes, traffic speed, bicyclist proximity to adjacent vehicle 
traffic and parked cars, and potential conflicts with turning, stopping, and idling cars, trucks, and 
buses. The City of Boston has developed a Bicycle Level of Traffic Stress (“BLTS”) methodology, 
which is an indication of how stressful a certain facility is for a cyclist, on a scale from 1 to 4. BLTS 
1 indicates the most favorable, lowest-stress conditions, while BLTS 4 indicates the least 
favorable, highest-stress conditions. The BLTS analysis will be conducted consistent with the City’s 
methodology.

The Project Site is surrounded by a mix of buildings and open areas, including Smith Field to the

The exterior materials for the Project have not been finalized. Building exteriors are expected to 
be constructed of a mixture of modern and traditional building materials that include brick, stone, 
pre-cast concrete, and glass. At this time, reflective glass is not anticipated for the Project. The 
Project will be designed so as not to present an adverse safety impact on Project area traffic as a

Air Quality 
Potential long-term air quality impacts can be generated by the Project’s mechanical equipment, 
and pollutant emissions from vehicular traffic generated by the development of the Project. 
Harvard has an extensive TDM program to minimize vehicle trips, and the minimal new parking is 
anticipated to encourage alternative modes of transportation. 
Any new stationary sources will be reviewed by the Massachusetts Department of Environmental 
Protection (“MassDEP”) during permitting under the Environmental Results Program, if required. 
It is expected that all stationary sources will be small, and any impacts from stationary sources 
would be minimal. 
Short-term air quality impacts from fugitive dust may be expected during the demolition and early 
phases of construction and from site preparation activities. Plans for controlling dust during 
construction will include wetting during periods of high wind and careful removal of debris by 
covered trucks. The construction contracts will provide for a number of strictly enforced measures 
to be utilized by contractors to reduce emissions and minimize impacts. These are expected to 
include: 
♦ Using wetting agents where needed on a scheduled basis; 
♦ Using covered trucks; 
♦ Minimizing exposed storage debris on-site; 
♦ Monitoring actual construction practices to ensure that unnecessary transfers and 
mechanical disturbances of loose materials are minimized; 
♦ Locating aggregate storage piles away from areas having the greatest pedestrian activity 
where and when possible; and 
♦ Periodic cleaning of streets and sidewalks to minimize dust accumulations.

Sustainability 
Sustainable design is a character defining element of the overall development project. The design 
of the Project incorporates measures to reduce energy use, takes advantage of Harvard’s District 
Energy Facility, and seek to further Harvard’s goal to be fossil fuel neutral by 2026 and fossil fuel 
free by 2050. Living Building Challenge Core, certification enacted by the International Living 
Future Institute (“ILFI”), is a philosophy, advocacy tool and certification program that promotes 
the measurement of sustainability in the built environment and will be pursued for each of the 
two Project Components. In addition, each Component will be designed to meet LEED certification 
at the Gold level. This section provides an overview of the proposed design measures and the 
approach to achieve LEED certification. The LEED scorecards for each Project Component are 
included at the end of this section. 
3.14.1 
Performance Center Component 
3.14.1.1 
Overview 
The Performance Center Component design will incorporate several measures to reduce carbon 
emissions, including a high-efficiency building envelope, connection to Harvard’s District Energy 
Facility which provides efficient heating, cooling, and electricity, a proposed PV array, and passive-
assisted mechanical ventilation (described in more detail below). In addition, the Performance

Center team seeks to reduce the entire life cycle carbon footprint of building, operating, and 
eventually decommissioning through low-carbon design strategies. The design is evaluating the 
use of existing building materials, hybrid timber-steel structure, timber procurement from 
sustainable forestry practices, and concrete mix-design optimization. 
Passive-Assisted Mechanical Ventilation 
The building will utilize stack ventilation for natural ventilation. Stack ventilation, or "buoyancy-
driven ventilation," moves air using temperature and height differences between openings. 
During natural ventilation mode, cool air will enter the building from intakes to the underfloor 
plenum. Then, the air will enter through displacement ventilation supply grills to the west stage, 
and east stage. The air will absorb heat in the room, rise when it is heated, then leave the space 
through the upper plenum and roof openings. This process will create a partial vacuum that pulls 
more air in through the air intake. Stack ventilation does not rely on wind, which can be highly 
unpredictable, to move air. Mechanical ventilation and conditioning will be used when conditions 
for natural ventilation are not suitable. 
3.14.1.2

As required under Article 37 of the Zoning Code, projects that are subject to Article 80B, Large 
Project Review, shall be LEED certifiable. The LEED rating system tracks the sustainable features 
of the Project by achieving points in the following categories: Integrative Process; Location and 
Transportation; Sustainable Sites; Water Efficiency; Energy and Atmosphere; Materials and 
Resources; Indoor Environmental Quality; Innovation; and Regional Priority Credits. 
The Performance Center Component is being designed to achieve the Harvard Green Building 
Standard (“HGBS”) and will pursue the following certifications: LEED Gold Certification using the 
LEED for New Construction v4/v4.1 rating system and Living Building Challenge (“LBC”) Core

programs, and communication has commenced with the certification bodies. 
It is important to note that certification is viewed as the result of good design, and the intent is to 
ensure that sustainability strategies add value to the design via improved performance, better 
occupant health, and high-quality design - not simply box checking. The sustainable design 
strategies reflect the environmental and social values of the A.R.T. and demonstrate Harvard’s 
ethos of sustainability and goal to be fossil fuel neutral by 2026 and fossil fuel free by 2050. 
Regenerative Design is an overarching theme for sustainability at the Performance Center.

3.16 
Urban Design and Landscape Architecture 
3.16.1 
Urban Design 
Building on a tradition of arts, music and performance, Allston, and specifically Barry’s Corner, is 
an increasingly dynamic center for publicly oriented cultural activities. The area now includes Ed 
Portal, Artlab, iLab, the Harvard Ceramics Program, Zone 3, Artisan's Asylum and Allston Branch 
Public Library. In addition, a growing number of actively programmed public spaces such as Smith 
Field and Playground, The Grove, and Ray Mellone Park are attracting diverse users, families, and 
students to the neighborhood. Additional housing and retail spaces also create activities for 
students and the public, including Soldiers Field Park, One Western, and Continuum. 
The Project dovetails with the growth in numbers and diversity of the area, bringing new residents 
and attracting theatergoers from around the city and the world. Programmatically and materially, 
the Project evokes Allston’s historically urban and industrial character with activated street 
frontage and dense residential use. The two Project Components will have characteristics unique 
to their respective uses, while a common palette of glass and brick brings cohesion to the block. 
Informed by masonry loft building construction, painted masonry facades of the Performance 
Center building will continue a tradition of adaptation and re-use within Allston. The Housing 
building will include brick coursework and details that will break down the massing into 
discernable residential-unit scale. Soldier-coursed lintels, punched windows, robust piers and 
columns will distinguish the Housing facade while maintaining a material consistency with the 
Performance Center. Both buildings will employ storefront glass and iron-spot brick to provide a 
continuous ground-floor datum from building to building, from which the Performance Center’s 
yard emerges to draw visitors around and into this new neighborhood destination. A bike pavilion 
located at the residential courtyard along Ivy Lane will create a linear extension of the 
Performance Center’s site fence, providing continuity of the street wall of the two buildings. See 
Figure 3-21 at the end of this section for a diagram of Ivy Lane’s streetwall. Housing’s graduate 
commons storefronts, visually transparent, generous residential lobby entries facing McCurdy 
Track, Smith Field and the residential courtyard, and townhouses fronting Smith Field will be 
scaled appropriately for street activation while fostering a sense of local community. Figures 3-22 
to 3-36 at the end of this section include views and sections of the Project.

Rising from Barry’s Corner toward McCurdy Track and culminating with a beacon effect at its 
pinnacle, the Project reads clearly as an extension of Allston’s history of industriousness, urban 
vitality and density. In contrast with the more uniform parapets of Continuum, the Housing 
building massing will increase in height by two-story increments from the established Allston 
neighborhood to the south, transitioning in scale in relation to the stadium to the north. 
The Project Site provides a variety of outdoor places to gather, converse, and relax outdoors, and 
promotes a diversity of use. Along the north side of the Project Site, the Project will include an 
outdoor, urban edge bookended by the Performance Yard to the east and residential lobby and 
GCP spaces to the west, while a more contemplative courtyard primarily designed for use by 
Affiliate Housing residents occupies the center of the block. By working in concert, both Project 
Components create an activated site which amplifies the evolving urban ecosystem of activities 
in Allston. 
3.16.2 
Landscape Architecture 
The Unified Block 
The Project Site lies at the intersection of two main thoroughfares in Allston: North Harvard 
Street, which offers a north-south connection to Harvard’s Cambridge campus, and the future 
Academic Way, an east-west connection between Smith Playground to the planned Harvard ERC 
Greenway. 
Three primary landscape spaces are proposed to support the Project: a residential courtyard that 
is designed for residents but open for public access will occupy the space between the two 
buildings; the Performance Yard, envisioned as a flexible outdoor space associated with the lobby 
of the Performance Center, and the surrounding streetscape that will wrap the perimeter of the 
block. 
Along with the architectural elements shared between the two buildings, the streetscape 
dimensions and materials will help unite the two Project Components within the block, and to the 
larger Allston community. Street trees, furnishing zones, sidewalks, and exterior light fixtures will 
conform to the standards of the Design Guidelines described in Section 3.4 of the IMP. A “shared 
porch” will offer a direct route between the yard and the lobby of the Housing building on the 
north side of the block, further integrating the Project Components. 
Regenerative design principles guide the approach to the landscape design with the careful 
incorporation of stormwater infiltration and storage, biophilic walls, and the use of varied native 
plantings to encourage biodiversity. This approach extends to the landscaping of the roof 
featuring sedum roofs, PV panels, and opportunities for growing food.

Performance Center Component Landscape 
The frontage zone along North Harvard Street is designed to welcome visitors and the Allston 
community into the building. A proposed small herb garden at the corner of Ivy Lane will enliven 
a newly integrated bus stop. A long run of stairs and sloped walks will ease travel into the main 
lobby and the yard. The Performance Yard is envisioned as a flexible outdoor room with a simple 
floor of permeable brick pavers and bi-fold shutters, offering the Performance Center maximum 
flexibility in programming and regulating the space for a variety of social, artistic and community 
events throughout the year. 
Affiliate Housing Component Landscape 
Along South Campus Drive, seat walls and plantings will be used to separate the public sidewalk 
from an accessible-path walkway leading to a series of townhomes within the Affiliate Housing 
Component. At Ivy Lane, a bike pavilion is subtly inserted into the topography as a bounding 
element between the Project Components to hold the Ivy Lane streetwall and create a residential 
courtyard. This layered courtyard landscape between the Project Components will soften 
elevational differences to tie the Project Components together. At a higher elevation to the west 
within the courtyard, a residential terrace will be constructed over the parking garage and feature 
a central lawn for gathering and events, with smaller outdoor spaces connected to building 
entrances and amenity rooms which allow activities to spill out from interior to exterior. As this 
terrace is slightly elevated from the lower area towards the theater, gentle grade transitions 
including sloped walks and seat steps will soften the topographic changes down towards the 
theater to the east. The subtle grade changes and planted landscape together create a smooth, 
barrier-free transition from street elevation to the ground floor which has been raised for 
resiliency. 
The areas within the courtyard will connect the public sidewalks to the residential terrace through 
a series of outdoor spaces of varied experiences. These include an entry gateway, a terraced 
hangout space, a walk-through lush vegetation, a porch with swing benches and stone block 
seating, and access to the bike pavilion with a bike workstation beyond. Layers of vegetation 
including canopy trees, ornamental trees, shrubs, grasses and other understory planting will 
create a diverse and desirable landscape for residents to be immersed in.

3.17.1.1 
Sewer Infrastructure 
There is an existing Boston Water and Sewer Commission (“BWSC”) dedicated sewer main located 
in North Harvard Street. The main is an 18-inch line which increases to 24-inch at a manhole in 
the intersection of North Harvard Street and Ivy Lane. The main flows in a southwesterly direction 
down North Harvard Street. 
Various sewer services for the existing Continuum Building discharge to a 10-inch private sewer 
line in Ivy Lane which transitions to a 12-inch private sewer line midway down Ivy Lane. This sewer 
line flows southeasterly towards North Harvard Street. The Continuum Building is the only 
building discharging sewage to Ivy Lane currently. There is an existing 8-inch sewer stub near the 
intersection of Ivy Lane and North Harvard Street which reaches up north towards the Project Site 
and connects to the 12-inch line in Ivy Lane. Sewer flow from the 12-inch line in Ivy Lane then 
flows east where it connects to the previously mentioned BWSC 24-inch sewer main in North 
Harvard Street. 
There is a 30-inch MWRA sewer line which flows northeast in an easement just to the west of 
South Campus Drive which connects to the Charles Relief Sewer line. 
There is also an existing 6-inch sewer line on the Project Site which runs southeast along the 
existing 175 North Harvard Street building. This 6-inch line connects to the previously mentioned 
18-inch BWSC sewer main in North Harvard Street. 
The existing sewer system is illustrated in Figures 3-37 and 3-38.

3.17.2.1 
Water Infrastructure 
Water for the Project Site will be provided by the BWSC. There are four water systems within the 
City, and these provide service to portions of the City based on ground surface elevation. The four 
systems are Southern Low (commonly known as low service and abbreviated SL), Southern High 
(commonly known as high service and abbreviated SH), Northern Low, and Southern Extra-High

There is an existing BWSC water main in North Harvard Street that is a 12-inch cement lined

North Harvard Street. The existing water system is illustrated in Figure 3-39.

consumption, system losses and other usages to estimate an average daily water demand. The 
Project’s total estimated domestic water demand is 64,506 GPD. The water for the Project will be 
supplied by the private water line in Ivy Lane. 
The existing building at the Project Site has a BWSC water account (1295021). The historical water 
use for the service to the existing buildings are estimated to be between 230 gpd and 18,840 GPD 
(7,690 average GPD). This estimate is based on the water meter billing history provided by BWSC 
for the existing account located at the Project Site from September 2020 to October 2021.

Stormwater 
There is an existing 18-inch BWSC drain line in North Harvard Street which flows northeast. Just 
before the intersection of North Harvard Street and South Campus Drive, the 18-inch line 
becomes a 24-inch line. 
There are existing private 12-inch lines in Ivy Lane which direct water from catch basins in Ivy Lane 
as well as roof drainage from the building on the south side of Ivy Lane to an underground 
infiltration system in Ivy Lane. Flow leaving this system flows southeast where it connects to the 
previously mentioned BWSC 18-inch line in North Harvard Street. 
On South Campus Drive near the northeast corner of the Project Site, there are a series of private 
12-inch and 15-inch drain lines which direct flow to an underground infiltration system in South 
Campus Drive. Overflow travels east in a private 18-inch pipe where it connects to the BWSC 
drainage main in North Harvard Street. 
Stormwater at the Project Site currently travels via over land flow to various catch basins and area 
drains around the existing site. There is a private 15-inch line on the Project Site which picks up 
the various site drainage and the roof drainage. This 15-inch line flows southeast where it 
connects to the previously mentioned BWSC drainage line in North Harvard Street, near the 
location where it increases in size from 18-inches to 24-inches. The existing BWSC and private 
storm drain system is illustrated in Figures 3-37 and 3-38. 
3.17.3.1 
Proposed Project Stormwater Management 
The Project is expected to result in an increase in impervious areas. The Project will meet or 
reduce the existing peak rates of stormwater discharge from the Project Site and promote 
stormwater recharge.

The Project will provide stormwater storage for 1.25 inches of runoff from the impervious site. 
Different approaches to stormwater recharge will be assessed. It is anticipated that subsurface 
stormwater recharge systems will work to passively infiltrate runoff into the ground with a gravity 
system in conjunction with a green roof and porous pavers. The underground recharge systems, 
green roof, and any required site closed drainage systems will be designed so that there will be 
no increase in the peak rate of stormwater discharge from the Project Site in the developed 
condition compared to the existing condition.

service connections, and assessment of Project demands and system capacity.

Water Quality Impact 
It is not anticipated that the Project will affect the water quality of nearby water bodies. Erosion

ARTICLE 80 – ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST 
A Requirement of the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) 
Article 80 Development Review Process 
 
The Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities works to reduce architectural barriers that impact accessibility in 
Boston’s built environment. This Checklist is intended to ensure that accessibility is planned at the beginning of projects, 
rather than after a design is completed. It aims to ensure that projects not only meet minimum MAAB/ ADA requirements, 
but that they create a built environment which provides equitable experiences for all people, regardless of age or ability. 
 
All BPDA Small or Large Project Review, including Institutional Master Plan modifications, must complete this Checklist to 
provide specific detail and data on accessibility. An updated Checklist is required if any project plans change significantly. 
 
For more information on compliance requirements, best practices, and creating ideal designs for accessibility throughout 
Boston's built environment, proponents are strongly encouraged to meet with Disability Commission staff prior to filing.

Glossary of Terms: 
 
1. 
Accessible Route – A continuous and unobstructed path of travel that meets or exceeds the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 20 
2. 
Accessible Guestrooms – Guestrooms with additional floor space, that meet or exceed the dimensional requirements set forth 
by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 8.4 
3. 
Age-Friendly – Implementing structures, settings and polices that allow people to age with dignity and respect in their homes 
and communities 
4. 
Housing – Group 1 Units – Residential Units that contain features which can be modified without structural change to meet the 
specific functional needs of an occupant with a disability, per MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.3 
5. 
Housing – Group 2 Units – Residential units with additional floor space that meet or exceed the dimensional and inclusionary 
requirements set forth by MAAB 521 CMR: Section 9.4 
6. 
Ideal Design for Accessibility – Design which meets, as well as exceeds, compliance with AAB/ ADA building code requirements 
7. 
Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) – Program run by the BPDA that preserves access to affordable housing opportunities in 
the City. For more information visit: http:/ / www.bostonplans.org/ housing/ overview 
8. 
Public Improvement Commission (PIC) – The regulatory body in charge of managing the public right of way in Boston. For more 
information visit: https:/ / www.boston.gov/ pic 
9. 
Social Equity LEED Credit – Pilot LEED credit for projects that engage neighborhood residents and provide community 
benefits, particularly for persons with disabilities

QUESTIONNAIRE 
The City of Boston is working to cultivate a broadband ecosystem that serves the current 
and future connectivity needs of residents, businesses, and institutions.  The real estate 
development process offers a unique opportunity to create a building stock in Boston that 
enables this vision.  In partnership with the development community, the Boston Planning 
and Development Authority and the City of Boston will begin to leverage this opportunity 
by adding a broadband readiness component to the Article 80 Design Review.  This 
component will take the form of a set of questions to be completed as part of the Project 
Notification Form.  Thoughtful integration of  future-looking broadband practices into this 
process will contribute to progress towards the following goals:
1. Enable an environment of competition and choice that results in all residents and
businesses having a choice of 2 or more wireline or fixed wireless high-speed Internet
providers
2. Create a built environment that is responsive to new and emerging connectivity
technologies
3. Minimize disruption to the public right of way during and after construction of the
building

The information that is shared through the Broadband Ready Buildings Questionnaire will 
help BPDA and the City understand how developers currently integrate 
telecommunications planning in their work and how this integration can be most 
responsive to a changing technological landscape.  
Upon submission of this online form, a PDF of the responses provided will be sent to the 
email address of the individual entered as Project Contact.  Please include the PDF in the 
Project Notification Form packet submitted to BPDA.
 If necessary, you may edit form responses prior to final submission. A link to edit the 
form will be generated upon submission.
Learn more about the Broadband Ready Buildings Questionnaire at the link below:
http://www.bostonplans.org/projects/development-review/article-80-design-review-
broadband-ready-buildings

______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) Board 
(1) approve a two-year renewal of the 2013 Institutional Master Plan 
for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (the “Harvard IMP”) 
pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, Section 80D-8, and 
Section 51-29(6) of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) and (2) 
authorize the Director to take all actions and execute all documents 
deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director in connection with 
such renewal of the Harvard IMP. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The 2013 Institutional Master Plan for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (the 
“Harvard IMP”) was approved by the BRA Board in October 2013 and by the Boston 
Zoning Commission in November 2013. The BRA Board approved five amendments 
to the Harvard IMP; the First Amendment in 2016; the Second, Third, and Fourth 
Amendments in 2017; and the Fifth Amendment on December 15, 2022. The BRA 
Board approved a four-year renewal of the original 2013 Institutional Master Plan in 
December 2017. 
 The term of the 2017 renewal of the Harvard IMP runs until

March 20, 2023 pursuant to Chapter 53 of the Acts of 2020, which tolled the 
expiration date of local permits and approvals during the Covid State of Emergency. 
 
On September 8, 2022, Harvard submitted an IMPNF for the Fifth IMP Amendment 
(the “IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment”), for the 92 Seattle Street Project. The IMPNF 
for Fifth IMP Amendment also included a request for the renewal of the Harvard 
IMP (the “Renewal Request”) pursuant to Section 51-29(6) of the Code, which 
provides that colleges and universities in Allston/Brighton are required to renew 
their Institutional Master Plans every four years. The Renewal Request proposes no 
new Proposed Institutional Projects; no changes to the Harvard IMP that would 
constitute a change in the use, dimensional, parking, or loading elements of the 
Harvard IMP; and no significantly greater impacts would result from continued 
implementation of the approved Harvard IMP than were originally projected. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 
The Renewal Request is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review, and qualified 
for a waiver of further review in accordance with Section 80D5.2(e) and 80D-6 in 
that (i) the Renewal Request proposes no new Proposed Institutional Projects; (ii) 
no changes to the Harvard IMP are proposed that would constitute a change in the 
use, dimensional, parking, or loading elements of the Harvard IMP; and (iii) no 
significantly greater impacts would result from continued implementation of the 
approved Harvard IMP than were originally projected. The Renewal Request seeks 
approval of the renewed Harvard IMP for a period of two years. Harvard intends to 
start the process of preparing a new Institutional Master Plan pursuant to Section 
80D-8 of the Code in 2023. 
 
The IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment, which included the Renewal Request, was 
filed on September 8, 2022, initiating a 30-day comment period. Harvard presented 
the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment to the Harvard-Allston Task Force on 
September 22, 2022. The BPDA approved the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment on 
December 15, 2022, with the Renewal Request to be considered separately prior to 
the expiration of the previous renewal. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA Board authorize 
the Director to (1) approve a two-year renewal of the 2013 Institutional Master Plan 
for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (the “Harvard IMP”) pursuant to Section

Zoning Code (the “Code”) and (2) authorize the Director to take all actions and 
execute all documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director in 
connection with such renewal of the Harvard IMP. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That in connection with the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
for the Fifth Amendment to the 2013 Institutional Master Plan for 
Harvard University’s Campus in Allston, filed by Harvard University on 
September 8, 2022, and after consideration of the request included 
therein (the “Renewal Request”) for the two-year renewal of the 2013 
Institutional Master Plan for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (as 
so renewed, the “Harvard IMP”) the BRA hereby find that (1) the 
Harvard IMP conforms to the provisions of Article 80D of the Code; (2) 
the Harvard IMP conforms to the general plan for the City of Boston as 
a whole; and (c) on balance, nothing in the Harvard IMP will be 
injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public 
welfare, weighing all the benefits and burdens; and 
 
VOTED: 
That the BRA waives further review of the Renewal Request pursuant 
to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the Code 
and approves the Harvard IMP for a period of two (2) years from the 
date of approval of this renewal vote by the BRA, that is January 19, 
2025; and 
 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute any and all 
documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director in 
connection with the renewal of the Harvard IMP.

1. Introduction

9
1.1. Overview
This Institutional Master Plan Notification Form ("IMPNF") is being submitted by the 
President and Fellows of Harvard College ("Harvard" or "the University") to present the 
proposed development plans to be included in the next ten-year Institutional Master Plan 
("IMP") for Harvard University's campus in Allston, in accordance with Section 80D-5 of 
the Boston Zoning Code (the "Zoning Code"). In total, Harvard owns approximately 358 
acres of land in Allston and the land area subject to the IMP consists of approximately 184 
acres used by Harvard for institutional purposes. 
The Allston campus is currently guided by an Institutional Master Plan approved by the 
Boston Planning & Development Agency (''BPDA'') in 2013 (the''2013 IMP''). The 2013 
IMP, which had an original term of ten years, was extended to January 2025 pursuant to 
the approval of the BPDA in January 2023. 
This IMPNF identifies six Institutional Projects (herein referred to as the “IMP Projects”). 
Three out of the six proposed Institutional Projects were previously approved in the 2013 
IMP and are the following: 
•	Harvard Business School ("HBS") Faculty & Administrative Office Building; New 
construction, approximately 110,000 square feet ("SF"). Please note that all 
references to square feet in this document refer to Gross Floor Area as defined in 
Article 2 of the Boston Zoning Code.
•	Gateway Project; New construction, approximately 300,000 SF
•	Harvard Stadium Renovation & Addition; approximately 46,000 new SF beyond 
existing envelope, approximately 34,000 new SF within existing envelope, and 
approximately 130,500 SF renovation
In the 2013 IMP, these three previously approved projects were analyzed for impacts and 
accounted for in Harvard's IMP Cooperation Agreement.
The three new IMP Projects to be included in the IMP are the following:
•	Tennis & Squash Racquet Center; New construction, approximately 200,000 SF
•	Mignone Field Support Building; New construction, approximately 20,000 to 30,000 
SF
•	Crimson Catering; Change of use and partial renovation, approximately 8,150 SF
Over the next decade, Harvard's IMP will focus its efforts on campus stewardship, 
sustainability, and resiliency, while advancing both new development (approximately 
720,000 SF) and renovation and reuse (approximately 138,500 SF). 
These aspirations looking toward 2034 will build upon the planning principles that guided 
the 2013 IMP—connectivity, enhancement of the open space network, best practices 
in urban design, and respect for community context. In addition to undertaking the six 
specified IMP Projects in the coming decade, Harvard expects to continue to invest in and 
maintain its other campus facilities to ensure a high-quality academic environment. 

10
While the University's building program proposed in the IMP is largely carried over 
from the 2013 IMP, Harvard will nonetheless develop, with community input, a plan 
for significant community benefits during the term of the IMP in connection with the 
new projects described herein. Concurrently, Harvard is advancing the planning and 
development of its non-institutional landholdings in Allston, principally the Enterprise 
Research Campus (“ERC”) and Beacon Park Yard (“BPY”), as part of distinct and 
complementary processes that fall outside of the IMP and are noted herein as an 
acknowledgment of the area context.

1.2. Institutional Priorities
1.2.1. Institutional Objectives and Needs
Harvard is an educational institution dedicated to excellence in teaching, learning, 
and research, with an academic mission to advance new ideas and promote enduring 
knowledge. New technologies, pioneering discoveries, and emerging societal issues 
require facilities that strengthen collaboration and innovation. Harvard’s campus in 
Allston offers an opportunity to expand and improve campus resources to support the 
University’s teaching and research, and meet the needs of Harvard’s Schools and Units.
Harvard’s planning for its Allston campus is shaped by several larger objectives. The 
University seeks to strengthen cross-disciplinary initiatives, cultivate the arts and 
humanities, invest in science and engineering education, and encourage the translation 
of new discoveries into solutions that benefit humankind. The University is committed 
to responding to the great challenges we face as a society, such as climate change and 
public health crises. Harvard seeks to accelerate sustainable development to protect 
the climate and the environment, advance a more equitable society, and promote the 
wellbeing of people. Harvard’s core values of equity, diversity, inclusion, and belonging 
call for fostering a campus where everyone can thrive. The University remains committed 
to creating a welcoming setting for living and learning, with a focus on attractive 
common spaces, cultural amenities, and residential environments. Harvard aims to 
design a campus that is sensitive to the surrounding built environment and to support 
partnerships that contribute to the vibrancy and well-being of the Allston community.
Harvard’s planning for Allston responds to the space need projections and facility 
conditions assessments of Harvard’s academic faculties and administrative units. The 
IMP Projects proposed in this IMPNF reflect the University’s currently anticipated needs 
for additional academic space, athletic space, and other space to support the University.

1.2.2. Harvard Allston Campus Planning Principles 
The Allston campus faces complex challenges and opportunities: an evolving and growing 
residential neighborhood to its south and west; a dynamic commercial, office, and lab real 
estate market; hybrid work-life and learning modalities; anticipated increases in climate 
exposure; evolving transportation patterns; as well as a growing shift toward increased 
sustainability and fossil fuel reductions.
Harvard has established planning principles to ensure that design and implementation 
decisions are balanced and sound. Planning must not only be consistent with the 
University’s broader goals and vision, but also recognize the planning context of the 
neighborhood and the surrounding regulatory environment. These planning principles 
include:
•	Community: Respect community context through sensitivity to the surrounding 
neighborhood and land use patterns. Contribute to an enhanced public realm. 
Support the activation of Barry’s Corner through urban design, welcoming 
streetscapes and programming.
•	Equity: Foster a welcoming campus physical environment that promotes inclusion 
and belonging.
•	Campus Character: Ensure that new development respects the campus character 
in terms of massing, visual axes and edges, while celebrating contemporary design 
informed by societal needs, technology, and sustainability
•	Balance: Preserve the existing Allston campus while celebrating contemporary 
architecture that is informed by current societal needs, technology, and 
sustainability.
•	Connectivity: Enhance connectivity through a multimodal approach to bridging 
the people, places, and activities on the campus.
•	Public Realm: Preserve and enhance campus open spaces and landscape 
elements, and improve pedestrian orientation.
•	Sustainability: Promote sustainability, and address climate, health and equity, by 
dramatically reducing greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging high-performance 
and healthier buildings, and strengthening climate resilience.
•	Stewardship: Invest in existing facilities and, where possible, reuse existing 
campus assets to meet emerging needs through reinvestment and adaptive re-use.

14
1.2.3. Equity, Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging 
Initiatives
The experience of Harvard’s physical campus is augmented by University efforts to foster 
a campus culture where everyone can thrive. This is the intent of Harvard’s commitment 
to championing and supporting inclusive excellence. Harvard, through its Office for 
Equity, Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging ("OEDIB"), is continually working to create 
and maintain a community that draws on the widest possible pool of talent to unify 
excellence and diversity—one that fully embraces individuals from varied backgrounds, 
cultures, races, identities, life experiences, and values. The aspiration to achieve inclusive 
excellence is rooted in the understanding that the diversity of Harvard's community is 
a source of excellence and is a fulfillment of Harvard's educational mission to include 
people of different backgrounds and beliefs to engage with and learn from each other.
Harvard and its representative Schools and Units have taken on a vast array of 
initiatives—policies, programs, spaces, events, resources, and more—to advance 
inclusive excellence on campus. A small sampling of these efforts includes the following: 
•The Inclusive Hiring Initiative provides guidelines and training on compliant and 
inclusive hiring practices at Harvard.
•The Harvard Construction Inclusion Plan has established minimum standards 
for the inclusion of underrepresented business enterprises and for the employment 
of women and people of color on significant construction projects.
•The Presidential Initiative on Harvard & the Legacy of Slavery is an effort 
to understand and address the enduring legacy of slavery within the University 
community.

development planning, as follows:

This chapter outlines the specific projects the University aims to complete over the next 
decade, including new construction, renovation, and maintenance projects, to realize 
strategic goals in both academic and community development.

changes since the approval of the 2013 IMP. The history of institutional planning on the

vehicular, transit, bicycle, and pedestrian facilities. An overview of anticipated impacts 
related to the IMP Projects and areas for further study in the IMP transportation analysis 
are also presented. 
Sustainability (Chapter 5)
Harvard continues to advance a holistic strategy to optimize outcomes across climate, 
health, and equity, including goals related to sustainable design and operations. A review 
of Harvard's efforts is provided, including reducing emissions while transitioning to a 
fossil fuel-free future and sharing knowledge on how to translate research into practice 
at scale, such as eliminating classes of harmful chemicals and embodied carbon from 
building materials and the supply chain.

climate, given the University’s long-established presence along the Charles River Basin. 
A review of future climate conditions and Harvard’s previous planning related to climate 
resiliency are covered in this chapter.

with a summary of improvements made since the 2013 IMP and a review of anticipated 
impacts and mitigation strategies due to IMP Projects.

priorities, and potential benefit areas that will be discussed with the community and the 
City of Boston (the "City").

2.1.2. Zoning and IMP Area
Zoning
Harvard University’s Allston campus, is the subject of this IMPNF and will be governed by 
the zoning parameters established in the IMP as approved by the BPDA and the Boston 
Zoning Commission. The IMP Projects will be subject to future BPDA and community 
review under Article 80 of the Zoning Code. The IMP will establish guidelines and 
parameters as applicable for proposed development which will constitute the basis for 
the Allston campus as it evolves. Once approved by the Boston Zoning Commission 
(anticipated in 2024), the IMP for the Allston campus will have a term of ten years, 
consistent with the previous IMP term.
IMP Area
Harvard proposes to subtract approximately 2.5 net acres of land from the IMP Area 
approved in 2013. This proposal reflects the following changes:
•	Addition of approximately 1.1 acres at 168 Western Avenue to convert an existing 
commercial kitchen to a University catering kitchen and to include a section of the 
institutional parking lot at the rear of the site that is incorporated into the parking at 
28 Travis Street.
•	Adjustment of the west and north IMP boundaries at the District Energy Facility 
("DEF") adjacent to the Planned Development Area of the ERC, resulting in a net loss 
of approximately 0.15 acres from the IMP Area. This adjustment will allow the DEF to 
accommodate future sub-surface equipment, storage tanks, etc. It will also create a 
consistent right-of-way for DEF Drive.
•	Redesignation of approximately 3.5 acres from the IMP Area that is associated with 
the Greenway in an effort to recognize its public, community use and to establish it 
more clearly as one defined area. Though the Greenway will be outside of the IMP 
Area, it will occasionally support institutional uses, including those associated with 
the Treehouse Conference Center.

potential for either field renovation or replacement and the inclusion of new support 
structures to provide amenities, such as permanent seating, press box, restrooms, 
concessions, storage, team rooms, and other athletic support necessary for maintaining 
the athletic programs which currently use those fields.
Harvard also anticipates the installation of an array of photovoltaic panels at 114 Western 
Avenue in furtherance of the University's long-term goal of fossil fuel-free operation.

 2.1.5. Public Review 
Harvard-Allston Task Force
Harvard works regularly with a task force of neighborhood representatives regarding 
planning and development in Allston. The Harvard-Allston Task Force (the “Task Force”) 
was first convened in the mid-1980’s in preparation for the University’s first IMP, filed in 
1989.
In January 2006, then Boston Mayor Thomas M. Menino announced a new 
Harvard-Allston Task Force to serve as an advisory group to the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority (now doing business as the BPDA) as Harvard began a new institutional master 
planning process for the Allston campus. Since 2006, Harvard has met regularly with this 
Task Force. It is composed of representatives, nominated by the City, to help the BPDA 
determine appropriate strategies to mitigate the social and environmental impacts of 
Harvard’s institutional projects and other associated development.
MEPA Review
Harvard University's campus in Allston is subject to a Special Review Procedure under 
the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act (“MEPA”). The Special Review Procedure 
requires certain project documentation to be submitted to the MEPA office to confirm 
consistency with the 2013 IMP. Harvard will consult with the MEPA office to determine the 
appropriate approach to future filings for the IMP.

3.1. History
3.1.1. Early Institutional History and Original Mission 
In 1636, the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony allocated funding 
for the establishment of “a school or college.” A professor was appointed the following 
year and the institution, established in Cambridge and known as Harvard College, 
enrolled nine students in 1638.
In 1650, the Great and General Court approved Harvard’s charter of incorporation. The 
charter named the corporation the “President and Fellows of Harvard College” and 
assigned them the duties of managing the College’s finances, properties, and donations, 
and acting as a legal entity in courts of law. The President and Fellows of Harvard College 
(also known as the Harvard Corporation) is considered the oldest corporation in the 
Western Hemisphere. 
Since 1636, Harvard has undergone significant physical growth driven by emerging 
societal needs, changing approaches to teaching and research, the rise of specialized 
academic fields, and the desire to create a residential campus setting. Harvard is at 
the frontier of academic and intellectual discovery. Beginning with the introduction of 
medical education in 1782, Harvard added graduate and professional programs over the 
course of two centuries, becoming a university in name as well as function. Those who 
venture to Harvard—to learn, research, teach, work, and grow—join nearly four centuries 
of students and scholars in the pursuit of truth, knowledge, and a better world.

38
3.1.2. Harvard’s Development in Allston
Harvard University has maintained a presence in Allston since the late 1800s. In 1870, 
poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, along with his family and a few friends, gave 70 acres 
of meadowland on the Charles River to Harvard. In 1890, Bostonian Henry Lee Higginson 
donated an additional 31 acres to the University and the area became known as Soldiers 
Field. Development of Harvard’s property in Allston began shortly thereafter. Harvard 
Stadium—the country’s first large reinforced concrete structure—was built in 1903. Soon 
after its construction, Allston became the center of the University’s athletic programs. 
In the early part of the 20th century, Harvard expanded its Allston campus to 
accommodate the Graduate School of Business Administration (now HBS), which had 
formally opened on the Cambridge Campus in 1908. After World War I, HBS was faced 
with surging enrollment and increased competition for space on the Cambridge Campus 
and in the surrounding residential areas. At the same time, HBS had solidified its role 
as the leading provider of graduate business education and business research, and 
sought to accommodate a larger faculty and administrative staff. To meet these needs 
in a modern and cohesive environment, Harvard constructed approximately 500,000 
SF of classroom, library, office, and residential space in Allston in accordance with a plan 
developed by the firm of McKim, Mead & White. The new campus opened in 1927.
The space needs of Harvard’s Athletics program and Business School drove development 
of its Allston campus through much of the 20th century, combined with the desire to 
provide residential accommodations for growing numbers of graduate students and 
other Harvard affiliates. The Soldiers Field Park housing complex, developed by Harvard 
University, opened in 1974, adding more than 450 apartment units to the Allston campus. 
Planning in the 1970s, in part to respond to the expansion of women's athletics under 
Title IX, resulted in the creation of Blodgett Pool, Gordon Track, and the Bright-Landry 
Hockey facility.
In more recent decades, HBS added McArthur Hall, Spangler Center, and Hawes Hall 
pursuant to the 1997 IMP. The Science and Engineering Complex, originally proposed in 
2007, was completed in 2021. The Harvard Innovation Labs and Tata Hall were proposed 
in 2011, and a number of other projects, including the Chao Center and Klarman Hall 
and a major renovation of the University's Soldiers Field Park housing, were completed 
following the 2013 IMP. 

39
3.1.3. North Allston History 
North Allston's development began in the early 17th century as an agricultural and cattle-
raising outpost of Cambridge. Since then, it has witnessed intense transformations: 
from a market town and center for the beef industry; to a streetcar suburb built along 
Western Avenue that continues to serve as North Allston’s Main Street; to a major rail 
transportation center; to textile factories; to the small- and medium-sized businesses 
scattered through the neighborhood.
The area of North Allston centered on the intersection of Western Avenue and North 
Harvard Street, known as Barry’s Corner, is less densely built when compared with other 
areas of Boston and Cambridge and is somewhat isolated within the larger region. This 
development pattern is in part a result of North Allston’s separation by the river and the 
Massachusetts Turnpike, but is also due to the proximity of low density land uses, such 
as athletic fields and City and State park land. As a result, few access/egress points serve 
the area, challenging the University’s efforts to create strong links with its Cambridge 
Campus and to activate Barry’s Corner.
North Allston’s residential streets provide ample evidence of the neighborhood’s historic 
stability with rows of well-maintained houses. At one time, many North Allston residents 
walked to nearby jobs at the railyards and mills; today, they are more likely to commute to 
work in other areas of Boston and the surrounding region.

40
3.2. Existing Conditions
3.2.1. University Profile 
Harvard’s operations are located primarily within its three main campus areas: 
Harvard’s original campus in Cambridge, centered on Harvard Square; the North 
Allston neighborhood of Boston (the subject of this IMPNF); and its facilities within the 
Longwood Medical and Academic Area (“LMA”) in Boston. In addition, Harvard’s Arnold 
Arboretum occupies 281 acres in the Jamaica Plain and Roslindale neighborhoods of 
Boston. Harvard’s facilities in the LMA and at the Arboretum are the subject of their own 
Institutional Master Plans. 
Today, Harvard has a total enrollment of approximately 25,000 degree candidates, 
including approximately 7,000 undergraduates and 14,000 graduate students as well 
as approximately an additional 3,900 students are enrolled part-time in the Harvard's 
Division of Continuing Education. 
Harvard has approximately 2,400 faculty members, as well as 17,200 staff who work in 
Cambridge and Boston. Of the total faculty and staff population employed at Harvard, 
approximately 3,400 are residents of Boston. In addition, Harvard has more than 12,000 
faculty at its 15 affiliated teaching hospitals, including but not limited to Massachusetts 
General Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical 
Center, and Boston Children’s Hospital.

broader context of Harvard's landholdings in the Metro Boston area can be seen in Figure

3.2.5. Neighborhood Context 
Harvard’s campus in Allston abuts the North Allston neighborhood, creating opportunities 
for appropriate transitions between the scale and uses of the institution and the 
neighborhood. North Harvard Street and Western Avenue intersect at Barry’s Corner, an 
important public realm link between the neighborhood and the University. 
Today, North Allston is home to newly arrived immigrants, professionals, students, and 
long-term residents. Over the last decade, Harvard has worked to increase the density 
of activity in and around Barry’s Corner with the goal to create a vibrant, pedestrian-
friendly neighborhood with attractive amenities, a vision Harvard shares with the City 
and community. Much of the area surrounding the Allston campus has been transformed 
through new partnership projects being developed on Harvard-owned land south of 
Western Avenue and at Barry’s Corner, as well as by mixed-used developments on 
privately-owned land west of Barry’s Corner.
South of Western Avenue, the Phase A of the ERC is currently being developed as part 
of Planned Development Area #115. The BPDA is leading the pending Harvard ERC 
District and Greenway Plan, a longer-term planning study for the remaining ERC areas. 
The ERC project site is located in an area that has historically served transportation-
related industrial uses. Prior to its acquisition by Harvard, the ERC site area was used 
by CSX Transportation and a sublease primarily for warehousing and freight forwarding 
via an easement from the Massachusetts Turnpike Authority (now the Massachusetts 
Department of Transportation). Phase A of the ERC project will include approximately 
900,000 SF of mixed-use development consisting of residential, office/lab, hotel, 
conference center, restaurant, retail, research and development, service, open space 
(including programmed open space), and parking uses. 
The Greenway is the principal open space resource planned for this area of Allston, linking 
the neighborhood edge at North Harvard Street, through the ERC, towards the Charles 
River. The Greenway will serve as a publicly accessible civic landscape, an infrastructure 
corridor, and an important component of the area’s long-term climate resiliency effort. 
The recently-developed Rena Path together with the Ray Mellone Park form the western 
terminus of the Greenway and serve as a green link between the community and the 
campus.
Recent investments in and west of Barry’s Corner include the creation of the Harvard 
Ed Portal at 224 Western Avenue, completion of the Continuum residential complex and 
connected grocery and retail outlets, the new Science and Engineering Complex and 
ArtLab buildings, enhancement of The Grove open space, and the Zone 3 commercial and 
public art initiative along Western Avenue. Informed by the newly adopted Western Avenue 
Corridor and Rezoning Study, other mixed-use partnership projects on Harvard-owned 
land include a mixed use project at 176 Lincoln Street, approved by the BPDA, and 180 
Western Avenue, presently under BPDA review. Area private development projects, such 
as Allston Labworks at the Allston Innovation Corridor, WBZ-TV/CBS Studio, and 1170-
1190 Soldiers Field Road, will include more than 1.3 million gross square feet of new office, 
laboratory, retail and residential space, a new broadcast facility for WBZ-TV, and public 
realm improvements. 

50
Given the multiple planning processes in Allston, Harvard is committed to maintaining 
a high level of coordination with the City and stakeholders to ensure a successful and 
integrated outcome. This commitment to coordination also holds true for construction 
management and mitigation, both for Harvard and its partners. Harvard undertakes a 
comprehensive construction planning and mitigation approach to pre-empt, minimize, 
and/or eliminate the negative impacts large construction and renovation projects 
can have on neighborhoods, businesses, the City, and the Harvard community, 
while collaborating with contractors to ensure the timely and efficient completion of 
construction activities.
3.2.6. Housing Context 
Harvard is committed to supporting a range of affordable housing initiatives throughout 
Allston-Brighton, as well as providing a broad housing portfolio for its student and 
affiliate population. This commitment includes ensuring the University continues to meet 
its goal for graduate student housing capacity, supplying the affiliate community with 
modern accommodation options, providing funding and land for several homeownership 
initiatives throughout the community, and partnering with developers whose goal is to 
build new housing that meets or exceeds the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy. 
Affiliate Housing
To support Harvard’s core campuses, the University maintains over 8,700 units with 
approximately 15,000 beds in its total affiliate housing portfolio in Boston, Cambridge, 
and Somerville. More than one-third of the housing portfolio serves as Undergraduate 
housing. Approximately 1,755 units, are in the Allston neighborhood of Boston, located 
in the HBS dormitories and Harvard University affiliate housing. At HBS, there are nine 
residence halls with over 1,000 units available to HBS students. Six of these residence 
halls house MBA and doctoral students. The remaining three residential buildings 
(Esteves, McArthur, and Tata) are dedicated to the Executive Education program and offer 
short-term housing as most of their programs are typically only a few weeks in length. As 
a result, one hundred percent of Executive Education students are housed on-campus 
for their programs. The Harvard University Housing (“HUH”) portfolio of Harvard-owned 
affiliate housing consists of approximately 2,900 apartment units, located in Cambridge, 
Boston, and Somerville, of which about 700 are located within Allston at the One Western 
Avenue and Soldiers Field Park apartment complexes. The Soldiers Field Park housing 
complex, originally built in 1974, recently underwent a phased renovation completed in 
2020 and included modernization efforts to significantly expand its amenity program and 
provide site and landscape improvements. HUH’s existing portfolio will expand further 
upon completion of the proposed housing at 175 North Harvard Street.
Harvard currently has the capacity to house more than 50 percent of its graduate 
students, which remains the University’s benchmark. Many affiliate housing facilities are 
open to all full-time Harvard graduate students, while some are school specific. Most 
students tend to select housing that provides the proximity for a meaningful academic 
experience. Consequently, most of the demand for on-campus housing in Allston is from 
HBS students as housing close to academic buildings is considered a strategic part of 
the learning and living immersive experience. With a total population of approximately

Aiming to provide additional capacity to house Harvard graduate students and affiliates, 
Harvard’s Sixth Amendment to the 2013 IMP proposed a new affiliate housing building 
at 175 North Harvard Street. The residential building is planned to contain approximately 
275,000 SF with approximately 275 housing units for Harvard graduate students, faculty, 
staff, and their families. By offering a varied mix of unit configurations, the building will 
accommodate a wide range of household types, including individuals who may opt either 
for the privacy of a studio or the more cost-effective option of a single bedroom in a

occupancy cost spectrum, an individual affiliate may share a unit with others, while at the 
upper end a larger household may occupy an entire unit. 
HUH has implemented several policies to help with the affordability of affiliate housing. 
This includes offering lower than typical “barriers to entry” in that affiliates are not 
required to pay brokerage fees, provide security or last month’s rent deposits or undergo 
credit checks. University leasing practices encourage apartment sharing to increase 
the efficient utilization of housing inventory. HUH maintains prevailing market rates 
for housing, which is consistent with the University’s affiliate housing rental policy 
and amenable to graduate student budgets. Many graduate student affiliates receive 
financial aid towards living expenses from the University appropriate to their particular 
circumstance.

3.3.3. Changing Context
Harvard University's campus in Allston and its neighborhood context has undergone 
significant change since the approval of the 2013 IMP. Harvard has made major investments 
into buildings and facilities, infrastructure, open space, and the activation of Barry’s Corner. 
This campus development has been complemented by a host of other public improvements 
and private sector development in Allston. Planning studies have refined the vision for the 
area and sustainability and climate resiliency policies and strategies, at Harvard and beyond, 
have advanced considerably during this past decade.
Changes Initiated by Harvard
•	New and Renovated Institutional Buildings: Harvard completed the construction 
of several major new buildings, including the SEC, DEF, ArtLab, Klarman Hall and Chao 
Center. Additionally, comprehensive renovations were undertaken at the Soldiers Field 
Park housing development, Esteves Hall, and 114 Western Avenue. In total these projects 
represented over 900,000 SF of new development and over 600,000 SF of renovation.
•	Partnership Developments: Harvard has engaged with development partners to 
create multi-faceted, mixed-use projects on Harvard-owned land that add to Allston's 
vibrancy. The Continuum housing and retail complex was the first partnership project 
in the heart of Barry’s Corner. Harvard’s ERC recently secured approval for its Phase A 
mixed-use development, consisting of residential, office/lab, hotel, conference center, 
and restaurant and retail uses. In addition, mixed-use partnership projects are underway 
at several other sites, including the BPDA Board approved 176 Lincoln Street, and 180 
Western Avenue and 287 Western Avenue, both of which are currently under review by 
the BPDA.
•	Transportation and Utility Infrastructure: To support Harvard's other area 
projects, as well as future development, Harvard made extensive transportation and 
utility infrastructure improvements in Allston between 2013 and 2023, including new 
underground utilities, streets, sidewalks, and landscape amenities along Western Avenue, 
Stadium Road, Academic Way, Science Drive, Ivy Lane, South Campus Drive, and Kresge 
Way. Harvard created a mobility hub at Stadium Road, supporting campus shuttle 
circulation and bicycle parking, thereby improving the convenience of alternatives to 
single-occupant-vehicle use. The sum of these transportation improvements and utility 
enhancements serve not just Harvard University but the Allston neighborhood as a 
whole.
•	Open Space: Between 2013 and 2023, Harvard developed new open spaces at Rena 
Path (adjacent to the City’s Raymond Mellone Park) and the SEC, and made open 
space improvements to The Grove at the Barry’s Corner intersection, the Soldiers Field 
Park housing complex, and HBS’s Schwartz Common and Pavilion. The University also 
undertook a campus-wide initiative to improve pedestrian wayfinding, which resulted in 
new directional signage on the Allston campus. 
•	Placemaking: Since 2013, Harvard and its partners have worked to make the Western 
Avenue corridor in Allston a more vibrant and active pedestrian and retail environment. 
The Continuum project added street-facing retail to the Barry’s Corner intersection. 
The renovated Harvard Ed Portal and Ceramics Program turned the former light 
industrial building at 224 Western Avenue into an active contributor to street life. The art 
installations, pop-up food venues such as Rabottini's Pizza, Café Beatrice, and Jamaica 
Mi Hungry, and programming associated with Harvard’s Zone 3 initiative have all added 
considerable vitality to Western Avenue.

61
•	Space Requirements: A lasting impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, for Harvard 
and beyond, is an increase in hybrid and remote work models. Fostering hybrid 
environments at the University often requires flexible and efficient layouts, enhanced 
collaboration spaces, improved communication technology, and a priority on occupant 
health. As space use changes, Harvard is prioritizing opportunities to repurpose 
existing space whenever possible before considering the creation of new spaces.
•	Sustainability and Climate Resiliency: Harvard’s ambitious Sustainable Building 
Standards, in place since 2009, have resulted in many projects on the Allston campus 
receiving Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (“LEED”) and Living 
Building Challenge certifications. Harvard has instituted sustainable site maintenance 
standards for organic landscape maintenance, composting and recycling programs, 
sustainable cleaning standards, electric campus shuttle bus use, and a program for 
healthier building products and furnishings. Harvard’s University-wide climate goals 
are to be fossil fuel-neutral by 2026 and fossil fuel-free by 2050 to address broader 
impacts of fossil fuels beyond just carbon. Since 2013, the University has participated 
actively with the City of Boston and other partners on sustainability and climate 
resiliency strategies for the campus, City, and region.
Changes Initiated by Public and Private Sector 
•	Public Improvements: The City and State have reinvested in Allston’s mobility, 
utility, and open space infrastructure since 2013, with major renovations of the state-
managed Anderson Memorial Bridge and John Weeks Bridge, a comprehensive 
redesign of the City’s William F. Smith Playground which the University helped 
actualize, and water and sewer main improvements undertaken by the BWSC.
•	Private Sector Development: Since 2013, the Allston neighborhood has seen 
substantial levels of activity and investment by private-sector and non-profit real 
estate developers. Projects are in planning or currently underway at the WBZ campus, 
250-280 Western Avenue (Allston Labworks), Studio Allston Hotel, and 365 Western 
Avenue.
•	Planning for the Future: Beyond the campus, Allston has been and continues to be 
the subject of multiple public planning efforts on a range of topics. The BPDA is leading 
public planning processes to advance land use, urban design, mobility, equity, and 
assessment of community needs in Allston that inform policies, plans, and regulations. 
These planning initiatives, some complete, some in progress, others upcoming, 
include: Western Avenue Transit Study, Western Avenue Corridor Study and Rezoning, 
Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan, ERC planning, BPY planning, and Allston-Brighton 
Needs Assessment. Concurrently, the State through the Massachusetts Department 
of Transportation is advancing the Allston Multimodal Project, intended to enhance 
regional mobility while improving local connectivity and livability. Harvard is an active 
participant in all of these processes, partnering with City, state officials, and community 
members to collaborate on a shared future of Allston.
