4.1. Existing Mobility Conditions
Mobility conditions for pedestrians, bicyclists, transit users, and motorists in the IMP Area 
are shaped by the nature of the regional and local multimodal transportation networks and 
the presence of the Charles River. This section discusses the existing mobility conditions 
considering these regional and local network changes from the 2013 IMP, as illustrated in 
Figure 4.1; presents preliminary potential impacts from the proposed IMP Projects; and 
proposes areas for further study in the IMP transportation analysis. 
Three of the six currently proposed IMP Projects were included in the 2013 IMP and their 
respective transportation impacts were identified and evaluated at that time. The relative 
impacts of those three projects are anticipated to be comparable with those presented 
and analyzed in the 2013 IMP, as discussed below. Transportation analyses in Allston 
subsequent to the 2013 IMP have included the impact of these three projects. A set of 
transportation improvements were presented in the 2013 IMP to address impacts of the 
projects and several improvements have advanced since that time. Additional review under 
Article 80B of the Zoning Code, which requires evaluation of impacts, will be completed for 
the IMP Projects as required.
4.1.1. Active Transportation 
Accommodations for active transportation modes—walking, bicycling, mobility devices —
have evolved and improved since the 2013 IMP with investments by Harvard and others.
Harvard owns and maintains a network of campus paths within its Allston campus that 
provides internal connections and links to networks on the periphery of the campus. Public 
sidewalks, bicycle facilities, and shared-use paths are primarily under the jurisdiction of the 
Department of Conservation and Recreation (“DCR”), the Massachusetts Department of 
Transportation (“MassDOT”), and the City of Boston.
Recent Investments: The University and others have started to improve long-standing 
transportation mobility challenges stemming from outdated, inaccessible infrastructure 
and large-scale, impenetrable zones with former industrial uses:
•	Public streets adjacent to the Allston campus are under the jurisdiction of the City of 
Boston. Recently, the University reconstructed sections of Western Avenue, improving 
east-west pedestrian and bicycle mobility: sidewalks in the northwest corner of Barry’s 
Corner were reconstructed in 2015 as part of the Continuum development, a privately 
owned building on Harvard-owned land.
•	Improvements along Western Avenue were completed as part of the SEC project in 
2021. These improvements include:
•	Sidewalk reconstruction on both sides of Western Avenue between Travis 
Street and Batten Way with street tree buffers.
•	Protected bike lanes in both directions on Western Avenue between Academic 
Way and Soldiers Field Road.
•	Bike accommodations at the intersection of Western Avenue at Soldiers Field 
Road.

64
•	DCR has jurisdiction over the shared use paths along the Charles River and Soldiers 
Field Road and the pedestrian bridges that cross them: the John W. Weeks Bridge and 
the Sinclair Weeks Bridge, respectively. In 2015, DCR completed renovation of the John 
W. Weeks Bridge, funded by Harvard, which included pedestrian and bicycle accessibility 
improvements that have enhanced connectivity across the Charles River.
•	MassDOT has jurisdiction over the Anderson Memorial, Western Avenue and River Street 
bridges. MassDOT completed renovation of the Anderson Memorial Bridge in 2016, 
which included improved pedestrian accommodations, the addition of bike lanes in both 
directions, and accessibility enhancements. 
New Roadways: Harvard has begun to create a more fine-grained transportation network 
integrating its campus and the Allston community, with robust pedestrian accommodations 
and enhanced bike infrastructure: 
•	In 2015, South Campus Drive and Ivy Lane were constructed to support the Continuum 
development, northwest of Barry’s Corner. South Campus Drive includes a shared use 
path on the north/west side north of Ivy Lane, and sidewalks on both sides of the street, 
and a two-way cycle track south of Ivy Lane. Ivy Lane includes sidewalks on both sides of 
the street.
•	Rena Path was completed in 2017 and includes a shared use path, connecting North 
Harvard Street to Science Drive.
•	In 2021, Academic Way, Science Drive, and Stadium Road were constructed as part of the 
SEC Enabling Roadways project. Academic Way includes a shared use path on the east 
side of the street and a sidewalk on the west side. Science Drive includes a sidewalk on 
the north side of the street. Stadium Road includes a shared use path on the east side of 
the street and sidewalks on both sides of the street.
These improvements support internal site circulation; promote connectivity to/from and 
within the campus and to adjacent sites, transit stops, and bicycle amenities such as 
Bluebikes stations; and enhance the overall connectivity of Harvard’s campus in Allston with 
its campus in Cambridge, to the adjacent residential neighborhood, and to the riverfront.
Further enhancing bicycle mobility, Harvard supports six Bluebikes stations in Allston at 
Harvard Stadium, 175 North Harvard Street, Innovation Lab, Soldiers Field Park, Honan-
Allston Branch Library, and Brighton Mills. Harvard also supports seven stations in 
Cambridge and one station in the LMA.
Bicycle parking is an important part of the transportation system on the Allston campus, 
where the University provides more than 1,500 bike parking spaces. Harvard significantly 
increased bicycle parking capacity with the completion of the SEC. Harvard constructed 
the Allston Mobility Hub on Stadium Road, which added approximately 264 bicycle parking 
spaces to the network available to Harvard University ID holders. In addition, over 300 more 
uncovered or partially covered bicycle spaces were constructed to support the SEC.
Harvard is committed to providing students, faculty and staff with safe, healthy, and 
sustainable transportation options. Harvard will continue collaborating with DCR, MassDOT, 
and the City of Boston to provide a robust active transportation network in Allston.

4.1.3. Roadway Network
Allston is strategically located on the western edge of Boston at the crossroads of the 
Massachusetts Turnpike/I-90, Soldiers Field Road, North Harvard Street, and Western 
Avenue. Regional highway access to and from the Allston campus is principally provided by 
the I-90 to/from the east/west (linking to I‑95/Route 128 to the west); Soldiers Field Road 
to/from the east; I-93 to/from the north and south; Route 2 to/from the west; and Route 1 
to/from the north. 
Regional Roadways
I-90 is a toll road under the jurisdiction of MassDOT and is an interstate highway with 
an interchange that is located less than one-quarter mile from the Allston campus. I-90 
provides regional connections to downtown Boston, Logan Airport, and the larger regional 
highway system that serves metropolitan Boston and New England including I-93 to the 
east.

68
Soldiers Field Road, which is under the jurisdiction of DCR, is adjacent to the Allston 
campus with interchanges at Cambridge Street, Western Avenue and North Harvard 
Street. Soldiers Field Road is a parkway that is restricted to travel by autos and permitted 
vehicles only. This roadway connects Allston with downtown Boston, Back Bay, 
Cambridge, and communities to the west like Watertown and Newton. Soldiers Field Road 
becomes Storrow Drive east of the BU Bridge, providing connections to the north via I-93 
and Route 1.
Local Streets
Western Avenue is a two-way, east-west arterial roadway under the jurisdiction of the City 
of Boston with daily weekday traffic volumes of approximately 6,100 vehicles as it passes 
through the Allston campus. The roadway has one lane in each direction, turn lanes at 
signalized intersections, and striped bike lanes. The bike lanes are protected in both 
directions between Academic Way and Soldiers Field Road. On-street parking is provided 
on the northern side of the street across the SEC in a floating parking lane that protects 
an on-road bike lane. On-street pick-up/drop-off is provided on the southern side of 
the street in front of the SEC with a sidewalk-level separated bike lane. The roadway 
width and the existing bike lanes, varies from approximately 44 to 46 feet in the section 
between North Harvard Street and Soldiers Field Road.
North Harvard Street is a two-way, north-south arterial roadway under the jurisdiction 
of the City of Boston with daily weekday traffic volumes of approximately 8,700 vehicles 
as it passes through the Allston campus. The roadway has one lane in each direction, 
turn lanes at signalized intersections and at Gate 8 (Harvard Stadium), and striped bike 
lanes. On-street parking is provided on the eastern side of the street next to Shad Hall. 
The roadway width is approximately 40 feet between Western Avenue and Soldiers Field 
Road.
Since the 2013 IMP, Harvard constructed South Campus Drive and Ivy Lane as part of the 
Continuum development completed in 2015, and constructed Academic Way, Science 
Drive, and Stadium Road as part of the SEC development completed in 2021. These new 
streets provide local circulation opportunities and additional on-street parking to support 
a portion of the parking demands from institutional uses and the new housing and retail 
uses at the Continuum development. These new streets are generally low-volume, low-
speed streets that provide pedestrian and local bicycle and motorized vehicle circulation 
opportunities and access to adjacent land uses.

69
4.1.4. Transportation Demand Management
Harvard has an extensive Transportation Demand Management (“TDM”) program that 
is an important tool in managing vehicular travel to the campus. Over the past two years, 
more employees returned to campus after working remotely, and commuting patterns and 
habits continue to change. While many employees have returned to campus fully, many 
others continue in hybrid work models. In response to these changing commuter dynamics, 
Harvard has adapted its programs and services to meet the evolving commuting needs of 
the Harvard community. Key components of the program include:
•	Marketing: Harvard continues to maintain an extensive CommuterChoice website.
•	Transit: Harvard provides a 50 percent subsidy on MBTA monthly passes for eligible 
affiliates such as faculty, staff, and postdocs. Nine Harvard Graduate Schools offer 
a Semester Pass program offering subsidies between 11 and 50 percent. There is 
no MBTA subsidy for undergraduates. In addition, Harvard offers a flexible pre-tax 
transportation debit card for staff who wish to alternate between parking or transit 
commuting.
•	Bicycle: The CommuterChoice program works to continually improve the cycling 
environment through marketing and education initiatives and participation in the 
Bluebikes bikeshare program. Harvard supports six Bluebikes stations in Allston at 
Harvard Stadium, 175 North Harvard Street, Innovation Lab, Soldiers Field Park, Honan-
Allston Branch Library, and Brighton Mills. Harvard also supports seven stations in 
Cambridge and one station in the LMA. Harvard affiliates are offered a $31 (24 percent) 
discount from the Bluebikes Annual Membership.
•	Carpool/Vanpool:The CommuterChoice program provides benefits to employees 
who carpool or vanpool on their commutes. Harvard offers discounted and preferential 
carpool and vanpool parking in the largest garages and several surface lots, and has 
arranged for additional carpool/vanpool spaces as needed. Harvard provides a 50 
percent subsidy for two-person carpools and 75 percent subsidy for three-or-more 
person carpools on an annual parking permit for employees that commute to work with 
one or more colleagues either four or five days per week. Harvard also provides a 50 
percent subsidy off the cost of a vanpool (consisting of five to 15 commuters) through 
the CommuterChoice program, and vanpools park free of charge.
•	ZipCar: Harvard currently provides six ZipCar vehicles for Harvard affiliate use who are 
eligible for discounted memberships. ZipCars are located within Allston at the off-street 
lots of Soldiers Field Parking Visitors Lot, 2 Hague Street, 125 Western Avenue, 28 
Travis Street, and 302 Western Avenue. In addition, two car share spaces are provided 
on Ivy Lane (under Harvard jurisdiction) and three car share spaces are provided on 
Spurr Street (under City of Boston jurisdiction).
•	Guaranteed Ride Home:Harvard offers a guaranteed ride home for faculty and staff 
who walk, bike, take transit, carpool or vanpool to work. The reimbursement is up to 
$100 to take a taxi, ride hailing service, transit, ZipCar or rental car in the event of a 
qualified emergency up to four times per year.
•	Digital Tools:During the fully remote work months of the pandemic, the 
CommuterChoice office phased out paper forms and applications and implemented 
virtual platforms in order to accommodate remote work environments and employee 
safety. The CommuterChoice Program continues to provide Harvard affiliates with 
commuter information and resources across multiple transportation modes including 
public transit, cycling, walking, and ride share programs.

70
•	Event Management:Harvard accommodates transportation demands related 
to athletic, commencement, and HBS events through police detail traffic control/
management, parking demand management, temporary signage, etc.
Harvard will maintain and continue to review and refine as necessary the TDM program 
to support alternative modes as a major component of day-to-day transportation 
operations supporting the IMP development program.
4.1.5. Parking
The existing Harvard parking facilities on the Allston campus consist of 20 surface lots 
and two parking garages, totaling approximately 3,116 institutional spaces. These spaces 
are used by eligible staff and faculty, students and affiliates living on campus, and visitors. 
In response to hybrid work needs, Harvard offers hourly and daily parking options with 
reduced rates and flexible three-day annual parking permits.
The institutional parking supply also supports evening and weekend events at Athletics 
and other campus venues by allowing event attendees to park for a fee in spaces that are 
used by daytime campus commuters. In addition, a limited number of public on-street 
parking spaces are located along North Harvard Street and Western Avenue adjacent to 
the Allston campus, as well as along South Campus Drive, Ivy Lane, and Stadium Road.
All University parking is controlled and administered by the Harvard University Parking 
Office as a University-wide resource with a permitting system, specific parking lot 
assignments, and fee schedule.

4.2. Anticipated Future Mobility 
Conditions
A number of significant, multimodal transportation improvements are planned or 
proposed for North Allston that will continue to enhance mobility conditions, including:
MBTA Bus Network Redesign Project: The MBTA released a revised Bus Network 
Redesign map in November 2022 and a final report in February 2023. The plan 
was adopted by the MBTA board and the resulting bus network is anticipated to be

from Central Square to Kendall Square in Cambridge and shortened to end at 
Waltham Center in Waltham.
•	Route 86: Headways of 45 minutes or better, with approximately 25-minute 
headways during peak periods. Route 86 will be shortened to between Harvard 
Square and Reservoir Station.
City of Boston Western Avenue Separated Bike Lanes: Through discussions during 
the Western Avenue Corridor Study and Rezoning and as part of the Better Bike Lanes 
initiative, separated bike lanes have been planned on Western Avenue between North

Enterprise Research Campus Roadways: Portions of “Milestone Street”, “Trotting 
Avenue” and “Axle Way” as well as an extension of Science Drive will be constructed to

to provide pedestrian, bicycle, transit and vehicle circulation opportunities and access to 
adjacent land uses. They also will begin to frame a street grid south of Western Avenue 
that will eventually connect south of Cambridge Street as part of the Allston Multimodal 
Project, discussed below.

72
Allston-Brighton Neighborhood Transit Link: As part of the Allston-Brighton Mobility 
Plan, the Allston Brighton TMA is currently conducting a study for the BPDA to inform 
the creation of a Neighborhood Transit Link Service to serve the Allston and Brighton 
neighborhoods. The service is envisioned to be open to the public and two draft routes 
are currently being considered:
•	North-south route connecting Harvard Square, Boston Landing, and Washington 
Square via Western Avenue and North Harvard Street.
•	East-west route connecting Coolidge Corner, Boston Landing, and Oak Square.
MassDOT Allston I-90 Viaduct Preservation and Cambridge Street Project: 
MassDOT is currently advancing a bridge preservation project for the I-90 viaduct in

Allston Multimodal Project, discussed below. The scale and scope of the Cambridge

MassDOT Allston Multimodal Project: Over the next decade, MassDOT is expected to

planning processes, such as the BPDA's Western Avenue Transitway Study, throughout

4.3. Transportation Demand 
Implications of IMP Projects
The transportation analysis for the IMP will evaluate the traffic impacts of the IMP Projects. 
The Harvard Stadium Addition & Renovation, HBS Faculty & Administrative Office Building, 
and the Gateway Project were included in the 2013 IMP and their transportation impacts 
were identified and evaluated. The relative impacts of these IMP Projects are anticipated 
to be generally comparable with those presented and analyzed in the 2013 IMP and all 
subsequent analyses which considered the impacts of these projects. The discussion 
presented below updates the preliminary trip generation analysis to reflect current best 
practices and recently available data.
The Harvard Stadium Addition and Renovation is not expected to generate more traffic, 
as the addition/renovation will upgrade amenities but not increase the number of seats. 
Further, this project is anticipated to add little to no new typical daily or peak hour 
transportation demands and therefore has not been evaluated. 
The proposed Tennis Squash and Racquet Center will include the replacement of the 
existing Beren Tennis Center and relocation of courts from other campus locations, 
consolidating them into a new facility. While the racquet center will offer more year-round 
use than the existing facilities, it is anticipated that during typical periods, this new facility 
will accommodate a level of activity similar to the existing sites. Further, this project is 
anticipated to add little to no new typical daily or peak hour transportation demands and 
therefore has not been evaluated. 
The proposed Mignone Field Support Building will upgrade athletic facilities that support 
the women's rugby program that are currently housed in temporary trailers on-site. It is 
anticipated that during typical periods, these upgraded facilities will accommodate a level 
of activity similar to the existing site. Further, this project is anticipated to add little no new 
typical daily or peak hour transportation demands and therefore has not been evaluated.
Person-trips were estimated for the HBS Faculty & Administrative Office Building, the 
Gateway Project, and Crimson Catering using the most recent Institute of Transportation 
Engineers (“ITE”) trip generation rates and data at existing Harvard facilities. The results of 
a preliminary person-trip generation analysis indicate that these projects would generate 
approximately 10,400 new daily person-trips. During the morning peak hour, there would 
be approximately 750 new person-trips (approximately 650 in and approximately 100 
out). During the evening peak hour, there would be approximately 1,050 new person-trips 
(approximately 300 in and approximately 750 out).
Vehicle trips were estimated by applying an automobile mode share and an average vehicle 
occupancy rate (“VOR”) to the person trip generation estimates. These estimates are 
based on Boston Transportation Department’s published mode share data by trip purpose 
for Area 17 (the zone for Allston) and Harvard’s 2019 Commuter Survey responses. 

74
The results the estimated vehicle generation analysis indicate that these projects would 
generate approximately 4,000 new daily vehicle trips (including private vehicle and 
Transit Network Company ("TNC"; such as Uber, Lyft) trips). During the morning peak 
hour, there would be approximately 350 new vehicle trips (approximately 300 in and 
approximately 50 out). During the evening peak hour, there would be approximately 400 
new vehicle trips (approximately 100 in and approximately 350 out).
The Ten-Year Plan also describes a number of maintenance and improvement projects 
(Section 2.1.4.) that are not expected to generate new traffic or parking demands and 
therefore are not included in this preliminary transportation assessment. 
The COVID-19 pandemic has had a major impact on the local and regional transportation 
network, travel behaviors, and transportation choice. Conditions have not yet reached 
a steady state and it is unlikely that the transportation network will be used in the same 
manner as pre-pandemic conditions as many employers and institutions, including 
Harvard, continue to refine policies such as flexible work schedules. It is anticipated that 
future condition activity levels (traffic volumes and transit ridership) and trip generation 
estimates will be refined in the IMP and subsequent Large Project Review submissions to 
reflect a reasonable estimate of post-pandemic transportation demands and behaviors.

75

Analysis for IMP

5.1. Introduction 
Ensuring a sustainable planet and protecting it for future generations is among the 
greatest challenges of our time. Harvard University has a proud legacy of taking 
institutional action to advance sustainability by accelerating the adoption of systems and 
practices that protect the climate and environment, advancing a more equitable society, 
and promoting the wellbeing of people at Harvard and beyond.
Harvard launched its first comprehensive Sustainability Plan in 2014, making it one of 
the first universities to define clear goals and targets across its organization. Harvard has 
taken significant steps since then, including meeting its first climate action goal in 2016, a 
30 percent absolute reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from a 2006 baseline.
To ensure a healthy, safe, equitable, and resilient future, Harvard adopted an updated 
and more ambitious agenda in May 2023 built on the latest research and lessons learned 
from implementing its first sustainability plan. This updated Sustainability Action Plan 
holistically integrates climate and the environment, societal equity, and the health and 
wellbeing of people into the actions it proposes and how it measures success. Harvard 
is aiming to advance sustainability by transforming how it powers, builds, operates, and 
leads.

78
5.2. Pathway to Fossil Fuel-Free
Harvard aims to power all campus operations without the use of fossil fuels by 2050. 
In February 2018, Harvard set goals to be fossil fuel-neutral by 2026 and fossil fuel-free 
by 2050. In adopting the concept of "fossil-fuel-free," Harvard is focused on the wider 
impacts of fossil fuels, not just greenhouse gas emissions. This will enable the University 
to drive progress across the issues of climate, health, and equity.
The University expects to meet these climate goals by zeroing out fossil fuels in four key 
areas: its district energy systems, its buildings (on-site use of fossil fuels), its purchased 
electricity, and its vehicle fleet. The complexity and scale of this energy transition is 
significant. Harvard has begun this “Roadmap to Fossil Fuel-Free by 2050” strategy with a 
University-wide planning effort overseen by the Presidential Committee on Sustainability 
(“PCS”). This multi-year planning effort will engage key internal stakeholders as well 
as critical external partners, including the utility providers and the cities of Boston and 
Cambridge.
1.	 District Energy Systems: Harvard’s Sustainability Action Plan involves evaluating 
a variety of technological solutions for transitioning the University's fossil fuel-based 
energy systems over time, including electrification, green hydrogen, and other innovative 
solutions.
2.	Buildings: Harvard is evaluating the feasibility of decarbonizing all building types by 
assessing the infrastructure needed to eliminate on-site combustion from boilers, kitchen 
appliances, and other equipment and systems. Coordination with external partners, such 
as utility providers and supply chains, is needed for this scale of capital planning and 
execution. 
3.	Vehicles and Fleet: Harvard is working to transition its entire vehicle fleet to electric 
power and is developing targets by vehicle type. An initial area of focus is the transition 
of Harvard’s shuttle bus fleet, building on the success of the first four electric buses 
launched in, fall 2021.
4.	Electricity Supply: Harvard is helping to develop new large-scale renewable 
electricity projects that address both carbon emissions and air pollution, and undertaking 
studies to quantify related climate and health benefits. Harvard will continue to evaluate 
on-site solar opportunities beyond the 3 megawatts ("MW") already installed on 
Harvard’s campuses, including Allston.

79
5.3. Sustainable Built Environment 
Initiatives
Harvard began to require the application of its Sustainable Building Standards to capital 
projects on its campuses in 2009. The University has upgraded and adjusted these 
standards in the years since. Through these innovative standards, the University has 
made significant progress towards its climate, health, and equity goals.
Harvard is continuing to develop its Sustainable Building Standards and building 
operational best practices to address the changing climate as well as health and equity 
in the built environment. Revisions to the Sustainable Building Standards undergo a 
University-wide review process focused on data-driven decision-making and informed by 
faculty research and best practices at Harvard and other industry leaders. The Standards 
apply to all capital projects and have resulted in significant emissions reductions, 
higher performance, better indoor air quality, healthier and more sustainable materials, 
improved equity, and accessibility. The Standards have been applied University-wide in a 
consistent way to capital projects, campus planning, and ongoing building operations. 
The Standards are the result of a collaborative effort led by the Office for Sustainability 
and informed by faculty through a subcommittee of the PCS, engaging with hundreds of 
facility leaders and project managers across the University’s Schools and Units.
Harvard’s current Sustainable Building Standards call for new construction and major 
renovations to be certified as either Living Building Challenge Core (“LBC Core”) or LEED 
v4 Gold, and use the Harvard Healthier Building Academy requirements to reduce or 
eliminate the use of harmful classes of chemicals in 14 interior product categories and 
provide excellent indoor air quality.
LEED and Living Building Challenge Projects
Harvard has 148 LEED-certified spaces across campus, including the first and second 
LEED v4 commercial interiors projects in Massachusetts. Recently, both the SEC and 
the Swartz Hall projects achieved LEED Platinum certification, the highest level of 
certification in the rating system. The SEC is also the largest building and first research 
laboratory building to achieve the International Living Future Institute’s (“ILFI”) 
Living Building Challenge ("LBC") Petal certification in Materials, Equity and Beauty. 
LBC certification defines the highest measure of sustainability possible in the built 
environment based on the best science, and holds organizations accountable to an 
exceedingly high standard while recognizing that true sustainability is an ongoing journey.
An additional two projects in Boston, the Treehouse Conference Center, and 175 North 
Harvard Street project are pursuing LBC Core certification. LBC Core seeks to rapidly 
diminish the gap between the highest levels of established green building certification 
programs and the aspirations of the LBC. Certification is achieved based on actual, 
not modeled, performance and all ten imperatives are required; there are no elective 
requirements.

80
LBC Core certification is aligned not only with Harvard’s holistic approach to 
sustainability and focus on climate, health, and equity, but also with the City’s climate and 
equity goals. For example, LBC Core requires no on-site combustion, a 20% reduction 
in embodied carbon, exceeds Boston Water and Sewer Commission stormwater 
requirements, and includes equity via the inclusion imperative. These projects exemplify 
how Harvard is leading on sustainability in the built environment.
Harvard Healthier Building Academy (“HHBA”)
The HHBA, launched in 2016, is a partnership led by the Office for Sustainability together 
with researchers from the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, SEAS, and HMS. 
Since 2014, Harvard has required building project teams to reduce and eliminate specific 
classes of chemicals. The current HHBA requirements eliminate classes of chemicals 
from 14 interior product categories and are helping to send a clear market signal for 
healthier, sustainable products with positive impacts throughout the supply chain, 
including where products are manufactured. 
Harvard continues to work with vendors and suppliers, leveraging University purchasing 
power, to accelerate the transition to healthier building materials and more transparent 
supply chains. Harvard also shares lessons learned with public schools, affordable 
housing and other large owners and non-profits to help expedite solutions to this global 
systemic challenge.
On-site Renewable Energy
Over 3 MW (equivalent to powering over 2,200 homes) of on-site solar projects have 
been installed on Harvard’s rooftops, including 1.8 MW of installed storage. In addition 
to on-campus solar installations, Harvard has implemented other types of on-campus 
renewable energy sources including roof-mounted wind turbines, geothermal energy 
(ground-source heat pumps), solar hot water, and energy storage.
Embodied Carbon Reductions
In keeping with the University’s leadership on the cutting-edge of sustainable design, 
the Sustainability Action Plan and Sustainable Building Standards emphasize tracking 
and reductions of embodied carbon emissions from building materials throughout their 
life cycle, including cement with non-fossil fuel replacements to lower embodied carbon 
emissions.
Green Lab Program 
Harvard continues to advance lab sustainability efforts through its Green Lab Program 
established in 2008. Through the Lab Inhalation Risk Assessment, the University works 
to right-size laboratory ventilation using equipment that measures and analyzes chemical 
exposure. Harvard also developed a Lab Ventilation Management Plan (“LVMP”) which 
saves energy through optimizing air change rates and keeping researchers safe during 
experiments. For example, the SEC operates on an LVMP which allows the building to 
adjust the airflow to different spaces based on usage and activities. This saves energy – 
more than 30 percent of a typical lab in New England – and creates healthier conditions 
for researchers and all occupants and visitors.

81
Alignment with Massachusetts and Boston Climate Action Goals
Harvard’s commitment to climate action and sustainability are well aligned with the State 
and City goals, including:
•	The Commonwealth of Massachusetts Global Warming Solutions Act.
•	The City of Boston’s adoption of the Municipal Opt-in Specialized Stretch Energy 
Code, promoting electrification of building systems and carbon emission reductions.
•	The City of Boston’s Building Emissions Reduction and Disclosure Ordinance 
(“BERDO”) which incentivizes energy and emissions reductions.
Waste Reduction and Recycling
Harvard takes a systemic approach to waste prevention and reduction, aiming to ensure 
the materials that the University purchases and handles are used effectively and for 
as long as possible. Harvard is also strategically preventing waste throughout its value 
chain, while minimizing on-campus municipal solid waste (or trash) and sustainably 
managing other waste streams, including plastics, recyclables, and organics, as well 
as construction, demolition, and hazardous waste through Recycling and Waste 
Management.
As the primary campus waste hauler, Recycling and Waste Services is responsible for 
sustainable materials management across Harvard’s Cambridge, Allston, and Longwood 
campuses. The department manages municipal solid waste, single stream recycling, 
and food waste streams, both through its own drivers and through contracted vendors. 
Services they coordinate also include mattress recycling, textile recycling, e-waste and 
universal waste recycling, furniture and appliance pickup, waste audits, reuse events, and 
repair events.
Harvard began measuring its rate of recycling in 1989, which has since increased from 5 
percent to more than 50 percent. Continuing to improve this diversion rate is necessary 
for the Harvard community to be an effective steward of the environment and the 
materials that come in and out of that environment. These ongoing efforts, managed by 
Recycling and Waste Management, are multi-dimensional and include active participation 
from the building management community, students and student organizations, 
procurement and purchasing staff, occupant engagement groups, the Office for 
Sustainability, Environmental Health and Safety and University leadership.
Harvard measures and reports data annually for its major waste streams and is 
developing a strategic zero-waste plan by the end of 2024, which will include guidance 
and resources to help Schools and Units create their own zero-waste plans and goals.

82
Transportation
The University is developing and investing in sustainable modes of transportation, 
described previously in Chapter 4, ensuring that walking, cycling, and public transport 
are affordable and accessible. 
To improve the sustainability of its fleet, Harvard transitioned one-third of its shuttle 
buses to electric vehicles in 2021. The University also installed more than 50 electric 
vehicle charging stations for the community. 
In its Sustainability Action Plan, Harvard set the following objectives to continue to 
advance sustainable transportation options:
•	Complete the transition of Harvard’s shuttle-bus fleet to electric by 2035 and set 
new target dates for its remaining fleet vehicle types by the end of 2026 as part of 
the University’s commitment to be fossil fuel-free by 2050. This roadmap will include 
an outline for installing more charging infrastructure for university vehicles and 
equipment.
•	Maintain at least gold-level status in the League of American Bicyclists’ Bicycle 
Friendly University Program, which evaluates whether universities are effectively 
encouraging bicycling and protecting cyclists’ rights.
•	Support and enhance the pedestrian experience and sufficiently accommodate other 
personal transportation, such as Bluebikes, e-bikes, and scooters.
•	Continuously improve sustainable transportation opportunities, programs, and 
incentives for Harvard affiliates.

83
5.4. Education & Research
Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability
The Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability at Harvard is a groundbreaking new 
entity that will advance and catalyze research programs across all of Harvard’s Schools, 
turn climate research into real-world climate solutions, and enable comprehensive cross-
university education in climate and the environment. Launched in 2022, the Institute was 
made possible by a gift from Melanie and Jean Eric Salata and is led by James Stock, the 
University’s inaugural Vice Provost for Climate and Sustainability.
The Institute works closely with faculty, students, staff, and academic leadership from 
across the University to guide and further develop Harvard’s strategies for advancing 
climate research and its global impact. It also advises and collaborates across the 
University with various faculty-driven initiatives and centers as well as with the PCS and 
Office for Sustainability. The Institute will be operating at a time of transformational 
change, both in the climate and in society, as energy-source transitions and other 
climate-related changes accelerate.
The Climate Research Clusters Program is an interdisciplinary initiative that unites 
Harvard faculty, post-docs, students, practitioners, and external collaborators to research 
and propose actionable, concrete solutions to an aspect of the climate crisis. 
In its first cycle, the fund will provide more than $8.1 million over three years to projects 
that bring together 30 faculty members from several disciplines as they work toward 
ambitious and meaningful, real-world progress on important climate problems.

84
Campus as a Living Lab
Harvard is using its campus as a living lab to serve as a model for how organizations can 
help accelerate the transition to a healthier, fossil fuel-free future. Faculty and students 
are collaborating with staff to translate research into practice by piloting and proving 
exciting new solutions that can be scaled up on the local, regional, and global levels.
For instance, the SEC, completed in 2021, was certified as one of the healthiest, most 
sustainable, and energy-efficient laboratories in the world. The SEC was awarded the 
LBC Petal for Materials, Beauty, and Equity, and LEED Platinum certification. With a 
firm foundation in Harvard research, the SEC, with its innovative construction methods, 
is not only a successful demonstration project and blueprint for others, but has also 
helped influence the market to create better, healthier buildings today and for future 
generations.
During the construction of the SEC, the HHBA evaluated 6,000+ building materials and 
collaborated with 1,200 companies, ultimately motivating those companies to publicly 
disclose the ingredients in their products and create labels to help others make healthier 
decisions. The result led many manufacturing partners to reformulate their products 
to remove harmful classes of chemicals (e.g., PFAS “forever chemicals”, chemical flame 
retardants, etc.) not just for Harvard, but for all customers, and this helps protect 
communities along the supply chain as well as people in the building. OFS also worked 
with faculty researchers who published peer-reviewed science demonstrating that 
when healthier materials are bought, the reduction of chemicals of concern, like PFAS 
and chemical flame retardants, in interior spaces can be measured, as well as other 
innovative research documenting the importance of creating a healthier supply chain.

85
5.5. Community Engagement & 
External Partnerships
Green Ribbon Commission
The Boston Green Ribbon Commission (“GRC”) was established to provide advice and 
counsel to the City of Boston on the design and implementation of its Climate Action 
Plan. The GRC accelerates Boston toward a climate safe, carbon free, equitable future. 
GRC members are also working to align the resources of the key sectors, serving as 
advocates, and showing their peers what progress looks like by adopting and promoting 
leading efficiency and clean energy practices.
Harvard was the founding Chair of the Higher Ed Working Group (“HEWG”) and chaired 
the HEWG for 10 years. The HEWG leverages the higher education sector’s capabilities 
for climate action by sharing knowledge and fostering collaboration within and across 
sectors to support the City in meeting its climate goals. 
Two key reports issued by the HEWG include a lab energy use benchmarking study 
and renewable energy procurement white paper. The lab benchmarking study was 
commissioned to better understand how Boston-area lab buildings compare to 
each other and to other lab buildings nationally. The study included 121 lab buildings 
from seven institutions. It was anonymized and made publicly available to national 
benchmarking efforts. The renewable energy procurement report provided early 
guidance on the important difference between various renewable energy projects and 
how to account for the impacts of reducing emissions. 
In addition to research, the HEWG has organized multiple events for its community and 
other sectors to learn from national experts, share best practices, and discuss lessons 
learned to create shared solutions and advance collective action on climate change.
Building Emissions Reduction and Disclosure Ordinance
BERDO is a key policy for the City of Boston to achieve its Climate Action Plan and 2050 
carbon neutrality goal. Over the past ten years, the HEWG has collaborated with the City 
and other GRC working groups on policy recommendations, research, and expertise for 
the City and beyond.
Harvard, through the HEWG, has been an active and engaged stakeholder with the City as 
it established BERDO. One of the key accomplishments identified in the HEWG strategic 
plan 2021-2025 includes the HEWG providing aligned, clear group feedback and input 
on BERDO. Harvard and the HEWG continue to support the City’s Climate Action goals 
though continued feedback as the City creates new regulations and policies to implement 
BERDO.

86
Student Sustainability Leadership
Harvard has a variety of programs that engage students in sustainability action. For 
instance, the Council of Student Sustainability Leaders (“CSSL”), managed by the 
Harvard Office for Sustainability, comprises Harvard graduate and undergraduate 
students who lead and are involved in sustainability-related student groups on campus. 
CSSL also advises the PCS and OFS on University-wide sustainability strategy and 
priorities.
Harvard Innovation Labs
Harvard Innovation Labs ("i-lab") is an ecosystem that supports Harvard students and 
select alumni as they explore the world of innovation and entrepreneurship. Its Climate 
Entrepreneurs Circle is a selective incubation program for the next generation of climate 
entrepreneurs who are actively uncovering new, unexpected ways to take on climate 
change.

6. Climate Resiliency 
6. Climate Resiliency 
Photo Credit: Peter Vanderwarker

89
6.1. Introduction 
The 2013 IMP recognized the need to consider future climate conditions when planning 
for new buildings and facilities on the Allston campus. It identified potential site 
impacts related to changes in air temperature, sea surface temperature, sea levels, and 
precipitation, as well as potential resilience strategies related to each type of impact 
based on information available at the time. Newer, site-specific climate projections are 
now available and are being incorporated into Harvard’s IMP planning efforts.
In addition, several climate change adaptation-related studies and regulations have been 
published/promulgated since 2013, including Climate Ready Boston, Heat Resilience 
Solutions for Boston, the Boston Urban Forest Plan, the Department of Public Works’ 
Climate Resilient Design Standards, and the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District. 
All of this information is being incorporated into Harvard’s current planning, and the 
forthcoming IMP will address strategies for campus-wide implementation of those plans’ 
recommendations for improving resilience to increased precipitation, sea level rise, and 
extreme heat.
This section identifies the vulnerability of the Allston campus to projected climate 
impacts; describes Harvard’s past, ongoing, and future planned programs and policies 
related to climate change adaptation; and identifies adaptation strategies for the HBS 
Faculty & Administrative Office Building, the Gateway Project, the Harvard Stadium 
Addition & Renovation, the Tennis and Squash Racquet Center, the Mignone Field 
Support Building, and Crimson Catering.

90
6.2. Campus Context 
Like many areas of Boston, the Allston campus is vulnerable to future flooding and 
extreme heat resulting from climate change. According to the currently effective Federal 
Emergency Management Agency (“FEMA”) Flood Insurance Rate Map, the campus is 
not within the 1 percent annual chance floodplain. However, the campus will become 
increasingly subject to coastal storm flooding in the near-, medium- and long-term as 
sea levels rise (although less so upon implementation of the downstream district-scale 
flood protection measures recommended in Climate Ready Boston reports). Based on 
this information, parts of the campus could experience flooding 5.5 to 7.5 feet above the 
current elevation of the Charles River. (See Figure 6.1.)
The Allston campus is likely to experience precipitation-based flooding due to the 
probability that the depth of the 10-year, 24-hour design storm will increase over time, 
reaching 6 inches by the end of the century. According to the Boston Water and Sewer 
Commission’s Inundation Model Viewer, barring system-wide improvements that may be 
implemented within the next 50 years, much of the IMP Area could be subject to flooding 
during the 2070 100-yr Nor’easter storm event, with more than two feet of flooding 
expected in the vicinity of Harvard Stadium, the new HBS Administrative & Faculty 
Building, and the Mignone Field Support Building, as well as up to two feet of flooding 
in the vicinity of the Gateway Project and Crimson Catering projects. Small areas of the 
campus are likely to be vulnerable to shallow flooding during other types of storm events 
(100-year tropical storm and 10-year thunderstorm) by 2030.

91
Photo Credit: Peter Vanderwarker

92
6.3. Initiatives, Programs, and Policies
The 2013 IMP provided a framework of climate change resilience strategies and adaptation 
measures. The goal was to ensure that the buildings remain sound, that all damage from 
climate impacts would be minor and easily repairable, and that occupants remain safe. 
Harvard has made significant progress on many of the previously identified measures by 
utilizing its $12 million Green Revolving Fund which provides capital for high-performance 
campus design, operations, and maintenance, and its Office for Sustainability Grant Program 
which has awarded more than 100 grants to student projects that use Harvard’s campus as a 
living lab to create a sustainable community. 
The 2013 IMP discussed the following resilience strategies and adaptation measures:
Stormwater Management
•	Build infrastructure to withstand and recover from severe storm impacts, including 
extended flooding events: Harvard continues to sustainably manage its on-campus 
stormwater and runoff, while leveraging research related to water pollution and public 
health to inform purchasing decisions that can have impacts along the value chain.
•	Design stormwater management plans for extreme precipitation events; consider 
Adaptive Management Techniques: Klarman Hall has been renovated with multiple 
infiltration beds and a stormwater storage tank to efficiently deal with runoff. Non-
potable water collected can be used for irrigation.
Flood Damage Prevention
•	Elevate buildings to or above expected 100-year flood elevations. Methods include 
building on alternative fill, pier and beams, or bored piles: The two new buildings at 175 
North Harvard Street (Performance Center and Affiliate Housing) have been designed 
to meet the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District requirements and are elevated for 
flood protection. Klarman Hall, SEC, and DEF were designed to be above flood elevations.
•	Locate critical facilities above the first floors and basements of structures: The DEF was 
relocated from the subsurface level of the SEC to an above-grade facility above future 
flood levels, as reported out in the First Amendment to the 2013 IMP.
•	Work with the DCR to ensure that the Charles River Dam continues to be able to regulate 
the level of the Charles River in the face of severe storms and sea level rise: Harvard 
coordinates regularly with the DCR on regional resilience issues, including potential 
flooding. 
Energy Resilience
•	Diversify the energy supply to buildings, incorporate redundant energy systems, and 
incorporate innovative renewable energy options to the extent feasible to hedge against 
grid power outages: Harvard has made great strides in adding thermal and solar energy 
to the Allston campus. Completed in 2021, the SEC has been certified as one of the 
healthiest, most sustainable, and energy-efficient laboratories in the world. Thermal 
energy comes from a portfolio of equipment at the DEF allowing the University to switch 

93
between multiple supply and production configurations. As of 2022, Harvard had installed 
3 MW of solar panel capacity across all campuses including the Allston campus. Solar PV 
installations have recently been installed on Batten Hall, Chao Center, Klarman Hall, and 25 
Travis Street.
•	Create a microgrid to generate, distribute and regulate energy within the Allston campus: 
Electric power is supplied to more than 250 buildings on the Cambridge and Allston 
campuses through Harvard's 13,800-volt micro-grid. It provides redundant distribution 
circuits that can be powered via its cogeneration facility or an upstream utility.
•	Locate mechanical and electrical installations on the roof, with mechanisms to refuel in 
anticipation of potential power outages: Mechanical equipment is located on the roof of many 
buildings including the SEC. The life safety emergency generator is equipped with an on-site 
fuel tank in case of a power outage.
•	Create energy efficient building envelopes that reduce the electricity load of the building, 
especially in the summer months: The SEC was awarded the LBC Petal for Materials, Beauty, 
and Equity, and LEED Platinum certification. Its facade has been engineered to minimize 
energy consumption and maximize natural light, with a patterned envelope that protects the 
interior from solar heat gain during warmer months while letting the sun enter during the 
winter, reducing both cooling and heating demands. 
Heat Island Mitigation
•	Strategically plant trees to provide shading around buildings, thus providing natural shading 
canopies: Nearly 700 trees have been planted on campus in the past decade. Based on 
Harvard's latest tree inventory, the number of trees on the Allston campus increased by 32% 
between 2013 and 2022. A tree inventory will be included as part of the upcoming Institional 
Master Planning ("IMP") process. 
•	Design facilities to reduce the urban heat-island effect; Require green roofs or white roofs 
to reduce the summer cooling loads: Harvard had 148 LEED-certified buildings on campus. 
Green roofs have been installed at multiple buildings including Chao Center, Shad Hall, 
Klarman Hall, McArthur/McCollum Hall, Tata Hall, Class of 1959 Chapel, and the SEC. White 
roofs have been installed at Klarman Hall. 
The framework included additional strategies (primarily related to flood damage prevention) 
that have not yet been implemented, but which Harvard will continue to evaluate for the projects 
proposed as part of the IMP and as additional improvements are made to the campus. These 
include:
•	Design and construct buildings to withstand flood loads and the pressure of rising water – 
both still and moving.
•	Retrofit buildings to include appropriate flood proofing measures up to future projected 100-
year flood elevations.
•	Incorporate non-mechanical strategies to support building functionality during climate 
events.
Moving forward, Harvard will continue to review the climate adaptation strategies presented in 
documents such as Climate Ready Boston (“CRB”), Heat Resilience Solutions for Boston, and the 
Boston Urban Forest Plan, and will determine how to best incorporate those and other strategies 
with the goal of increasing the campus’ resilience to the impacts of climate change.

94
6.4. Adaptation Strategies 
The IMP Projects will be designed to be resilient to future climate conditions.
The Harvard Stadium Addition and Renovation, the Tennis and Squash Racquet Center, 
and Mignone Field Support Building projects are located within the Coastal Flood 
Resilience Overlay District ("CFROD"). The proposed work associated with each of these 
projects are subject to this ordinance as per Section 25A-4.1.(a)(i) because they include 
the erection or extension of one or more buildings that results in the addition of an 
aggregate gross floor area of 20,000 or more square feet. These projects will utilize a sea 
level rise design flood elevation (“SLR-DFE”) of 16 feet Boston City Base (“BCB”), which 
is one foot higher than the sea level rise base flood elevation (“SLR-BFE”) indicated for 
this location.¹
Although the new HBS Faculty and Administrative Office Building, Gateway Project, and 
Crimson Catering are outside of the CFROD, these buildings may also be vulnerable to 
flooding during their design lives. As such, Harvard will consider the CFROD SLR-DFE 
during the design process. No exterior renovations are planned at this time in conjunction 
with the Crimson Catering project.
The IMP Projects will demonstrate compliance with CFROD as part of Large Project 
Review or Small Project Review, as applicable.

7.1. Introduction
Since the 2013 IMP, Harvard has completed the following Boston Water and Sewer 
Commission (“BWSC”)-owned utility infrastructure improvements within and adjacent 
to the Allston campus, which have provided additional capacity and relief for the Allston 
neighborhood as well as in support of Harvard projects such as the SEC:
•	Replacement of approximately 2,000 linear feet (“LF”) of an existing BWSC 12-inch 
water main with a new 16-inch ductile iron water main along Western Avenue from 
North Harvard Street to Hague Street.
•	Replacement of approximately 1,000 LF of existing BWSC 36-inch storm drain with 
a new 72-inch reinforced concrete trunkline along Rena Path from North Harvard 
Street to Science Drive at the SEC site, as the initial phase of the North Allston Storm 
Drain Extension Project (“NASDEP”).
•	Structural lining of approximately 1,500 LF of existing BWSC 24-inch sanitary sewer 
culvert along Western Avenue, from One Western Avenue to 114 Western Avenue.
•	Installation of approximately 4,000 LF on new 12-inch ductile iron water main loops 
within the Allston campus as part of the SEC Enabling Project to provide additional 
redundancies in the BWSC system and connecting the formerly dead-end main in 
Seattle Street to new infrastructure in Western Avenue.
•	The University has commenced work on the NASDEP 84-inch culvert installation 
from the SEC site towards the DEF and future outfall to the Charles River.
In addition, stormwater management design for all new projects have improved 
previously developed and untreated areas to incorporate elements of water quality 
treatment, rainwater harvesting (SEC), bioretention basins, and infiltration prior to 
discharge to the BWSC storm drain system.

7.3. Stormwater Management and 
Regulatory Compliance
The IMP Projects will present opportunities for Harvard to continue to improve the 
quality and quantity of stormwater runoff from areas within the Allston campus. Projects 
will develop thoughtful stormwater management strategies in compliance with BWSC 
standards, particularly relative to low-impact development techniques, phosphorus and 
total suspended solids reduction, promotion of stormwater recharge, and mitigation of 
peak runoff rates. The IMP Projects will also be developed and executed in accordance 
with the Environmental Protection Agency National Pollutant Discharge Elimination 
System Construction General Permit requirements.

8.1. Introduction to Community 
Benefits 
As part of the iterative regulatory process to review and approve Harvard’s IMP, Harvard 
will propose and develop, with community input, a ten-year plan for community benefits 
commensurate with the size and scale of the institutional projects anticipated within the 
ten-year IMP duration. This will build on the success of the 2013 Cooperation Agreement 
that covered all of the 2013 IMP Projects including the three previously approved projects 
included in this IMPNF.
Similar to an earlier Allston-Brighton Community Needs Assessment dating back to 
2008, Harvard agreed to fund and participate in a City of Boston-run Allston-Brighton 
Community Needs Assessment as a community benefit associated with the July 2022 
BPDA approval for Phase A of the ERC project. The upcoming results and learnings of the 
Allston-Brighton Community Needs Assessment will inform Harvard’s IMP community 
benefits proposal.
Harvard deeply values, and has benefited greatly, from longtime relationships and 
partnerships with individuals and organizations that contribute to the vitality of Allston-
Brighton and the City of Boston. Over the course of the IMP review process, Harvard 
will access these existing relationships and partnerships to develop a renewed ten-year 
community benefit package. As in the past, Harvard will rely on and respond to feedback 
from local residents, the Harvard-Allston Task Force, Allston-Brighton’s delegation of 
elected officials, and policymakers and partners at the City of Boston and BPDA to 
inform and deliberate on community benefit priorities, culminating in an IMP cooperation 
agreement associated with the IMP approval. 
Harvard reports out annually on the implementation and impact of numerous 
cooperation agreements for community benefits associated with various institutional and 
commercial projects. Harvard had made enormous investments in creating, growing, and 
measuring the impact of programs and community benefits emanating from the Harvard 
Ed Portal, providing a helpful basis of existing programming. 
Given the enormous success and impacts emanating from the Harvard Ed Portal 
since the initial 2008 iteration, and most especially since the culmination of Harvard’s 
commitment to a transformative project for Allston-Brighton residents delivered via 
the 2015 opening of a greatly expanded Harvard Ed Portal in a newly renovated facility 
at 224 Western Avenue, Harvard’s initial thinking on IMP community benefits assumes 
continued full operation and delivery of programming and partnerships at the Harvard Ed 
Portal. 
As the regulatory and community engagement process to develop, review and approve 
a IMP and associated community benefits package begins, Harvard will continue to 
operate and staff the Harvard Ed Portal at full capacity. Harvard’s initial thinking on the 
IMP community benefits discussion is to encourage an assessment of past and ongoing 
benefit areas organized across the following categories:

102
Education 
Past agreements have included: Funding and Operation of Harvard Ed Portal, Adult 
Education and Workforce Development, Ongoing relationships with Boston Public 
Schools. 
Public realm
Past agreements have included: Maintenance of Public Parks such as Ray Mellone Park, 
Public Realm Improvements, Greenway Planning.
Grant making 
Past agreements have included: Harvard Allston Partnership Fund and Harvard- Allston 
Public Realm Flexible Fund.
Housing
Past agreements have included: the donation of Brookline Machine, the Harvard Allston 
Housing Fund.
Harvard’s goal is for community benefits discussion associated with the IMP to continue 
to achieve high impact, establish long-term programming continuity, and maintain 
programmatic flexibility to meet the evolving needs of Allston-Brighton and City 
residents.

INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN AMENDMENT
The Joslin Diabetes Center, Inc. (“Joslin”) is submitting this Institutional Master Plan
Amendment pursuant to Article 80D-9 of the Zoning Code of the City of Boston (the “Code”).
1.
Introduction and Background
1.1
2003 Institutional Master Plan
An Institutional Master Plan (the “2003 Institutional Master Plan”) for the 89,433 square feet
(2.05 acres) of land (the “2003 Institutional Master Plan Area”) owned by Joslin within the
Longwood Medical and Academic Area (“LMA”) bounded generally by Brookline Avenue,
Jos in Place, Pilgrim Road and Longwood Avenue was approved in 2003. On May 1, 2003
pursuant to Article 80D-5 of the Code, the Authority approved a “Modified Institutional Master
Plan” filed by Joslin on February 25, 2003, as the 2003 Institutional Master Plan. Map
Amendment No. 421, which was adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission on May 28, 2003,
approved the 2003 Institutional Master Plan and established the land subject to the 2003
Institutional Master Plan as an Institutional Master Plan Area. The Mayor approved the Map
Amendment on May 29, 2003. The 2003 Institutional Master Plan was for a five (5) year period
from May 1, 2003 through April 30, 2008.
The 2003 Institutional Master Plan proposed one major research project (the “2003 IMP
Project”) that would house laboratory, office and clinic space, a residential component, and
parking for 350 cars. Ultimately, Joslin did not pursue the 2003 IMP Project.
1.2
2008 Institutional Master Plan Amendment
On April 29, 2008, Joslin filed an Institutional Master Plan Amendment (the “2008 IMP
Amendment”) in order (a) to remove the 2003 IMP Project from the 2003 Institutional Master
Plan and to remove the 44,656 square foot parcel (the “PDA Project Site”) from the 2003
Institutional Master Plan Area; and (b) to extend the term of the Joslin IMP for a period of ten
(10) years from the date of BPDA’s approval thereof (i.e., from April 29, 2008 to April 29,
2018). The BPDA Board approved the 2008 IMP Amendment on April 29, 2008. The Boston
Zoning Commission approved the 2008 IMP Amendment and the accompanying Map
Amendment on May 29, 2008 (the “2008 Map Amendment”). After approval of the 2008 IMP
Amendment and the 2008 Map Amendment, the Joslin Institutional Master Plan Area (the “IMP
Area”) was revised to consist of 44,777 square feet bounded generally by Brookline Avenue,
Joslin Place, Pilgrim Road and the PDA Project Site, which Site is known commonly as 415
Brookline Avenue and is depicted on Figure 1.2 below.

2018 Institutional Master Plan Amendment
The purpose of this Institutional Master Plan Amendment is (a) to renew the term of the
Institutional Master Plan Amendment for five (5) years from April 29, 2018 to April 29, 2023;
and (b) to add to the allowed first-floor uses permitted by the Institutional Master Plan (which

Master Plan Amendment, to amend it by renewing the term of the Institutional Master Plan from

Restaurant Uses) and Service Uses within the first-floor of the Institutional Master Plan Area,
and to, where appropriate, update the information presented as to matters such as Workforce
Development.

2.
Mission and Objectives
2.1
Joslin Mission Statement
The healthcare epidemic of our time, diabetes, affects more than 20 million Americans. In the
face of this public health crisis, Joslin Diabetes Center, a Harvard Medical School-affiliated
institution, is executing the largest categorical attack on the disease in the world.
Joslin is the world’s largest diabetes research center, diabetes clinic and provider of diabetes
education. Its concentrated focus on a single disease allows it to rapidly discover, create and
distribute new knowledge about diabetes prevention, treatment options and research toward a
cure.
Joslin is committed to addressing the challenges of diabetes from all angles, to deliver
exceptional, compassionate care and education to not only treat, but also empower patients and
their families to help manage diabetes and improve their overall health and quality of life.
The ultimate goal of this approach is to help people with diabetes live long, healthy lives and
offer real hope and progress toward prevention and a cure. Our mission is to improve the lives of
people with diabetes and its complications through innovative care, education and research that
will lead to the prevention and cure of the disease.
2.2
Major Operating Divisions
Among the Harvard Medical School-affiliated institutions, Joslin is one of the most research-
intensive academic medical centers and is unique in its sole focus on diabetes.
Founded in 1898 by a single physician, Elliott P. Joslin, M.D., Joslin today employs
approximately 480 individuals in the following major areas:
• Joslin Research: a highly collaborative team of people undertaking the largest research
program aimed at preventing and curing type 1 and type 2 diabetes and their long-
term complications.
• Joslin Clinic, Inc.: the world’s first and most respected diabetes care facility, which
cares for approximately 23,000 adult and pediatric patients a year.
Joslin Education and Care: Provides innovative learning programs that expand the
availability of Joslin knowledge and expertise to people with diabetes and the
clinicians who care for them domestically and across the globe.
Joslin Administration: Provides administrative and operational support in Finance,
Human Resources, IT and other administrative areas.

2.2.1
Joslin Research
Joslin research comprises the most comprehensive and productive effort in diabetes research
anywhere in the world. Joslin researchers focus on unraveling the biologic, biochemical and
genetic processes that underlie the development of type 1 and type 2 diabetes and related
complications.
Joslin research is highly innovative and imaginative, employing the newest tools in genetics,
genomics and proteomics to identify abnormalities that may play a role in the development of
diabetes and its complications. Joslin Clinic patients, and others with diabetes, have the option of
participating in clinical trials at Joslin to help translate basic research into treatment innovations.
Joslin has one of the largest diabetes training programs in the world, educating approximately
130 physicians and Ph.D. researchers each year, many of whom go on to lead diabetes initiatives
at leading institutions all over the globe. Three Joslin researchers are members of the prestigious
National Academy of Science, a rare accomplishment even in large academic medical and
research institutions.
Joslin’s research budget has grown 15-fold since 1983, with strong support from the National
Institutes of Health. Other support for Joslin research comes from the Juvenile Diabetes Research
Foundation, the American Diabetes Association, as well as from individuals, foundations and
industry.
2.2.2
Joslin Clinic, Inc.
Joslin Clinic, since its inception, has focused on comprehensive care of the patient. Joslin’ s team
consists of board-certified physicians expert in treating diabetes, Certified Diabetes Educators,
Behavioral Health experts providing the patient with all care needed to live a full and productive
life with Diabetes. Joslin has a large patient database and the largest patient population using
insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors. Joslin’s 23,000 patients benefit from highly
specialized care.
Dr. Elliott P. Joslin is credited with creating modern day diabetes care, which utilizes a combined
medical and educational team approach to empower patients to manage their disease in order to
prevent complications. Dr. Joslin was an early champion of tight glucose control and was proven
right 75 years later by the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT).
Today, Joslin’s care teams are made up of highly specialized and multi-skilled experts in all
facets of diabetes, including adult and pediatric diabetes, kidney disease, eye care, mental health
and pregnancy, as well as Certified Diabetes Educators — nurses, dietitians, exercise
physiologists, nurse practitioners and mental health professionals. Joslin clinicians are relentless
in their pursuit of diabetes complications, which are a devastating burden to the patient, their
family and the national healthcare system.
6
4824-2646-6656.4

The impact Joslin has in preventing complications is second to none. Our care model is proof
that with the recommended standard of care and management, complications of diabetes can be
prevented or reversed. Joslin Clinic consistently ranks among the best in the care of patients with
diabetes as measured by national quality indicator data collected by American Diabetes
Association, National Committee on Quality Assurance and numerous private and for-profit
health data consortiiims, including Bridges to Excellence.
Beetham Eye Institute: Integral to patient care is the delivery of the world’s finest diabetes eye
treatment through Joslin’s Beetham Eye Institute. Techniques pioneered at the Beetham have
preserved the vision of more than nine million people around the globe.
Pediatric Health Services: Joslin Clinic provides pioneering care and support of pediatric
patients and their families. Joslin cares for a large portion of children with diabetes in
Massachusetts and more than a quarter of all children with diabetes in New England. Joslin
provides the widest range of patient and family support programs anywhere.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center: Joslin Clinic is affiliated with the Beth Israel
Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), a teaching hospital affiliate of Harvard Medical School.
Together, Joslin assists BIDMC primarily in the inpatient setting at the hospital.
2.2.3
Joslin Care and Education Initiatives
Joslin’ s care and education initiatives focus on improving the quality of diabetes care around the
globe. These programs include professional medical education, telemedicine services,
Publications, Affiliated Centers and education provided directly to hospital physicians and nurses
at various locations around the world. Joslin has the largest and most expansive diabetes
continuing medical education program in the world. Since 2002, Joslin professional education
has reached more than 500,000 healthcare providers.
Joslin also provides a wealth of patient education through books, videos and online services,
allowing people around the globe to learn how Joslin experts recommend they manage their
disease.
2.3
Collaboration with Other Institutions
Our affiliation with Harvard Medical School gives Josh11 researchers opportunities to collaborate
with other investigators with complementary interests and expertise. Most Joslin researchers and
clinicians have academic appointments at Harvard Medical School and several are involved in
Ph.D. training at the Medical School.
Our investigators are advancing science at an unusually fast pace due to Joslin’s unique
environment. For example, Joslin’s Diabetes Endocrinology Research Center (DERC) provides
the infrastructure necessary to support research efforts across all the disciplines and encourage
the development of young scientists. The DERC offers researchers specialized technical
assistance as well as a network of colleagues from across the medical and scientific community.
The DERC framework facilitates translational research—that is, the collaboration between basic

scientists and clinical investigators—resulting in breakthroughs that make a difference to the
millions of people living with diabetes.
These types of collaborations offer an incredibly rich setting in which to work, and provide a
significant asset to our researchers. Two other important examples are our affiliations with Beth
Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, which enables Joslin researchers
to work with investigators with complementary interests and expertise through such programs as
the Harvard Stem Cell Institute; the Clinical Islet Transplantation Program at Harvard Medical
School; and the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation Center on Immunological Tolerance in
Type 1 Diabetes. In addition, Joslin is part of the Boston Autologous Islet Replacement Therapy
Program (BAIRT), an academic and industry sponsored research program that looks to link a
patient’s own insulin producing cells to cure Diabetes.
Joslin maintains close links to other LMA institutions, including Children’s Hospital for
pediatrics inpatient care and training of fellows in pediatric endocrinology.

3.
Existing Property and Uses
3.1
Description of Existing Campus
The Joslin campus as it appears today is essentially one building comprised of two separate
wings. The original Joslin research and clinic facility was constructed at the corner of Pilgrim
Road and Joslin Place in 1956 and remains in active use today supporting clinical and research
programs (the “1950s Building”).
A second wing, the Howard F. Root Wing on Brookline Avenue was completed in 1976, to
provide Joslin with additional space for research and clinical activities. This structure was
originally four stories in height (50 feet) and included retail space on the first floor level along
Brookline Avenue. At the time it was constructed, the design allowed for three additional floors.
Joslin subsequently completed the expansion of this building in 1991, by adding three stories
along Brookline Avenue and raising the courtyard to the Pilgrim Road level. A portion of the
courtyard was enclosed for visitor and staff lounge fl4nctions.
Joslin presently occupies approximately 242,300 gsf~ consisting of research, clinic, and
administrative space. In addition, Joslin has historically leased retail, office and restaurant space
on the first floor along Brookline Avenue (approximately 12,000 gsf). At the time of its 1991
expansion, Joslin was issued permission for conditional use and variance from the City of
Boston, Board of Appeal (BZC -15190 dated November 19, 1991) allowing for aFAR of 3.9.
This variance allowed Joslin to achieve a maximum height of 100 feet from average site grade
(eight stories) along Brookline Avenue.
After approval of the IMP Area under the 2008 IMP Amendment, the FAR of the existing
improvements on the IMP Area was increased to approximately 5.4.
3.2
Pedestrian Access
Pedestrian access to the main reception area of Joslin is accessible via Joslin Place. Through the
main entrance Joslin’s Beetham Eye unit can be accessed. The Pilgrim Road access provides
access to Pediatrics and Adult Diabetes clinics on the second floor. All entrances are
handicapped accessible.
3.3
Parking and Loading Facilities
Joslin’s parking needs are provided by garages located in the Longwood Medical Area. Joslin
does not have any parking available of its own. Employee parking is offered through Joslin’s
affiliation with MASCO and area parking companies. Loading dock and trash disposal functions
are accommodated within the completed PDA Project, known as Longwood Center, by virtue of
a lease agreement between the owner of the PDA Project and Joslin.

4.
Needs of the Institution
4.1
Regional and National Trends
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, diabetes affects approximately
30.3 million Americabs and is the seventh leading cause of death in the U.S. Recently released
data from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) shows that in 2015, diabetes claimed more
than 252,806 lives. Increases in types 1 and 2 diabetes, as well as obesity, are also being
observed in children and adolescents presenting future challenges to the healthcare system.
Meanwhile, the financial burden associated with diabetes is staggering. In 2012, between
healthcare costs and lost productivity, diabetes costs the nation $245 billion annually. The ADA
estimates that one out of every five healthcare dollars is spent caring for someone with diabetes.
4.2
Strengths and Weaknesses of the Existing Campus
Joslin’ s present location in the LMA is ideal for multi-institutional research collaborations and
its major partners for clinical care are located in this area. However, while Joslin’s existing
facilities have served it well in its quest to eradicate diabetes, the prevalence of diabetes
continues. Additional research, alternative health care approaches, and an increased amount of
educational programs are necessary. The cu~ent infrastructure limits Joslin’s ability to expand
its research programs and its staff, to promote innovative approaches, and to support stronger
educational outreach programs. Research and clinical space are used to capacity.
Joslin anticipates that the greatest infrastructure needs will be in three areas:
• Well-trained staff: As the complexity of research and demands for clinical services
increase, the need for well-trained staff with a broad range of expertise will grow.
• Patient care and Administration: Joslin may need additional space to care for the ever
growing diabetic population.
• Lab and Research Facilities: Existing facilities are becoming antiquated and are
increasingly inadequate to optimally house even Joslin’s current programming needs.
The facility age and limitations impede Joslin’s ability to achieve its mission, as well as
the needed growth in research and administrative functions.
