5.
Proposed Future Projects
5.1
Long-term Planning
Joslin is in the process of developing long-range space plans (e.g. beyond the 5-year term of this
Institutional Master Plan) that may include renovations of the buildings to ensure suitability for
use as a world-class research and clinical care facility.
5.2
Effect of Approval of the IMP Amendment
Pursuant to Article 80D of the Code, upon approval of this Institutional Master Plan Amendment
by the BPDA, uses or structures existing or described in this Institutional Master Plan will be
deemed to be in compliance with the use, dimensional, parking and loading requirements of
underlying zoning (including special purpose overlay districts) and may be reconstructed after
casualty, notwithstanding any provision of underlying zoning to the contrary and without the
requirement of further zoning relief.
So long as the existing uses or structures are consistent with the provisions of this Institutional
Master Plan, the existing uses or structures may be located on multiple contiguous parcels or
lots, whether or not any portion of the existing uses or structures satisfies the provisions of the
underlying zoning. Consistent therewith, any yard and setback requirements shall be measured
at the exterior property lines of the IMP Area, and shall not apply to any interior lots that may
exist or be created within the IMP Area. Building Height shall have the same meaning as
defined in Article 2A and shall be measured to the top of the last occupiable floor.
5.3
Future Building Renovation and Maintenance Projects
Throughout the term of this Institutional Master Plan, Joslin may conduct ongoing building
renovation projects and other campus improvements which may consist of an erection of
extension of an Institutional Use but which may be below the threshold for IMP Review or Large
Project Review. So long as each such project or improvement are below 20,000 SF GFA in the
aggregate, such work may be conducted without amendment of this Institutional Master Plan and
the permitted FAR under this Institutional Master Plan shall be deemed adjusted accordingly to
not greater than approximately 5.9. In accordance with Article 80D-7 of the Code, Joslin will
submit biannual updates from the date of approval of the IMP. These biannual updates will
include updates on any building renovation and maintenance projects.
5.4
Future Leased or Purchased Space
Joslin has no current plans to purchase or lease additional space located outside of the IMP Area.
Any such facility, to the extent it exceeds IMP exemption thresholds, would not require an
amendment to this Institutional Master Plan as long as the use category of the underlying zoning
which most closely described the use of such facility is either allowed as of right by the
underlying zoning or is allowed by zoning relief obtained by the property owner. This will give
Joslin the needed flexibility to meet its space and parking needs. In accordance with Article 80D-

From time to time during the term of this Institutional Master Plan, Joslin may reallocate Gross
Floor Area among the various Hospital Subuses, including certain High Impact Subuses (Facility

reallocation will not require an amendment to this Institutional Master Plan as long as the Gross
Floor Area devoted to High Impact Subuses is not increased. This will give Joslin the needed
flexibility to meet its operational needs.

Introduction/Consistency with LMA Interim Guidelines For Transportation
Under the LMA Interim Guidelines, the LMA’s transportation guidelines are applicable to

Transportation Demand Management (“TDM”)

o Biking — Joslin provides on-site bike racks for employees.

System-wide Transportation Projects

Current Workforce Development Efforts
Joslin has invested heavily in Workforce Development Programs and has an extensive array of
programs to help retain current workers, improve their skills, and help them qua1if~r for

time and full-time.

• ESL Training - There are three levels of instruction in English as a Second Language
offered in partnership with Dana Farber Cancer Institute. The levels of instruction range
from beginner to advanced, and is based on communications proficiency in speaking,
listening, conversational skills and vocabulary.
• Tuition Reimbursement Program - Tuition and laboratory fees are reimbursed based
on length of service, up to the company maximums per fiscal year. Courses eligible for
reimbursement include those related to the employee’s current position, are required as
part of a degree-granting program, or taken for career advancement within Joslin.
Reimbursement is paid upon satisfactory passing of the class.

public speaking, and leadership skills, as well as specialized computer applications.

internship opportunities. Joslin averages 10 interns and 5-6 mentors per year. One mentor

8.
Community Benefits
8.1
Impact on the Surrounding Area
Joslin is one of the most significant assets to the patient and medical community in Boston, a city
regarded as the country’s preeminent medical center. Here, Joslin plays a vital role as the only
Harvard Medical School Affiliated institution with a sole focus on diabetes. Joslin’s invaluable
educational programs and care resources benefit patients in the surrounding neighborhood, the
City of Boston and the New England region. Some of these benefits include:
• Joslin is aunique resource for people with diabetes and its complications. With 40
physicians on staff—the world’s largest team of board-certified physicians treating
diabetes— Joslin has a concentration of knowledge and support to help people manage
this difficult disease. Joslin has the largest patient database in the world—23,000 active
patients who make more than 70,000 visits a year, commuting to Boston from
surrounding towns and from all over New England for the best diabetes care available.
• Diabetes affects more than 6.2% of the population in Massachusetts. Joslin cares for 51-
76% of kids with diabetes in Massachusetts and 23-34% of kids with diabetes in New
England.
8.2
Special Programs
As part of Joslin’s clinical services, Joslin serves groups at high risk of developing diabetes, such
as African Americans, Latinos and Asian Americans. Two of Joslin’s programs offer unique
opportunities for Latinos and Asian Americans to receive diabetes care that is both linguistically
appropriate and culturally relevant.
8.2.1
Latino Diabetes Initiative (LDI)
The LDI at Joslin is designed to improve health outcomes for Latinos, who are one and one-half
times more likely to develop diabetes than non-Latino Caucasian Americans. Through vigorous
community outreach initiatives that aim to address common myths and perceptions about
diabetes, and in tandem with clinic services in Spanish, Joslin delivers innovative and specialized
care to Latinos in Boston, and from around the world. Outreach programs include: Beisbol y
Salud (Mo Peace Foundation), Bailey Salud (Dance for Health) — community dance program,
group visits, outreach to churches and other community gathering places, Rosa’s Story novella.
8.2.2
Asian American Diabetes Initiative (AADI)
The AADI was established in recognition of the growing challenge of diabetes in the Asian
American population. Joslin has implemented educational outreach programs that increase
awareness of diabetes in Asian communities, and draw these populations to the Joslin Clinic.
Through the AADI, patients receive culturally appropriate diabetes care from a team of doctors,
as well as a JoslinCare ambassador that offers translation services, coordinates appointments,

Department Comments
Included here are Boston Public Works Department (PWD) comments for the Massachusetts College of Pharmacy
and Health Sciences IMPNF.
Project Coordination:
The developer should coordinate with the City of Boston if proposing any changes in use, dimensional, parking, or
loading elements.
Project Specific Scope Considerations:
The developer should coordinate with BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for
pedestrians and cyclists in the area.
Pedestrian Access:
The developer should consider extending the scope of sidewalk improvements along the site frontage.
Site Plan:
The developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb
functionality on both sides of all streets that abut the property.
 
Construction Within The Public vs Private Right-of-Way:
Although the general comments below apply specifically to work associated with the project within the public
right-of-way, it is preferred and encouraged for construction in the private right-of-way to be consistent with City
standards for public ways, as well, to the extent possible. Should these streets ever become public ways, they must
conform to the City standards as outlined below.
All work within the public way shall conform to Boston Public Works Department (PWD) standards. Any
non-standard materials proposed within the public way will require approval through the Public
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification
(LM&I) Agreement with the PIC.
Sidewalks:
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet
current American’s with Disabilities Act (ADA)/ Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines,
including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections
abutting the project site if not already constructed to ADA/AAB compliance per Code of Massachusetts Regulations
Title 521, Section 21 (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/521-CMR-21-curb-cuts). This includes converting apex
ramps to perpendicular ramps at intersection corners and constructing or reconstructing reciprocal pedestrian
ramps where applicable. Plans showing the extents of the proposed sidewalk improvements associated with this
project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb geometry
will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC.
Please note that at signalized intersections, any alteration to pedestrian ramps may also require upgrading the
traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and
Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) requirements. Any changes to the traffic signal system must
be coordinated and approved by BTD.

All proposed sidewalk widths and cross-slopes must comply to both City of Boston and ADA/AAB standards.
The developer is encouraged to contact the City’s Disabilities Commission to confirm compliant accessibility within
the Public ROW.
Green Infrastructure:
The developer shall work with PWD, the Green Infrastructure Division, and the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission (BWSC) to determine appropriate methods of green infrastructure and stormwater management
systems within the Public ROW. The ongoing maintenance of such systems shall require an LM&I Agreement with
the PIC.
Driveway Curb Cuts
Any proposed driveway curb cuts within the Public ROW will need to be reviewed and approved by the PIC. All
existing curb cuts that will no longer be utilized shall be closed.
Discontinuances
Any discontinuances (sub-surface, surface or above surface) within the Public ROW must be processed through
the PIC.
Easements
Any easements within the Public ROW associated with this project must be processed through the PIC.
Landscaping
The developer must seek approval from the Chief Landscape Architect with the Parks and Recreation Department
for all landscape elements within the Public ROW. The landscaping program must accompany a LM&I with the
PIC.
Street Lighting
The developer must seek approval from the PWD Street Lighting Division, where needed, for all proposed street
lighting to be installed by the developer. All proposed lighting within the Public ROW must be compatible with the
area lighting to provide a consistent urban design. The developer should coordinate with the PWD Street Lighting
Division for an assessment of any additional street lighting upgrades that are to be considered in conjunction with
this project. All existing metal street light pull box covers within the limits of sidewalk construction to remain shall be
replaced with new composite covers per PWD Street Lighting standards. Metal covers should remain for pull box
covers in the roadway. For all sections of sidewalk that are to be reconstructed in the Public ROW that contain or
are proposed to contain a City-owned street light system with underground conduit, the developer shall be
responsible for installing shadow conduit adjacent to the street lighting system. Installation of shadow conduit and
limits should be coordinated through the BPDA Smart Utilities team.
Roadway
Based on the extent of construction activity, including utility connections and taps, the developer will be responsible
for the full restoration of the roadway sections that immediately abut the property and, in some cases, to extend the
limits of roadway restoration to the nearest intersection. A plan showing the extents and methods for roadway
restoration shall be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval.
Additional Project Coordination
All projects must be entered into the City of Boston Utility Coordination Software (COBUCS) to review for any
conflicts with other proposed projects within the Public ROW. The developer must coordinate with any existing
projects within the same limits and receive clearance from PWD before commencing work.

Resiliency:
Proposed designs should follow the Boston Public Works Climate Resilient Design Guidelines
(https://www.boston.gov/environment-and-energy/climate-resilient-design-guidelines) where applicable.
Please note that these are the general standard and somewhat specific PWD requirements. More detailed
comments may follow and will be addressed during the PIC review process. If you have any questions, please feel
free to contact me at jeffrey.alexis@boston.gov or at 617-635-4966.

1.1 
INTRODUCTION 
Pursuant to Section 80D-8 and 80D-5(2)(e) of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”), MCPHS 
University (f/k/a Massachusetts College of Pharmacy and Health Sciences, and hereinafter “MCPHS” 
or the “University”) submits this Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) to the City of 
Boston Planning Department (“BPD”) to commence the process for renewing and extending the 
approved 2014-2024 MCPHS University Institutional Master Plan (“MCPHS IMP” or “IMP”) for two 
years so that the MCPHS IMP will then be set to expire July 23, 2026. In addition, pursuant to 
Section 80D-7 of the Code, MCPHS is providing its biannual update to the IMP. 
The MCPHS IMP was approved by the then Boston Redevelopment Authority on June 19, 2014, and 
by the Boston Zoning Commission on July 23, 2014, with an effective date of July 23, 2014. The 
IMP was amended for the first time on August 10, 2017, to approve the Brant House expansion 
project at 704 Huntington Avenue. 
This IMPNF renewal and extension request summarizes below (i) the need for an IMP renewal and 
extension, (ii) an update on the institutional projects, campus updates and improvements, future 
potential projects, and public benefits of the IMP, and (iii) a request for a two-year renewal and 
extension of the IMP. 
1.2 
THE NEED FOR AN IMP RENEWAL & EXTENSION 
The current MCPHS IMP is set to expire on July 23, 2024, and given the shifting demographic and 
market conditions that not only generally impact higher education institutions, but also specifically 
impact health science focused institutions, MCPHS seeks an extension of the IMP to fully analyze 
and determine next steps for its Boston Campus. 
MCPHS is a private, coeducational university offering graduate, professional and undergraduate 
degrees in health sciences. Founded in 1823, the University is the oldest institution of higher 
education in the City of Boston, and is home to the second oldest college of pharmacy in the United 
States. Its main campus is located in Boston’s Longwood Medical and Academic Area (the “Boston 
Campus”), and in addition, the University has campuses in Worcester, Massachusetts and 
Manchester, New Hampshire. MCPHS has a diverse offering of professional and undergraduate 
degrees in pharmacy and pharmaceutical science, nursing, physician assistant studies, dental 
hygiene, optometry, radiologic sciences, health psychology, public health, chemistry, and 
premedical and health studies. Graduate programs are offered in drug regulatory affairs and health 
policy, pharmaceutical economics and policy, drug discovery and development, pharmaceutical 
sciences, medicinal chemistry, pharmaceutics, pharmacology, and clinical research. 
The University’s short-term and long-term program needs and objectives are based on the 
institution’s internal goals, but are also heavily influenced and impacted by external factors and 
trends; most notably: shifts in demographics, market demands for specific program types, and 
housing. Externally, the University grapples with the same larger demographic constraints facing 
all other institutions of higher education – especially in the Northeastern United States – which is 
that due to a drop in the birth rates since the “Great Recession” or 2008, institutions are expecting 
to compete for approximately 20% fewer students by the middle of this decade. In addition, shifting

Chapter 1: Introduction
Pursuant to Section 80D-8 and 80D-5(2)(e) of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”), New England 
Conservatory (“NEC”) submits this Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) to the Boston 
Planning and Development Agency (“BPDA”) to commence the process for renewing the approved New 
England Conservatory Institutional Master Plan 2012-2022 (“NEC IMP” or “IMP”) for two years extending the 
expiration date to September 13, 2024.
In addition, pursuant to Section 80D-7 of the Code, New England Conservatory is providing its biannual 
update to the IMP. 
The New England Conservatory IMP was approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA,” now 
“BDPA”) on July 12, 2012, the effective date of the NEC IMP was September 13, 2012 (Map amendment #552).
1.1 Institutional Master Plan Renewal Request & Update
The current NEC IMP is set to expire on September 13, 2022. In January of 2019, the conservatory welcomed 
a new President, Andrea Kalyn. President Kalyn, along with board leadership and members of both faculty and 
staff, spent the remainder of 2019 developing an initial Strategic Planning framework. This Strategic Planning 
framework resulted in the creation of four strategic pillars: student experience, social cultural relevance, 
technology, and financial sustainability along with a guiding vision that NEC will advance music’s role in society 
by cultivating musical minds. NEC exists at the nexus of excellence and exploration, educating musicians of 
profound artistry with unparalleled expertise, innovation, technical mastery, and collaboration. Driven by 
passion and curiosity, NEC faculty and students will forge new pathways for musicianship that elevate the lives 
of individuals, communities, and society writ large.
Supporting the Strategic Planning framework, NEC held a series of initial kick-off meetings for its internal 
Campus Master Planning effort in February 2020. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, this initiative did not 
proceed beyond these preliminary meetings. 
Coming out of the 2021-22 academic year, New England Conservatory is laying the framework to look forward 
and having the time to focus the Conservatory’s attention on its future translating the Strategic Plan into the 
next IMP. The Conservatory hopes to begin working in earnest on its next ten-year Institutional Master Plan 
no later than the first quarter of 2023.
Since March 2020, the Conservatory has been focused on its response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Presented 
with unprecedented barriers through 2020 and 2021, NEC’s partners and students rose to the challenge; the 
2020-2021 academic year saw NEC students teach over 1,200 virtual hours, lead over 1,000 teaching visits, 
perform nearly 100 virtual performances and events, and reach an estimated 10,000 people. From teaching 
front line workers through our partnership with Massachusetts General Hospital, to meeting young students 
virtually for band lessons in East Boston schools, to mastering the technology for virtual performances in 
nursing homes, schools, and libraries; through it all, these students and partners went above and beyond with 
an abundance of trust, resiliency, and true generosity of spirit. We could not be prouder of the collaborative 
achievements and of the relationships that have contributed towards education, growth, and healing in the 
Boston community.

Chapter 2: New England Conservatory Background
The oldest independent school of music in the United States, NEC was founded in 1867 by Eben Tourjée at 
a time when post- Civil War society was demanding American-centric musical culture. The Conservatory’s 
curriculum is remarkable for its wide range of styles and traditions, with the school growing from seven rooms 
rented above Music Hall on Tremont Street to its own dedicated facility in Jordan Hall in 1903 where it has 
operated since. 
NEC’s mission is to educate and train musicians of all ages from around the world, drawing on the talent and 
deep reservoir of experience of its distinguished faculty. NEC is dedicated to inculcating the highest standards 
of excellence and nurturing individual artistic sensibility and creative growth. Understanding that music is 
one of the transcendent expressions of human civilization, NEC aspires to ensure it has a central place in 
contemporary society.
In support of this mission, NEC features undergraduate and graduate-level training in classical, jazz, 
contemporary improvisation, world, and early music. Through expanded education programs, including 
the Preparatory School, NEC provides training and performance opportunities for a 5-year average of 1,600 
children, pre-college students, adults, and seniors. Through its Community Performances and Partnerships 
(CPP) projects, NEC offers young musicians the opportunity to engage with community-based audiences in 
schools, hospitals, community centers and nursing homes, bringing pleasure to new young listeners, the 
elderly, and other underserved audiences, and enlarging the universe for classical music and many other 
genres. 
Looking to the future, NEC will continue to be central to the future of music. Propelled by profound artistry, 
bold creativity, and deep compassion, NEC will amplify the impact of musicians to advance shared humanity. 
Fusing artistic excellence with access, rigor with risk-taking, tradition with technology, collaboration with 
community, NEC will embody the shared tenant that music connects and enlivens. 
NEC students will be empowered to meet a dynamic world head-on, equipped with the tools and emboldened 
with the confidence needed to forge multidimensional lives of artistic depth and relevance. NEC will continue 
to be an incubator for artistic excellence and a hub of disciplined artistic exploration. Through the art of 
sound, NEC will inspire the future. 
2.1 History, Mission, and Vision
NEC presents more than 900 free concerts each year, many of them held in its world-renowned Jordan Hall, a 
National Historic Landmark famous for its superb acoustics and beautifully restored interior. These programs 
range from solo recitals to chamber music to orchestral programs to jazz, contemporary improvisation, and 
opera scenes. Every year, NEC’s Opera Studies department also presents two fully staged opera productions.
NEC is a founding partner of Project STEP, Boston Children’s Chorus, and the String Training and Education 
Program, which for more than 40 years has provided rigorous pre-professional music preparation for BIPOC 
children. NEC is also a member of the Fenway Alliance, a consortium of 21 nationally and internationally 
renowned cultural and academic institutions located in the Fenway that creates innovative and relevant 
programming in the Boston community. As part of the Fenway Alliance, NEC has participated in the Opening 
Our Doors festival - an annual day of free cultural experiences - for the past twenty years, as well as Fenway 
Porchfest, a partnership of Fenway Alliance, Fenway CDC, and Fenway Civic Association.

Since 2019 and through the support of the Mellon Foundation, NEC has also hosted the Boston Bridge to 
Equity and Achievement in Music (BEAM) program. In collaboration with Boston Youth Symphony Orchestras, 
the Community Music Center of Boston, Project STEP, and the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Boston BEAM’s 
mission is to create a region-wide collective solution for supporting and sustaining musical excellence 
among young musicians of historically excluded populations who self-identify as aspiring to careers in the 
classical music profession. BEAM’s primary goal is to increase racial and ethnic diversity in post-secondary 
instrumental classical music programs to increase diversity in the field of classical music, especially in 
orchestras. 
In the 2020-21 academic year, the CPP program had 124 partnerships with schools, senior centers, community 
centers, hospitals, libraries, museums, and historic landmarks. More than 100 NEC students taught over 1,200 
virtual hours, led over 1,000 teaching visits, performed nearly 100 virtual performances and events, and 
reached over 10,000 people. 
NEC’s work with Boston Public Schools dates to the inception of the CPP program in 2003 and has prioritized 
alignment at the district level to meet student needs during in school and out of school time. Over the last 
decade, CPP has worked on average with 15 schools annually, reaching 5,000 students through performances, 
weekly teaching, project-based residencies, workshops, and an annual touring children’s opera. During the 
pandemic, NEC successfully partnered with teachers at 9 Boston Public Schools to provide remote lessons, 
group classes, performances, and residencies. Through a generous grant, CPP will begin a pilot program 
during the 2022-23 school year focused on students in grades 5 and 6 to offer 200-250 hours of private music 
lessons. Following the initial pilot, NEC hopes to expand the opportunity to more grade levels and partners.
NEC looks forward to building upon the success of these relationships to provide more access to private 
lesson instruction, as well as create more robust pipelines for teaching artists entering the field. This 
includes opportunities for students to develop as teachers—practicing artists with the complementary skills, 
curiosities, and habits of mind of educators—who can apply their musicianship to learning in, through, and 
around the arts. Students will engage artistically, effectively, and ethically with diverse communities through 
practical coursework, mentoring, and experiential opportunities in a broad range of settings, including 
in Boston schools, after-school programs, senior living facilities, and community organizations. At the 
Preparatory School, NEC has plans to expand its offerings and continue the development of strong community 
partnerships, to further remove barriers to the delivery of a meaningful and engaging music education 
experience. In addition to educating future musicians, NEC will focus the work of its Prep School to create the 
audience of tomorrow for musicians.

The 2012 NEC Institutional Master Plan projected a ten-year vision for the Conservatory and incorporated the 
following key projects:

“Learning Center” project on the current 33 Gainsborough Street site.

Additionally, NEC identified continued investments on various ongoing projects to maintain and improve 
existing facilities throughout the IMP. These ongoing projects may include (but are not limited to): repair 
and maintenance-related projects and activities, minor additions to or removal of minor portions of 
existing facilities, additions to or removal of on-campus parking spaces, improvements to existing building 
finishes, infrastructure, and systems, and/or change of uses of portions of existing buildings on the NEC 
campus to accommodate on-campus relocation of various functions related to NEC’s ongoing operations 
and the development of the Proposed Projects.
NEC has completed Phase 1, with the SLPC opening in September 2017. The SLPC houses approximately 
255 students, and together with the library and dining commons, is the new campus center for students, 
faculty, staff, and visitors. The Center’s three modestly-scaled new performance spaces – a 200-seat Black Box 
theater, orchestra rehearsal room, and ensemble/recording room - are used by students for performances and 
rehearsals, as well as for public performances. The adjacent dining areas serve dual functions as breakout and 
reception areas for evening and other performance events, in addition to providing modern, affordable dining 
options to NEC students, faculty and staff, and to members of the public.
The only Institutional Project not yet completed from the 2012-2022 IMP is Phase 2; this project was 
intended to follow Phase 1, the SLPC project, and was contingent on the reallocation of the program from 
33 Gainsborough. The future program needs of Phase 2 are currently being refined to match the emerging 
Strategic Plan direction and vision for curricular development. It is anticipated that the next IMP for NEC will 
re-frame these objectives. There are no plans to advance this project before the submission of NEC’s next 10-
year IMP.

•	
Establishing Green Building Practices for Campus:
NEC has incorporated several green practices in existing facilities across campus. These include the 
incorporation of food waste composting from the dining hall, recycling of paper, plastic, and metal, water 
bottle fill stations, as well as an electronics recycling program aimed at redirecting waste from operations. 
Additionally, carbon neutral carpet tiles have been specified as standard floor covering to reduce the 
operational impact of interior materials. Further, NEC has been working to install high albedo roofing 
material to reduce heat island effect and the amount of heat energy absorbed. 
•	
Decreasing Energy and Wastewater Through Efficiency Upgrades: 
NEC has installed metered faucets, low-flow toilets, and shower heads as well as a comprehensive LED 
retrofit of existing facilities replacing incandescent and fluorescent lighting and occupancy sensors in

controls update allowing equipment operations to be managed more effectively.

initiative.

population on campus. The addition of these spaces, coupled with recent renovations in 241 St. Botolph

Technology upgrades have been constantly implemented over the course of the 2012 – 2022 NEC IMP. A 
focus on redundancy, reliability, and access have driven many of the on-campus upgrades. The COVID-19 
pandemic has also driven innovation and upgrades in technology to enable hybrid classroom formats, 
as well as creating low-latency connections within buildings allowing practitioners to collaborate from 
separate spaces with minimal signal latency. Upgrades were also made in NEC’s concert halls to improve 
streaming capabilities, enabling the sharing of free concerts in person and online to the community.

New Revenue
NEC continues to explore new revenue models and opportunities through diversification of its 
programming, with an emphasis on the Prep School and summer programming, as well as increasing 
available performance spaces on campus for rental.

3.4 Update on Community and Public Benefits
New England Conservatory has a long tradition of supporting the surrounding community through free 
Jordan Hall concerts, scholarships to Boston Preparatory program students, the Community Performances 
and Partnerships Program, and Boston Bridge to Equity and Achievement in Music (BEAM) initiative. NEC has 
long been an outstanding partner with numerous Boston Public Schools and local non-profit social services 
organizations in providing free access to classical music education and performance, as well as providing on-
campus space for community partners. Through the COVID-19 pandemic, NEC has adjusted its offerings to 
provide virtual programming and engagement to the public. 
3.5 Cultural Equity and Belonging
As a pillar of the strategic planning process, NEC announced in April 2021 Monique Van Willingh as the 
inaugural Director of the Cultural Equity and Belonging (CEB) program. This new position led to the 
establishment of community-wide plans and programming, the building of partnerships within NEC, and the 
advancement of institutional goals around equity, diversity, inclusion, and belonging.
Prior to launching CEB, consultants engaged in one-on-one conversations with over 140 people representing 
members of NEC’s stakeholder groups. Following this engagement, the Center for CEB was established 
both as a physical space and support for all NEC community members. The Center for CEB has four pillars: 
Dialogue, Learning, Collaboration, and Support and Resources. The focus of the inaugural CEB year was to 
build relationships across campus, to build NEC’s CEB practice, and to build resources. This was accomplished 
through providing support for students, student clubs, faculty, and staff individually and in teams; providing 
CEB workshops, listening circles, Perspectives Forums (dialogue spaces); facilitating team problem-solving 
and brainstorming sessions; activating a faculty think tank; and collaborating with staff teams such as Human 
Resources and the Preparatory School to explore department-specific goals.
Based on student and NEC community feedback, the goals for 2022-23 include establishing a larger baseline 
understanding of CEB in teaching and staff practices; establishing Human Resources practices that promote 
CEB; and ensuring that every point of welcome at NEC promotes CEB. Additionally, individual and team 
support for the entire NEC community will continue to be a central function of the Center for CEB. These goals 
and themes will serve to inform the Strategic Plan and Institutional Master Plan moving forward.

3.6 Community Engagement Through COVID-19
NEC’s programming centers around engagement of both performers and audience. Through the COVID-19 
pandemic, the traditional outreach and engagement venues were not available. Through commitment and 
engagement, NEC’s faculty, staff, and students developed new approaches, systems, and offerings to bring 
music where it was most needed. 
Born out of the earliest days of the pandemic, Boston Hope Music (BHM) was created to address the need for 
artistic healing at the Boston Hope Medical Center, a field hospital established to treat COVID patients during 
the spring of 2020. NEC students were integral to creating virtual playlists for patients at the hospital that 
were used to augment healing for the duration of the hospital’s existence (Apr - Jun 2020).
An organic outgrowth of NEC’s work with hospitalists at MGH, 6 NEC students joined forces with Harvard 
Medical students to deliver 23 virtual bedside concerts to patients and their families over the Thanksgiving 
and Winter Holidays (Nov – Dec 2020).
Another aspect of NEC’s partnership with Boston Hope Music and Massachusetts General 
Hospital this spring was the BHM Music & Song Project, led by NEC Teaching Fellows and Contemporary 
Improvisation graduates. In a five-week virtual workshop series, nurses, respiratory therapists, social workers, 
and doctors who had been on the front lines of the COVID-19 pandemic reflected upon their experiences and 
generated original music in an atmosphere of vulnerability and trust.
Responding to the vaccination phase of the COVID-19 Pandemic, Boston Hope Music created the initiative 
Vacci-Nation, designed to bring live music to vaccination centers in the Boston Area. Throughout the duration 
of these sites (Mar – Jun 2021) Boston Hope staff, NEC alumni, and current students performed at mass 
vaccination sites at Fenway Park, Assembly Row (Somerville), and the Reggie Lewis Center (Roxbury).
NEC’s virtual presence during this time drastically expanded, providing live streams of numerous student 
and group performances. From March 2020 through June 2020 NEC content received 1.7 million video views 
across all platforms with 200k on YouTube alone. This expanded engagement continued through the 2020 - 
2021 academic year with 1.3 million video views across all platforms with 427k views on YouTube.

Chapter 2: New England Conservatory Background
The oldest independent school of music in the United States, NEC was founded in 1867 by Eben Tourjée at 
a time when post- Civil War society was demanding American-centric musical culture. The Conservatory’s 
curriculum is remarkable for its wide range of styles and traditions. As the school grew from seven rooms
rented above Music Hall on Tremont Street to its own dedicated facility in Jordan Hall in 1903, the programs, 
reach, and impact have established NEC as a national and international leader among music schools.
NEC’s mission is to educate and train musicians of all ages from around the world, drawing on the talent and
deep reservoir of experience of its distinguished faculty. NEC is dedicated to inculcating the highest standards
of excellence and nurturing individual artistic sensibility and creative growth. Understanding that music is
one of the transcendent expressions of human civilization, NEC aspires to ensure it has a central place in
contemporary society.
New England Conservatory offers rigorous training to approximately 784 undergraduate, graduate, and 
doctoral music students from around the world in an intimate, nurturing community. Its college faculty of 220 
boasts internationally esteemed artist-teachers and scholars. Its alumni go on to fill orchestra chairs, concert 
hall stages, jazz clubs, recording studios, and arts management positions worldwide. Nearly half of the Boston 
Symphony Orchestra is composed of NEC trained musicians and faculty. The great majority of NEC-trained 
musicians devote at least some of their professional lives to teaching, sharing their knowledge and skills with 
children, young people, and adults.
On the college level, the school offers undergraduate and graduate-level training in classical, jazz, 
Contemporary Musical Arts, world, and early music. Through its Preparatory School and Expanded Education, 
NEC provides training and performance opportunities for an average of 1,400 children and pre-college 
students. Through its Community Performances and Partnerships projects, NEC offers young musicians
the opportunity to engage with community-based audiences in schools, hospitals, community centers and 
nursing homes, bringing pleasure to new young listeners, the elderly, and other underserved audiences, and 
increasing appreciation of classical music and many other genres.
2.1 History, Mission, and Vision
NEC presents more than 900 free concerts each year, many of them held in its world-renowned Jordan Hall, a 
National Historic Landmark famous for its superb acoustics and beautifully restored interior. These programs 
range from solo recitals to chamber music to orchestral programs to jazz, contemporary musical arts, and 
opera scenes. Every year, NEC’s Opera Studies department also presents two fully staged opera productions.
NEC is a founding partner of Project STEP, Boston Children’s Chorus, and the String Training and Education 
Program, which for more than 40 years has provided rigorous pre-professional music preparation for BIPOC 
children. NEC is also a member of the Fenway Alliance, a consortium of 21 nationally and internationally 
renowned cultural and academic institutions located in the Fenway that creates innovative and relevant 
programming in the Boston community. As part of the Fenway Alliance, NEC has participated in the Opening 
Our Doors festival - an annual day of free cultural experiences - for the past twenty years, as well as Fenway 
Porchfest, a partnership of Fenway Alliance, Fenway CDC, and Fenway Civic Association.
Since 2019 and through the support of the Mellon Foundation, NEC has also hosted the Boston Bridge to 
Equity and Achievement in Music (BEAM) program. In collaboration with Boston Youth Symphony Orchestras, 
the Community Music Center of Boston, Project STEP, and the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Boston BEAM’s 
mission is to create a region-wide collective solution for supporting and sustaining musical excellence
among young musicians of historically excluded populations who self-identify as aspiring to careers in the 
classical music profession. BEAM’s primary goal is to increase racial and ethnic diversity in post-secondary 
instrumental classical music programs to increase diversity in the field of classical music, especially in 
orchestras.
In December 2022, President Kalyn and Mayor Michele Wu established and announced a partnership 
between NEC and the City of Boston. The conservatory secured a $14.5 million grant to substantially increase 
access to high-quality music education for Boston’s children, which includes expansion of early childhood 
music education as well as increased scholarships to NEC’s Preparatory School with a focus on welcoming 
students from underrepresented communities.
NEC hosted a music program for 3rd-5th grade students in Summer 2023 called “Everyone Can Make Music” 
designed to introduce students from the City of Boston to music through song, instruments, composition, and 
theory, with a final showcase in NEC’s Jordan Hall. Participants from the summer program, as well as other 
students from the Boston community, have enrolled in NEC Prep academic year programming through the 
NEC Prep scholarships, which have been endowed in order to provide increased scholarship opportunities for 
years to come.
In October 2023, NEC launched a three-year pilot program for Early Childhood music, which provides weekly 
music lessons to nearly 600 young students across five sites throughout Boston in Bradshaw, Dorchester, 
and Mattapan in partnership with ABCD Head Start, and in the South End and Jamaica Plain in partnership 
with Ellis Early Learning. As part of NEC’s commitment to increased access to high quality music education, 
the institution continues to work in coordination with city partners to support recruitment for the NEC Prep 
scholarships and expansion of Early Childhood music education offerings.

finishes, infrastructure, and systems, and/or change of uses of portions of existing buildings on the NEC 
campus to accommodate on-campus relocation of various functions related to NEC’s ongoing operations 
and the development of the Proposed Projects.
The only Institutional Project not yet completed from the 2012-2022 IMP is Phase 2; this project was

year IMP.
3.1 Update on Institutional Projects
With the completion of IMP projects, New England Conservatory has advanced the goals of its 2012-2022 IMP. 
•	
Scholarship and Financial Aid
Each year, thousands of young musicians from the U.S. and abroad apply for admission to NEC. For many, 
scholarships and financial aid are crucial factors in their ability to attend the Conservatory, or even to 
consider pursuing a career in music. In the current academic year, 2023-24, NEC awarded scholarship 
funds to 784 students from 43 U.S. states and 37 foreign countries. The primary goal of NEC’s financial- 
aid allocation is to offer students financial aid packages that cover a high percentage of students’ overall 
financial needs. Scholarships are crucial to help NEC pursue its core academic and artistic missions, and to 
cultivate the unique creative community that thrives here.
•	
Distinctive Faculty and Programs
The SLPC has unlocked new opportunities to recruit, grow, and expand programs and faculty with the 
inclusion of specialized venues supporting Jazz, Contemporary Musical Arts, and Opera programs. 
Eben Jordan Ensemble Room, Burnes Hall, and the Plimpton Shattuck Black Box Theatre unlock new 
opportunities for faculty and students to collaborate and expand the impact of the NEC curriculum.
•	
Student-Centric Campus Redevelopment
Additionally, the SLPC focuses on student-centric experiences. With the inclusion of a new residential 
tower, the SLPC facility modernizes and expands the on-campus residential capacity of NEC. The dining 
commons, library, and common areas of the SLPC support the residential and non-residential student 
population on campus. The addition of these spaces, coupled with recent renovations in 241 St. Botolph, 
support the Community Engagement and Professional Studies (CEPS) program as well as the Cultural 
Equity and Belonging (CEB) programs on campus. The linkage of this space and these programs to the 
SLPC have created a Main Street of student services and student programming targeted to enhance the 
student experience.
•	
Technology
Technology upgrades have been constantly implemented over the course of the 2012 – 2022 NEC IMP. 
A focus on redundancy, reliability, and access have driven many of the on-campus upgrades. Additional 
investments focus on innovation and upgrades of technology to enable hybrid classroom
formats. The introduction of low-latency connections within buildings allows practitioners to collaborate 
from separate spaces with minimal signal latency. Upgrades were also made in NEC’s concert halls
to improve streaming capabilities, enabling the sharing of free concerts in person and online to the 
community.
•	
New Revenue
Recent institutional projects have enabled the Conservatory to explore new revenue models by 
diversifying programming as well as increasing available performance space on campus for rentals.

3.4 Update on Community and Public Benefits
New England Conservatory has a long tradition of supporting the surrounding community through free 
Jordan Hall concerts, scholarships to Boston Preparatory program students, the Community Performances 
and Partnerships Program, and Boston Bridge to Equity and Achievement in Music (BEAM) initiative. NEC has 
long been an outstanding partner with numerous Boston Public Schools and local non-profit social services 
organizations in providing free access to classical music education and performance, as well as providing on- 
campus space for community partners.
3.5 Cultural Equity and Belonging
The Cultural Equity and Belonging (CEB) program is a core element of the Strategic Planning process. This 
initiative led to the establishment of community-wide plans and programming, the building of partnerships 
within NEC, and the advancement of institutional goals around equity, diversity, inclusion, and belonging.
The Center for CEB has four pillars: Dialogue, Learning, Collaboration, and Support and Resources. The focus 
of the inaugural CEB year was to build relationships across campus, to build NEC’s CEB practice, and to build 
resources. This was accomplished through providing support for students, student clubs, faculty, and staff 
individually and in teams; providing CEB workshops, listening circles, Perspectives Forums (dialogue spaces); 
facilitating team problem-solving and brainstorming sessions; activating a faculty think tank; and collaborating 
with staff teams such as Human Resources and the Preparatory School to explore department- specific goals.
The second year of CEB focused on deepening collaboration and partnerships across campus
and emphasized community-focused events. NEC’s Intercultural Institute became a branch of CEB and 
curated multiple cultural learning experiences and a symposium on Bimusicality. Community events included 
the Candid Conversations series (informal and student-led conversations between faculty and students), 
CEB Music and Poetry Open Mic evenings, and CEB campaigns that promoted a sense of belonging through 
affirming cultural identities (such as a library rotating CEB display and proactively connecting with the 
community through interactive tabling).
Based on student and NEC community feedback, the goals for 2023-24 included establishing a larger baseline 
understanding of CEB in teaching and staff practices; establishing Human Resources practices that promote 
CEB; promoting a sense of connectedness and community for the NEC campus; and ensuring that every point 
of welcome at NEC promotes CEB. Additionally, individual and team support for the entire NEC community 
will continue to be a central function of the Center for CEB. These goals and themes will serve to inform the 
Strategic Plan and Institutional Master Plan moving forward.
3.6 Community Engagement with City of Boston
In addition to the newly formed partnership between NEC and the City of Boston, NEC is proud to celebrate 
the 20th anniversary of our Community Performances and Partnerships (CPP) program. In 2003, NEC 
introduced the community engagement program to offer students a chance to connect the skills they were 
developing as musicians to a broad array of civic aims and aspirations in Boston and beyond. In just a few 
years, what started as a relatively modest initiative led by a single staff member blossomed into a full-blown 
department at NEC. Nearly a quarter of all NEC students were participating in community-based programming 
on an annual basis, enabling NEC to develop a robust network of collaborators in disparate fields such as 
public education, health, and the visual arts.
In the 2023-24 academic year, the CPP program had 125 partnerships with schools, senior centers, community 
centers, hospitals, libraries, museums, and historic landmarks. More than 300 NEC students and alumni 
taught 1,260 hours, performing at 158 events, and reaching over 12,500 people. This year, NEC expanded its 
partnership within the Boston Public Schools (BPS) through a foundation-supported pilot to provide ongoing 
private and small group lessons at three BPS locations.
NEC’s work with Boston Public Schools dates to the inception of the CPP program in 2003 and has prioritized 
alignment at the district level to meet student needs during in school and out of school time. Over the last 
decade, CPP has worked on average with 15 schools annually, reaching 5,000 students through performances, 
weekly teaching, project-based residencies, workshops, and an annual touring children’s opera.
NEC looks forward to building upon the success of these relationships to provide more access to private 
lesson instruction, as well as create more robust pipelines for teaching artists entering the field. This 
includes opportunities for students to develop as teachers—practicing artists with the complementary skills, 
curiosities, and habits of mind of educators—who can apply their musicianship to learning in, through, and 
around the arts. Students will engage artistically, effectively, and ethically with diverse communities through 
practical coursework, mentoring, and experiential opportunities in a broad range of settings, including
in Boston schools, after-school programs, senior living facilities, and community organizations.
3.7 Request for IMP Extension and Renewal for Two Years
The New England Conservatory IMP is set to expire on September 15, 2024. Because New England 
Conservatory continues to develop its strategic planning process, to be followed by a new campus master 
planning process, to be followed by a new institutional master planning process – all impacted by the effects 
of the global COVID-19 pandemic – the Conservatory respectfully requests a two-year renewal and extension 
to its existing 2012-22 IMP.

1.3 
Progress on the 2013-2023 IMP Projects 
Northeastern’s specific objectives, as reflected in its 2013-2023 IMP include: 
• 
Development of superior academic facilities to serve Northeastern’s increasingly 
sophisticated teaching environment; 
• 
Development of superior research facilities to support Northeastern’s growing research 
programs, including those in the fields of health, security and sustainability; 
• 
Continued expansion and enhancement of Northeastern’s student residential facilities, to 
help attract and retain qualified students; and 
• 
Consolidation of administrative and other non-academic uses, so as to maximize the 
availability of space and resources in the central campus area to better serve 
Northeastern’s academic priorities. 
• 
Creation of 1,000 new student beds, as part of mixed-use projects on University-owned 
property. 
The IMP included eleven new projects with specific project sites to be refined and finalized during 
the ten-year term of the IMP. The IMP sought to accommodate over 2,000,000 GSF of academic 
and student life facility growth, including athletic facilities and additional housing on the 
Northeastern campus. To satisfy this scale of needed facilities, while remaining within the 
confines of the existing campus, the IMP proposed to increase the built density through the re-
purposing of under-utilized areas such as parking lots, and replacing low-rise, aging buildings, with 
taller, more economically and environmentally efficient construction.

Northeastern focused initially on completing a proposed Interdisciplinary Science and Engineering 
Complex (ISEC) as well as completing the 720-bed East Village (formerly named GrandMarc) 
residence hall before commencing additional projects. The ISEC completed construction in 
December 2016 and construction of the East Village residence hall was completed in November 
2014 and occupied by students starting in January 2015. The LightView project, previously known 
as the Columbus Avenue Housing Project, was developed in partnership with American Campus 
Communities (ACC). This residential community opened in August 2019 and welcomed 
Northeastern students to the 825 new student beds that the project provides. Northeastern 
students were eager to live in this new residential community as evidenced by the property being 
fully preleased in just a few months. In May of 2019 Northeastern submitted a Project Notification 
Form for the building known as EXP. This project was approved by the BPDA Board in October 
2019. Construction began in June 2020 and occupancy is slated for the third quarter of 2023. 
While projects such as those included in the IMP remain a priority, the global pandemic has 
necessitated a closer look at Northeastern’s development pipeline, both from the perspective of 
University expenditures as well as changing patterns of space use and implications for the campus’ 
built form. This closer look is under way and will be presented in the full ten-year IMP.

Update on Benefits 
Following extensive consultation with the BPDA-appointed Northeastern IMP Task Force, the 
broader community, elected officials, and the BPDA, Northeastern committed to a robust package 
of public benefits in association with the eleven projects considered in the IMP. These specific 
commitments are over and above the diverse array of more than 240 community focused 
programs and services that Northeastern developed over the years in response to community 
need and which the University continues to support. An extensive annual update on the IMP 
community benefits is available online at: 
https://bpda.app.box.com/s/wh0ijtvonjsjyylh6iwh3e39ijhsh7a0 
The guidelines that Northeastern relied on to develop the package of community benefits 
associated with the IMP included the following: 
 The benefit serves the mutual interests of the community and Northeastern and can be 
recognized to be of benefit in the local community and beyond; 
 The benefit leads to sustainable partnerships in the community designed to promote the 
development of thriving communities along Northeastern's institutional borders, 
especially in Roxbury; 
 The benefit builds on existing programmatic strengths and core competencies of the 
University, or builds upon other strengths that can be leveraged or harnessed; 
 The benefit strives for innovative ways to optimize resources that build a strong 
community and a strong University; and

INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL INFORMATION 
1.1 
Overview 
Northeastern University (“Northeastern” or the “Proponent”) is pleased to submit this 
Institutional Master Plan Notification Form/Project Notification Form (this “IMPNF/PNF”) to the 
Boston Redevelopment Authority, doing business as Boston Planning & Development Agency 
(herein, the BPDA). With this submission, Northeastern is initiating the process for approval of a 
10-year Institutional Master Plan (the “IMP”) pursuant to Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code 
(the Code) and initiating Large Project Review under Article 80B of the Code to enable the 
development of the projects outlined herein. 
This IMPNF/PNF will provide an organizational framework for creating a physical plan and 
infrastructure for the Boston campus that will strengthen and celebrate Northeastern’s mission. 
Guided by its 2013 Institutional Master Plan (the “2013 IMP”), Northeastern is planning for the 
next ten years through the construction of several new projects and the redevelopment of older 
and underutilized buildings within the campus core (the “IMP Projects”). These projects, 
described in Chapter 3 hereof, will largely be driven by Northeastern’s academic mission as a 
global research university, powered by experience. Northeastern is renowned for its experiential 
learning model, high-impact research, deep partnerships, and worldwide reach, and its physical 
presence in Boston is organized in such a way to meet the current and future needs in education 
and research. 
As part of this IMPNF/PNF, Northeastern also seeks to initiate Large Project Review for the 
redevelopment of the 262 St. Botolph Street site, which currently houses Matthews Arena and a 
surface parking lot, and is bounded by St. Botolph Street to the north, the MBTA Orange Line, 
Commuter Rail and Amtrak right-of-way to the south, Public Alley 823 to the east, and 
Gainsborough Street to the west (the “Project Site”). Northeastern proposes to construct a new, 
approximately 290,000 square foot (sf) multi-purpose facility (the “262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility” or “Project”) that will support Northeastern’s athletic capabilities 
for its Division I athletes, intramural teams, and club sports. It is anticipated the new facility will 
provide an inviting and diverse space for current and future students and elevate the profile of 
collegiate athletics in Boston. As detailed in Chapter 4, the Project will enhance the overall campus 
plan, aesthetically integrate with, and complement, the surroundings of this unique Site, while 
providing for Northeastern’s varsity athletics programs and student recreation programming. 
1.2 
Institutional Mission, Objectives, and Needs 
Founded in 1898, Northeastern University is a top-tier, nonprofit research university located on 
both sides of Huntington Avenue on the edges of the Back Bay, Fenway, Mission Hill, Roxbury, 
and South End neighborhoods of Boston. Grounded in its signature cooperative education 
program, Northeastern provides its students with unprecedented experiential learning 
opportunities around the world.

Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
Northeastern’s undergraduate colleges, myriad of graduate programs, and part-time divisions 
offer bachelor’s, master’s, professional and doctoral degrees in a wide variety of academic 
disciplines and professional areas. Northeastern offers its students opportunities for professional 
work, research, service, and global learning in more than 130 countries. Northeastern’s rapidly 
growing research enterprise is strategically aligned with three national and global imperatives: 
health, security, and sustainability. 
Northeastern’s physical presence in Boston serves as a testament to the university’s rich history 
and more recent evolution. With its roots as a commuter college, the campus has transformed its 
surface parking lots into a vibrant academic hub, nestled amidst Boston’s diverse neighborhoods. 
As its physical footprint has evolved, its commitment to learning, research, impact, and 
experiential education remains at the core of the university’s mission, manifested in its campus 
design, buildings and open spaces. The Boston campus serves as a living laboratory: a backdrop 
for innovation and discovery, as well as a bridge to community and real-world applications of 
higher education. 
Planning for Northeastern’s Boston campus—as with its network of global campuses—responds 
to space need projections and facility conditions assessments of the present day. Events in this 
past decade, notably changes in the global landscape as a response to the global pandemic, have 
provided an opportunity to rethink the environments in which we learn, research, and work in 
ways yet to be fully defined. However, the pandemic has reinforced the value of flexibility and 
adaptability, which can be supported by space design. The IMP Projects described in this IMPNF 
reflect the university’s currently anticipated needs with an understanding that these needs will 
undoubtedly evolve over time. This IMPNF offers a framework for such needs, including the need 
to plan and build flexibly to allow for adaptability to meet the demands of the current day. 
1.3 
IMP History 
Northeastern has filed Institutional Master Plans for its Boston campus since 1999. Most recently, 
Northeastern’s 2013 IMP was approved by the BPDA Board in November 2013 and by the Boston 
Zoning Commission in December 2013. In October 2023, the BPDA approved a two-year renewal 
of Northeastern’s 2013 IMP. The two-year extension to the 2013 IMP allowed for the completion 
of the Third Amendment to the 2013 IMP, which was approved in March 2024. 
Since the 2013 IMP, five IMP Amendments have been approved, as described below. 
First Amendment 
The First Amendment to the 2013 IMP added the approximately 825-bed dormitory now known 
as LightView, located at 744 Columbus Avenue. The First Amendment was approved by the BPDA 
Board on July 14, 2016, and the new residential community opened in August 2019.

the BPDA Board on March 14, 2024, and the 840 Columbus Avenue project and the Renaissance 
Park Renovation Project are currently in planning and design.

International Village residence halls to add up to approximately 900 beds across the two buildings. 
The Fourth Amendment was approved by the BPDA Board on March 10, 2022, and the residence 
halls were upsized fall 2022. 
Fifth Amendment 
The Fifth Amendment to the 2013 IMP consisted of interior renovations and a new first floor 
enclosure at the existing Snell Library. The Fifth Amendment was approved by the BPDA Board on 
September 15, 2022. The Snell Library renovations are now in progress.

2.1 
University Profile 
Today, Northeastern enrolls approximately 40,000 degree-seeking students in Boston, including 
approximately 21,000 undergraduate students and approximately 19,000 part-time and full-time 
graduate students. These figures fluctuate from year to year, due in part to Northeastern’s 
cooperative education model in which students alternate semesters of academic study with 
periods of full-time work, as well as the recent expansion of Northeastern’s global network of 
campuses in Oakland, California, London, England and most recently, New York, New York to 
accommodate the university’s growing undergraduate population. 
Northeastern has approximately 2,800 faculty members, as well as 3,500 staff in Boston. Of the 
total faculty and staff employed at Northeastern, approximately 26% are residents of Boston.

Northeastern’s campus is adjacent to the Back Bay, Fenway, Mission Hill, Roxbury, and South End 
neighborhoods of Boston and has a variety of residential, commercial, and institutional neighbors. 
Northeastern and the surrounding neighborhoods are connected through the activities of 
students and faculty of Northeastern, who are involved in a multitude of programs and activities 
that engage community organizations and neighborhood residents. Within these diverse 
neighborhoods are wide arrays of land uses, including institutional, high- and medium-density 
residential, commercial, and recreational uses.

3.0 
TEN-YEAR PLAN 
3.1 
Introduction 
Since the 2013 IMP, new development on Northeastern’s Boston campus has primarily 
concentrated along Columbus Avenue. The IMP for the next ten years will shift focus to the core 
of the campus by focusing on the renewal and redevelopment of older, outmoded buildings and 
underutilized spaces in the heart of the campus. This shift aims to create a more cohesive and 
vibrant campus experience, enhancing the sense of campus community and fostering 
interdisciplinary collaboration by improving research, student life, and academic space resources 
in ways that reflect Northeastern’s forward-looking approach to learning and community 
partnership. 
The proposed IMP Projects will include the renovation and expansion of existing academic 
buildings, the creation of new student life and recreation facilities, and the development of 
additional green spaces and pedestrian-centered environments. By concentrating future growth 
within the campus core, Northeastern seeks to optimize its highly physically-constrained land use, 
address necessary capital renewal and maintenance of older buildings on campus, create a more 
sustainable and resilient campus, and continue to ensure that the campus’ evolution contributes 
positively to the broader urban fabric of the city of Boston. This IMPNF identifies eight sites for 
new construction (redevelopment), nine major renovations, and three areas of additional 
interest. Of these eight redevelopment sites, six are carried over from the 2013 IMP. See Figure 
3-1 for the proposed ten-year plan. 
3.2 
Planning Framework 
3.2.1 
Planning and Urban Design Goals 
The planning principles for the IMP reflect Northeastern’s unique identity as an institution that 
values experiential learning, global engagement, and interdisciplinary collaboration, shaping a 
campus environment that fosters innovation, inclusion, and a strong sense of community both 
within the campus and with its surrounding neighborhoods. The following five principles guide 
the IMP: 
♦ Flexibility and Agility: Plan for space on the Boston campus that supports the mobility of 
students, faculty and staff across the university’s global network. 
♦ Impactful Learning and Collaboration: Promote collaborative, multidisciplinary research 
and experiential learning.

3.2.2 
Campus Communities 
Northeastern’s campus can be divided into seven areas described as “campus communities.” 
While the campus population participates in all of these areas, each has their own distinct identity, 
character and functions. The physical space that comprise these campus communities feature a 
diversity of programmatic uses, including learning spaces; areas for gathering, studying, and 
socializing; as well as open spaces that contribute to the overall vibrancy and identity within each 
community. See Figure 3-2 for the seven campus communities. 
University Square 
University Square, anchored by the iconic Krentzman Quad, serves as the traditional core of 
Northeastern's campus, featuring the university's historic buildings, such as Ell Hall, Dodge Hall, 
and Richards Hall. This campus community also includes buildings central to the contemporary 
campus experience, including the Curry Student Center and the Snell Library. With a 
predominance of academic and administrative buildings, Krentzman Quad lies at the heart of 
University Square, serving as an iconic open space. 
East End 
The East End campus community will be home to the new 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project, as well as a new academic and research quad anchored by the 
redevelopment of Mugar Life Sciences building, Cullinane Hall, and Gainsborough Garage. These 
transformative projects will establish the East End as a vibrant research and student activity hub, 
and the re-envisioning of a meaningful quad situated between what are now Mugar, Hurtig and 
Robinson Halls (now known as Robinson Quad), will connect the East End to University Square. 
South Landing 
Located in the southern part of Northeastern’s campus, South Landing is a thriving hub for 
research and innovation and student housing. Home to two major research facilities, ISEC and 
EXP, this campus community will soon welcome a residence hall at 840 Columbus Avenue. South 
Landing's mix of research spaces, the City’s Carter Playground, local retail, and modern student 
amenities exemplifies Northeastern's commitment to fostering an environment that supports 
academic excellence and connection to City and the neighboring community.

3.2.3 
Public Realm and Landscape 
Northeastern’s public realm and landscape, collectively referred to here as open spaces, play an 
integral role in both the campus experience and local environmental conditions. The open space 
network on the Boston campus consists of a range of space types and planting schemes, which 
work together to provide a distinctive setting for an urban campus. 
Part of the vision for Northeastern’s physical campus design for the Boston campus is to create a 
cohesive and connected network of open spaces that serves critical social, academic, and 
environmental functions, while linking to Boston’s neighborhoods. The Boston campus open 
space network interventions seek to: 
♦ Support the university’s academic mission and student life goals; 
♦ Serve as a destination for the community beyond Northeastern; 
♦ Be inclusive and welcoming, through the embrace of universal design principles; 
♦ Unite the campus’ diverse architecture; and 
♦ Enhance the ecological and environmental performance of the campus. 
The university’s landscape-based approaches for ecological and environmental performance 
include optimizing green infrastructure and addressing water conservation and inland flood 
resilience while adhering to various guidelines, processes, and regulations, such as the Green 
Building and Climate Resiliency Guidelines, Groundwater Conservation Overlay District, BWSC Site 
Plan Approval, and MassDEP Stormwater Standards. 
Northeastern strives to be a model of a sustainable, healthy, interconnected, and just community. 
The university's landscape and public realm priorities focus on supporting informal social 
interaction and formal programming, enhancing pedestrian experience and throughput, 
maximizing pervious surfaces in an urban context, utilizing a stormwater toolkit to improve water 
quality, and elevating the Arboretum to Level III status to further enhance biodiversity and 
understanding of local ecology. These efforts demonstrate Northeastern's commitment to social 
and environmental stewardship and its goal of increasing "plant space" where possible on an 
urban campus. 
Northeastern recognizes the importance of stewarding the Arboretum, which is essential to 
supporting an ecologically healthy campus and sense of belonging on campus. The university aims 
to continue upholding the City of Boston's Urban Forest Plan Goals by replacing trees at a 
minimum 1:1 ratio, aiming for a net increase in tree quantity and achieving greater species 
diversity in the urban canopy through strategic removals, transplants, and additions. 
Northeastern is also committed to exploring opportunities to remove physical barriers for open 
space access across campus. Over the next decade, the university intends to redesign core campus 
landscapes to prioritize pedestrian movement while still enabling service and emergency vehicles.

3.2.4 
Campus Life 
Northeastern's educational model - centered on experiential learning, global mobility, and 
community service - fosters a student experience that is both globally focused and locally 
engaged. With a network of campuses around the world, Northeastern encourages students to 
explore diverse cultures, perspectives, and opportunities. Physical spaces are meant to reinforce 
and inspire this sense of exploration, not just in the classroom and in laboratories, but within 
residence halls, recreational facilities, and spaces devoted to celebration and collaboration. 
Through its recently announced mergers with Mills College in Oakland, California and Marymount 
Manhattan College in New York City, Northeastern is pursuing a global mobility model, in which 
students have the option to study at one of its numerous residential campuses. These mergers, 
coupled with the expansion of global co-op opportunities, comprise Northeastern’s global 
mobility programs. These programs broaden student’s horizons as students seek opportunities 
outside of Boston throughout their academic experience. 
Northeastern's location in four of Boston’s neighborhoods is an integral part of the student 
experience. The university cherishes being part of the City’s fabric and remains committed to 
providing comprehensive student life facilities to meet the needs of its student population, 
reducing the pressure on neighborhood resources. In recent years, Northeastern has made 
significant strides in improving its student life facilities. The Marino Center and the Curry Student 
Center continue to serve as central hubs for student activities, offering a range of amenities and 
social outlets. Please see Figure 3-3 for campus life amenities.

Student Housing Plan 
Over the last ten-year Institutional Master Plan, Northeastern exceeded its commitment to 
deliver 1,000 additional student housing beds, by building, leasing, and securing permitting for 
more than 3,000 beds. Currently Northeastern requires first and second year students to live in

off-campus, particularly after their second year, due to a greater range of price points, unit types, 
and amenities available in the open market. Northeastern is committed to supporting a range of 
affordable and attractive housing options for students throughout their time at the university. 
This commitment includes maintaining the existing supply and increasing its portfolio through 
innovative housing solutions and partnerships.

International Village residence halls to add up to approximately 900 beds across the two buildings.

a lease agreement in the building formerly known as the South Tower of the Sheraton Boston 
Hotel located at 60 Belvidere Street (formerly known as 39 Dalton Street) whereby the university 
is leasing approximately 250,000 sf within the building resulting in an additional 854 student beds.

3.2.5 
Mobility 
The campus’ urban location provides access to a wide range of transportation options, with 
particularly robust access to public transit, micromobility networks, and bike facilities, while the 
compact nature of the campus contributes to a highly walkable environment. In recent years, 
Northeastern has made significant strides in promoting cycling as a healthy and environmentally 
friendly mode of transportation by investing in bike infrastructure and amenities. Mobility is 
discussed further in Chapter 5. 
3.2.6 
Sustainability and Resilience 
Northeastern has demonstrated a strong commitment to sustainability and resilience through its 
research, experiential education, and investment into the physical campus and surroundings. In 
late 2022, the university launched its Climate Justice Action Plan (CJAP) process through which a 
diverse steering committee comprised of representatives from the university and from 
community organizations, has been engaged to explore and create a framework for sustainable 
and just climate solutions. The CJAP goals address various aspects of sustainability, including 
greenhouse gas emissions, air quality, transportation, waste, climate resilience, local economies, 
community relationships, and research practices. The university's efforts to evolve its Boston 
campus will be informed by the CJAP, ensuring that new developments consider not only 
environmental factors but also social and economic impacts on the surrounding local 
communities. 
The university has also recently initiated a Decarbonization and Resilience Plan (DRP) to develop 
a phased, implementable plan for decarbonizing its Boston campus while addressing resilience 
and climate justice. Anticipated to be completed in 2025, the DRP will establish precise 
decarbonization goals and milestones aligned with the campus' growth and development. It will 
build upon Northeastern's existing utility planning work, including an analysis of electrical load

In recent years, Northeastern has made significant strides in sustainability through a multifaceted 
approach that encompasses buildings, transportation, and open space. The university has 
reduced greenhouse gas emissions per square foot of building space through fuel switching, 
energy conservation measures, and sustainable building design, with new buildings like the ISEC 
and EXP achieving high levels of sustainability through energy efficiency efforts and green 
infrastructure. Northeastern also supports sustainable transportation, with a majority of faculty, 
and staff using public transit, biking, or walking to commute to campus. The university has 
expanded its composting and recycling programs, diverting 48% of waste from landfills in 2023 
and partnering with local worker-owned cooperatives for composting services. Northeastern's 
Arboretum, with over 1,400 trees and 5,400 shrubs, contributes to urban green space, supporting 
community activity, filtering pollution, and mitigating heat islands. Additionally, the university has 
implemented initiatives to address heat resilience, indoor air quality, and water conservation, 
including rainwater collection systems, bioswales, and sustainable design standards for new 
buildings. Sustainability and Climate Resilience is discussed further in Chapter 6.
