4.0 
262 ST. BOTOLPH STREET MULTIPURPOSE ATHLETIC FACILITY 
4.1 
Purpose and Need 
Northeastern’s athletics and recreational buildings support 17 Division I athletic teams and more 
than 100 intramural and club teams. The university is committed to providing state-of-the-art, 
safe, and engaging facilities that meet Conference, NCAA, National and International Federation 
rules and regulations and recreational needs for the student community. In addition to 
intercollegiate athletics, intramural, and club sports, these facilities support university sanctioned 
events and a variety of public programming. Northeastern proposes to redevelop the 238-262 St. 
Botolph Street Site, currently housing the George J. & Hope M. Matthews Arena, with an 
approximately 290,000 square foot (sf), 115 foot tall multipurpose athletic building (the “262 St. 
Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility,” “Multipurpose Athletic Facility,” or the “Project”). 
The new building at 238-262 St. Botolph Street will be a four-story multipurpose facility that will 
provide improved spaces for varsity, club and intramural athletic programs, and new spaces for 
student recreation. The improved spaces for varsity games and training are vital to 
Northeastern’s recruitment opportunities and advancement of Northeastern’s Division I 
programs. Furthermore, the new recreation spaces are necessary to provide relief of 
overcrowding in other facilities on campus, offering all students greater access to wellness and 
fitness opportunities. The Multipurpose Athletic Facility will also further Northeastern’s diversity, 
equity, and inclusion efforts by including spaces for all-gender restrooms, lactation rooms for staff 
and visitors, space dedicated to visitors with sensory needs, and equity of space across men’s and 
women’s varsity hockey and basketball programs. 
The Project endeavors to serve all students, not just varsity athletes, in both its building program 
and design. The design of the arena will allow for natural light as well as visual connections 
between the street, concourse, recreation spaces, and arena bowl. This improved student, visitor, 
and public realm experience will also create an exciting interaction with collegiate activities and 
sporting events. Additionally, the new space will provide opportunities for more community 
events, such as Boston Public School commencement ceremonies and serving as a polling 
location. 
4.1.1 
Current Project Site Uses 
Matthews Arena is currently used as a facility for women’s and men’s varsity, club and intramural 
hockey practice and games, figure skating, men’s varsity basketball games, and gathering space 
for events such as commencement ceremonies. The building also provides hockey offices, training 
conditioning spaces, and offices for facilities staff. Despite efforts to renovate the existing building 
components, the team lockers, training spaces, and coaches’ offices in the current arena are 
lacking in modern amenities, building systems, and technology. The existing building is not fully 
accessible. Further, existing public spaces do not meet the university’s goals for diversity, equity, 
and inclusion. Varsity programs rely on space in other facilities on campus for training and 
practices and women’s varsity basketball has no space in the current building. There are also no 
spaces in the current arena dedicated to general student fitness and recreation.

Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
As the first project to advance in the IMP, the Project will anchor the edge of campus through 
public realm enhancements and connections with public transit. 
4.1.1.1 
Condition of the Building 
Over the building’s history prior to Northeastern’s ownership, it has endured many physical 
changes as a result of multiple fires, major structural changes, increasing space demands, and 
changing uses and owners. In 1948, the building was cited for potential structural collapse of the 
rear wall, which required it to be entirely reconstructed in 1949. During the 1949 renovation, the 
entire top floor of the building was removed. 
The building has consistently had issues with structural stability and fire safety. While 
Northeastern has invested in the facility to address these issues, including most recently installing 
temporary bracing to mitigate safety concerns associated with differential settlement, the facility 
has been deemed beyond repair. Redevelopment has emerged as the preferred approach from a 
financial and programmatic perspective, in line with Northeastern’s goals as an institution as well 
as a community partner. Figures 4-1 and 4-2 show the existing conditions. 
Consistent with the 2013 IMP, Northeastern begun investigating the potential for an addition to 
Matthews Arena in early 2019. As a result of that work, Northeastern discovered the building’s 
limitations, the gravity of the structural deficiencies previously noted, and the implications such 
an addition would have on the structural integrity of the facility. As a result of those studies, 
Northeastern proceeded with temporary structural improvements to the existing facility and is 
proposing redevelopment of the Arena with the Proposed Project.

Project Description 
4.2.1 
Project Site and Area Context 
Acquired by Northeastern in 1979, Matthews Arena has served as a home for Northeastern 
women’s and men’s hockey for over 45 years. Northeastern invested millions of dollars through 
multiple renovations in the 1980s and 1990s to bring the facility up to the then modern standards. 
In 1982, the arena was renamed the Matthews Arena in honor of George (former chairman of 
Northeastern’s board of trustees) and his late wife Hope. 
The approximately 97,969 sf Project Site is in the Fenway neighborhood located at 238-262 St. 
Botolph Street, within Northeastern’s East End campus community (see Figure 4-3). The Project 
Site, which currently houses Matthews Arena and a surface parking lot, is bounded by St. Botolph 
Street to the north, the MBTA tracks to the South, Public Alley 823 to the east, and Gainsborough 
Street to the west. The Project Site is an ideal location for a pedestrian- and transit-oriented 
multipurpose arena: athletes, students, and visitors can easily access the Massachusetts Avenue 
MBTA Station, which is adjacent to the Project Site and provides access to the MBTA Orange Line 
and numerous local bus routes. 
The building located at 238-262 St. Botolph Street, historically known as the Boston (Matthews) 
Arena (BOS.15498) has a long history with Boston sports and hosted many events in Boston’s 
history including visiting celebrities and dignitaries. Over the building’s history, it has endured 
many changes as a result of increasing space demands, fires, and changing uses and owners. 
Never rising to the prominence of the Boston Garden, the arena was always a secondary or a 
tertiary location of events in Boston. A devasting fire in 1918 resulted in the building being largely 
rebuilt, with only the entry portion of its original 1910 structure remaining. While the building has 
a long history with Boston, the substantial loss of integrity makes it ineligible for listing on the 
National Register of Historic Places.

4.2.2 
Proposed Project 
Northeastern intends to replace Matthews Arena and build a new, innovative and creatively 
designed multipurpose athletic facility. As the first project within the IMP, the Project will connect 
to the overall campus plan and aesthetically integrate with and complement, the surroundings of 
this Site, while providing critical program for Northeastern’s varsity athletics programs and 
student recreation programming. The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project will address both the short and long-term needs of the university’s athletics 
program and enhance the student-athlete experience by providing critical athlete support and 
recruiting amenities. The Project will also bring to the campus expanded space for recreation to 
be shared by the wider campus community. As designed, the building is approximately 290,000 
sf, or approximately 72,500 sf per floor over four floors of high bay, long span space. 
The program for basketball will accommodate two new basketball practice facilities, coaches’ 
offices, and all the required supporting space to include strength and conditioning, athletic 
training, team meeting rooms, men’s and women’s locker rooms, storage, and team laundry. The 
program for hockey will accommodate a new ice sheet, coaches’ offices, and all the required 
supporting space to include strength and conditioning, athletic training, team meeting rooms, a 
shooting station, and men’s and women’s locker rooms. In addition to the varsity athletics 
program, the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will add approximately 
54,000 sf of multipurpose recreation and fitness space that will serve as additional passive 
recreation space for students and event space. See Figure 4-4 to 4-6 for the massing design and 
site plans. 
Considering the large civic arena use, the ground floor will consist of a main building entry 
prominently facing Gainsborough Street with one secondary entrance along St. Botolph Street 
and one entrance along Gainsborough Street. The main entrance will provide an iconic arrival 
sequence to a new public lobby that will accommodate gameday peak foot-traffic and gatherings. 
The Gainsborough Street entrance is designed for transparency and connectivity to the future 
planned entrance to the MBTA Massachusetts Avenue Orange Line stop. 
The current construction cost is estimated between $300M and $350M.

Project Benefits 
In addition to the community benefits that will be provided by Northeastern through the IMP 
Projects, the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will include numerous 
benefits to the neighborhood and the City of Boston, including but not limited to: 
♦ Creation of approximately 350 construction jobs. 
♦ Improvement of the urban design characteristics and aesthetic character of the 
neighborhood by replacing the existing aging structure and a surface parking lot with 
active ground floor public uses and introducing high-quality architecture and landscape 
to the Project Site. 
♦ Consistent with Article 37 and Article 80 of the Code, the 262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will be designed to Leadership in Energy and 
Environmental Design (LEED) certifiable at the Gold level. New high performance building 
systems will serve the new facility, utilizing a fossil fuel free approach paired with a 
photovoltaic array on the roof. 
♦ Improvements to the public streetscapes along St. Botolph and Gainsborough Streets 
with new street trees, site furnishings, and seating opportunities, all in compliance with 
City of Boston Complete Streets Guidelines 
♦ Continued support for public programs that currently take place at Matthews Arena, 
including but not limited to Boston Public School commencement ceremonies, City of 
Boston polling, blood drives, and other community events. 
4.2.4 
Preliminary Project Schedule 
The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is anticipated to begin 
construction in winter 2025 and be completed by summer of 2028. 
4.3 
Urban Design 
The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project design aims to create a unique 
building for the campus while responding to the surrounding neighborhood context. The scale of 
the proposed project is driven by the modern athletic and recreational program requirements, 
and architectural design moves aim to break down building’s massing to create dynamic, inviting, 
and people-centric spaces for building users, guests, and the community at large. 
Paving along both St. Botolph and Gainsborough Streets will relate in style to the existing 
enhanced streetscape across the street by the New England Conservatory of Music and further 
north along Gainsborough Street, stitching the Project into the fabric of the greater 
neighborhood.

Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
The Project design will provide an inviting open space that promotes sustainable transportation 
options, including walking, cycling, and public transit. In addition to sidewalk reconstruction, site 
furnishings will include bike racks, planters, and seating. The plaza paving will extend, where 
possible, towards the Massachusetts Avenue MBTA Station, creating a holistic visual connection 
between the Project Site and public transit. 
4.3.1 
Tree Protection and Removal Plan 
Design of the public realm for the Project intends to provide conditions for street trees to flourish. 
While all existing plant material within the property line will be removed during construction, an 
effort will be made to relocate trees following a feasibility assessment. While more mature trees 
may not survive relocation, it is anticipated that the much younger street trees will survive. 
Relocation will be addressed further in the design process, in consultation with the contractor. In 
general, however, all trees removed as part of the Project will be replaced with new trees on 
campus. As part of the public realm improvement for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project, 22 trees are currently anticipated to be planted throughout the Project 
Site, including along Gainsborough Street which currently has no existing street trees. The average 
caliper of the trees is anticipated to be 4” at time of planting. These trees will be planted within 
large soil volumes. Where possible, the tree planting areas will be provided with continuous 
volumes of structural soil to support healthy tree growth. Additionally, trees which are planted 
within hardscape plazas or more urban conditions will be provided with extended structural soil 
or soil structures (such as silva cells) to reduce soil compaction and ensure adjacent pavements 
are not heaved over time. Tree species selected will be appropriate for street tree conditions, 
with columnar forms where in closer proximity to building façade. 
4.4 
Public Realm and Open Space Improvements 
The landscape design for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project includes 
improvements to the streetscape along St. Botolph and Gainsborough Streets with new street 
trees, site furnishings, lighting and seating opportunities, all in compliance with City of Boston 
Complete Streets Guidelines. See Figure 4-13 for the existing St. Botolph Street section and 
Figures 4-14 and 4-15 for the proposed St. Botolph Street section, Figure 4-16 for the existing 
Gainsborough section and Figures 4-17 and 4-18 for the proposed Gainsborough sections. 
The proposed design provides an inclusive space with a continuous concrete sidewalk with 
accessible slopes that meet or exceed existing sidewalk width. Beyond the clear concrete 
sidewalk, paving patterns are designed to relate to the building architecture and program and site 
context. The dynamic paving patterns, façade elements, and site furnishings all contribute to a 
vibrant public realm.

4.5 
Zoning 
The Project Site is located within: (i) an Institutional subdistrict within the Fenway Neighborhood 
District (Map 1Q of the Code); (ii) the Restricted Parking Overlay District; (iii) the Northeastern 
Institutional Master Plan Area; (iv) the Institutional Master Plan Overlay District; and (v) the 
Groundwater Conservation Overlay District. The Project Site is subject to Northeastern’s 
Institutional Master Plan Area. 
Northeastern is submitting this IMPNF/PNF pursuant to Articles 80D and 80B of the Code, and will 
subsequently file a new IMP, which will include the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project as an IMP Project. When the IMP is approved, the 262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will be permitted without requiring any further zoning relief 
in accordance with Section 80D-11 of the Code, subject to obtaining a Certification of Consistency 
with the IMP pursuant to Section 80D-10 of the Code and a Certification of Compliance under 
Large Project Review pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code. Section 80D-11 provides that an IMP 
project which has obtained a Certification of Consistency and, if applicable, a Certification of 
Compliance “shall be deemed to be in compliance with the use, dimensional, parking and loading 
requirements of the underlying zoning (including special purpose overlay districts established 
districts established pursuant to Section 3-1A), notwithstanding any provision of the underlying 
zoning to the contrary and without the requirement of further Zoning Relief.” 
The university has long-contemplated how to make use of the existing building to adequately 
serve its programmatic needs and to support the community in meaningful ways, and in the 2013 
IMP, Northeastern proposed an expansion to the existing arena. However, through further 
investigation and due to the structural issues beyond repair, the 262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project, which will replace the existing arena, will meet current and 
future programmatic demands and will better serve the Northeastern community and City of 
Boston neighbors.

transfers. The Project will require a state permit but a MEPA threshold is not anticipated to be 
met and thus, Northeastern anticipates that MEPA review will not be required for the 262 St.

5.1 
Overview 
This chapter describes the transportation-related components of this IMPNF/PNF in accordance 
with the Boston Transportation Department’s (BTD’s) Transportation Access Plan (TAP) Guidelines 
and the BPDA’s IMP Review process. The following sections provide an overview of the 
transportation conditions on Northeastern’s Boston Campus including key changes since the 2013 
IMP; ongoing and planned transportation initiatives; and the relevant impacts associated with the 
proposed IMP projects. This information is intended to assist the community and the City agencies 
in identifying transportation-related issues that they would like to see further addressed in the 
IMP, which will include a more detailed analysis of traffic, parking, transit, short-term construction 
period impacts, and pedestrian and bicycle conditions within and around the Campus. 
Concurrent with the IMP, Northeastern intends to submit a Draft Project Impact Report (DPIR) for 
the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project that is proposed within this 
IMPNF/PNF. The DPIR will include a detailed transportation study that adheres to the BTD’s TAP 
Guidelines and the BPDA ’s Article 80 Large Project Review process. The DPIR will include an 
evaluation of the existing conditions, future conditions, and projected impacts to the overall 
campus parking supply, loading/delivery plan, transit services, pedestrian and bicycle activity, 
transportation demand management (TDM) strategies for the Project, and construction-period 
impacts. The proposed Multipurpose Athletic Facility will be required to enter into a 
Transportation Access Plan Agreement (TAPA); the TAPA will set forth the specific TDM measures 
and agreements between Northeastern and the City of Boston. 
5.1.1 
Context 
Northeastern is within walking distance of a variety of transportation options including public 
transit, Bluebikes shared bicycle facilities, and regional off-street pathways, as well as designated 
locations for car-sharing services. 
For Northeastern students, faculty, and staff, commuting by public transit is the most common 
mode of access to and from the Boston campus. Northeastern has excellent access to a wide 
variety of public transportation options including 14 Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority 
(MBTA) bus routes, rapid transit on the MBTA’s Orange and Green Lines, and commuter rail 
service on three lines (Franklin/Foxborough, Needham, and Providence/Stoughton). According to 
the 2023 Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP) Rideshare Survey, 
transit accounts for approximately 37% of faculty and staff trips and 46% of student trips. 
Bicycling and walking are the next most common modes of access to and throughout the Boston 
campus for students and are a key mode of access for faculty and staff. The Boston campus has 
direct access to the Southwest Corridor and proximity to the Back Bay Fens and Emerald Necklace. 
According to Northeastern’s 2023 DEP Rideshare Survey, approximately 39% of all students and 
approximately 12% of all faculty/staff walk or bike to campus.

Car-Sharing Services 
Car-sharing services enable easy access to short-term vehicular transportation. Vehicles are 
rented on an hourly or daily basis, and all vehicle costs (gas, maintenance, insurance, and parking) 
are included in the rental fee. Vehicles are checked out for a specific time period and returned to 
their designated location. Pick-up/drop-off locations are typically in existing parking lots or other 
parking areas throughout neighborhoods as a convenience to users of the services. Nearby car-
sharing services provide an important transportation option and reduce the need for private 
vehicle ownership. 
Zipcar is the primary car-share company in the Boston car-sharing market; however other 
companies such as Turo and Getaround also operate within the City. Four Zipcar locations (Leon 
Street, Renaissance Park Garage, Gainsborough Street, and Matthews Lot) and one EV from 
Good2Go (Columbus Garage) is located within the vicinity of the campus. Additional Zipcar 
locations are located within a five-minute walk (one-quarter mile) from the campus (Westland

MBTA Orange Line 
The MBTA’s Orange Line subway provides service from Forest Hills Station in Jamaica Plain 
through downtown Boston to Oak Grove Station in Malden. The Orange Line provides inbound 
and outbound service approximately every eight minutes Monday through Friday and every 10 to 
13 minutes on Saturday and Sunday. Two MBTA stations along the Orange Line are located within 
walking distance of the campus and used by the Northeastern community: Ruggles and 
Massachusetts Avenue stations. Ruggles Station is located in the south campus at the corner of 
Ruggles and Tremont Streets. The Massachusetts Avenue Station is located in the east campus on 
Massachusetts Avenue between Columbus Avenue and St. Botolph Street. A secondary egress 
from Massachusetts Avenue station is provided on the Camden footbridge. Proposed MBTA 
Ruggles Station improvements include constructing a station entrance accessible from the 
Camden Street footbridge and Gainsborough Street. 
MBTA Green Line 
The MBTA Green Line E Branch provides trolley service between Heath Street and Lechmere 
Stations. The E Branch operates on eight-minute headways during the weekday morning and 
afternoon peak periods and on eight- to nine-minute headways during off-peak periods. Weekend 
service runs approximately every nine minutes. The Museum of Fine Arts, Northeastern, 
Symphony, and Prudential Center Stations are all located along Huntington Avenue adjacent to 
the campus. 
MBTA Bus Service 
As shown in Table 5-5 and Figure 5-5, the Northeastern campus is located within convenient 
walking distance to 14 MBTA bus routes. The primary MBTA bus route serving the Northeastern 
campus is the #39 Bus, which provides service between Forest Hills Station and Back Bay Station 
via Huntington Avenue. The buses operate on seven- to ten-minute headways during the weekday 
morning and afternoon peak periods. Bus-Bike-Only lanes were installed along a one-mile section 
of Huntington Avenue between Brigham Circle and Gainsborough Street in 2022–2023 along the 
#39 route to improve bus efficiency and reliability. 
The campus is also located adjacent to the MBTA #43 bus on Tremont Street that provides service 
between Ruggles Station and Park Street Station. 
MBTA Commuter Rail 
Three MBTA commuter rail lines run through Ruggles Station: the Providence/Stoughton Line, the 
Franklin/Foxboro Line, and the Needham Line. Commuter rail trains provide access from Boston 
to the southern and southwestern regions of Massachusetts and Rhode Island.

minutes during peak periods and less frequently during off-peak hours. 
The Franklin/Foxboro Line has 20 inbound trains and 18 outbound trains that stop at Ruggles

5.2.3.2 
Northeastern Shuttle Connections 
The following other transit connections are available for Northeastern students, faculty, and staff. 
Northeastern RedEye Shuttle 
Northeastern operates the RedEye shuttle, an off-campus safety ride service, which is available 
for students who live within two miles of the center of campus. Every night from 5 p.m. until 6 
a.m., the RedEye van will pick students up at Egan Access Road behind Snell Library. Students can 
book a ride in advance using the RedEye App or at the RedEye dispatch center located at the 
Northeast Security office in the Ruggles Substation. The on-demand App matches riders to similar 
direction and destinations into a shared vehicle for efficient drop off loops that pick up from 
campus every 30 minutes. 
Northeastern Loop Shuttle 
The Northeastern loop shuttle runs on a continuous “loop” between Forsyth Circle and university 
housing near the Prudential Center, notably 60 Belvidere Street (former Sheraton Hotel) between 
6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. The loop shuttle operates on a first come, first 
served basis with no reservation system and was introduced in 2021 with the addition of a long-
term lease for university undergraduate student housing at 60 Belvidere Street. 
Northeastern Boston-Burlington Shuttle 
Northeastern provides shuttle service for faculty, students, and staff traveling between Boston 
and Burlington for the purposes of research, co-ops, and classes. Shuttles operate from 7:30 a.m. 
to 6:45 p.m and run approximately every two hours with additional service mid-day. The Boston-
Burlington shuttle was introduced in 2022 to provide more research opportunities for students, 
to offer more flexible working hours for co-ops, and to allow staff more options for collaboration 
between campuses.

MasParc Connect 
MasParc provides access to and from the Boston campus via on-demand electric vehicles to local

operates Monday to Saturday from 10:00 a.m. – 8:00 p.m. Rides are requested by Northeastern

transport staff, patients, and students to and around the LMA area via shuttle services from public 
transit stops and off-site parking facilities. The Longwood Collective shuttle buses serve stops at 
Ruggles Station, JKF/UMass, Andrews Square, Fenway, Landsdowne Station, Landmark Center, 
and the Renaissance and Columbus garages. 
5.2.4

5.2.4.1 
Pedestrian Access 
Sidewalks are provided on both sides of all roadways within the study area. Crosswalks and ramps 
are provided at all study area intersections. 
5.2.4.2 
Bicycle Access 
Separated bicycle lanes are provided along Columbus Avenue east of Melnea Cass Boulevard. 
Additionally, there are share-the-road arrows (sharrows) along Ruggles Street, north of Tremont 
Street. The Melnea Cass Bike Path, a two-way multi-use path, is located on the north side of 
Melnea Cass Boulevard between Tremont Street and Massachusetts Avenue to the south. The 
City of Boston’s “Bicycle Level of Traffic Stress Map” last updated in 2022 designates Ruggles 
Street, Huntington Avenue, Massachusetts Avenue, and Tremont Street as intermediate routes, 
or routes which do not have on-road bicycle markings or signage and are suitable for riders with 
some on-road experience. Recently, Bus-Bike-Only lanes have been installed on Huntington 
Avenue and separated bicycle lanes and Bus-Bike-Only lanes have been installed on 
Massachusetts Avenue north of Melnea Cass Boulevard and across the Massachusetts Avenue 
Bridge into Cambridge. The Southwest Corridor path, which follows the north edge of Columbus 
Avenue, is designated as a beginner route – i.e., a path, trail, or car-free roadway suitable for all 
riders including new cyclists with no on-road experience. Bicycle facilities in the area are

5.2.4.3 
Bicycle Sharing 
Numerous bicycle-sharing stations, located throughout the campus, are provided by Bluebikes, 
Boston area’s largest bicycle sharing service which was launched in 2011 and currently consists of 
more than 4,000 shared bicycles at more than 400 stations throughout 13 metro-Boston 
communities, including Boston, Brookline, Cambridge, Chelsea, Somerville, and Everett. As shown 
in Figure 5-6, five Bluebikes stations are located on or near campus and additional stations are 
located within one-half-mile of the campus. Northeastern has contributed to a number of these 
stations and offers discounts to Northeastern users. 
5.2.4.4 
Bicycle Storage and Demand 
Northeastern is continually evaluating on-campus bicycle usage and storage, and actively adds 
bicycle racks and/or relocates existing racks to meet changing demand patterns as bicycle usage 
continues to evolve. Northeastern has significantly increased on-campus bicycle storage from only 
141 rack spaces at eight locations in 2000 to approximately 2,000 rack spaces at nearly 40 
locations throughout the campus in 2023. 
The East Village (GrandMarc) Project was the first campus building to provide a dedicated bicycle 
storage room within a residence hall facility with a capacity of approximately 80 bicycles. Since 
that time, LightView (537 bicycle spaces), Interdisciplinary Science and Engineering Complex 
(ISEC) (104 bicycle spaces), and EXP (128 bicycle spaces), have all added internal covered and 
secured long-term bicycle storage accommodations in addition to external short-term visitor 
racks. The BPDA Board recently approved 840 Columbus Avenue, which will include an additional 
approximately 246 bicycle spaces in a ground floor bicycle room and approximately 70 short-
term, exterior spaces for visitors on outdoor racks. 
These new bicycle accommodations will bring the campus-wide storage total up to approximately 
1,095 secure/internal bicycles, and 1,151 external visitor bicycles. 
Table 5-6 and Figure 5-8 show bicycle rack locations on campus, both covered and uncovered, and 
locations where bikes are parked without formal bike racks. Approximately one-half of the bicycle 
racks are covered. Designated bicycle parking is well-used during peak periods; bicycles were also 
observed chained to poles, etc. in the most heavily used areas. Seven different types of bicycle 
storage racks can be found on campus as shown in Figure 5-9.

5.2.5 
Loading, Service, and Emergency Access 
Northeastern’s Transportation, Receiving, and Warehousing Department is responsible for 
administering the campus’s central receiving and distribution system, which is run from a central 
warehouse in Jamaica Plain. The department receives vendor deliveries, stores equipment and 
materials as necessary, and completes deliveries to on-campus locations, as well as from one 
campus location to another. Most buildings on campus also receive regular deliveries of mail, 
supplies, and food, some of which, such as those by courier or express delivery, occur within the 
public way. 
On campus, the building housing the university’s mail center at 716 Columbus Avenue is 
scheduled for renovation and upgrades. The renovations include upgrades to the mail center to 
accommodate broader receiving and delivery needs and the installation of an additional delivery 
window on the lower level. Construction on the centralized mail facility will be completed in 2024. 
Campus loading docks and access restrictions are summarized in Figure 5-10. As shown, in 
addition to the main service road along the MBTA Orange Line tracks, several other routes within 
the campus are used by vehicles servicing buildings. 
To the extent possible, all deliveries and pickups are coordinated to minimize impacts to the 
community. In addition, as further described below, Northeastern coordinates student move-in 
days with BTD, neighborhood residents, and other affected parties to minimize traffic disruption.

5.2.5.2 
Trash/Recycling 
Staff empties outdoor waste/recycling containers throughout the day seven days per week, 
consolidating materials to other locations on campus. 
Consolidated trash and recycling materials are picked up starting at approximately 7:00 a.m. via 
hauler trucks on routes that vary by day, time, duration, and service stops. Recycling materials 
are picked up by facilities staff who operate five box trucks throughout the campus; materials are 
actively picked up across campus during typical recycling staff shift hours (6:00 a.m. – 2:30 p.m.) 
and occasionally earlier or later to accommodate special situations. Approximately 20 
compactors are located on the campus. Compactors are emptied as needed, with service ranging 
from once per week to once per month. 
5.2.5.3 
Food Waste 
In addition to trash and recycling, food waste is also picked daily, generally in the time frame of 
5:00 a.m. – -8:00 a.m. Conversion of food waste to compost helps to divert waste from landfills 
and is part of a broader commitment to reducing Northeastern’s environmental footprint. 
5.2.5.4 
Emergency Service Access 
Emergency access to the campus is provided by the City street network, principally the arterial 
streets of Massachusetts Avenue, Huntington Avenue, Ruggles Street, and Columbus Avenue. 
Access into the campus is provided by local streets and a network of service roadways and 
pathways throughout the campus. 
5.2.6 
Student Move-in Move Out 
Since 2000, Northeastern has prepared Move-In/Move-Out Plans each academic year for BTD. 
The Move-Out Plan is usually a less formalized document since that process is more gradual, 
taking place over a longer timeframe. The elements of the Move-In Plan include: 
♦ Notifying neighbors about the move-in process and arranging parking for neighbors in the 
Camden Lot and Gainsborough garages for the weekend. 
♦ Avoiding moving students into the Fenway area on September 1 due to expected 
congestion. 
♦ Working with the neighborhoods on August 31 and September 1. 
♦ Assisting coordination of trash removal and police presence. 
♦ Reaching out to neighboring businesses and institutions (i.e., the Symphony, Wentworth) 
in early May and early June to notify them of Northeastern’s move-in plans.

5.2.7 
Transportation Demand Management (TDM) 
As outlined in its 2013 IMP, Northeastern has made a strong commitment to TDM and continues 
to make improvements to TDM initiatives to help reduce single-occupant automobile commuting 
to and from its campus, and to promote non-automobile alternatives. It is expected that enhanced 
bicycle storage, expansion of car-sharing opportunities, provisions for alternative fuel vehicles, 
and continued attention to parking availability and pricing will be priority efforts over the term of 
the IMP. As the parking supply on campus is reduced due to new building projects, parking ratios 
for students and staff will decrease. This reduced availability typically leads to higher fees for 
automobile users, further serving as a demand management measure. 
The following promotions and incentives are offered to faculty, staff, and students: 
♦ Posting of schedules, maps, fare information; 
♦ MBTA semester pass program; 
♦ Pre-tax purchase of MBTA passes for employees; 
♦ On-campus Bluebikes stations; 
♦ Bluebikes membership subsidies; 
♦ Indoor, secured bicycle spaces and outdoor visitor bicycle spaces across campus; 
♦ Preferential parking for carpools and vanpools; 
♦ Access to EV charging; and 
♦ Limited overnight parking for campus residents.

5.3 
Future Conditions 
The following sections provide a summary of the future transportation conditions and proposed 
improvements occurring in the area. 
5.3.1 
Ongoing Transportation Initiatives 
Northeastern is actively engaged with various City and State agencies on a number of initiatives 
to improve transportation conditions in and around the campus, as described in the following: 
♦ Tremont Street Improvements. The Tremont Street Design Project, completed in fall 
2023, was intended to make Tremont Street safer for everyone with an emphasis on 
pedestrian safety at intersections along Tremont Street between Massachusetts Avenue 
and Herald Street in the South End. 
♦ Roxbury Resilient Corridors. Corridor improvements are in initial planning stages for 
Malcolm X Boulevard, Melnea Cass Boulevard, and Warren Street. Concept designs will 
include the roads, sidewalks, green infrastructure, and public spaces of these three major 
corridors in Roxbury. Corridor improvements are proposed in two phases: 
o Phase 1. Community engagement for Malcolm X Boulevard (12-18 months) leading to 
final concept design. This Phase will require tight coordination and collaboration with 
the MBTA. 
o Phase 2. Community engagement and concept design for Warren Street and Melnea 
Cass Boulevard will start in 2025. The beginning of Phase 2 may overlap with the last 
months of Phase 1. 
♦ Roxbury-Fenway Connector. The Roxbury to Fenway Connector is a proposed "Green 
Link” that would include a path within the existing double row of trees on Ruggles Street 
between Ruggles Station and Parker Street. 
♦ Northeastern Boston Campus Bike Parking Framework. Building on existing analyses of 
bicycle parking usage, locations, and types, the university is formalizing bike parking 
approaches and policies in a framework plan. The framework will establish guidance for 
rack location selection, style, installation, and maintenance on the Boston campus. 
♦ Ruggles Street Improvements. Ruggles Street between the Parker Street intersection and 
the Southwest Corridor has been identified in the BTD’s GoBoston 2030 report as a 
candidate corridor in the continuing expansion of the Boston Green Links initiative to 
improve access to green spaces and active transportation options. New pedestrian paths, 
bicycle facilities, and safer road crossings have been recently constructed.

♦ MBTA Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Extensions. The MBTA Columbus Avenue Bus Lanes 
Project constructed New England’s first center-running bus lane. Phase 1 of the Columbus 
Avenue bus lane operates between Jackson Square and Walnut Avenue. Phase 2 of the 
Columbus Avenue center bus lane would extend the existing center-running bus lanes on 
Columbus Avenue north from Jackson Square to Ruggles Station. The design includes 
center platforms with shelters and real-time arrival information, redesigned circulation 
to reduce bus travel times throughout the corridor, improvements to pedestrian 
crossings, and added green infrastructure to make the area more welcoming for everyone 
who lives, studies, and travels along the corridor. 
♦ MBTA Better Bus Project. The Better Bus Project was created as part of the MBTA’s $9.6 
billion, five-year capital investment plan in 2018 to improve bus service throughout the 
MBTA service area. Initial changes were implemented in 2019 to provide more frequent, 
consistent, and reliable service, as well as a small number of new connections. In addition 
to service changes, the Better Bus Project is constructing bus priority infrastructure, 
including bus layover spaces, bus stops, signage, and signals. 
♦ 840 Columbus Avenue. The recently-approved 840 Columbus Avenue project will be set 
back from the property lines to create wider sidewalks on Columbus Avenue, Melnea Cass 
Boulevard, and Tremont Street; design and install a street-level two-way, separated 
bicycle lane on Columbus Avenue; design and install a sidewalk-level, separated bicycle 
lane on Melnea Cass Boulevard; and design and construct accessibility and Complete 
Street improvements to the intersections of Melnea Cass Boulevard/Columbus Avenue 
and Melnea Cass Boulevard/Tremont Street, including curb ramps and their reciprocal 
ramps, protected bicycle facilities, and traffic signals. Investment into new or existing 
Bluebike stations are included in the project. 
♦ 716 Columbus Avenue. Northeastern is reconstructing sidewalks along Benton Street 
adjacent to the building. New streetlights, street trees, bicycle racks, and curb extensions 
are included in the project.

SUSTAINABILITY AND CLIMATE RESILIENCE 
6.1 
Approach and Goals 
Northeastern University has a longstanding commitment to sustainability and resilience through 
its research, experiential education, and support of the physical campus and its surroundings. In 
2007, university President Joseph Aoun was a founding member of the American College & 
University Presidents Climate Commitment. In 2010, the Northeastern Facilities Division released 
the university’s first sustainability plan, which made a commitment to reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions by 80 percent by 2050. Northeastern has made great progress since then, reducing 
emissions by 42 percent while emphasizing resiliency, or the ability to withstand change and adapt 
quickly. 
Northeastern’s pride in these accomplishments is matched by an interest in moving forward to 
broaden efforts for collective action at the intersection of climate change and related social justice 
issues. Events like the Flint water crisis, COVID-19, and the 2020 racial awakening have highlighted 
the unequal burdens of climate change, along with sustainability and social justice. Climate justice 
calls for a transition away from the extraction of resources, both human and natural, and connects 
the climate crisis to social, racial, and environmental issues, in which it is deeply entangled. Higher 
education has an opportunity, and a responsibility, for greater impacts by working with City and 
community partners to address the systems that interconnect with climate justice and 
sustainability. Moreover, by using citywide frameworks as the basis for university sustainability 
planning, Northeastern ensures its commitment to act in service of the broader community and 
planet. Plans like the Boston Climate Action Plan and Urban Forest Plan help establish the 
foundation for the university’s sustainability plans and strategies, while policies like BERDO and 
the Specialized Stretch Energy Code act as key measures to ensure robust building standards. 
Climate Justice Action Plan (CJAP) 
In late 2022, Northeastern partnered with campus and community members to launch its Climate 
Justice Action Plan (CJAP) planning process. The Climate Justice and Sustainability Hub, part of 
Northeastern’s Planning, Real Estate and Facilities division, and its community partners, co-
designed a process that ensured the plan would be responsive to the concerns of locally impacted 
communities and aligned with the university’s research, teaching and physical plant stewardship 
goals. The steering committee, made up of community representatives, students, frontline 
workers, faculty, and Northeastern staff, has worked closely for over 15 months towards a 
consensus on goals and strategy recommendations for the plan. 
The resulting CJAP goals, strategies, and actions have created a framework for Northeastern in its 
pursuit of sustainable and just solutions to climate and intersecting issues. A summary of CJAP’s 
goals and strategies has been provided in Table 6-1.

6.2 
Sustainable Campuses 
Northeastern has made significant strides in campus sustainability over the past decade, including 
sustainable buildings, landscape, and commuter mode choices that reduce emissions and 
congestion. Northeastern requires that all new major buildings or renovations achieve a minimum 
of LEED Gold certification, with the goal of achieving LEED Platinum. This and other sustainability 
standards are outlined in Northeastern’s recently updated Sustainable Design Standards1. To 
date, Northeastern has seven LEED certified projects in Boston, including ISEC certified LEED Gold 
in 2018, East Village certified LEED Gold in 2016, and LightView student housing certified LEED 
Platinum in 2021. The recently completed EXP building has committed to LEED Platinum 
certification. The new Pedestrian Crossing bridge (PedEx) received an Envision Bronze certification 
for sustainable infrastructure. 
6.2.1 
Building Decarbonization and Energy Resilience 
6.2.1.1 
Greenhouse Gas Emissions & Local Air Quality 
Between 2005 and 2021, greenhouse gas emissions per square foot of building space on 
Northeastern’s Boston campus declined by 42%. In 2023, Northeastern received a Mass Save 
Climate Leader award for its energy efficiency efforts, including an extensive LED lighting upgrade. 
ISEC and EXP, the two largest developments to be constructed since the 2013 IMP, were designed 
creatively to achieve high levels of sustainability. ISEC, which is LEED gold certified, achieved 50% 
energy savings when compared to a typical lab building through solutions such as a cascading air 
system and a solar veil. EXP, a multidisciplinary science and learning complex completed in fall 
2023, is committed to achieving LEED Platinum certification. From triple glazing to heat recovery 
chillers, energy efficiency efforts lead to a 50% reduction in energy use, and a 74% reduction in 
natural gas use compared to a baseline building. The reduction in fossil fuel use contributes not 
only to a reduction in carbon emissions but also to better air quality. 
Across existing buildings, the university has identified which roofs are suitable for solar PV and is 
also planning the addition of solar arrays on roofs due for replacement. The university is currently 
negotiating a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) to install solar panels on the roof of the Curry 
Student Center, which was replaced in 2023 and designed to support solar panels. This follows 
the recent installation of solar panels on the roof of Snell Library in spring 2024.

Decarbonization and Resiliency Planning and Other Utility Planning Efforts 
Northeastern’s approach to decarbonization includes 1) reducing the energy use intensity of its 
buildings, and 2) transitioning to clean energy sources. The university’s DRP will turn this approach 
into an implementable plan that ties building-level interventions into a campus-wide strategy for 
energy, decarbonization, and resiliency. 
The DRP team is currently engaged in an early recommendations phase to ensure that near-term 
large investments align with and create assets for future zero carbon options. Following 
identification and assessment of alternative decarbonization scenarios, the university is targeting 
an approved multi-year DRP by Fall 2025. 
The DRP will build off growth and development planning established in this IMPNF/PNF to identify 
load, opportunities, and phasing that aligns with development and capital needs over the next 
decade. In turn, it will ensure that development approved through the 2024 IMP is implemented 
in-line with a realistic plan to meet or exceed Northeastern’s, the State’s, and City’s 
decarbonization goals. 
The DRP also builds from Northeastern’s utility planning work, including an early analysis of 
electrical load growth, identification of Energy Conservation Measures (ECM’s), and solar PV 
potential. In the summer, the current peak load on campus for electricity is nearly 18MW and 
peak steam load is about 135M pounds/hr. 
The Boston campus currently faces electric distribution limitations and failing steam lines. To 
ensure resilience and reliability, the university is switching parts of the campus’ existing steam 
system from a natural gas-fired central plant to Vicinity’s high-pressure steam, while negotiating 
towards purchase of their “e-steam” product. This transition will decrease on-site fossil fuel 
emissions associated with existing building operations on campus. Eventual decommissioning of 
the central campus heating plant will also reduce scope one emissions and associated local air 
pollutants. 
Once finalized, the DRP and related planning efforts will enable Northeastern to describe more 
precisely the university’s plans for electrical load growth, solar PV, installation, long-range district 
system, as well as the university’s timeline to meet goals, regulations, and interim milestones. In 
the interim, the university is on track to comfortably exceed BERDO requirements through 2029.

described in Chapter 5, a large percentage of on-campus students utilize walking and/or running

bicycle, scooter, skateboard). According to the 2023 Massachusetts Department of Environmental 
Protection (MassDEP) Rideshare Survey, transit accounts for approximately 37% of faculty and 
staff trips and 46% of student trips. Furthermore, Northeastern’s practice over the years of

Diversion 
In 2022, Northeastern expanded its composting services to include all dining halls, which resulted

Reduction and Reuse 
Northeastern seeks to reduce and reuse materials in capital projects, purchases, and practices 
across the university. Northeastern’s Capital Projects team targets furniture reuse and, where 
unable, identifies partners or needs in the community where items in good condition can get a 
second life. This has ranged from 700 pounds of office supplies being donated to the Great 
Exchange to gently used appliances being donated to Boston Building Resources. 
The university’s updated Sustainable Design Standards address embodied carbon, requiring new 
buildings and whole building renovations to perform whole building life cycle carbon analysis and 
reduce embodied carbon of primary materials by 20% from a typical design. 
“OZZI” containers in dining halls are reusable to-go containers that provide convenience and 
flexibility while reducing the volume of paper and foam products in landfills. Meanwhile, to 
reduce plastic waste, there are also over 250 water bottle filling stations throughout campus. 
Northeastern is actively exploring additional procurement opportunities to further reduce the 
purchase and use of single-use plastics.

Climate Resilience 
6.2.4.1 
Arboretum 
Urban green space contributes notably not only to ecology but also to human health and 
wellbeing. These spaces support community activity, filter pollution, mitigate heat islands, 
support water retention and filtration, and more. Northeastern University’s Arboretum was 
awarded a Level II Accreditation through ArbNet. Level II-accredited arboreta have 100 species, 
varieties or cultivars of trees or woody plants, an arboretum collections policy describing the 
development and professional management of plants and enhanced educational and public 
programming. Northeastern’s Boston campus has more than 1,400 individual trees and 5,400 
shrubs, representing 320 different wood species that shelter the walkways between buildings and 
surround the open green spaces, creating an urban oasis. This mature canopy provides respite, 
helps mitigate urban heat island, and supports management of stormwater runoff. 
Beyond its own campus, Northeastern supports trees by urban forestry efforts, helping to 
maintain urban street trees and partnering with community groups to support their urban 
canopy. For example, Northeastern staff and co-ops recently partnered with Mission Hill 
Neighborhood Housing Services to help Fitzgerald Park become certified as a Level I arboretum.

Excessive heat is a serious threat to health and wellbeing that disproportionately impacts 
vulnerable communities. In summer 2023, following Mayor Wu’s call for local institutions to 
support the City’s response to extreme heat, the university piloted its Hot Summer: Cool Break 
initiative. Northeastern joined community partners to host Community Heat Breaks at summer 
camps or residential communities on hot afternoons. These festive gatherings for children and

Projects completed during the 2013 IMP paid particular attention to water use and green

6.3.3.1 
Introduction 
Northeastern has reviewed climate change conditions as further detailed, more frequent and 
severe weather events, including higher maximum and mean temperatures, longer and more 
extreme heat events, increased droughts, and severe precipitation events. A copy of the 
completed Climate Resiliency Checklist is included in Appendix E. 
6.3.3.2 
Extreme Heat Events 
According to “Climate Ready Boston,” the City of Boston can expect that the number of days with 
temperatures greater than 90°F will increase. Between 1971 and 2000, Boston experienced an 
average of eleven days per year over 90 degrees and may experience between 25 and 90 days 
annually by 2070, depending on the extent of greenhouse gas emissions over the next several 
decades. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project design incorporates 
measures to minimize the impact of high temperature events, including: 
♦ High-albedo roofing materials; 
♦ New street trees to provide shade;

6.3.3.3 
Flooding Events 
Because of climate change, New England is expected to experience an increased frequency of 
intense storms that generate significant volumes of precipitation. Such precipitation events have 
the potential to overwhelm existing stormwater infrastructure capacity and may result in inland 
flooding with the potential to damage buildings. Improper conveyance of stormwater during 
precipitation events may also cause overflows of combined sewer systems that allow wastewater 
from buildings connected to the combined sewer to discharge to local waterways, or that 
surcharge the system and cause overflow at other locations. 
To mitigate the effects of extreme precipitation events, the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project’s stormwater management system will be designed to minimize the 
volume of stormwater runoff from the Project Site and promote groundwater recharge to the 
greatest extent practicable. Part of the stormwater management strategy is to include pervious 
pavers, where feasible, on the Project Site. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project will retain the first 1.25-inch of stormwater runoff from the Site’s impervious 
areas. 
6.3.3.4 
Drought Conditions 
Under the high emissions scenario evaluated by Climate Ready Boston, the occurrence of 
droughts lasting one to three months could increase by as much as 75% over existing conditions 
by the end of the century. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will 
approach potential drought impacts by reducing the amount of water used within the building 
and across the Project Site for irrigation. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility 
Project will include low-flow fixtures and water conserving appliances, to the extent feasible, to 
minimize the amount of water used by the building’s occupants.

7.1.7.2 
Groundwater Conditions 
Groundwater observation wells have been installed and are being monitored at the Project Site. 
Based on groundwater level measurements dating back to 2012, groundwater levels generally 
range between El. 4 and El. 7 Boston City Base Datum. 
Groundwater levels are influenced by the presence of stormwater recharge systems at the north 
and southwest portions of the Project Site. Site groundwater levels will vary with season, 
precipitation, construction activity in the area, below-grade structures, leakage from utilities, and 
other factors. 
7.1.7.3 
Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD) 
The Project Site is located within the Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD), 
therefore specific requirements of Article 32 of the Boston Zoning Code and the Boston Water 
and Sewer Commission (BWSC) policy will apply. Construction of a building that falls within the 
district must not negatively impact groundwater levels in the area. A suitably designed 
groundwater recharge system will be constructed as part of the 262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. The lowest level of the new building and ice rink slab are 
anticipated to be at El. 11’-7” or higher and above El. 7 BCB and area groundwater levels. 
Therefore, no permanent groundwater pumping or underslab drainage systems are necessary for 
new building construction. A “no harm” letter regarding groundwater will be submitted to the 
BPDA and the Boston Groundwater Trust. 
7.1.7.4 
Foundation Construction Methodology 
Northeastern anticipates that the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will 
support the building on deep foundations bearing in bedrock. High capacity, low displacement 
steel H-piles will be used for new building column support. Piles will be vibrated to the top of the 
bedrock bearing stratum to mitigate noise and potential impacts to abutting structures. Following 
installation to top of bedrock, piles will be driven to final end bearing resistance. Appropriate 
vibration performance criteria will be developed for levels not to be exceeded during 
construction. 
The replaced ice rink slab will be supported on a combination of existing and new concrete 
caissons (drilled shafts) bearing within the Marine Clay Deposit. 
Excavation will be required for construction of new pile caps and various below grade features. 
Excavation depths will vary from approximately 5 to 13 feet deep at isolated locations depending 
on existing conditions and new construction requirements. Temporary support of excavation 
requirements are anticipated to be limited. 
Excavation for new substructure construction will generally be above Site groundwater levels. 
Temporary construction dewatering will be required for short term deeper excavations and to 
control surface water runoff into excavations during rain events. Any temporary dewatering

7.2.3.4 
DEP Stormwater Management Policy Standards 
In March 1997, MassDEP adopted a new Stormwater Management Policy (the Policy) to address 
non-point source pollution. In 1997, MassDEP published the Massachusetts Stormwater 
Handbook as guidance on the Policy, which was revised in February 2008. The Policy prescribes 
specific stormwater management standards for development projects, including urban pollutant 
removal criteria for projects that may impact environmental resource areas. Compliance is 
achieved through the implementation of Best Management Practices (BMPs) in the stormwater 
management design. The Policy is administered locally pursuant to MGL Ch. 131, s. 40. 
A brief explanation of each Policy Standard and the system compliance is provided below: 
Standard #1: No new stormwater conveyances (e.g. outfalls) may discharge untreated 
stormwater directly to or cause erosion in wetlands or waters of the Commonwealth.

cause erosion to, wetlands or waters. Therefore Standard #1 will be met. 
Standard #2: Stormwater management systems shall be designed so that post-development peak 
discharge rates do not exceed pre-development peak discharge rates. This Standard may be 
waived for discharges to land subject to coastal storm flowage as defined in 310 CMR 10.04 
The proposed stormwater management system will be designed so that there is no increase in

Standard #3: Recharge to groundwater 
Loss of annual recharge to groundwater shall be eliminated or minimized through the use of 
environmentally sensitive site design, Low Impact Development techniques, stormwater best 
management practices, and good operation and maintenance. At a minimum, the annual 
recharge from the post- development site shall approximate the annual recharge from pre-
development conditions based on soil type. This Standard is met when the stormwater 
management system is designed to infiltrate the required recharge volume as determined in 
accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. 
Soil testing will be done to determine the Hydrologic soil types. The Project will be required to 
infiltrate a volume of runoff equal to 1.25 inch of rainfall times the total footprint of proposed 
impervious area / building on-site to meet BWSC requirements. Therefore, Standard #3 is 
anticipated to be met. 
Standard #4: Stormwater management systems shall be designed to remove 80% of the average 
annual post-construction load of Total Suspended Solids (TSS). This Standard is met when: 
a. Suitable practices for source control and pollution prevention are identified in a long-term 
pollution prevention plan, and thereafter are implemented and maintained; 
b. Structural stormwater best management practices are sized to capture the required water 
quality volume determined in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook; 
and 
c. Pretreatment is provided in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. 
Most of the Project Site will be occupied by the proposed building, which includes roof runoff that 
will be routed to new infiltration system to meet the BWSC requirements, thus meeting the 80% 
TSS removal for majority of the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. 
Therefore, Standard #4 is anticipated to be met.

8.1 
Historic Resources 
This chapter briefly addresses the historic designations of the potential development sites 
described in this IMPNF/PNF, and specifically, the proposed development of the 262 St. Botolph 
Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. As other IMP Projects proceed to permitting, some 
may be subject to Article 80B, Large Project Review or Article 85, Demolition Delay Review. As 
Northeastern University continues to develop the specifics of other IMP Projects, regulatory 
requirements for each of the potential development sites will be discussed in the subsequent 
filings related to those projects. 
The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is located in the 
Fenway Neighborhood District of Boston. The Project Site is included in the Inventory of Historic 
and Archaeological Assets of the Commonwealth, but it is not listed in the State or National 
Registers of Historic Places. The Project Site, also currently known as the Matthews Arena, was 
initially constructed in 1910, the building (then known as the Boston Arena) consisted of a two-
story masonry entry block on the north elevation connecting to a large arena building, which was 
destroyed in a fire in 1918 and replaced with the present arena in 1920. Subsequent additions 
were added circa 1950 and in 2010 along with substantial alterations to the arena and entry block 
including removal of windows, infilling window openings with masonry and cladding over original 
masonry as well as removal of the entry block’s towers. During the late twentieth century, 
changes prior to the purchase of the arena by Northeastern were devastating to the building’s 
historic architecture. Historic features such as windows, doors, towers, decorative masonry, 
stairs, and terra cotta ornamentation were removed and/or covered over, stripping the building 
of its historic integrity. The substantial loss of integrity makes Matthews Arena ineligible for listing 
on the National Register of Historic Places. 
For additional information, please refer to the Historical Significance and Architectural Evaluation 
that has been provided in Appendix G.

Street, and Massachusetts Avenue will be limited. Further, the proposed size and massing of the 
262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project are consistent with the surrounding 
streetscape, as well as the historic and evolving use of the property as an arena and athletic 
facility. 
Further information regarding the potential development sites and visual impacts, if any, will be 
provided in subsequent filings for specific IMP Projects. 
8.4.3 
Shadow Impacts to Historic Resources 
The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is being designed to 
minimize new shadows on open spaces, sitting areas, or pathways to the extent feasible. 
Northeastern will conduct a shadow study for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project and include the results in the DPIR. 
8.5 
Consistency with Other Historic Reviews 
8.5.1 
Article 85 
The demolition of buildings over 50-years of age at potential development sites, including the 
Mathews Arena (BOS.15498) at 238-262 St. Botolph Street, will be subject to review of the Boston 
Landmarks Commission under Article 85 of the Code.

Massachusetts Historical Commission 
At this time, no state or federal funding, licensing, permits and/or approvals requiring review by

action is identified as required for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project, 
an MHC Project Notification Form will be filed in compliance with State Register Review (950 CMR 
71.00) and/or Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act (36 CFR 800).

Rowan Williams Davies & Irwin Inc. (RWDI) has prepared this letter of opinion to comment 
on the expected wind conditions around the proposed redevelopment of Matthews Arena at 
Northeastern University in Boston, MA. This qualitative assessment is based on a review of 
the local wind climate, the project information received by RWDI on May 14, 2024, the 
existing surroundings, and our experience and professional judgment. Detailed modeling 
and assessments will be carried out to quantify the predicted wind conditions and develop 
wind control solutions. 
Site & Project Information 
The Project is located at 238-262 St Botolph St, west of Massachusetts Avenue and South of 
Huntington Avenue in Boston (Image 1). The site is adjacent to the Massachusetts Avenue 
transit station and near the William E. Carter School grounds that are located to the 
southeast and south. Tall buildings that are 10-17 stories tall exist near the site on St 
Botolph Street to the north, west and southwest. The extended surroundings comprise a 
dense arrangement of generally six-storey buildings in the easterly and westerly directions, 
with midrise buildings of the order of eight to 20 stories to the southwest, and high-rise 
buildings to the north (Image 2). 
The existing Matthews Arena at the same site will be demolished to allow for the 
construction of a new facility (Image 3). The Athletic program presumes a maximum 
building size of 290,000 square feet of gross floor area, which includes a 4,000-seat arena, 
hockey and basketball team support facilities, a basketball practice facility, and a multi-use 
athletic and recreation turf/court space. Key areas of focus in this assessment include public 
areas (sidewalks and transit station) and the school grounds.

Meteorological Data 
Wind statistics recorded at Boston Logan International Airport between 1995 and 2020, 
inclusive, were analyzed to be used for this project. Image 4 graphically depicts the 
directional distribution of wind frequency and speeds on an annual and seasonal basis. 
When all winds are considered, those blowing from the northwest and southwest quadrants 
are predominant. Strong winds of a mean speed greater than 20 mph (indicated by red 
bands in the wind roses) measured at the airport (at an anemometer height of 30 ft) occur 
more often during the colder months of the year and are predominantly from the west-
northwest and northeast directions. The west-northwest winds are frequent and strongest 
in the winter, but also very prevalent in the spring and fall.

BPDA Wind Criteria 
The BPDA has adopted two standards for assessing the relative pedestrian wind conditions. 
First, the BPDA wind design guidance criterion states that an effective gust velocity (hourly 
mean wind speed +1.5 times the root-mean-square wind speed) of 31 mph should not be 
exceeded more than one percent of the time. The second set of criteria used by the BPDA 
to determine the acceptability of specific locations is based on the work of Melbourne and is 
used to determine the relative level of pedestrian wind comfort for activities such as sitting, 
standing, or walking. The criteria are expressed in terms of benchmarks for the one-hour 
mean wind speed exceeded 1% of the time. 
Although detailed results are not presented at this time, please note that the preliminary 
comments provided herein are based on the safety and comfort criteria as defined by the 
BPDA.

Preliminary Findings 
The proposed building will be taller (approximately 115 ft) than the existing Matthews Arena 
facility (approximately 65 ft), and comparable in height to the taller buildings that exist along 
St Botolph Street. The shorter but densely built massings in the surroundings to the 
southwest, northwest and northeast (Image 2) will precondition the approaching winds 
from those directions. 
The wind speeds at the existing site are expected to be inherently low to moderate, with the 
conditions being appropriate for the use of the public sidewalks, transit station entrance and 
the school grounds, given the surrounding urban landscape. The addition of the proposed, 
taller building will result in the redirection of more wind along the surrounding streets. 
However, due to the existing low wind speeds in the area, the redirected winds are not 
expected to be problematic in most areas. Wind speeds on the sidewalks around the Project 
are expected to continue to be appropriate for pedestrian use; high and potentially 
uncomfortable wind speeds may occur on an annual basis at the street intersections 
adjacent to the Project. These conditions can be quantified during later detailed modeling 
studies and the effectiveness of potential mitigation measures will be evaluated. 
The project is not expected to negatively affect wind conditions in the William E. Carter 
School grounds park (Image 1), as the park would be sheltered from the predominant winds 
from the northwest and southwest by the Project. A slight increase in wind speeds may be 
expected in the school tennis courts located to the south of the Project site across the transit 
line (Image 2). However, conditions are expected to continue to be appropriate for the 
expected use on an annual basis. 
The qualitative assessment of potential wind conditions around the proposed project 
provided herein is based on our experience, knowledge of the local climate and 
understanding of the current building designs. The wind impact of the Project will be 
quantified using detailed modeling. 
Conclusions 
The proposed development site is favorably surrounded by densely built areas that 
precondition the prevailing approach winds. The addition of the proposed building, that will 
be comparable in height or taller than most existing buildings in the immediate vicinity, is 
expected to moderately increase wind speeds along the sidewalks adjacent to the Project. 
Owing the low-moderate existing wind conditions, the moderately higher wind speeds are 
expected to continue to be appropriate for pedestrian uses on an annual basis. The 
predicted wind conditions will be quantified using detailed modeling.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
 
The building located at 238 St. Botolph Street, historically known as the Boston (Matthews) Arena 
(BOS.15498) has a long history with Boston sports and hosted many events in Boston’s history 
including visiting celebrities and dignitaries. Over the building’s history, it has endured many 
changes as a result of increasing space demands, fires, and changing uses and owners. Never 
rising to the prominence of the Boston Garden, the arena was always a secondary or a tertiary 
location of events in Boston. A devasting fire in 1918 resulted in the building being largely rebuilt, 
with only a portion of its original 1910 structure remaining. It is the late twentieth century 
changes prior to the purchase of the arena by Northeastern University, which have been 
devastating to the building’s historic architecture. Historic features such as windows, doors, 
towers, decorative masonry stairs and terra cotta ornamentation have been removed and/or 
covered over, stripping the building of its historic character and integrity. While the building has 
a long history with Boston, the substantial loss of integrity makes it ineligible for listing on the 
National Register of Historic Places.

INTRODUCTION 
1.1 
Purpose and Scope 
Epsilon was retained to assist with documentation and research related to the proposed removal 
of the existing building at 238 St. Botolph Street, historically known as the Boston (Matthews) 
Arena (BOS.15498) and proposed construction of a new multi-purpose facility for Northeastern 
University. The proposed demolition of the building is subject to review by the Boston Landmarks 
Commission (BLC) under Article 85. The enclosed report is intended to assist in the evaluation of 
the building for potential historic significance. 
 
Epsilon researched the history of the property to confirm the dates of construction of the existing 
building sections and subsequent additions and alterations. Research was conducted using 
collections of the Boston Globe, Boston Inspectional Services Department, Massachusetts 
Historical Commission, Digital Commonwealth and Northeastern University Collections. Epsilon 
used the information gathered to create the enclosed narrative detailing the property’s history 
and analysis of architectural integrity. 
 
Epsilon also completed photography and assessment of the property’s existing condition during 
a site visit. A detailed exterior photographic record of the property assisted with assessing the 
property’s historic integrity and alterations over time. The enclosed report summarizes the 
findings of the site visit and historical research and provides an analysis of the property’s historical 
significance and architectural integrity.

HISTORIC NARRATIVE 
2.1 
Property Location and Context 
238 St. Botolph Street (Parcel ID# 0402262000) is located in the Fenway section of Boston on an 
approximately two-acre parcel. The parcel is fairly level and bordered on the northeast by Public 
Alley 823, to the southeast by the MBTA line, to the southwest by Gainsborough Street and to the 
west by St. Botolph Street. Surrounding properties are multi-story institutional and multi-family 
residential buildings. 
2.2 
Development 
2.2.1 
Initial Construction 
Designed by the Boston based architecture firm of Funk and Wilcox, the Boston Arena opened in 
1910. Initially, its purpose was largely to host hockey games and could seat 5,000 people. Games 
from local colleges and universities as well as high school hockey games were played here as well 
as curling and skating events. In addition to ice activities at the arena, political rallies (such as 
hosting Teddy Roosevelt in 1912) and other public events were hosted here. In order to expand 
programming options, the building would later be converted to include an indoor bicycle racing 
track and roller-skating track. Capacity and fire concerns quickly became an issue for the building 
as the owners (Boston Arena Company) wished to host larger and larger events. The owners’ 
request to erect additional temporary wooden stands within the building for additional seating 
was denied by the City of Boston.

While the arena portion of the building was largely utilitarian in design featuring red brick, Funk 
and Wilcox designed an elaborate entrance to entice visitors. The entry block included two 
towers, terra cotta trim and arches, cherubs, finials, a marquee and other detailing. A circa 1930 
postcard (Figure 7) suggests the towers were multi-colored with gold roofs. The interior of the 
arena had first floor and balcony seating as well as a three-story section at the end, and overall 
was essentially a large oval with a large skylight in the ceiling.

2.3 
Second Arena 
In 1918, a fire destroyed the arena portion of the building. The entry block survived, while the 
arena collapsed, requiring it to be fully reconstructed. Funk and Wilcox were again selected to 
design the new arena. For the second arena, there initially was no balcony level and instead of 
arched steel trusses, the design used a triangular truss system mounted to concrete piers to 
support the gable roof. The second arena also had much larger windows and greater fireproofing, 
including concrete grandstands. Like the original arena, a large skylight system ran down the 
center of the roof. Windows on the second arena were much larger featuring steel industrial glass 
panels with operable sections and could bring far more light into the building than before. 
 
Funk and Wilcox put greater design efforts toward ornamentation on the second arena. The 
second arena was given a grand entrance on the west elevation, independent of the 1910 entry 
block featuring a large staircase with kneewall leading to a series of recessed panel doors with 
transoms above. In addition, there were decorative bands of masonry above and around the 
entrance. The second arena also had a greater use of concrete with concrete piers separating

2.4 
 
Subsequent Changes to Second Arena and Entry Block 
2.4.1 
Early to Midtwentieth Century Changes 
As soon as 1922, only two years after the construction of the second arena, there were complaints 
of overcrowding during events. In addition to all the previous uses the arena had it also now 
began to host other acts including diving competitions and circus performances. To satisfy egress 
requirements new exits were constructed, additional staircases were added and moved and 
additional entrances and exits added to the building. The ice area was reduced, and additional 
rows of seats were added, however this proved insufficient as demand for seats only increased. 
The Boston Bruins played their first home game in the arena and defeated the Montreal Maroons, 
2-1, on December 1, 1924. 
 
In 1926 a full balcony level was constructed which could seat an additional 2,200 people. Built 
from reinforced concrete for fireproofing, the balcony also required entry and exit doors to be cut 
into the exterior of the building and fire escapes added. In total by 1926, the arena could seat 
8,600 with standing room for an additional 2,000. Even with the additional capacity it still did not 
meet demand. On November 15, 1926, members of a nearby parade of roughly 1,500 people, 
including some unruly individuals tried to gain entry to see a boxing match, and when no tickets

One of the most significant events in the history of the arena is the construction of the Boston 
Garden in 1928. The Boston Garden would ultimately supplant the arena as the premier sports 
entertainment facility in Boston. The Boston Bruins would move their games immediately to the
