Boston Garden after its construction. The Boston Celtics played their first home game at the arena 
in 1936 and would continue to play there until 1955, when they too moved to the Boston Garden. 
The effect of the construction of the Boston Garden was not immediate, but its presence started 
the decline of the arena. The Boston Garden was simply a bigger venue and designed to have 
spectators as close to the action as possible, making it far more popular. 
 
During the latter years of World War II, the arena was shut down and used as a barracks. The 
building was converted to a barracks housing 85 men on the second floor in 1944 and then only a 
year later the floor of the arena was replaced, and the building converted back to arena use. By 
1945, the successive changes over time and use had taken its toll on the building and the roof was 
replaced, the entire rear (south) elevation was reconstructed, and top floor of the building was 
removed after being cited by the Inspectional Services department for structural failure and 
bowing of the building. It is likely that the skylight was removed at this time. 
2.4.2 
Late Twentieth Century Changes 
In 1934 the ownership of the Boston Garden and Boston (Matthews) Arena merged, and the arena 
operated as a secondary location. Ultimately, the owners decided to sell the property as it was 
no longer in demand. In 1953, the Metropolitan District Commission (MDC) bought the arena for 
$280,000. The arena continued to be used for a variety of events including concerts and 
graduations as well as collegiate and high school hockey and skating. With the growing use of 
electrification for lighting and increases in lighting technology, the exterior windows were 
removed and infilled with concrete block and those at the top of the building were removed and 
covered over with metal paneling. It is likely at this time that the formerly exposed red brick was 
painted.

The MDC owned the arena for over 20 years, renting it out for various uses. Ultimately, 
Northeastern University expressed interest in acquiring it and purchased the arena in 1979. 
Northeastern invested millions of dollars over multiple renovations in the 1980s and 1990s to 
bring the facility up to modern standards. In 1982, the arena was renamed the Matthews Arena 
in honor of George (former chairman of Northeastern’s board of trustees) and his late wife Hope. 
By the time the arena was purchased by Northeastern, the character defining features of the 
building had already been removed or significantly altered, such as the masonry on the entry 
block, and the windows, doors and skylights on the arena.

ARCHITECTURAL EVALUATION 
3.1 
Architectural Description 
The Boston (Matthews) Arena located at 238 St. Botolph Street is situated on the east side of St. 
Botolph Street in the Fenway neighborhood of Boston. The earliest portion of the building is a 
two-story masonry entry block on the north elevation. The entry block is roughly three by one 
bay at the two-story height and then steps down to one-story in height, where it is three by two 
bays and then further reduces to two bays in width for an additional 18 bays in length. As the 
entry block proceeds to the east, the grade slopes downward creating a full height basement level. 
Except for a portion of the decorative inner terra cotta arch, original features of the decorative 
portion entry block have been stripped away and covered over with red brick. The remaining long 
section of the entry block has had all its original windows and doors removed, window and door 
openings infilled and has been painted, where it was originally exposed red brick.

The original massing and design of the 1910 entry block was significantly altered in 1943 when

covered over and not lost, was re-exposed. (Fig. 10)

Over time the Boston (Matthews) Arena had substantial interior and exterior alterations. In 1926, 
a balcony level was added to the interior and numerous interior alterations were made over the 
decades, removing and expanding seating, replacing the arena playing floor, relocating and 
expanding the press box and remodeling locker rooms, bathrooms and other public areas as well 
as numerous alterations for fire safety and structural issues. In 1944, during World War II, the 
building was converted to serve as a barracks, which created substantial interior alterations. In 
1945, it was converted back to arena use.

The building has consistently had issues with structural stability and fire safety, causing repeated 
replacement of flooring in the arena and reinforcement of the foundation of the building as well 
as additional entrances and exits in the event of an emergency. Aside from the fire that destroyed 
the original arena in 1918, there was an additional fire in 1932. The 1932 fire destroyed one of 
the locker rooms and damaged adjacent areas. In 1948 the building was cited for potential 
structural collapse of the rear wall, which required it to be entirely reconstructed in 1949. During 
the 1949 renovation, the building was re-roofed and the top floor of the building was removed. 
The most significant alterations to the arena and affecting its character are the removal of all of 
the original windows and infilling the openings with concrete block and the removal of the 
skylight. Historically, the windows and skylight were important features and provided necessary 
light to the interior, without them the building both interior and exterior feels like a solid mass of 
masonry. 
 
 
Fig. 14

occurred including removal of the skylight, doors and windows as well as 
significant masonry detailing around the entrance. 
 
 
By the time the building was purchased by Northeastern in 1979 significant alterations had 
already occurred stripping the building of its historic character. After purchase of the building by 
Northeastern University, the arena went through renovations in the 1980s and 1990s 
substantially updating the facility. Due to the many changes and episodic renovations within the 
building, the interior of the arena portion of the building retains minimal historic fabric.

3.2 
Current Appearance 
The present Boston (Matthews) Arena does not represent the original form and massing of either 
the surviving original 1910 entry block or the later replacement 1920 main block of the arena. 
Changes made to the entry block including truncating it and the removal of the towers and portion 
of the arch as well as the marquee and its recladding have caused irreparable damage to its 
historic integrity. At the 1920 main block of the arena, a later circa 1950 rear addition, a 2010 
addition as well as the addition of structural bracing, the removal of every original door and 
window, infilling window openings with concrete block and painting the red brick exterior have 
degraded its historic integrity. Decorate masonry features and original exterior staircases have 
been removed and modern metal cladding added around the perimeter of the building. The 
building has also undergone substantial interior renovations over its history. The extensive 
alterations over time have degraded the building’s historic integrity. 
Detailed existing conditions photographs are included as Appendix A. Figures documenting 
changes to the property over time are included as Appendix B.

ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
Describe architectural features. Evaluate characteristics of this building in terms of other buildings within the 
community. 
Matthews Arena occupies most of the block bounded by St. Botolph Street (N), Massachusetts Avenue (E), Gainsborough 
Street (W), and the MBTA railroad tracks (S). It is set back from St. Botolph with surface parking to the west and the rear 
walls of buildings on Massachusetts Avenue to the east. St. Botolph Street is a narrow side street, behind and parallel to 
Huntington Avenue. It is developed with a mix of building types, most dating to the early twentieth century. 
Matthews Arena is a large building with a basically rectangular plan; a main entrance and vestibule projects from the 
northeast corner. The arena space, which rises to a side-gable roof with ventilators, accounts for most of the building. The 
arena is surrounded by two story wings that contain support and circulation spaces except at the southwest corner. The 
arena and side wings are red brick with segmental arch window and door openings, many of which have been bricked in. 
The narrow north and south wings are standard reinforced concrete frame structures. A multi-door entrance with segmental 
arched openings and crenellated parapet is centered on the north front wing. The original large window openings on both 
north and south wings have been bricked in. The architectural highlight of this building when completed in 1910 was the 
entrance vestibule at the northeast corner. It consisted of a massive terra-cotta arch entrance framed by paired towers and 
fronted by an ornate metal and glass hood. The towers were removed in 1940 and the remaining facade was covered in the 
1970s. In 1990, the terracotta arch with its elaborate guilloche, braided, and leaf and dart moldings, was exposed. The 
classical ornament on the interior of the vestibule remains intact. Sanborn maps describe the construction as fireproof with 
the exception of wing roofs. A steel truss roof covers the arena. 
HISTORICAL NARRATIVE 
Discuss the history of the building. Explain its associations with local (or state) history. Include uses of the 
building, and the role(s) the owners/occupants played within the community. 
The Boston Arena was built in 1906 as "the premier hockey and boxing emporium" in Boston, hi 1914, eight years after 
opening, the main building was leveled by fire; only the ornate arch and towers on the northeast side and refrigerator plant 
to the southwest remained. The damage was estimated at $250,000. After the fire the building was expanded to include a 
second deck. Another fire caused $5,000 damage in 1931. 
After the Boston Garden was built in November 17, 1928, the Arena's stature as a sports venue declined. The 1931 
Bromley Atlas shows the Boston Arena building also housed Police Station 21 and the Boston University gym. In 1941, 
The Boston Globe referred to the "ancient face of the old skating emporium" in an article that continues "since the building 
of the Garden, the Arena has slipped into oblivion which it never quite deserved. Everything of importance that comes to 
Boston during the winter season goes into the Garden. The Arena owned by the same corporation [Boston Garden-Arena 
Corporation merged in 1934] has been getting the leavings for the past dozen years." In 1944, 85 servicemen were lodged 
on the second floor. The Boston Celtics played their last game in the Arena in 1959. 
Owners wanted to sell it to a New York group that would use it as an industrial plant. Public groups and private citizens 
rallied to save it primarily for hockey leagues. Mayor John B. Hynes said Boston "couldn't purchase the building for 14 
high school hockey teams." A retired naval officer offered to buy the building for $100,000 and give it to the city. That 
state legislature debated what it was worth. Finally, the Metropolitan District Commission bought the building for 
$280,000 in July 1953.

Northeastern bought the property for $250,000 in 1979 and invested over $3 million in remodeling it. A second series of 
renovations, at an estimated cost of $2 million, was completed in 1995, bringing the arena's facilities up-to-date. In 1982, 
the building was renamed Matthews Arena in honor of the chairman of the University Corporation and Board of Trustees, 
George J. Matthews and the late Hope M. Matthews.

1.0 
INTRODUCTION AND GENERAL INFORMATION 
1.1 
Overview 
Northeastern University (“Northeastern” or the “Proponent”) is pleased to submit this 
Institutional Master Plan Notification Form/Project Notification Form (this “IMPNF/PNF”) to the 
Boston Redevelopment Authority, doing business as Boston Planning & Development Agency 
(herein, the BPDA). With this submission, Northeastern is initiating the process for approval of a 
10-year Institutional Master Plan (the “IMP”) pursuant to Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code 
(the Code) and initiating Large Project Review under Article 80B of the Code to enable the 
development of the projects outlined herein. 
This IMPNF/PNF will provide an organizational framework for creating a physical plan and 
infrastructure for the Boston campus that will strengthen and celebrate Northeastern’s mission. 
Guided by its 2013 Institutional Master Plan (the “2013 IMP”), Northeastern is planning for the 
next ten years through the construction of several new projects and the redevelopment of older 
and underutilized buildings within the campus core (the “IMP Projects”). These projects, 
described in Chapter 3 hereof, will largely be driven by Northeastern’s academic mission as a 
global research university, powered by experience. Northeastern is renowned for its experiential 
learning model, high-impact research, deep partnerships, and worldwide reach, and its physical 
presence in Boston is organized in such a way to meet the current and future needs in education 
and research. 
As part of this IMPNF/PNF, Northeastern also seeks to initiate Large Project Review for the 
redevelopment of the 262 St. Botolph Street site, which currently houses Matthews Arena and a 
surface parking lot, and is bounded by St. Botolph Street to the north, the MBTA Orange Line, 
Commuter Rail and Amtrak right-of-way to the south, Public Alley 823 to the east, and 
Gainsborough Street to the west (the “Project Site”). Northeastern proposes to construct a new, 
approximately 290,000 square foot (sf) multi-purpose facility (the “262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility” or “Project”) that will support Northeastern’s athletic capabilities 
for its Division I athletes, intramural teams, and club sports. It is anticipated the new facility will 
provide an inviting and diverse space for current and future students and elevate the profile of 
collegiate athletics in Boston. As detailed in Chapter 4, the Project will enhance the overall campus 
plan, aesthetically integrate with, and complement, the surroundings of this unique Site, while 
providing for Northeastern’s varsity athletics programs and student recreation programming. 
1.2 
Institutional Mission, Objectives, and Needs 
Founded in 1898, Northeastern University is a top-tier, nonprofit research university located on 
both sides of Huntington Avenue on the edges of the Back Bay, Fenway, Mission Hill, Roxbury, 
and South End neighborhoods of Boston. Grounded in its signature cooperative education 
program, Northeastern provides its students with unprecedented experiential learning 
opportunities around the world. 

6927/Northeastern University IMPNF/PNF 
1-2 
Introduction and General Information 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
Northeastern’s undergraduate colleges, myriad of graduate programs, and part-time divisions 
offer bachelor’s, master’s, professional and doctoral degrees in a wide variety of academic 
disciplines and professional areas. Northeastern offers its students opportunities for professional 
work, research, service, and global learning in more than 130 countries. Northeastern’s rapidly 
growing research enterprise is strategically aligned with three national and global imperatives: 
health, security, and sustainability. 
Northeastern’s physical presence in Boston serves as a testament to the university’s rich history 
and more recent evolution. With its roots as a commuter college, the campus has transformed its 
surface parking lots into a vibrant academic hub, nestled amidst Boston’s diverse neighborhoods. 
As its physical footprint has evolved, its commitment to learning, research, impact, and 
experiential education remains at the core of the university’s mission, manifested in its campus 
design, buildings and open spaces. The Boston campus serves as a living laboratory: a backdrop 
for innovation and discovery, as well as a bridge to community and real-world applications of 
higher education. 
Planning for Northeastern’s Boston campus—as with its network of global campuses—responds 
to space need projections and facility conditions assessments of the present day. Events in this 
past decade, notably changes in the global landscape as a response to the global pandemic, have 
provided an opportunity to rethink the environments in which we learn, research, and work in 
ways yet to be fully defined. However, the pandemic has reinforced the value of flexibility and 
adaptability, which can be supported by space design. The IMP Projects described in this IMPNF 
reflect the university’s currently anticipated needs with an understanding that these needs will 
undoubtedly evolve over time. This IMPNF offers a framework for such needs, including the need 
to plan and build flexibly to allow for adaptability to meet the demands of the current day. 
1.3 
IMP History 
Northeastern has filed Institutional Master Plans for its Boston campus since 1999. Most recently, 
Northeastern’s 2013 IMP was approved by the BPDA Board in November 2013 and by the Boston 
Zoning Commission in December 2013. In October 2023, the BPDA approved a two-year renewal 
of Northeastern’s 2013 IMP. The two-year extension to the 2013 IMP allowed for the completion 
of the Third Amendment to the 2013 IMP, which was approved in March 2024. 
Since the 2013 IMP, five IMP Amendments have been approved, as described below. 
First Amendment 
The First Amendment to the 2013 IMP added the approximately 825-bed dormitory now known 
as LightView, located at 744 Columbus Avenue. The First Amendment was approved by the BPDA 
Board on July 14, 2016, and the new residential community opened in August 2019.

Second Amendment 
The Second Amendment to the 2013 IMP included two small projects: (i) an increase in the 
amount of leased space in the Christian Science Church Complex to include the Publishing House 
building and (ii) a small building addition of approximately 3,800 square feet to the Badger and 
Rosen Squashbusters Center. The Second Amendment was approved by the BPDA Board on May 
26, 2017, and the addition was completed in fall 2017. 
Third Amendment 
The Third Amendment to the 2013 IMP added the approximately 453,800 sf, 23-story mixed-use 
building, located at 840 Columbus Avenue, which will contain an active community-focused 
ground floor and student housing above, anticipated to accommodate up to 1,370 beds as well as 
a student amenity space on the second floor. In addition, the Third Amendment to the 2013 IMP 
included (i) a lease of the building formerly known as the South Tower of the Sheraton Boston 
Hotel located at 39 Dalton Street whereby the university leased approximately 250,000 square 
feet within the building, and (ii) the Renaissance Park Renovation Project consisting of interior 
renovations of Floors 5-8 of the Renaissance Park building by converting approximately 75,000 SF 
of formerly leased office space back to university uses. The Third Amendment was approved by 
the BPDA Board on March 14, 2024, and the 840 Columbus Avenue project and the Renaissance 
Park Renovation Project are currently in planning and design. 
Fourth Amendment 
The Fourth Amendment to the 2013 IMP consisted of upsizing the existing East Village and 
International Village residence halls to add up to approximately 900 beds across the two buildings. 
The Fourth Amendment was approved by the BPDA Board on March 10, 2022, and the residence 
halls were upsized fall 2022. 
Fifth Amendment 
The Fifth Amendment to the 2013 IMP consisted of interior renovations and a new first floor 
enclosure at the existing Snell Library. The Fifth Amendment was approved by the BPDA Board on 
September 15, 2022. The Snell Library renovations are now in progress. 
1.4

conversations and partnership with the BPDA, Mayor’s Office, elected officials, IMP Task Force, 
and other interested parties, Northeastern commits to the proposal and development of 
community benefits over the next ten years commensurate with the size and scale of the 
institutional projects associated with the ten-year IMP. Such plan will build upon the success of 
the 2013 Cooperation Agreement and the robust package of public benefits associated with the

BACKGROUND AND EXISTING CONDITIONS 
2.1 
University Profile 
Today, Northeastern enrolls approximately 40,000 degree-seeking students in Boston, including 
approximately 21,000 undergraduate students and approximately 19,000 part-time and full-time 
graduate students. These figures fluctuate from year to year, due in part to Northeastern’s 
cooperative education model in which students alternate semesters of academic study with 
periods of full-time work, as well as the recent expansion of Northeastern’s global network of 
campuses in Oakland, California, London, England and most recently, New York, New York to 
accommodate the university’s growing undergraduate population. 
Northeastern has approximately 2,800 faculty members, as well as 3,500 staff in Boston. Of the 
total faculty and staff employed at Northeastern, approximately 26% are residents of Boston. 
2.2 
Existing Boston Campus 
Northeastern’s campus is adjacent to the Back Bay, Fenway, Mission Hill, Roxbury, and South End 
neighborhoods of Boston and has a variety of residential, commercial, and institutional neighbors. 
Northeastern and the surrounding neighborhoods are connected through the activities of 
students and faculty of Northeastern, who are involved in a multitude of programs and activities 
that engage community organizations and neighborhood residents. Within these diverse 
neighborhoods are wide arrays of land uses, including institutional, high- and medium-density 
residential, commercial, and recreational uses.

million square feet. The land area associated with Northeastern facilities in Boston is 
approximately 67 acres. Figure 2-1 presents a map of Northeastern’s existing facilities on the 
Boston Campus and Appendix A presents an inventory list of the same.

flexibility year over year as those units are considered university managed housing. The following

Progress on 2013 IMP 
The 2013 IMP included eleven new projects with specific project sites to be refined and finalized 
during the ten-year term of the 2013 IMP. The 2013 IMP sought to accommodate over two million 
square feet of academic and student life facility growth, including athletic facilities and additional 
housing, on the existing Northeastern campus. To satisfy this scale of needed facilities, while 
remaining within the confines of the existing campus, the 2013 IMP proposed to increase density

facilities to support its growing student body and research endeavors. The university has

Science and Engineering Complex (ISEC) and the multidisciplinary EXP building, both designed 
with a focus on sustainability and energy efficiency. These new facilities provide cutting-edge 
laboratories, classrooms, and collaborative spaces for students and faculty across various 
disciplines. Additionally, Northeastern has invested in the development of new residence halls, 
such as the recently completed LightView apartment complex and recently permitted 840 
Columbus Avenue, to accommodate demand for on-campus housing. The university has also 
made improvements to existing buildings, incorporating sustainable features and updating 
infrastructure to create a more efficient and environmentally friendly campus. See Figure 2-3 for 
the campus development progress since the 2013 IMP.

TEN-YEAR PLAN 
3.1 
Introduction 
Since the 2013 IMP, new development on Northeastern’s Boston campus has primarily 
concentrated along Columbus Avenue. The IMP for the next ten years will shift focus to the core 
of the campus by focusing on the renewal and redevelopment of older, outmoded buildings and 
underutilized spaces in the heart of the campus. This shift aims to create a more cohesive and 
vibrant campus experience, enhancing the sense of campus community and fostering 
interdisciplinary collaboration by improving research, student life, and academic space resources 
in ways that reflect Northeastern’s forward-looking approach to learning and community 
partnership. 
The proposed IMP Projects will include the renovation and expansion of existing academic 
buildings, the creation of new student life and recreation facilities, and the development of 
additional green spaces and pedestrian-centered environments. By concentrating future growth 
within the campus core, Northeastern seeks to optimize its highly physically-constrained land use, 
address necessary capital renewal and maintenance of older buildings on campus, create a more 
sustainable and resilient campus, and continue to ensure that the campus’ evolution contributes 
positively to the broader urban fabric of the city of Boston. This IMPNF identifies eight sites for 
new construction (redevelopment), nine major renovations, and three areas of additional 
interest. Of these eight redevelopment sites, six are carried over from the 2013 IMP. See Figure 
3-1 for the proposed ten-year plan. 
3.2 
Planning Framework 
3.2.1 
Planning and Urban Design Goals 
The planning principles for the IMP reflect Northeastern’s unique identity as an institution that 
values experiential learning, global engagement, and interdisciplinary collaboration, shaping a 
campus environment that fosters innovation, inclusion, and a strong sense of community both 
within the campus and with its surrounding neighborhoods. The following five principles guide 
the IMP: 
♦ Flexibility and Agility: Plan for space on the Boston campus that supports the mobility of 
students, faculty and staff across the university’s global network. 
♦ Impactful Learning and Collaboration: Promote collaborative, multidisciplinary research 
and experiential learning. 
♦ Inclusion and Belonging: Foster an inclusive physical and social environment where 
individuals of all backgrounds can thrive. 
♦ Sustainability and Resilience: Expand the campus’ leadership role in sustainability and 
resilience and implement sensible solutions to address the climate crisis.

Campus Communities 
Northeastern’s campus can be divided into seven areas described as “campus communities.” 
While the campus population participates in all of these areas, each has their own distinct identity, 
character and functions. The physical space that comprise these campus communities feature a 
diversity of programmatic uses, including learning spaces; areas for gathering, studying, and 
socializing; as well as open spaces that contribute to the overall vibrancy and identity within each 
community. See Figure 3-2 for the seven campus communities. 
University Square 
University Square, anchored by the iconic Krentzman Quad, serves as the traditional core of 
Northeastern's campus, featuring the university's historic buildings, such as Ell Hall, Dodge Hall, 
and Richards Hall. This campus community also includes buildings central to the contemporary 
campus experience, including the Curry Student Center and the Snell Library. With a 
predominance of academic and administrative buildings, Krentzman Quad lies at the heart of 
University Square, serving as an iconic open space. 
East End 
The East End campus community will be home to the new 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project, as well as a new academic and research quad anchored by the 
redevelopment of Mugar Life Sciences building, Cullinane Hall, and Gainsborough Garage. These 
transformative projects will establish the East End as a vibrant research and student activity hub, 
and the re-envisioning of a meaningful quad situated between what are now Mugar, Hurtig and 
Robinson Halls (now known as Robinson Quad), will connect the East End to University Square. 
South Landing 
Located in the southern part of Northeastern’s campus, South Landing is a thriving hub for 
research and innovation and student housing. Home to two major research facilities, ISEC and 
EXP, this campus community will soon welcome a residence hall at 840 Columbus Avenue. South 
Landing's mix of research spaces, the City’s Carter Playground, local retail, and modern student 
amenities exemplifies Northeastern's commitment to fostering an environment that supports 
academic excellence and connection to City and the neighboring community.

West Village, located on the western edge of Northeastern's campus, is a vibrant community that

3.2.3 
Public Realm and Landscape 
Northeastern’s public realm and landscape, collectively referred to here as open spaces, play an 
integral role in both the campus experience and local environmental conditions. The open space 
network on the Boston campus consists of a range of space types and planting schemes, which 
work together to provide a distinctive setting for an urban campus. 
Part of the vision for Northeastern’s physical campus design for the Boston campus is to create a 
cohesive and connected network of open spaces that serves critical social, academic, and 
environmental functions, while linking to Boston’s neighborhoods. The Boston campus open 
space network interventions seek to: 
♦ Support the university’s academic mission and student life goals; 
♦ Serve as a destination for the community beyond Northeastern; 
♦ Be inclusive and welcoming, through the embrace of universal design principles; 
♦ Unite the campus’ diverse architecture; and 
♦ Enhance the ecological and environmental performance of the campus. 
The university’s landscape-based approaches for ecological and environmental performance 
include optimizing green infrastructure and addressing water conservation and inland flood 
resilience while adhering to various guidelines, processes, and regulations, such as the Green 
Building and Climate Resiliency Guidelines, Groundwater Conservation Overlay District, BWSC Site 
Plan Approval, and MassDEP Stormwater Standards. 
Northeastern strives to be a model of a sustainable, healthy, interconnected, and just community. 
The university's landscape and public realm priorities focus on supporting informal social 
interaction and formal programming, enhancing pedestrian experience and throughput, 
maximizing pervious surfaces in an urban context, utilizing a stormwater toolkit to improve water 
quality, and elevating the Arboretum to Level III status to further enhance biodiversity and 
understanding of local ecology. These efforts demonstrate Northeastern's commitment to social 
and environmental stewardship and its goal of increasing "plant space" where possible on an 
urban campus. 
Northeastern recognizes the importance of stewarding the Arboretum, which is essential to 
supporting an ecologically healthy campus and sense of belonging on campus. The university aims 
to continue upholding the City of Boston's Urban Forest Plan Goals by replacing trees at a 
minimum 1:1 ratio, aiming for a net increase in tree quantity and achieving greater species 
diversity in the urban canopy through strategic removals, transplants, and additions. 
Northeastern is also committed to exploring opportunities to remove physical barriers for open

3.2.4 
Campus Life 
Northeastern's educational model - centered on experiential learning, global mobility, and 
community service - fosters a student experience that is both globally focused and locally 
engaged. With a network of campuses around the world, Northeastern encourages students to 
explore diverse cultures, perspectives, and opportunities. Physical spaces are meant to reinforce 
and inspire this sense of exploration, not just in the classroom and in laboratories, but within 
residence halls, recreational facilities, and spaces devoted to celebration and collaboration. 
Through its recently announced mergers with Mills College in Oakland, California and Marymount 
Manhattan College in New York City, Northeastern is pursuing a global mobility model, in which 
students have the option to study at one of its numerous residential campuses. These mergers, 
coupled with the expansion of global co-op opportunities, comprise Northeastern’s global 
mobility programs. These programs broaden student’s horizons as students seek opportunities 
outside of Boston throughout their academic experience. 
Northeastern's location in four of Boston’s neighborhoods is an integral part of the student 
experience. The university cherishes being part of the City’s fabric and remains committed to 
providing comprehensive student life facilities to meet the needs of its student population, 
reducing the pressure on neighborhood resources. In recent years, Northeastern has made 
significant strides in improving its student life facilities. The Marino Center and the Curry Student 
Center continue to serve as central hubs for student activities, offering a range of amenities and 
social outlets. Please see Figure 3-3 for campus life amenities.

deliver 1,000 additional student housing beds, by building, leasing, and securing permitting for 
more than 3,000 beds. Currently Northeastern requires first and second year students to live in 
university housing. Despite this increase in housing supply, students still seek alternative housing 
off-campus, particularly after their second year, due to a greater range of price points, unit types, 
and amenities available in the open market. Northeastern is committed to supporting a range of 
affordable and attractive housing options for students throughout their time at the university.

innovative housing solutions and partnerships.

a lease agreement in the building formerly known as the South Tower of the Sheraton Boston

is leasing approximately 250,000 sf within the building resulting in an additional 854 student beds.

3.2.5 
Mobility 
The campus’ urban location provides access to a wide range of transportation options, with 
particularly robust access to public transit, micromobility networks, and bike facilities, while the 
compact nature of the campus contributes to a highly walkable environment. In recent years, 
Northeastern has made significant strides in promoting cycling as a healthy and environmentally 
friendly mode of transportation by investing in bike infrastructure and amenities. Mobility is 
discussed further in Chapter 5. 
3.2.6 
Sustainability and Resilience 
Northeastern has demonstrated a strong commitment to sustainability and resilience through its 
research, experiential education, and investment into the physical campus and surroundings. In 
late 2022, the university launched its Climate Justice Action Plan (CJAP) process through which a 
diverse steering committee comprised of representatives from the university and from 
community organizations, has been engaged to explore and create a framework for sustainable 
and just climate solutions. The CJAP goals address various aspects of sustainability, including 
greenhouse gas emissions, air quality, transportation, waste, climate resilience, local economies, 
community relationships, and research practices. The university's efforts to evolve its Boston 
campus will be informed by the CJAP, ensuring that new developments consider not only 
environmental factors but also social and economic impacts on the surrounding local 
communities. 
The university has also recently initiated a Decarbonization and Resilience Plan (DRP) to develop 
a phased, implementable plan for decarbonizing its Boston campus while addressing resilience 
and climate justice. Anticipated to be completed in 2025, the DRP will establish precise 
decarbonization goals and milestones aligned with the campus' growth and development. It will 
build upon Northeastern's existing utility planning work, including an analysis of electrical load

growth, identification of Energy Conservation Measures (ECMs), and exploration of solar 
photovoltaic potential across the campus. Once finalized, the DRP will provide more precise 
information to the City regarding the university's timeline to meet its sustainability goals and 
interim milestones. 
In recent years, Northeastern has made significant strides in sustainability through a multifaceted 
approach that encompasses buildings, transportation, and open space. The university has 
reduced greenhouse gas emissions per square foot of building space through fuel switching, 
energy conservation measures, and sustainable building design, with new buildings like the ISEC 
and EXP achieving high levels of sustainability through energy efficiency efforts and green 
infrastructure. Northeastern also supports sustainable transportation, with a majority of faculty, 
and staff using public transit, biking, or walking to commute to campus. The university has 
expanded its composting and recycling programs, diverting 48% of waste from landfills in 2023 
and partnering with local worker-owned cooperatives for composting services. Northeastern's 
Arboretum, with over 1,400 trees and 5,400 shrubs, contributes to urban green space, supporting 
community activity, filtering pollution, and mitigating heat islands. Additionally, the university has 
implemented initiatives to address heat resilience, indoor air quality, and water conservation, 
including rainwater collection systems, bioswales, and sustainable design standards for new 
buildings. Sustainability and Climate Resilience is discussed further in Chapter 6.

262 ST. BOTOLPH STREET MULTIPURPOSE ATHLETIC FACILITY 
4.1 
Purpose and Need 
Northeastern’s athletics and recreational buildings support 17 Division I athletic teams and more 
than 100 intramural and club teams. The university is committed to providing state-of-the-art, 
safe, and engaging facilities that meet Conference, NCAA, National and International Federation 
rules and regulations and recreational needs for the student community. In addition to 
intercollegiate athletics, intramural, and club sports, these facilities support university sanctioned 
events and a variety of public programming. Northeastern proposes to redevelop the 238-262 St. 
Botolph Street Site, currently housing the George J. & Hope M. Matthews Arena, with an 
approximately 290,000 square foot (sf), 115 foot tall multipurpose athletic building (the “262 St. 
Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility,” “Multipurpose Athletic Facility,” or the “Project”). 
The new building at 238-262 St. Botolph Street will be a four-story multipurpose facility that will 
provide improved spaces for varsity, club and intramural athletic programs, and new spaces for 
student recreation. The improved spaces for varsity games and training are vital to 
Northeastern’s recruitment opportunities and advancement of Northeastern’s Division I 
programs. Furthermore, the new recreation spaces are necessary to provide relief of 
overcrowding in other facilities on campus, offering all students greater access to wellness and 
fitness opportunities. The Multipurpose Athletic Facility will also further Northeastern’s diversity, 
equity, and inclusion efforts by including spaces for all-gender restrooms, lactation rooms for staff 
and visitors, space dedicated to visitors with sensory needs, and equity of space across men’s and 
women’s varsity hockey and basketball programs. 
The Project endeavors to serve all students, not just varsity athletes, in both its building program 
and design. The design of the arena will allow for natural light as well as visual connections 
between the street, concourse, recreation spaces, and arena bowl. This improved student, visitor, 
and public realm experience will also create an exciting interaction with collegiate activities and 
sporting events. Additionally, the new space will provide opportunities for more community 
events, such as Boston Public School commencement ceremonies and serving as a polling 
location. 
4.1.1 
Current Project Site Uses 
Matthews Arena is currently used as a facility for women’s and men’s varsity, club and intramural 
hockey practice and games, figure skating, men’s varsity basketball games, and gathering space 
for events such as commencement ceremonies. The building also provides hockey offices, training 
conditioning spaces, and offices for facilities staff. Despite efforts to renovate the existing building 
components, the team lockers, training spaces, and coaches’ offices in the current arena are 
lacking in modern amenities, building systems, and technology. The existing building is not fully 
accessible. Further, existing public spaces do not meet the university’s goals for diversity, equity, 
and inclusion. Varsity programs rely on space in other facilities on campus for training and 
practices and women’s varsity basketball has no space in the current building. There are also no 
spaces in the current arena dedicated to general student fitness and recreation.

4.1.1.1 
Condition of the Building 
Over the building’s history prior to Northeastern’s ownership, it has endured many physical 
changes as a result of multiple fires, major structural changes, increasing space demands, and 
changing uses and owners. In 1948, the building was cited for potential structural collapse of the 
rear wall, which required it to be entirely reconstructed in 1949. During the 1949 renovation, the 
entire top floor of the building was removed. 
The building has consistently had issues with structural stability and fire safety. While 
Northeastern has invested in the facility to address these issues, including most recently installing 
temporary bracing to mitigate safety concerns associated with differential settlement, the facility 
has been deemed beyond repair. Redevelopment has emerged as the preferred approach from a 
financial and programmatic perspective, in line with Northeastern’s goals as an institution as well 
as a community partner. Figures 4-1 and 4-2 show the existing conditions. 
Consistent with the 2013 IMP, Northeastern begun investigating the potential for an addition to 
Matthews Arena in early 2019. As a result of that work, Northeastern discovered the building’s 
limitations, the gravity of the structural deficiencies previously noted, and the implications such 
an addition would have on the structural integrity of the facility. As a result of those studies, 
Northeastern proceeded with temporary structural improvements to the existing facility and is 
proposing redevelopment of the Arena with the Proposed Project.

Project Description 
4.2.1 
Project Site and Area Context 
Acquired by Northeastern in 1979, Matthews Arena has served as a home for Northeastern 
women’s and men’s hockey for over 45 years. Northeastern invested millions of dollars through 
multiple renovations in the 1980s and 1990s to bring the facility up to the then modern standards. 
In 1982, the arena was renamed the Matthews Arena in honor of George (former chairman of 
Northeastern’s board of trustees) and his late wife Hope. 
The approximately 97,969 sf Project Site is in the Fenway neighborhood located at 238-262 St. 
Botolph Street, within Northeastern’s East End campus community (see Figure 4-3). The Project 
Site, which currently houses Matthews Arena and a surface parking lot, is bounded by St. Botolph 
Street to the north, the MBTA tracks to the South, Public Alley 823 to the east, and Gainsborough 
Street to the west. The Project Site is an ideal location for a pedestrian- and transit-oriented 
multipurpose arena: athletes, students, and visitors can easily access the Massachusetts Avenue 
MBTA Station, which is adjacent to the Project Site and provides access to the MBTA Orange Line 
and numerous local bus routes. 
The building located at 238-262 St. Botolph Street, historically known as the Boston (Matthews) 
Arena (BOS.15498) has a long history with Boston sports and hosted many events in Boston’s 
history including visiting celebrities and dignitaries. Over the building’s history, it has endured 
many changes as a result of increasing space demands, fires, and changing uses and owners. 
Never rising to the prominence of the Boston Garden, the arena was always a secondary or a 
tertiary location of events in Boston. A devasting fire in 1918 resulted in the building being largely 
rebuilt, with only the entry portion of its original 1910 structure remaining. While the building has 
a long history with Boston, the substantial loss of integrity makes it ineligible for listing on the 
National Register of Historic Places.

4.2.2 
Proposed Project 
Northeastern intends to replace Matthews Arena and build a new, innovative and creatively 
designed multipurpose athletic facility. As the first project within the IMP, the Project will connect 
to the overall campus plan and aesthetically integrate with and complement, the surroundings of 
this Site, while providing critical program for Northeastern’s varsity athletics programs and 
student recreation programming. The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project will address both the short and long-term needs of the university’s athletics 
program and enhance the student-athlete experience by providing critical athlete support and 
recruiting amenities. The Project will also bring to the campus expanded space for recreation to 
be shared by the wider campus community. As designed, the building is approximately 290,000 
sf, or approximately 72,500 sf per floor over four floors of high bay, long span space. 
The program for basketball will accommodate two new basketball practice facilities, coaches’ 
offices, and all the required supporting space to include strength and conditioning, athletic 
training, team meeting rooms, men’s and women’s locker rooms, storage, and team laundry. The 
program for hockey will accommodate a new ice sheet, coaches’ offices, and all the required 
supporting space to include strength and conditioning, athletic training, team meeting rooms, a 
shooting station, and men’s and women’s locker rooms. In addition to the varsity athletics 
program, the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will add approximately 
54,000 sf of multipurpose recreation and fitness space that will serve as additional passive 
recreation space for students and event space. See Figure 4-4 to 4-6 for the massing design and 
site plans. 
Considering the large civic arena use, the ground floor will consist of a main building entry 
prominently facing Gainsborough Street with one secondary entrance along St. Botolph Street 
and one entrance along Gainsborough Street. The main entrance will provide an iconic arrival 
sequence to a new public lobby that will accommodate gameday peak foot-traffic and gatherings. 
The Gainsborough Street entrance is designed for transparency and connectivity to the future 
planned entrance to the MBTA Massachusetts Avenue Orange Line stop. 
The current construction cost is estimated between $300M and $350M.

4.3 
Urban Design 
The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project design aims to create a unique 
building for the campus while responding to the surrounding neighborhood context. The scale of 
the proposed project is driven by the modern athletic and recreational program requirements, 
and architectural design moves aim to break down building’s massing to create dynamic, inviting, 
and people-centric spaces for building users, guests, and the community at large. 
Paving along both St. Botolph and Gainsborough Streets will relate in style to the existing 
enhanced streetscape across the street by the New England Conservatory of Music and further 
north along Gainsborough Street, stitching the Project into the fabric of the greater 
neighborhood.

The Project design will provide an inviting open space that promotes sustainable transportation 
options, including walking, cycling, and public transit. In addition to sidewalk reconstruction, site 
furnishings will include bike racks, planters, and seating. The plaza paving will extend, where 
possible, towards the Massachusetts Avenue MBTA Station, creating a holistic visual connection 
between the Project Site and public transit. 
4.3.1 
Tree Protection and Removal Plan 
Design of the public realm for the Project intends to provide conditions for street trees to flourish. 
While all existing plant material within the property line will be removed during construction, an 
effort will be made to relocate trees following a feasibility assessment. While more mature trees 
may not survive relocation, it is anticipated that the much younger street trees will survive. 
Relocation will be addressed further in the design process, in consultation with the contractor. In 
general, however, all trees removed as part of the Project will be replaced with new trees on 
campus. As part of the public realm improvement for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project, 22 trees are currently anticipated to be planted throughout the Project 
Site, including along Gainsborough Street which currently has no existing street trees. The average 
caliper of the trees is anticipated to be 4” at time of planting. These trees will be planted within 
large soil volumes. Where possible, the tree planting areas will be provided with continuous 
volumes of structural soil to support healthy tree growth. Additionally, trees which are planted 
within hardscape plazas or more urban conditions will be provided with extended structural soil 
or soil structures (such as silva cells) to reduce soil compaction and ensure adjacent pavements 
are not heaved over time. Tree species selected will be appropriate for street tree conditions, 
with columnar forms where in closer proximity to building façade.

Public Realm and Open Space Improvements 
The landscape design for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project includes 
improvements to the streetscape along St. Botolph and Gainsborough Streets with new street 
trees, site furnishings, lighting and seating opportunities, all in compliance with City of Boston 
Complete Streets Guidelines. See Figure 4-13 for the existing St. Botolph Street section and 
Figures 4-14 and 4-15 for the proposed St. Botolph Street section, Figure 4-16 for the existing 
Gainsborough section and Figures 4-17 and 4-18 for the proposed Gainsborough sections. 
The proposed design provides an inclusive space with a continuous concrete sidewalk with 
accessible slopes that meet or exceed existing sidewalk width. Beyond the clear concrete 
sidewalk, paving patterns are designed to relate to the building architecture and program and site 
context. The dynamic paving patterns, façade elements, and site furnishings all contribute to a 
vibrant public realm.

5.1 
Overview 
This chapter describes the transportation-related components of this IMPNF/PNF in accordance 
with the Boston Transportation Department’s (BTD’s) Transportation Access Plan (TAP) Guidelines 
and the BPDA’s IMP Review process. The following sections provide an overview of the 
transportation conditions on Northeastern’s Boston Campus including key changes since the 2013 
IMP; ongoing and planned transportation initiatives; and the relevant impacts associated with the 
proposed IMP projects. This information is intended to assist the community and the City agencies 
in identifying transportation-related issues that they would like to see further addressed in the 
IMP, which will include a more detailed analysis of traffic, parking, transit, short-term construction 
period impacts, and pedestrian and bicycle conditions within and around the Campus. 
Concurrent with the IMP, Northeastern intends to submit a Draft Project Impact Report (DPIR) for 
the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project that is proposed within this 
IMPNF/PNF. The DPIR will include a detailed transportation study that adheres to the BTD’s TAP 
Guidelines and the BPDA ’s Article 80 Large Project Review process. The DPIR will include an 
evaluation of the existing conditions, future conditions, and projected impacts to the overall 
campus parking supply, loading/delivery plan, transit services, pedestrian and bicycle activity, 
transportation demand management (TDM) strategies for the Project, and construction-period 
impacts. The proposed Multipurpose Athletic Facility will be required to enter into a 
Transportation Access Plan Agreement (TAPA); the TAPA will set forth the specific TDM measures 
and agreements between Northeastern and the City of Boston. 
5.1.1 
Context 
Northeastern is within walking distance of a variety of transportation options including public 
transit, Bluebikes shared bicycle facilities, and regional off-street pathways, as well as designated 
locations for car-sharing services. 
For Northeastern students, faculty, and staff, commuting by public transit is the most common 
mode of access to and from the Boston campus. Northeastern has excellent access to a wide 
variety of public transportation options including 14 Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority 
(MBTA) bus routes, rapid transit on the MBTA’s Orange and Green Lines, and commuter rail 
service on three lines (Franklin/Foxborough, Needham, and Providence/Stoughton). According to 
the 2023 Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP) Rideshare Survey, 
transit accounts for approximately 37% of faculty and staff trips and 46% of student trips. 
Bicycling and walking are the next most common modes of access to and throughout the Boston 
campus for students and are a key mode of access for faculty and staff. The Boston campus has 
direct access to the Southwest Corridor and proximity to the Back Bay Fens and Emerald Necklace. 
According to Northeastern’s 2023 DEP Rideshare Survey, approximately 39% of all students and 
approximately 12% of all faculty/staff walk or bike to campus.

5.2.2 
Car-Sharing Services 
Car-sharing services enable easy access to short-term vehicular transportation. Vehicles are 
rented on an hourly or daily basis, and all vehicle costs (gas, maintenance, insurance, and parking) 
are included in the rental fee. Vehicles are checked out for a specific time period and returned to 
their designated location. Pick-up/drop-off locations are typically in existing parking lots or other 
parking areas throughout neighborhoods as a convenience to users of the services. Nearby car-
sharing services provide an important transportation option and reduce the need for private 
vehicle ownership. 
Zipcar is the primary car-share company in the Boston car-sharing market; however other 
companies such as Turo and Getaround also operate within the City. Four Zipcar locations (Leon 
Street, Renaissance Park Garage, Gainsborough Street, and Matthews Lot) and one EV from 
Good2Go (Columbus Garage) is located within the vicinity of the campus. Additional Zipcar 
locations are located within a five-minute walk (one-quarter mile) from the campus (Westland 
Avenue Garage and Symphony Hall). The nearby car-sharing locations are shown in Figure 5-4.

MBTA Orange Line 
The MBTA’s Orange Line subway provides service from Forest Hills Station in Jamaica Plain 
through downtown Boston to Oak Grove Station in Malden. The Orange Line provides inbound 
and outbound service approximately every eight minutes Monday through Friday and every 10 to 
13 minutes on Saturday and Sunday. Two MBTA stations along the Orange Line are located within 
walking distance of the campus and used by the Northeastern community: Ruggles and 
Massachusetts Avenue stations. Ruggles Station is located in the south campus at the corner of 
Ruggles and Tremont Streets. The Massachusetts Avenue Station is located in the east campus on 
Massachusetts Avenue between Columbus Avenue and St. Botolph Street. A secondary egress 
from Massachusetts Avenue station is provided on the Camden footbridge. Proposed MBTA 
Ruggles Station improvements include constructing a station entrance accessible from the 
Camden Street footbridge and Gainsborough Street. 
MBTA Green Line 
The MBTA Green Line E Branch provides trolley service between Heath Street and Lechmere 
Stations. The E Branch operates on eight-minute headways during the weekday morning and 
afternoon peak periods and on eight- to nine-minute headways during off-peak periods. Weekend 
service runs approximately every nine minutes. The Museum of Fine Arts, Northeastern, 
Symphony, and Prudential Center Stations are all located along Huntington Avenue adjacent to 
the campus. 
MBTA Bus Service 
As shown in Table 5-5 and Figure 5-5, the Northeastern campus is located within convenient 
walking distance to 14 MBTA bus routes. The primary MBTA bus route serving the Northeastern 
campus is the #39 Bus, which provides service between Forest Hills Station and Back Bay Station 
via Huntington Avenue. The buses operate on seven- to ten-minute headways during the weekday 
morning and afternoon peak periods. Bus-Bike-Only lanes were installed along a one-mile section 
of Huntington Avenue between Brigham Circle and Gainsborough Street in 2022–2023 along the 
#39 route to improve bus efficiency and reliability. 
The campus is also located adjacent to the MBTA #43 bus on Tremont Street that provides service 
between Ruggles Station and Park Street Station. 
MBTA Commuter Rail 
Three MBTA commuter rail lines run through Ruggles Station: the Providence/Stoughton Line, the 
Franklin/Foxboro Line, and the Needham Line. Commuter rail trains provide access from Boston 
to the southern and southwestern regions of Massachusetts and Rhode Island.

The Providence/Stoughton Line has 37 inbound trains and 36 outbound trains that stop at Ruggles 
Station. Inbound trains run between 4:15 a.m. and 1:01 a.m. approximately every 20 to 60 
minutes. Outbound trains run between 4:20 a.m. to 1:11 a.m. approximately every 45 to 60 
minutes during peak periods and less frequently during off-peak hours. 
The Franklin/Foxboro Line has 20 inbound trains and 18 outbound trains that stop at Ruggles 
Station on weekdays. Inbound trains run between 5:05 a.m. and 12:53 a.m. Outbound trains run 
between 5:45 a.m. to 1:15 a.m. Service to/from Franklin is approximately every 35 to 70 minutes 
during the peak periods and approximately 90 to 120 minutes during off-peak hours. Service 
to/from Foxboro is approximately every 90 minutes throughout the day. 
On weekdays, the Needham Line has 16 inbound trains and 15 outbound trains that stop at 
Ruggles Station. Inbound trains run between 5:05 a.m. and 10:42 p.m. Outbound trains run 
between 6:50 a.m. to 12:39 a.m. Peak hour headways are approximately 60 minutes. 
5.2.3.2 
Northeastern Shuttle Connections 
The following other transit connections are available for Northeastern students, faculty, and staff. 
Northeastern RedEye Shuttle 
Northeastern operates the RedEye shuttle, an off-campus safety ride service, which is available 
for students who live within two miles of the center of campus. Every night from 5 p.m. until 6 
a.m., the RedEye van will pick students up at Egan Access Road behind Snell Library. Students can 
book a ride in advance using the RedEye App or at the RedEye dispatch center located at the 
Northeast Security office in the Ruggles Substation. The on-demand App matches riders to similar 
direction and destinations into a shared vehicle for efficient drop off loops that pick up from 
campus every 30 minutes. 
Northeastern Loop Shuttle 
The Northeastern loop shuttle runs on a continuous “loop” between Forsyth Circle and university 
housing near the Prudential Center, notably 60 Belvidere Street (former Sheraton Hotel) between 
6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. The loop shuttle operates on a first come, first 
served basis with no reservation system and was introduced in 2021 with the addition of a long-
term lease for university undergraduate student housing at 60 Belvidere Street. 
Northeastern Boston-Burlington Shuttle 
Northeastern provides shuttle service for faculty, students, and staff traveling between Boston 
and Burlington for the purposes of research, co-ops, and classes. Shuttles operate from 7:30 a.m. 
to 6:45 p.m and run approximately every two hours with additional service mid-day. The Boston-
Burlington shuttle was introduced in 2022 to provide more research opportunities for students, 
to offer more flexible working hours for co-ops, and to allow staff more options for collaboration 
between campuses.

MasParc Connect 
MasParc provides access to and from the Boston campus via on-demand electric vehicles to local 
destinations that include the Prudential Center, the Longwood Medical Area, Fenway Park, 
Mission Hill, the Museum of Fine Arts, Target (1341 Boylston Avenue), multiple MBTA stops, and 
many other local businesses and offices through a program called MasParc Connect. The service 
operates Monday to Saturday from 10:00 a.m. – 8:00 p.m. Rides are requested by Northeastern

The Longwood Collective is a non-profit organization dedicated to enhancing Boston’s Longwood 
Medical and Academic (LMA) area with six different routes. The Longwood Collective helps

transit stops and off-site parking facilities. The Longwood Collective shuttle buses serve stops at 
Ruggles Station, JKF/UMass, Andrews Square, Fenway, Landsdowne Station, Landmark Center, 
and the Renaissance and Columbus garages.

Numerous bicycle-sharing stations, located throughout the campus, are provided by Bluebikes,

communities, including Boston, Brookline, Cambridge, Chelsea, Somerville, and Everett. As shown

5.2.4.4 
Bicycle Storage and Demand 
Northeastern is continually evaluating on-campus bicycle usage and storage, and actively adds 
bicycle racks and/or relocates existing racks to meet changing demand patterns as bicycle usage 
continues to evolve. Northeastern has significantly increased on-campus bicycle storage from only 
141 rack spaces at eight locations in 2000 to approximately 2,000 rack spaces at nearly 40 
locations throughout the campus in 2023. 
The East Village (GrandMarc) Project was the first campus building to provide a dedicated bicycle 
storage room within a residence hall facility with a capacity of approximately 80 bicycles. Since 
that time, LightView (537 bicycle spaces), Interdisciplinary Science and Engineering Complex 
(ISEC) (104 bicycle spaces), and EXP (128 bicycle spaces), have all added internal covered and 
secured long-term bicycle storage accommodations in addition to external short-term visitor 
racks. The BPDA Board recently approved 840 Columbus Avenue, which will include an additional 
approximately 246 bicycle spaces in a ground floor bicycle room and approximately 70 short-
term, exterior spaces for visitors on outdoor racks. 
These new bicycle accommodations will bring the campus-wide storage total up to approximately 
1,095 secure/internal bicycles, and 1,151 external visitor bicycles.

5.2.5 
Loading, Service, and Emergency Access 
Northeastern’s Transportation, Receiving, and Warehousing Department is responsible for 
administering the campus’s central receiving and distribution system, which is run from a central 
warehouse in Jamaica Plain. The department receives vendor deliveries, stores equipment and 
materials as necessary, and completes deliveries to on-campus locations, as well as from one 
campus location to another. Most buildings on campus also receive regular deliveries of mail, 
supplies, and food, some of which, such as those by courier or express delivery, occur within the 
public way. 
On campus, the building housing the university’s mail center at 716 Columbus Avenue is 
scheduled for renovation and upgrades. The renovations include upgrades to the mail center to 
accommodate broader receiving and delivery needs and the installation of an additional delivery 
window on the lower level. Construction on the centralized mail facility will be completed in 2024. 
Campus loading docks and access restrictions are summarized in Figure 5-10. As shown, in 
addition to the main service road along the MBTA Orange Line tracks, several other routes within 
the campus are used by vehicles servicing buildings. 
To the extent possible, all deliveries and pickups are coordinated to minimize impacts to the 
community. In addition, as further described below, Northeastern coordinates student move-in 
days with BTD, neighborhood residents, and other affected parties to minimize traffic disruption. 
5.2.5.1 
General Service and Deliveries 
To reduce impacts on pedestrians on campus, loading access has been prohibited all day at certain 
locations, and between 7:30 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. at others.

5.2.5.2 
Trash/Recycling 
Staff empties outdoor waste/recycling containers throughout the day seven days per week, 
consolidating materials to other locations on campus. 
Consolidated trash and recycling materials are picked up starting at approximately 7:00 a.m. via 
hauler trucks on routes that vary by day, time, duration, and service stops. Recycling materials 
are picked up by facilities staff who operate five box trucks throughout the campus; materials are 
actively picked up across campus during typical recycling staff shift hours (6:00 a.m. – 2:30 p.m.) 
and occasionally earlier or later to accommodate special situations. Approximately 20 
compactors are located on the campus. Compactors are emptied as needed, with service ranging 
from once per week to once per month. 
5.2.5.3 
Food Waste 
In addition to trash and recycling, food waste is also picked daily, generally in the time frame of 
5:00 a.m. – -8:00 a.m. Conversion of food waste to compost helps to divert waste from landfills 
and is part of a broader commitment to reducing Northeastern’s environmental footprint. 
5.2.5.4 
Emergency Service Access 
Emergency access to the campus is provided by the City street network, principally the arterial 
streets of Massachusetts Avenue, Huntington Avenue, Ruggles Street, and Columbus Avenue. 
Access into the campus is provided by local streets and a network of service roadways and 
pathways throughout the campus. 
5.2.6 
Student Move-in Move Out 
Since 2000, Northeastern has prepared Move-In/Move-Out Plans each academic year for BTD. 
The Move-Out Plan is usually a less formalized document since that process is more gradual, 
taking place over a longer timeframe. The elements of the Move-In Plan include: 
♦ Notifying neighbors about the move-in process and arranging parking for neighbors in the 
Camden Lot and Gainsborough garages for the weekend. 
♦ Avoiding moving students into the Fenway area on September 1 due to expected 
congestion. 
♦ Working with the neighborhoods on August 31 and September 1. 
♦ Assisting coordination of trash removal and police presence. 
♦ Reaching out to neighboring businesses and institutions (i.e., the Symphony, Wentworth) 
in early May and early June to notify them of Northeastern’s move-in plans.

5.2.7 
Transportation Demand Management (TDM) 
As outlined in its 2013 IMP, Northeastern has made a strong commitment to TDM and continues 
to make improvements to TDM initiatives to help reduce single-occupant automobile commuting 
to and from its campus, and to promote non-automobile alternatives. It is expected that enhanced 
bicycle storage, expansion of car-sharing opportunities, provisions for alternative fuel vehicles, 
and continued attention to parking availability and pricing will be priority efforts over the term of 
the IMP. As the parking supply on campus is reduced due to new building projects, parking ratios 
for students and staff will decrease. This reduced availability typically leads to higher fees for 
automobile users, further serving as a demand management measure. 
The following promotions and incentives are offered to faculty, staff, and students: 
♦ Posting of schedules, maps, fare information; 
♦ MBTA semester pass program; 
♦ Pre-tax purchase of MBTA passes for employees; 
♦ On-campus Bluebikes stations; 
♦ Bluebikes membership subsidies; 
♦ Indoor, secured bicycle spaces and outdoor visitor bicycle spaces across campus; 
♦ Preferential parking for carpools and vanpools; 
♦ Access to EV charging; and 
♦ Limited overnight parking for campus residents.

5.3 
Future Conditions 
The following sections provide a summary of the future transportation conditions and proposed 
improvements occurring in the area. 
5.3.1 
Ongoing Transportation Initiatives 
Northeastern is actively engaged with various City and State agencies on a number of initiatives 
to improve transportation conditions in and around the campus, as described in the following: 
♦ Tremont Street Improvements. The Tremont Street Design Project, completed in fall 
2023, was intended to make Tremont Street safer for everyone with an emphasis on 
pedestrian safety at intersections along Tremont Street between Massachusetts Avenue 
and Herald Street in the South End. 
♦ Roxbury Resilient Corridors. Corridor improvements are in initial planning stages for 
Malcolm X Boulevard, Melnea Cass Boulevard, and Warren Street. Concept designs will 
include the roads, sidewalks, green infrastructure, and public spaces of these three major 
corridors in Roxbury. Corridor improvements are proposed in two phases: 
o Phase 1. Community engagement for Malcolm X Boulevard (12-18 months) leading to 
final concept design. This Phase will require tight coordination and collaboration with 
the MBTA. 
o Phase 2. Community engagement and concept design for Warren Street and Melnea 
Cass Boulevard will start in 2025. The beginning of Phase 2 may overlap with the last 
months of Phase 1. 
♦ Roxbury-Fenway Connector. The Roxbury to Fenway Connector is a proposed "Green 
Link” that would include a path within the existing double row of trees on Ruggles Street 
between Ruggles Station and Parker Street. 
♦ Northeastern Boston Campus Bike Parking Framework. Building on existing analyses of 
bicycle parking usage, locations, and types, the university is formalizing bike parking 
approaches and policies in a framework plan. The framework will establish guidance for 
rack location selection, style, installation, and maintenance on the Boston campus. 
♦ Ruggles Street Improvements. Ruggles Street between the Parker Street intersection and 
the Southwest Corridor has been identified in the BTD’s GoBoston 2030 report as a 
candidate corridor in the continuing expansion of the Boston Green Links initiative to 
improve access to green spaces and active transportation options. New pedestrian paths, 
bicycle facilities, and safer road crossings have been recently constructed.

♦ MBTA Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Extensions. The MBTA Columbus Avenue Bus Lanes 
Project constructed New England’s first center-running bus lane. Phase 1 of the Columbus

Bluebike stations are included in the project.

adjacent to the building. New streetlights, street trees, bicycle racks, and curb extensions 
are included in the project.

5.3.3.3 
Trip Generation Methodology 
Trip generation is a complex, multi-step process that produces an estimate of vehicle, transit, and 
walk/bicycle trips associated with a proposed development and a specific land use program. A 
project’s location and proximity to different travel modes determines how people will travel to 
and from a site. 
Trip generation estimates for the faculty/staff, commuting students, and on-campus residential 
aspects of the IMP are based on a variety of sources specific to Northeastern, including the latest 
2023 MassDEP Rideshare survey data, and historical trip generation based on parking occupancy 
counts, parking lot/garage driveway counts, and parking permit data. 
Since the 2013 IMP, Northeastern has committed to providing additional on-campus housing for 
undergraduate students. For the IMP, Northeastern proposes to continue to commit to providing 
housing for 55% of undergraduate students. On-campus housing will continue to reduce 
undergraduate commuter trips to campus.

Construction Period Impacts 
Construction activities are expected to be accommodated within individual Project Site 
boundaries. Details of the overall construction schedule, working hours, number of construction 
workers, worker transportation and parking, number of construction vehicles, and routes will be 
addressed in detail in a CMP to be filed with BTD for each project in accordance with the City’s

coordinate all construction activities with other on-going construction work in the vicinity of the 
project to minimize impacts to area roadways.

6.1 
Approach and Goals 
Northeastern University has a longstanding commitment to sustainability and resilience through 
its research, experiential education, and support of the physical campus and its surroundings. In 
2007, university President Joseph Aoun was a founding member of the American College & 
University Presidents Climate Commitment. In 2010, the Northeastern Facilities Division released 
the university’s first sustainability plan, which made a commitment to reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions by 80 percent by 2050. Northeastern has made great progress since then, reducing 
emissions by 42 percent while emphasizing resiliency, or the ability to withstand change and adapt 
quickly. 
Northeastern’s pride in these accomplishments is matched by an interest in moving forward to 
broaden efforts for collective action at the intersection of climate change and related social justice 
issues. Events like the Flint water crisis, COVID-19, and the 2020 racial awakening have highlighted 
the unequal burdens of climate change, along with sustainability and social justice. Climate justice 
calls for a transition away from the extraction of resources, both human and natural, and connects 
the climate crisis to social, racial, and environmental issues, in which it is deeply entangled. Higher 
education has an opportunity, and a responsibility, for greater impacts by working with City and 
community partners to address the systems that interconnect with climate justice and 
sustainability. Moreover, by using citywide frameworks as the basis for university sustainability 
planning, Northeastern ensures its commitment to act in service of the broader community and 
planet. Plans like the Boston Climate Action Plan and Urban Forest Plan help establish the 
foundation for the university’s sustainability plans and strategies, while policies like BERDO and 
the Specialized Stretch Energy Code act as key measures to ensure robust building standards. 
Climate Justice Action Plan (CJAP) 
In late 2022, Northeastern partnered with campus and community members to launch its Climate 
Justice Action Plan (CJAP) planning process. The Climate Justice and Sustainability Hub, part of 
Northeastern’s Planning, Real Estate and Facilities division, and its community partners, co-
designed a process that ensured the plan would be responsive to the concerns of locally impacted 
communities and aligned with the university’s research, teaching and physical plant stewardship 
goals. The steering committee, made up of community representatives, students, frontline 
workers, faculty, and Northeastern staff, has worked closely for over 15 months towards a 
consensus on goals and strategy recommendations for the plan. 
The resulting CJAP goals, strategies, and actions have created a framework for Northeastern in its 
pursuit of sustainable and just solutions to climate and intersecting issues. A summary of CJAP’s 
goals and strategies has been provided in Table 6-1.

Northeastern also recognizes the urgency and significance of addressing our direct impact on the 
climate crisis by eliminating our greenhouse gas emissions and decarbonizing our buildings in line 
with or ahead of City and state goals. Thus, the university recently launched a robust 
Decarbonization and Resilience Plan (DRP) effort that will deliver a clear and actionable pathway 
to decarbonize Northeastern’s Boston campus. The planning process will enable the university to

IMPNF/PNF is delivered, along with renovations of existing campus buildings and infrastructure. 
As we move into the next decade in the IMP, Northeastern will move beyond aspirational goal 
setting and take concrete steps to eliminate emissions, improve air quality, and reduce congestion 
and waste. All done with an eye towards building resilience and advancing community health

Sustainable Campuses 
Northeastern has made significant strides in campus sustainability over the past decade, including 
sustainable buildings, landscape, and commuter mode choices that reduce emissions and 
congestion. Northeastern requires that all new major buildings or renovations achieve a minimum 
of LEED Gold certification, with the goal of achieving LEED Platinum. This and other sustainability 
standards are outlined in Northeastern’s recently updated Sustainable Design Standards1. To 
date, Northeastern has seven LEED certified projects in Boston, including ISEC certified LEED Gold 
in 2018, East Village certified LEED Gold in 2016, and LightView student housing certified LEED 
Platinum in 2021. The recently completed EXP building has committed to LEED Platinum 
certification. The new Pedestrian Crossing bridge (PedEx) received an Envision Bronze certification 
for sustainable infrastructure. 
6.2.1 
Building Decarbonization and Energy Resilience 
6.2.1.1 
Greenhouse Gas Emissions & Local Air Quality 
Between 2005 and 2021, greenhouse gas emissions per square foot of building space on 
Northeastern’s Boston campus declined by 42%. In 2023, Northeastern received a Mass Save 
Climate Leader award for its energy efficiency efforts, including an extensive LED lighting upgrade. 
ISEC and EXP, the two largest developments to be constructed since the 2013 IMP, were designed 
creatively to achieve high levels of sustainability. ISEC, which is LEED gold certified, achieved 50% 
energy savings when compared to a typical lab building through solutions such as a cascading air 
system and a solar veil. EXP, a multidisciplinary science and learning complex completed in fall 
2023, is committed to achieving LEED Platinum certification. From triple glazing to heat recovery 
chillers, energy efficiency efforts lead to a 50% reduction in energy use, and a 74% reduction in 
natural gas use compared to a baseline building. The reduction in fossil fuel use contributes not 
only to a reduction in carbon emissions but also to better air quality. 
Across existing buildings, the university has identified which roofs are suitable for solar PV and is 
also planning the addition of solar arrays on roofs due for replacement. The university is currently 
negotiating a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) to install solar panels on the roof of the Curry 
Student Center, which was replaced in 2023 and designed to support solar panels. This follows 
the recent installation of solar panels on the roof of Snell Library in spring 2024.
