Decarbonization and Resiliency Planning and Other Utility Planning Efforts 
Northeastern’s approach to decarbonization includes 1) reducing the energy use intensity of its 
buildings, and 2) transitioning to clean energy sources. The university’s DRP will turn this approach 
into an implementable plan that ties building-level interventions into a campus-wide strategy for 
energy, decarbonization, and resiliency. 
The DRP team is currently engaged in an early recommendations phase to ensure that near-term 
large investments align with and create assets for future zero carbon options. Following 
identification and assessment of alternative decarbonization scenarios, the university is targeting 
an approved multi-year DRP by Fall 2025. 
The DRP will build off growth and development planning established in this IMPNF/PNF to identify 
load, opportunities, and phasing that aligns with development and capital needs over the next 
decade. In turn, it will ensure that development approved through the 2024 IMP is implemented 
in-line with a realistic plan to meet or exceed Northeastern’s, the State’s, and City’s 
decarbonization goals. 
The DRP also builds from Northeastern’s utility planning work, including an early analysis of 
electrical load growth, identification of Energy Conservation Measures (ECM’s), and solar PV 
potential. In the summer, the current peak load on campus for electricity is nearly 18MW and 
peak steam load is about 135M pounds/hr. 
The Boston campus currently faces electric distribution limitations and failing steam lines. To 
ensure resilience and reliability, the university is switching parts of the campus’ existing steam 
system from a natural gas-fired central plant to Vicinity’s high-pressure steam, while negotiating 
towards purchase of their “e-steam” product. This transition will decrease on-site fossil fuel 
emissions associated with existing building operations on campus. Eventual decommissioning of 
the central campus heating plant will also reduce scope one emissions and associated local air 
pollutants. 
Once finalized, the DRP and related planning efforts will enable Northeastern to describe more 
precisely the university’s plans for electrical load growth, solar PV, installation, long-range district 
system, as well as the university’s timeline to meet goals, regulations, and interim milestones. In 
the interim, the university is on track to comfortably exceed BERDO requirements through 2029.

Reduction and Reuse 
Northeastern seeks to reduce and reuse materials in capital projects, purchases, and practices 
across the university. Northeastern’s Capital Projects team targets furniture reuse and, where 
unable, identifies partners or needs in the community where items in good condition can get a 
second life. This has ranged from 700 pounds of office supplies being donated to the Great 
Exchange to gently used appliances being donated to Boston Building Resources. 
The university’s updated Sustainable Design Standards address embodied carbon, requiring new 
buildings and whole building renovations to perform whole building life cycle carbon analysis and 
reduce embodied carbon of primary materials by 20% from a typical design. 
“OZZI” containers in dining halls are reusable to-go containers that provide convenience and 
flexibility while reducing the volume of paper and foam products in landfills. Meanwhile, to 
reduce plastic waste, there are also over 250 water bottle filling stations throughout campus. 
Northeastern is actively exploring additional procurement opportunities to further reduce the 
purchase and use of single-use plastics.

6.2.4.1 
Arboretum 
Urban green space contributes notably not only to ecology but also to human health and 
wellbeing. These spaces support community activity, filter pollution, mitigate heat islands, 
support water retention and filtration, and more. Northeastern University’s Arboretum was 
awarded a Level II Accreditation through ArbNet. Level II-accredited arboreta have 100 species, 
varieties or cultivars of trees or woody plants, an arboretum collections policy describing the 
development and professional management of plants and enhanced educational and public 
programming. Northeastern’s Boston campus has more than 1,400 individual trees and 5,400 
shrubs, representing 320 different wood species that shelter the walkways between buildings and 
surround the open green spaces, creating an urban oasis. This mature canopy provides respite, 
helps mitigate urban heat island, and supports management of stormwater runoff. 
Beyond its own campus, Northeastern supports trees by urban forestry efforts, helping to 
maintain urban street trees and partnering with community groups to support their urban 
canopy. For example, Northeastern staff and co-ops recently partnered with Mission Hill 
Neighborhood Housing Services to help Fitzgerald Park become certified as a Level I arboretum.

Excessive heat is a serious threat to health and wellbeing that disproportionately impacts 
vulnerable communities. In summer 2023, following Mayor Wu’s call for local institutions to 
support the City’s response to extreme heat, the university piloted its Hot Summer: Cool Break 
initiative. Northeastern joined community partners to host Community Heat Breaks at summer 
camps or residential communities on hot afternoons. These festive gatherings for children and

6.3.3.1 
Introduction 
Northeastern has reviewed climate change conditions as further detailed, more frequent and 
severe weather events, including higher maximum and mean temperatures, longer and more 
extreme heat events, increased droughts, and severe precipitation events. A copy of the 
completed Climate Resiliency Checklist is included in Appendix E. 
6.3.3.2 
Extreme Heat Events 
According to “Climate Ready Boston,” the City of Boston can expect that the number of days with 
temperatures greater than 90°F will increase. Between 1971 and 2000, Boston experienced an 
average of eleven days per year over 90 degrees and may experience between 25 and 90 days 
annually by 2070, depending on the extent of greenhouse gas emissions over the next several 
decades. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project design incorporates 
measures to minimize the impact of high temperature events, including:

♦ New street trees to provide shade;

6.3.3.3 
Flooding Events 
Because of climate change, New England is expected to experience an increased frequency of 
intense storms that generate significant volumes of precipitation. Such precipitation events have 
the potential to overwhelm existing stormwater infrastructure capacity and may result in inland 
flooding with the potential to damage buildings. Improper conveyance of stormwater during 
precipitation events may also cause overflows of combined sewer systems that allow wastewater 
from buildings connected to the combined sewer to discharge to local waterways, or that 
surcharge the system and cause overflow at other locations. 
To mitigate the effects of extreme precipitation events, the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project’s stormwater management system will be designed to minimize the 
volume of stormwater runoff from the Project Site and promote groundwater recharge to the 
greatest extent practicable. Part of the stormwater management strategy is to include pervious 
pavers, where feasible, on the Project Site. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project will retain the first 1.25-inch of stormwater runoff from the Site’s impervious 
areas. 
6.3.3.4 
Drought Conditions 
Under the high emissions scenario evaluated by Climate Ready Boston, the occurrence of 
droughts lasting one to three months could increase by as much as 75% over existing conditions 
by the end of the century. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will 
approach potential drought impacts by reducing the amount of water used within the building 
and across the Project Site for irrigation. The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility 
Project will include low-flow fixtures and water conserving appliances, to the extent feasible, to 
minimize the amount of water used by the building’s occupants.

7.1.7.2 
Groundwater Conditions 
Groundwater observation wells have been installed and are being monitored at the Project Site. 
Based on groundwater level measurements dating back to 2012, groundwater levels generally 
range between El. 4 and El. 7 Boston City Base Datum. 
Groundwater levels are influenced by the presence of stormwater recharge systems at the north 
and southwest portions of the Project Site. Site groundwater levels will vary with season, 
precipitation, construction activity in the area, below-grade structures, leakage from utilities, and 
other factors. 
7.1.7.3 
Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD) 
The Project Site is located within the Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD), 
therefore specific requirements of Article 32 of the Boston Zoning Code and the Boston Water 
and Sewer Commission (BWSC) policy will apply. Construction of a building that falls within the 
district must not negatively impact groundwater levels in the area. A suitably designed 
groundwater recharge system will be constructed as part of the 262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. The lowest level of the new building and ice rink slab are 
anticipated to be at El. 11’-7” or higher and above El. 7 BCB and area groundwater levels. 
Therefore, no permanent groundwater pumping or underslab drainage systems are necessary for 
new building construction. A “no harm” letter regarding groundwater will be submitted to the 
BPDA and the Boston Groundwater Trust. 
7.1.7.4 
Foundation Construction Methodology 
Northeastern anticipates that the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project will 
support the building on deep foundations bearing in bedrock. High capacity, low displacement 
steel H-piles will be used for new building column support. Piles will be vibrated to the top of the 
bedrock bearing stratum to mitigate noise and potential impacts to abutting structures. Following 
installation to top of bedrock, piles will be driven to final end bearing resistance. Appropriate 
vibration performance criteria will be developed for levels not to be exceeded during 
construction. 
The replaced ice rink slab will be supported on a combination of existing and new concrete 
caissons (drilled shafts) bearing within the Marine Clay Deposit. 
Excavation will be required for construction of new pile caps and various below grade features. 
Excavation depths will vary from approximately 5 to 13 feet deep at isolated locations depending 
on existing conditions and new construction requirements. Temporary support of excavation 
requirements are anticipated to be limited. 
Excavation for new substructure construction will generally be above Site groundwater levels. 
Temporary construction dewatering will be required for short term deeper excavations and to 
control surface water runoff into excavations during rain events. Any temporary dewatering

that will connect to existing BWSC 10-inch DICL Southern Low Main in St. Botolph Street.

Storm Drainage System 
7.2.3.1 
Existing Storm Drainage System 
There is an existing BWSC drainage main in Gainsborough Street, St. Botolph Street, and Public 
Alley No. 823 adjacent to the Project Site. 
The Project Site currently consists mostly of impervious areas, such as the existing Matthews 
Arena building and bituminous asphalt that has some planted and grassed areas. Stormwater 
runoff from the Project Site is captured by existing catch basins, which flow to the two existing 
infiltration systems within the Project Site, that ultimately overflow to the BWSC drain main in St. 
Botolph Street. Stormwater in the roadways is captured by existing catch basins, which flow to 
the existing BWSC drain mains in Gainsborough Street, St. Botolph Street, and Public Alley No. 
823. 
Project Site

connecting to the 18-inch BWSC drain main at the intersection of St. Botolph Street. 
Gainsborough Street

connecting to the 30-inch BWSC drain main at the intersection of St. Botolph Street.

7.2.3.2 
Proposed Drainage Systems 
The Project is expected to substantially improve the stormwater quality runoff from the Project 
Site and will meet the BWSC’s Site Plan requirements. The existing drain main in St. Botolph Street 
appears to be of adequate capacity to service the needs of the 262 St. Botolph Street 
Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. The Project will meet or reduce the existing peak rates of 
stormwater discharge and will improve the stormwater quality and reduce the quantity of 
stormwater runoff being discharged to the City storm drain system through the installation of on-
site infiltration systems. Per BWSC requirements, the equivalent of 1.25-inch of rainfall over the 
Project Site’s impervious areas will be stored and recharged. 
In addition to the installation of on-site infiltration systems, stormwater runoff will be treated 
using deep sump hooded catch basins, manholes and, if necessary, stormwater quality treatment 
units to achieve the required pretreatment and reductions. A stormwater Operation and 
Maintenance Plan will be developed to support the long-term functionality of the proposed 
stormwater management systems. 
7.2.3.3 
Stormwater Quality 
The Project will improve the quality of stormwater leaving the Project Site through the installation 
of on-site infiltration systems and therefore is expected to have positive impacts on the water 
quality of the nearby water bodies. Erosion and sediment controls will be used during 
construction to protect adjacent properties and the municipal storm drain system. These controls 
will be inspected and maintained throughout the construction phase until the areas of 
disturbance have been stabilized through the placement of pavement, structure, or vegetative 
cover. 
Necessary dewatering will be conducted in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and BWSC 
discharge permits. Once construction is complete, the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project will be in compliance with BWSC Site Plan requirements. 
7.2.3.4 
DEP Stormwater Management Policy Standards 
In March 1997, MassDEP adopted a new Stormwater Management Policy (the Policy) to address 
non-point source pollution. In 1997, MassDEP published the Massachusetts Stormwater 
Handbook as guidance on the Policy, which was revised in February 2008. The Policy prescribes 
specific stormwater management standards for development projects, including urban pollutant 
removal criteria for projects that may impact environmental resource areas. Compliance is 
achieved through the implementation of Best Management Practices (BMPs) in the stormwater 
management design. The Policy is administered locally pursuant to MGL Ch. 131, s. 40. 
A brief explanation of each Policy Standard and the system compliance is provided below: 
Standard #1: No new stormwater conveyances (e.g. outfalls) may discharge untreated 
stormwater directly to or cause erosion in wetlands or waters of the Commonwealth.

The 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Althetic Facility Project will be designed so that 
stormwater conveyances (outfalls/discharges) do not discharge untreated stormwater into, or 
cause erosion to, wetlands or waters. Therefore Standard #1 will be met. 
Standard #2: Stormwater management systems shall be designed so that post-development peak 
discharge rates do not exceed pre-development peak discharge rates. This Standard may be 
waived for discharges to land subject to coastal storm flowage as defined in 310 CMR 10.04 
The proposed stormwater management system will be designed so that there is no increase in 
post construction discharge rates from the Project Site. Therefore, Standard #2 will be met. 
Standard #3: Recharge to groundwater 
Loss of annual recharge to groundwater shall be eliminated or minimized through the use of 
environmentally sensitive site design, Low Impact Development techniques, stormwater best 
management practices, and good operation and maintenance. At a minimum, the annual 
recharge from the post- development site shall approximate the annual recharge from pre-
development conditions based on soil type. This Standard is met when the stormwater 
management system is designed to infiltrate the required recharge volume as determined in 
accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. 
Soil testing will be done to determine the Hydrologic soil types. The Project will be required to 
infiltrate a volume of runoff equal to 1.25 inch of rainfall times the total footprint of proposed 
impervious area / building on-site to meet BWSC requirements. Therefore, Standard #3 is 
anticipated to be met. 
Standard #4: Stormwater management systems shall be designed to remove 80% of the average 
annual post-construction load of Total Suspended Solids (TSS). This Standard is met when: 
a. Suitable practices for source control and pollution prevention are identified in a long-term 
pollution prevention plan, and thereafter are implemented and maintained; 
b. Structural stormwater best management practices are sized to capture the required water 
quality volume determined in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook; 
and 
c. Pretreatment is provided in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook. 
Most of the Project Site will be occupied by the proposed building, which includes roof runoff that 
will be routed to new infiltration system to meet the BWSC requirements, thus meeting the 80% 
TSS removal for majority of the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. 
Therefore, Standard #4 is anticipated to be met. 
Standard #5: For land uses with higher potential pollutant loads, source control and pollution 
prevention shall be implemented in accordance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook to 
eliminate or reduce the discharge of stormwater runoff from such land uses to the maximum 
extent practicable. If through source control and/or pollution prevention all land uses with higher

Soil Erosion and Sediment Control Plan: 
The objectives of the Soil Erosion and Sediment Control Plan are to control erosion at its source

concentrate and distribute stormwater runoff through natural vegetation before discharging to 
BWSC drainage systems. Soil erosion control does not begin with a perimeter sediment trap. It 
begins at the source of the sediment, the disturbed land areas, and extends down to the control 
structure. 
The Soil Erosion and Sediment Control Plan will be enacted during construction. The erosion 
control devices will remain in place until all exposed areas have been stabilized with vegetation 
or impervious surfaces. 
The objective of the Soil Erosion & Sediment Control Plan that will be enacted on the Project Site 
is to control the vulnerability of the soil to the erosion process or the capability of moving water 
to detach soil particles during the construction phase(s). The Soil Erosion and Sediment Control 
Plan will be in place during the construction phase.

implemented to ensure that stormwater management systems function as designed.

controls will be developed. The plan will include owner(s); parties responsible for operation and 
maintenance; schedule for inspection and maintenance; and routine and non-routine

8.1 
Historic Resources 
This chapter briefly addresses the historic designations of the potential development sites 
described in this IMPNF/PNF, and specifically, the proposed development of the 262 St. Botolph 
Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project. As other IMP Projects proceed to permitting, some 
may be subject to Article 80B, Large Project Review or Article 85, Demolition Delay Review. As 
Northeastern University continues to develop the specifics of other IMP Projects, regulatory 
requirements for each of the potential development sites will be discussed in the subsequent 
filings related to those projects. 
The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is located in the 
Fenway Neighborhood District of Boston. The Project Site is included in the Inventory of Historic 
and Archaeological Assets of the Commonwealth, but it is not listed in the State or National 
Registers of Historic Places. The Project Site, also currently known as the Matthews Arena, was 
initially constructed in 1910, the building (then known as the Boston Arena) consisted of a two-
story masonry entry block on the north elevation connecting to a large arena building, which was 
destroyed in a fire in 1918 and replaced with the present arena in 1920. Subsequent additions 
were added circa 1950 and in 2010 along with substantial alterations to the arena and entry block 
including removal of windows, infilling window openings with masonry and cladding over original 
masonry as well as removal of the entry block’s towers. During the late twentieth century, 
changes prior to the purchase of the arena by Northeastern were devastating to the building’s 
historic architecture. Historic features such as windows, doors, towers, decorative masonry, 
stairs, and terra cotta ornamentation were removed and/or covered over, stripping the building 
of its historic integrity. The substantial loss of integrity makes Matthews Arena ineligible for listing 
on the National Register of Historic Places. 
For additional information, please refer to the Historical Significance and Architectural Evaluation 
that has been provided in Appendix G.

8.4.1 
Demolition of Existing Building 
Matthews Arena (BOS.15498), which is included in the Inventory of Historic and Archaeological 
Assets of the Commonwealth, but not listed in the State or National Registers of Historic Places, 
will be demolished and a new multipurpose facility will be constructed in its place. As stated 
previously, substantial alterations to the building have detrimentally affected its historic character 
and integrity. The loss of integrity makes it ineligible for listing on the National Register of Historic 
Places. Further information regarding the potential development sites and potential demolition 
of existing buildings associated with the IMP Projects (if any) will be provided in subsequent filings 
for such projects. 
8.4.2 
Visual Impacts to Historic Resources 
The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is in the vicinity of other 
historic resources listed in the State and National Registers of Historic Places. Surrounding 
buildings, including historic resources and modern construction, range from two to sixteen stories 
in height. As the proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is 
approximately four-stories in height with two stories of mechanical space, it will be visible from 
such historic resources in the immediate vicinity of the Project Site; however, due to the size and 
height of surrounding buildings, potential visibility of the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose 
Athletic Facility Project, outside of the immediate vicinity along St. Botolph Street, Gainsborough 
Street, and Massachusetts Avenue will be limited. Further, the proposed size and massing of the 
262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project are consistent with the surrounding 
streetscape, as well as the historic and evolving use of the property as an arena and athletic 
facility. 
Further information regarding the potential development sites and visual impacts, if any, will be 
provided in subsequent filings for specific IMP Projects. 
8.4.3 
Shadow Impacts to Historic Resources 
The proposed 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic Facility Project is being designed to 
minimize new shadows on open spaces, sitting areas, or pathways to the extent feasible. 
Northeastern will conduct a shadow study for the 262 St. Botolph Street Multipurpose Athletic 
Facility Project and include the results in the DPIR.

BPDA Wind Criteria 
The BPDA has adopted two standards for assessing the relative pedestrian wind conditions. 
First, the BPDA wind design guidance criterion states that an effective gust velocity (hourly 
mean wind speed +1.5 times the root-mean-square wind speed) of 31 mph should not be 
exceeded more than one percent of the time. The second set of criteria used by the BPDA 
to determine the acceptability of specific locations is based on the work of Melbourne and is 
used to determine the relative level of pedestrian wind comfort for activities such as sitting, 
standing, or walking. The criteria are expressed in terms of benchmarks for the one-hour 
mean wind speed exceeded 1% of the time. 
Although detailed results are not presented at this time, please note that the preliminary 
comments provided herein are based on the safety and comfort criteria as defined by the 
BPDA.

Preliminary Findings 
The proposed building will be taller (approximately 115 ft) than the existing Matthews Arena 
facility (approximately 65 ft), and comparable in height to the taller buildings that exist along 
St Botolph Street. The shorter but densely built massings in the surroundings to the 
southwest, northwest and northeast (Image 2) will precondition the approaching winds 
from those directions. 
The wind speeds at the existing site are expected to be inherently low to moderate, with the 
conditions being appropriate for the use of the public sidewalks, transit station entrance and 
the school grounds, given the surrounding urban landscape. The addition of the proposed, 
taller building will result in the redirection of more wind along the surrounding streets. 
However, due to the existing low wind speeds in the area, the redirected winds are not 
expected to be problematic in most areas. Wind speeds on the sidewalks around the Project 
are expected to continue to be appropriate for pedestrian use; high and potentially 
uncomfortable wind speeds may occur on an annual basis at the street intersections 
adjacent to the Project. These conditions can be quantified during later detailed modeling 
studies and the effectiveness of potential mitigation measures will be evaluated. 
The project is not expected to negatively affect wind conditions in the William E. Carter 
School grounds park (Image 1), as the park would be sheltered from the predominant winds 
from the northwest and southwest by the Project. A slight increase in wind speeds may be 
expected in the school tennis courts located to the south of the Project site across the transit 
line (Image 2). However, conditions are expected to continue to be appropriate for the 
expected use on an annual basis. 
The qualitative assessment of potential wind conditions around the proposed project 
provided herein is based on our experience, knowledge of the local climate and 
understanding of the current building designs. The wind impact of the Project will be 
quantified using detailed modeling. 
Conclusions 
The proposed development site is favorably surrounded by densely built areas that 
precondition the prevailing approach winds. The addition of the proposed building, that will 
be comparable in height or taller than most existing buildings in the immediate vicinity, is 
expected to moderately increase wind speeds along the sidewalks adjacent to the Project. 
Owing the low-moderate existing wind conditions, the moderately higher wind speeds are 
expected to continue to be appropriate for pedestrian uses on an annual basis. The 
predicted wind conditions will be quantified using detailed modeling.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
 
The building located at 238 St. Botolph Street, historically known as the Boston (Matthews) Arena 
(BOS.15498) has a long history with Boston sports and hosted many events in Boston’s history 
including visiting celebrities and dignitaries. Over the building’s history, it has endured many 
changes as a result of increasing space demands, fires, and changing uses and owners. Never 
rising to the prominence of the Boston Garden, the arena was always a secondary or a tertiary 
location of events in Boston. A devasting fire in 1918 resulted in the building being largely rebuilt, 
with only a portion of its original 1910 structure remaining. It is the late twentieth century 
changes prior to the purchase of the arena by Northeastern University, which have been 
devastating to the building’s historic architecture. Historic features such as windows, doors, 
towers, decorative masonry stairs and terra cotta ornamentation have been removed and/or 
covered over, stripping the building of its historic character and integrity. While the building has 
a long history with Boston, the substantial loss of integrity makes it ineligible for listing on the 
National Register of Historic Places.

2.0 
HISTORIC NARRATIVE 
2.1 
Property Location and Context 
238 St. Botolph Street (Parcel ID# 0402262000) is located in the Fenway section of Boston on an 
approximately two-acre parcel. The parcel is fairly level and bordered on the northeast by Public 
Alley 823, to the southeast by the MBTA line, to the southwest by Gainsborough Street and to the 
west by St. Botolph Street. Surrounding properties are multi-story institutional and multi-family 
residential buildings. 
2.2 
Development 
2.2.1 
Initial Construction 
Designed by the Boston based architecture firm of Funk and Wilcox, the Boston Arena opened in 
1910. Initially, its purpose was largely to host hockey games and could seat 5,000 people. Games 
from local colleges and universities as well as high school hockey games were played here as well 
as curling and skating events. In addition to ice activities at the arena, political rallies (such as 
hosting Teddy Roosevelt in 1912) and other public events were hosted here. In order to expand 
programming options, the building would later be converted to include an indoor bicycle racing 
track and roller-skating track. Capacity and fire concerns quickly became an issue for the building 
as the owners (Boston Arena Company) wished to host larger and larger events. The owners’ 
request to erect additional temporary wooden stands within the building for additional seating 
was denied by the City of Boston.

Fig. 2: 1915 pamphlet illustrating Boston (Matthews) Arena entry block 
While the arena portion of the building was largely utilitarian in design featuring red brick, Funk 
and Wilcox designed an elaborate entrance to entice visitors. The entry block included two 
towers, terra cotta trim and arches, cherubs, finials, a marquee and other detailing. A circa 1930 
postcard (Figure 7) suggests the towers were multi-colored with gold roofs. The interior of the 
arena had first floor and balcony seating as well as a three-story section at the end, and overall 
was essentially a large oval with a large skylight in the ceiling.

Historic Significance and Architectural Evaluation 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
 
 
Fig. 3: Circa 1915 photograph of Boston (Matthews) Arena interior. 
2.3 
Second Arena 
In 1918, a fire destroyed the arena portion of the building. The entry block survived, while the 
arena collapsed, requiring it to be fully reconstructed. Funk and Wilcox were again selected to 
design the new arena. For the second arena, there initially was no balcony level and instead of 
arched steel trusses, the design used a triangular truss system mounted to concrete piers to 
support the gable roof. The second arena also had much larger windows and greater fireproofing, 
including concrete grandstands. Like the original arena, a large skylight system ran down the 
center of the roof. Windows on the second arena were much larger featuring steel industrial glass 
panels with operable sections and could bring far more light into the building than before. 
 
Funk and Wilcox put greater design efforts toward ornamentation on the second arena. The 
second arena was given a grand entrance on the west elevation, independent of the 1910 entry 
block featuring a large staircase with kneewall leading to a series of recessed panel doors with 
transoms above. In addition, there were decorative bands of masonry above and around the 
entrance. The second arena also had a greater use of concrete with concrete piers separating

2.4 
 
Subsequent Changes to Second Arena and Entry Block 
2.4.1 
Early to Midtwentieth Century Changes 
As soon as 1922, only two years after the construction of the second arena, there were complaints 
of overcrowding during events. In addition to all the previous uses the arena had it also now 
began to host other acts including diving competitions and circus performances. To satisfy egress 
requirements new exits were constructed, additional staircases were added and moved and 
additional entrances and exits added to the building. The ice area was reduced, and additional 
rows of seats were added, however this proved insufficient as demand for seats only increased. 
The Boston Bruins played their first home game in the arena and defeated the Montreal Maroons, 
2-1, on December 1, 1924. 
 
In 1926 a full balcony level was constructed which could seat an additional 2,200 people. Built 
from reinforced concrete for fireproofing, the balcony also required entry and exit doors to be cut 
into the exterior of the building and fire escapes added. In total by 1926, the arena could seat 
8,600 with standing room for an additional 2,000. Even with the additional capacity it still did not 
meet demand. On November 15, 1926, members of a nearby parade of roughly 1,500 people, 
including some unruly individuals tried to gain entry to see a boxing match, and when no tickets

More damage to the building occurred in 1932 when a fire broke out inside the building, but was 
put out.

One of the most significant events in the history of the arena is the construction of the Boston 
Garden in 1928. The Boston Garden would ultimately supplant the arena as the premier sports 
entertainment facility in Boston. The Boston Bruins would move their games immediately to the

Historic Narrative 
Historic Significance and Architectural Evaluation 
 
 
Epsilon Associates, Inc. 
Boston Garden after its construction. The Boston Celtics played their first home game at the arena 
in 1936 and would continue to play there until 1955, when they too moved to the Boston Garden. 
The effect of the construction of the Boston Garden was not immediate, but its presence started 
the decline of the arena. The Boston Garden was simply a bigger venue and designed to have 
spectators as close to the action as possible, making it far more popular. 
 
During the latter years of World War II, the arena was shut down and used as a barracks. The 
building was converted to a barracks housing 85 men on the second floor in 1944 and then only a 
year later the floor of the arena was replaced, and the building converted back to arena use. By 
1945, the successive changes over time and use had taken its toll on the building and the roof was 
replaced, the entire rear (south) elevation was reconstructed, and top floor of the building was 
removed after being cited by the Inspectional Services department for structural failure and 
bowing of the building. It is likely that the skylight was removed at this time. 
2.4.2 
Late Twentieth Century Changes 
In 1934 the ownership of the Boston Garden and Boston (Matthews) Arena merged, and the arena 
operated as a secondary location. Ultimately, the owners decided to sell the property as it was 
no longer in demand. In 1953, the Metropolitan District Commission (MDC) bought the arena for 
$280,000. The arena continued to be used for a variety of events including concerts and 
graduations as well as collegiate and high school hockey and skating. With the growing use of 
electrification for lighting and increases in lighting technology, the exterior windows were 
removed and infilled with concrete block and those at the top of the building were removed and 
covered over with metal paneling. It is likely at this time that the formerly exposed red brick was 
painted.

The MDC owned the arena for over 20 years, renting it out for various uses. Ultimately, 
Northeastern University expressed interest in acquiring it and purchased the arena in 1979. 
Northeastern invested millions of dollars over multiple renovations in the 1980s and 1990s to 
bring the facility up to modern standards. In 1982, the arena was renamed the Matthews Arena 
in honor of George (former chairman of Northeastern’s board of trustees) and his late wife Hope. 
By the time the arena was purchased by Northeastern, the character defining features of the 
building had already been removed or significantly altered, such as the masonry on the entry 
block, and the windows, doors and skylights on the arena.

ARCHITECTURAL EVALUATION 
3.1 
Architectural Description 
The Boston (Matthews) Arena located at 238 St. Botolph Street is situated on the east side of St. 
Botolph Street in the Fenway neighborhood of Boston. The earliest portion of the building is a 
two-story masonry entry block on the north elevation. The entry block is roughly three by one 
bay at the two-story height and then steps down to one-story in height, where it is three by two 
bays and then further reduces to two bays in width for an additional 18 bays in length. As the 
entry block proceeds to the east, the grade slopes downward creating a full height basement level. 
Except for a portion of the decorative inner terra cotta arch, original features of the decorative 
portion entry block have been stripped away and covered over with red brick. The remaining long 
section of the entry block has had all its original windows and doors removed, window and door 
openings infilled and has been painted, where it was originally exposed red brick.

Boston (Matthews) Arena in 1921. The surviving original entrance was retained 
while an entire new arena was constructed to the rear.

The original massing and design of the 1910 entry block was significantly altered in 1943 when 
the towers were demolished. Subsequently, in the 1970s, it was reclad in brick losing the marquee 
and decorative terra cotta features. Then in 1990, the terra cotta inner arch, which had only been 
covered over and not lost, was re-exposed. (Fig. 10)

secondary entrances at the east and west elevations. 
The circa 1950 addition is two stories four by five bays. Like the main block of the arena, it has

Over time the Boston (Matthews) Arena had substantial interior and exterior alterations. In 1926, 
a balcony level was added to the interior and numerous interior alterations were made over the 
decades, removing and expanding seating, replacing the arena playing floor, relocating and 
expanding the press box and remodeling locker rooms, bathrooms and other public areas as well 
as numerous alterations for fire safety and structural issues. In 1944, during World War II, the 
building was converted to serve as a barracks, which created substantial interior alterations. In 
1945, it was converted back to arena use.

The building has consistently had issues with structural stability and fire safety, causing repeated 
replacement of flooring in the arena and reinforcement of the foundation of the building as well 
as additional entrances and exits in the event of an emergency. Aside from the fire that destroyed 
the original arena in 1918, there was an additional fire in 1932. The 1932 fire destroyed one of 
the locker rooms and damaged adjacent areas. In 1948 the building was cited for potential 
structural collapse of the rear wall, which required it to be entirely reconstructed in 1949. During 
the 1949 renovation, the building was re-roofed and the top floor of the building was removed. 
The most significant alterations to the arena and affecting its character are the removal of all of 
the original windows and infilling the openings with concrete block and the removal of the 
skylight. Historically, the windows and skylight were important features and provided necessary 
light to the interior, without them the building both interior and exterior feels like a solid mass of 
masonry.

By the time the building was purchased by Northeastern in 1979 significant alterations had 
already occurred stripping the building of its historic character. After purchase of the building by 
Northeastern University, the arena went through renovations in the 1980s and 1990s 
substantially updating the facility. Due to the many changes and episodic renovations within the 
building, the interior of the arena portion of the building retains minimal historic fabric.

3.2 
Current Appearance 
The present Boston (Matthews) Arena does not represent the original form and massing of either 
the surviving original 1910 entry block or the later replacement 1920 main block of the arena. 
Changes made to the entry block including truncating it and the removal of the towers and portion 
of the arch as well as the marquee and its recladding have caused irreparable damage to its 
historic integrity. At the 1920 main block of the arena, a later circa 1950 rear addition, a 2010 
addition as well as the addition of structural bracing, the removal of every original door and 
window, infilling window openings with concrete block and painting the red brick exterior have 
degraded its historic integrity. Decorate masonry features and original exterior staircases have 
been removed and modern metal cladding added around the perimeter of the building. The 
building has also undergone substantial interior renovations over its history. The extensive 
alterations over time have degraded the building’s historic integrity.

changes to the property over time are included as Appendix B.

ARCHITECTURAL DESCRIPTION 
Describe architectural features. Evaluate characteristics of this building in terms of other buildings within the 
community. 
Matthews Arena occupies most of the block bounded by St. Botolph Street (N), Massachusetts Avenue (E), Gainsborough 
Street (W), and the MBTA railroad tracks (S). It is set back from St. Botolph with surface parking to the west and the rear 
walls of buildings on Massachusetts Avenue to the east. St. Botolph Street is a narrow side street, behind and parallel to 
Huntington Avenue. It is developed with a mix of building types, most dating to the early twentieth century. 
Matthews Arena is a large building with a basically rectangular plan; a main entrance and vestibule projects from the 
northeast corner. The arena space, which rises to a side-gable roof with ventilators, accounts for most of the building. The 
arena is surrounded by two story wings that contain support and circulation spaces except at the southwest corner. The 
arena and side wings are red brick with segmental arch window and door openings, many of which have been bricked in. 
The narrow north and south wings are standard reinforced concrete frame structures. A multi-door entrance with segmental 
arched openings and crenellated parapet is centered on the north front wing. The original large window openings on both 
north and south wings have been bricked in. The architectural highlight of this building when completed in 1910 was the 
entrance vestibule at the northeast corner. It consisted of a massive terra-cotta arch entrance framed by paired towers and 
fronted by an ornate metal and glass hood. The towers were removed in 1940 and the remaining facade was covered in the 
1970s. In 1990, the terracotta arch with its elaborate guilloche, braided, and leaf and dart moldings, was exposed. The 
classical ornament on the interior of the vestibule remains intact. Sanborn maps describe the construction as fireproof with 
the exception of wing roofs. A steel truss roof covers the arena. 
HISTORICAL NARRATIVE 
Discuss the history of the building. Explain its associations with local (or state) history. Include uses of the 
building, and the role(s) the owners/occupants played within the community. 
The Boston Arena was built in 1906 as "the premier hockey and boxing emporium" in Boston, hi 1914, eight years after 
opening, the main building was leveled by fire; only the ornate arch and towers on the northeast side and refrigerator plant 
to the southwest remained. The damage was estimated at $250,000. After the fire the building was expanded to include a 
second deck. Another fire caused $5,000 damage in 1931. 
After the Boston Garden was built in November 17, 1928, the Arena's stature as a sports venue declined. The 1931 
Bromley Atlas shows the Boston Arena building also housed Police Station 21 and the Boston University gym. In 1941, 
The Boston Globe referred to the "ancient face of the old skating emporium" in an article that continues "since the building 
of the Garden, the Arena has slipped into oblivion which it never quite deserved. Everything of importance that comes to 
Boston during the winter season goes into the Garden. The Arena owned by the same corporation [Boston Garden-Arena 
Corporation merged in 1934] has been getting the leavings for the past dozen years." In 1944, 85 servicemen were lodged 
on the second floor. The Boston Celtics played their last game in the Arena in 1959. 
Owners wanted to sell it to a New York group that would use it as an industrial plant. Public groups and private citizens 
rallied to save it primarily for hockey leagues. Mayor John B. Hynes said Boston "couldn't purchase the building for 14 
high school hockey teams." A retired naval officer offered to buy the building for $100,000 and give it to the city. That 
state legislature debated what it was worth. Finally, the Metropolitan District Commission bought the building for 
$280,000 in July 1953.

DIVERSITY, EQUITY AND INCLUSION PLAN DISCLOSURE 
Introduction 
In August of 2022, the BPDA Board approved a new policy requesting that project proponents include 
information in their Article 80 filings describing their plans to advance diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) 
efforts in throughout the life of their projects from pre-development through construction and ongoing 
operations. 
Proponent Information 
In Boston, the field of higher education stands as a prominent source of employment, with Northeastern 
proudly employing over 1,800 local residents. We are committed to expanding our Boston based 
workforce’s number and diversity. Additionally, we acknowledge our crucial role in supporting small 
businesses, particularly those owned by minorities and women. Over the past ten years, our contributions 
have aligned with our Institutional Master Plan objectives and our broader university mission of 
strengthening communities. Some of the initiatives include providing members of the community with 
opportunities for education, networking, and employment. 
Northeastern University’s Goals 
Given the significant size of investment the university makes every year in goods and services, for capital 
projects and day to day operations, the university’s spending goals are expected to have significant impact 
on underrepresented businesses. The university’s goals to support this effort over time include the 
following: 
• 
Northeastern remains committed to increasing business with SLBEs to 20% of its discretionary 
spending and MWBEs to 12% of discretionary spending by 2023. 
• 
Furthering President Aoun’s goal, Northeastern is committed to doubling spend with diverse 
suppliers by 2026. Additional details can be found here - https://northeastern.edu/ 
diversity/our-progress/ 
• 
In FY2023 Northeastern continues to strategically direct 30% of major design/construction 
spending in the Northeastern IMP to MBEs and 10% to WBEs 
• 
10% of non-IMP design/construction spend continues to be directed to MBEs and WBEs 
 
In addition to the economic impact, Northeastern leverages strategic sourcing and vendor management 
to identify opportunities in which diverse vendors can become strategic partners. In early FY23 after 
performing an RFP, Northeastern selected a new travel management company (“TMC”), Christopherson 
Business Travel (“CBT”). CBT is a certified WBE, whose services complement and support Northeastern’s 
rapid growth. 
In addition, Northeastern University’s Planning, Real Estate, and Facilities (“PREF”) department took a 
progressive approach, soliciting diverse suppliers via RFP, for cleaning and janitorial services RFP. In lieu 
of awarding an entire contract to a large company with a small portion of the subcontract being 
awarded to a minority supplier, PREF broke out the janitorial contract into two bid packages - the first 
bid package covered 80% of the “cleanable” campus square footage and the second bid package

INTRODUCTION 
 
The SEMC Institutional Master Plan, dated January 26, 2007 (the “2007 IMP”) was 
approved by the BRA on March 29, 2007 and by the Boston Zoning Commission 
("BZC") on April 25, 2007 with an effective date of April 25, 2007, as amended by the 
IMPNF for Minor Amendment and Project Change ("First Amendment") filed on June 
10, 2008 and approved by the BRA on July 17, 2008. The most recent filing related 
to the IMP was the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form/Notice of Project 
Change approved by the BRA on May 15, 2012 ("SEMC IMP"). 
 
On September 6, 2019, SEMC filed an Institutional Master Plan Notification Form for 
the proposed IMP (“IMPNF”) to initiate review of the proposed Institutional Master 
Plan (“Proposed IMP”) pursuant to Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code, and a 
Project Notification Form (“PNF”) to initiate review of the proposed parking garage 
project (“Proposed Project”). The Proposed IMP and Proposed Project are described 
in greater detail in sections below. The BPDA issued a Scoping Determination on 
January 6, 2020 in response to both these filings. 
 
On November 5, 2021, SEMC filed the Proposed IMP and Draft Project Impact 
Report (“DPIR”) related to the Proposed Project as well as a Supplemental 
Information Document (“SID”) on February 3, 2022. The BPDA has since issued a 
Request for Supplemental Information (“Request”) in response to which SEMC 
submitted a second Supplemental Information Document on April 19, 2022. 
 
The Proposed IMP and Proposed Project have been reviewed by the Boston Civic 
Design Commission (“BCDC”) and received a vote of approval at the monthly 
meeting on May 3, 2022.

THE PROPOSED IMP 
 
The Proposed IMP provides an update on proposed and existing uses and facilities 
on the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center (“SEMC”) Campus and community benefits. The 
Proposed Project is a proposed institutional project within the Proposed IMP. 
 
SITE OF PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
The Proposed Project is located in the Brighton neighborhood within an 
approximately 42,450 square-foot area of the SEMC Campus bounded by 
Washington Street on the southeast, the SEMC Campus on the north, and the 
Overlook site on the southwest, which is currently being redeveloped for residential 
use. The Project Site is currently occupied by a sloped grassy hill and an at-grade 
parking lot with 47 spaces. The Project Site is located within the boundaries of the 
Proposed IMP.

DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Proposed Project includes construction of an approximately 203,000-square-
foot, six-floor parking garage at 253 Washington Street in Brighton, Massachusetts 
to consolidate existing parking accommodations currently spread throughout the 
neighborhood into a single location directly adjacent to critical care facilities. The 
Parking Garage will be served by an additional driveway from Washington Street 
and a driveway within the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center campus. The Project will 
add approximately 610 parking spaces, a secure bicycle room with approximately 
32 spaces, 32 covered bicycle parking spaces, and a rooftop solar array. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On November 20, 2018, the Proponent filed a Letter of Intent (“LOI”) in accordance 
with the BPDA’s policy regarding Provision of Mitigation by Development Projects in 
Boston. The St Elizabeth’s Medical Center Task Force, a long-standing body 
appointed to advise the BPDA on the Institutional Master Plan and related 
development projects, serves as the Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) for the 
Proposed Project. As the Task Force had been inactive for a period of time and has 
seen some attrition, on October 26, 2021, the BPDA reached out to existing 
members to confirm their interest and availability in continued participation. As 
memorialized in a BPDA Memorandum dated November 1, 2021, the Task Force 
was finalized with 6 members. 
 
The Proponent filed both an Expanded Project Notification Form (“PNF”) and an 
Institutional Master Plan Project Notification Form (“IMPNF”) on September 6, 2019, 
which initiated a public comment period that concluded on October 26, 2019. 
Notice of the receipt of the PNF and IMPNF by the BPDA was published in the 
Boston Herald on September 6, 2019. The notice, PNF, and the IMPNF were sent to 
the City’s public agencies/departments and elected officials pursuant to Section 
80A-2 of the Code. Additionally, copies of the PNF were sent to all Task Force 
members. 
 
Pursuant to Section 80B-5.3 of the Code, a Scoping Session related to the PNF and 
IMPNF was held with the City’s public agencies and elected officials to review and 
discuss the Proposed Project and the Proposed IMP. 
 

6 
 
On October 2, 2019, a Task Force Meeting was held. The Task Force Meeting was 
listed on the BPDA website. On October 15, 2019, a Public Meeting was held. The 
Public Meeting was advertised in the Boston Bulletin and listed on the BPDA 
website. 
 
On January 6, 2020, a Scoping Determination was submitted to the Development 
Team. In response to the Scoping Determination, on November 5, 2021, a Draft 
Project Impact Report (“DPIR”) was filed. The Proponent concurrently filed the 
Proposed IMP and the DPIR on November 5, 2021, which initiated a sixty (60) day 
public comment period. Both the DPIR and Proposed IMP comment periods were 
extended several times, ultimately concluding February 28, 2022. Notice of the 
receipt of the Proposed IMP by the BPDA was published in the Boston Herald on 
November 5, 2021. The notice, Proposed IMP, and DPIR were sent to the City’s 
public agencies/departments and elected officials pursuant to Section 80A-2 of the 
Code. Additionally, copies of the Proposed IMP and DPIR were sent to all of the Task 
Force members. The proposed IMP was dated November 5, 2021 and is described 
in Section 1.1 of the IMP as “SEMC Institutional Master Plan 2022-2026”. 
 
On December 9, 2021, a Virtual Task Force Meeting was held. The Virtual Task Force 
Meeting was listed on the BPDA website. On December 9, 2021, a Virtual Public 
Meeting was held. The Virtual Public Meeting was advertised in the Boston Bulletin 
and listed on the BPDA website. 
 
On February 8, 2022, a Supplemental Filing to the Proposed IMP providing details of 
a proposed Boston EMS Facility was filed by the Development Team. 
 
On February 17, 2022, a Virtual Task Force Meeting was held. The Virtual Task Force 
Meeting was listed on the BPDA website. On February 17, 2022, a Virtual Public 
Meeting was held. The Virtual Public Meeting was advertised in the Boston Bulletin 
and listed on the BPDA website. 
 
On March 21, 2022, a Request for Supplemental Information (“Request”) was 
submitted to the Development Team. In response to the Request, on April 19, 2022, 
a Supplemental Filing in response to the Request was filed. 
 
On May 3, 2022, the Proposed Project was approved by the Boston Civic Design 
Commission. 

7 
 
 
In addition to the above-mentioned meetings, the Proponent and BPDA also 
undertook community outreach efforts and participated in a series of meetings 
during the Article 80 Review process with local elected officials and the Allston Civic 
Association to discuss the Proposed IMP and Proposed Project and solicit feedback. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project improves accessibility and pedestrian safety in support of 
pedestrian circulation goals identified in the 2022-2026 St. Elizabeth's Medical 
Center (SEMC) Institutional Master Plan. In support of Steward’s green building 
goals, Parksmart design practices are employed within the proposed parking 
garage to provide sustainable building and parking operations at SEMC, and the 
proposed photovoltaic system will serve as an energy security and resiliency critical 
resource for SEMC. The program of the proposed parking garage will consolidate 
staff parking occurring in short-term leased remote satellite parking lots, provide 
reliable parking accommodations and significantly reduce staff commute time. This 
program serves the SEMC guiding principles to provide accessible care to all who 
seek its services and its effort to be the best place to work in health care, in addition 
to their overall commitment to better patient care. 
 
The Proposed Project is located in the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan area. The 
Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan provides a blueprint for improving how people move 
around Allston and Brighton by making it safer and more efficient for all modes of 
transportation—walking, biking, transit, and cars. The Plan will: improve the transit 
network, expand the bike network, improve walkability, enhance the main street 
and neighborhood experiences, and simplify intersections for all users. 
 
ZONING 
 
The Project Site is located in the Allston/Brighton Neighborhood District, Article 51 
of the Code, and also within an Institutional Master Plan Overlay District. In 
accordance with the provisions of Section 51.29.6, the term of the IMP is four (4) 
years in the Allston/Brighton Neighborhood District, and the four (4) year term of 
the IMP shall commence on the effective date of the approval of the IMP. 
 
 
 

8 
 
MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
MITIGATION 
 
The Proposed Project will provide mitigation and community benefits for the 
Allston/Brighton neighborhood and the City of Boston as a whole, including: 
 
• Improved Street and Pedestrian Environment 
These proposed improvements shall be completed before Certificate of 
Occupancy issuance for the Proposed Project and/or IMP and are subject to 
review and approval by the Boston Transportation Department (BTD), Public 
Works Department (PWD), Public Improvement Commission (PIC), and the 
BPDA. 
 
 The Proposed Project will activate the Washington Street corridor with 
enhanced streetscapes that will include the construction of new 
sidewalks, increased pedestrian activity, an upgraded public realm along 
the project frontage in and around the Project Site, and will include a 
bocce court for community use, bicycle parking accommodations, site 
furniture, pedestrian lighting, landscaping, and street trees in compliance 
with City of Boston Complete Street Guidelines. 
 As part of the Proposed Project, the Proponent has committed to 
implementing an interim condition for Washington Street across the 
project frontage, which will allow for the transition of these streetscapes 
until the full extent of the transportation improvements associated with 
Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan can be implemented by the City. These 
interim conditions will include new sidewalks, street trees, and associated 
utilities and landscape plantings along the project frontage. The proposed 
improvements shall be coordinated with and approved by BPDA and BTD 
and completed before Certificate of Occupancy issuance for the Proposed 
Project. 
 The Proponent has committed to installing at least forty-three (43) new 
trees, including nine (9) street trees along Washington Street corridor, in 
and around the Project Site as part of the site plan improvements and 
mitigation associated with the Proposed IMP. The installation of the 
proposed street trees along Washington Street shall be completed before 
Certificate of Occupancy issuance for the Proposed Project. 
 
 
 

9 
 
• Sustainable Design/Green Building 
 The Proposed Project is committed to the advancement of sustainable 
and environmentally conscious design and construction. To that end, the 
Proposed Project is being designed to meet the requirements of Article 37 
of the Code and has committed to design and construct the parking 
garage to Silver Level certifiability standards under the Parksmart rating 
system. 
 The Proposed Project is committed to installation of a new 19,500 square 
foot solar array that will provide approximately 431,000 kilowatts of 
energy annually. 
 Improvements throughout the medical campus and the surrounding 
public realm include measures to minimize the impact of high-
temperature events, including the enhancement of more than 1.5 acres of 
green space and planting of additional shade trees and other 
improvements to pedestrian/bicycle amenities throughout the 
Washington, Cambridge, and Nevins Streets corridors. 
 
• Increased Employment 
 The Proposed Project will create approximately ten (10) permanent and 
one hundred and fifty (150) construction jobs. 
 
• Water and Sewage Infrastructure 
 The Proposed Project is anticipated to contribute to the Boston Water and 
Sewer Commission (BWSC) for infiltration/inflow mitigation fund at a rate 
of 4:1 for any new wastewater flows added to the BWSC system. 
 
• Transportation Improvements and Mitigation 
 The Proposed Project will provide several multi-modal transportation 
improvements and implement various mitigation measures, including: 
o Creating a robust Transportation Demand Management (TDM) 
strategy that encourages employee and visitor use of public transit 
to minimize single occupant vehicle trips, designating an on-site 
employee transportation coordinator, employee transit subsidies, 
dedicated car sharing spaces, and provides showers/changing 
rooms for staff that bicycles to work (TDM measures valued at over 
$125,000). 
 

10 
 
o Active participation in the Allston-Brighton Transportation 
Management Association (TMA), including maintaining a leadership 
participation role in the TMA by a senior SEMC staff member. 
 
o Funding new Bluebikes stations for a total of 36 bike share bikes in 
or around the Project Site. Subject to review and approval by BTD, 
PWD, PIC, and the BPDA, and other applicable 
agencies/departments, the proposed Bluebikes stations would be 
located at intersection of Washington/Cambridge Streets and 
Warren/Nevins Streets in coordination with planned public realm 
improvements associated with the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan. 
Final location and financial contributions to support Bluebikes 
stations and operations will be approved by BTD. 
 
o Electric vehicle charging stations for 150 vehicles within the 
Proposed Project’s parking garage, consistent with the City’s 
Electric Vehicle (EV) Readiness Policy for New Developments. 
 
• Smart Utilities Policy 
 The Proponent shall complete the Smart Utilities review before obtaining 
a Certificate of Compliance. Based on the Proposed Project’s size and 
scope of work, the items to be reviewed and verified are listed below: 
o Stormwater retention of 1.25 inches over the impervious area; 
o Review the location of trees to ensure feasibility around other 
infrastructure (the review will be coordinated with BPDA’s Urban 
Design team); 
o An updated Utility Site Plan with the relevant utilities, including the 
items mentioned above as well as any other item included in 
previous comment letters; 
• Annual Property and Sales Tax Revenues 
 SEMC contributes more than $5,000,000 in property tax revenue annually 
to the City of Boston for SEMC facilities at 736 Cambridge Street, 45 
Nevins Street, and 253 Washington Street. 
 SEMC generates more $300,000 in sales tax revenue annually for the City 
of Boston. 
 
 
 

11 
 
• Charitable Care for the Community 
 SEMC provides approximately $200,000 annually in charitable care for 
under- and uninsured members of the Allston-Brighton neighborhood 
and surrounding communities. This charitable care provided by the 
Proponent combines with Health Safety Net (HSN) care through state 
reimbursements to total more than $2,000,000 annually in charitable care 
for the community. 
 
COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
In addition to the aforementioned mitigation, the Proposed Project includes the 
following community benefit commitments specific to the Proposed IMP and not 
included in other community benefit commitments to the Massachusetts 
Department of Public Health: 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to construct an approximately 2,300 square foot 
2-bay facility that can park two ambulance vehicles inside and has space for 
an office, lounge, locker & changing rooms with showers, full kitchen, toilet 
facilities and voice/data closet. This facility is estimated to be valued at more 
than $1,000,000 in construction costs and will be provided, as an additional 
community benefit, on a rent-free basis to EMS Boston subject to the terms 
of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between Steward Health Care 
and the Boston Public Health Commission dated June 8, 2022. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to maintain membership in the Allston-Brighton 
Transportation Management Association (TMA) with annual paid dues of 
appropriately $8,000 and contributions to key TMA initiatives for the 4-year 
term of the Proposed IMP. 
 
• 
The Proponent has agreed to work with BPDA, BTD, and MBTA staff to 
develop a preliminary conceptual design of a Bus Rapid Transit (“BRT”) lane 
from Parsons Street to Union Square. This work is valued at approximately 
$100,000. Scope of work will be determined by the time the TAPA is 
executed. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to make a snow emergency provision of 50 
parking spaces at 326 Washington Street (“the Elks Lot”) for use by Allston-
Brighton residents with valid City-issued Allston-Brighton neighborhood 
parking permits on a first-come-first-serve basis during City of Boston 

12 
 
declared snow emergencies. This parking provision is made for the 4-year 
term of the Proposed IMP. The Proponent is currently under lease 
agreement with the Elks Lot through 2026. Should the Proponent be unable 
to renew the parking lot lease at this location, provisions through end of the 
4-year term of the Proposed IMP for 50 snow emergency parking spaces will 
be made elsewhere on the SEMC campus. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to construct public realm streetscape 
improvements along Washington, Nevins, and Cambridge Streets along 
SEMC campus frontage to support future public right-of-way revitalization 
proposed through the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan. Construction of these 
public realm streetscape improvements are valued at more than $100,000 
for pedestrian hardscape surfaces, curbing, planting of shade trees and 
other landscape plant materials, signage, and other public realm 
improvements. Specific improvements may include, but are not limited to, 
left turn markings and overhead signs on Cambridge Street, installation of 
larger stop signs, and installation of flex posts to reinforce existing striping. 
Improvements will be coordinated with BPDA and BTD prior to design and 
installation and should be completed no later than by issuance of Certificate 
of Occupancy. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to make a financial contribution of five thousand 
dollars ($5,000) annually throughout the 4-year term of the Proposed IMP to 
support elder care and community programming for seniors through the 
Veronica Smith Senior Center for the Allston-Brighton community. The five-
thousand-dollar financial contribution shall be made payable to the 
“Veronica Smith Senior Center” for their use in supporting and enhancing 
community health care programs. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to make a financial contribution of fifty thousand 
dollars ($50,000) annually per year from 2024 to 2026to support community 
nutrition programming through the Allston Brighton Health Collaborative for 
the Allston-Brighton neighborhood. The fifty-thousand-dollar financial 
contribution shall be made payable to the “Allston Brighton Health 
Collaborative” in 2024, 2025, and 2026 for their use in supporting and 
enhancing community nutrition programs. 
 

13 
 
• The Proponent is committed to maintaining its annual scholarship program 
for Allston-Brighton residents pursuing a higher education degree in the 
health care field. This scholarship program is valued at $15,000 annually. 
 
• The Proponent is aware of a larger effort being undertaken by the City to 
improve pedestrian and bicycling conditions along Washington Street 
adjacent to the project site. No bus stop relocations, curb-changes, or other 
permanent improvements will be made on Washington Street by the project 
proponents prior to planning and design engagement with BPDA, the City of 
Boston, and MBTA service planning. However, to improve pedestrian safety 
along Washington Street adjacent to the project site prior to the City’s effort 
being implemented, the Proponent shall work with BPDA and BTD to design 
and install quick-build safety improvements along the corridor. The value of 
this is estimated to be approximately $25,000. 
 
The Proponent will provide the BPDA with evidence indicating that the above-
referenced mitigation and community benefits have been satisfied. BPDA approved 
construction signage must be installed at the Project construction site(s) before and 
during Project construction. The signage must be in the form of panels at highly 
visible locations at the construction site(s) or around the construction site 
perimeter and must be adjacent to each other. The BPDA will work with the 
Proponent to provide high-resolution graphics that must be printed at a large scale 
(minimum 8 feet by 12 feet). 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, the BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA Board: (1) 
approve the Proposed IMP, pursuant to Section 80D of the Code; (2) authorize the 
Director to petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the Proposed 
IMP for a term of four (4) years from the effective date of approval, pursuant to 
Article 80D of the Code; (3) issue a Preliminary Adequacy Determination waiving the 
requirement of further review pursuant to Article 80B-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code for the 
Proposed Project; (4) authorize the Director to issue a Certification of Compliance 
for the Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code and one or more 
Certifications of Consistency pursuant to Section 80D-10.1 (a) and (b) (i) and (ii) of 
the Code for the IMP Proposed Projects, upon successful completion of the Article 
80 Large Project Review process; and (5) authorize the Director to execute and 
deliver a Cooperation Agreement, which will include a provision requiring 
compliance with the Boston Residents Jobs Policy and any and all other documents 

14 
 
and agreements as the Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection 
with the Proposed Project and the Proposed IMP. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That, in connection with the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center Institutional 
Master Plan 2022-2026 (the “Proposed IMP”) describing the St. 
Elizabeth's Medical Center Parking Garage project (the “Proposed 
Project”) presented at a public hearing duly held pursuant to Section 
80D-5.4(c)(ii) of the Boston Zone Code (“Code”) by the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority (the “BRA”) on May 12, 2022, and after 
consideration of evidence presented at, and in connection with, the 
hearing on the Proposed IMP and the Proposed Project, the BRA finds 
that, in accordance with Section 80D-4 of the Code, that: (a) the 
Proposed IMP complies with the Scoping Determination issued in 
connection with the Expanded Plan Notification Form (“PNF”) 
submitted on August 20, 2019; (b) the Proposed IMP conforms to the 
provisions of Article 80D of the Code; (c) the Proposed IMP conforms 
to the general plan for the City as a whole; and (d) on balance, nothing 
in the Proposed IMP will be injurious to the neighborhood or 
otherwise detrimental to the public welfare, weighing all the benefits 
and burdens; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue an Adequacy 
Determination pursuant to Article 80D-5.4(c) of the Code approving 
the Proposed IMP; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to petition the Boston 
Zoning Commission for approval of the Proposed IMP for a term of 
four (4) years from the effective date of the approval, in substantial 
accord with that presented to the BRA at its public hearing on May 12, 
2022; and 
 
 
 

15 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue one or more 
Certifications of Consistency pursuant to Article 80D-10 of the Code 
when the Director finds that: (a) a Proposed Project is described 
adequately in the Proposed IMP and is consistent with the Proposed 
IMP, including the requirement of the subsection of (d) of Section 80D-
10 concerning the location of High Impact Subuses and (b) the 
Proposed IMP has been approved by the BRA and the Boston Zoning 
Commission in accordance with the applicable provisions of Article 
80D, lnstitutional Master Plan Review; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That following a virtual presentation of the Proposed Project at a 
public hearing held pursuant to section 80B-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code on 
May 12, 2022, the BRA hereby finds that the Proposed Project, as 
described in the Draft Project Impact Report (“DPIR”) dated November 
5, 2021, conforms to the general plan for the City of Boston as a whole 
and that nothing in the Proposed Project will be injurious to the 
neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Preliminary 
Adequacy Determination Waiving Further Review regarding the 
Proposed Project pursuant to Section 808-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code 
approving the DPIR dated November 5, 2021, and the Supplemental 
Filings of February 8, 2022 and April 19, 2022, and waiving the 
requirement for the filing and review of a Final Project Impact Report, 
subject to BRA design review; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue one or more 
Certifications of Compliance for the Proposed Project pursuant to 
Section 80B-6 of the Code upon successful completion of all Article 80 
processes for the Proposed Project; and 
 
 
 

16 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute and deliver 
a Cooperation Agreement, which will include a provision requiring 
compliance with the Boston Residents Jobs Policy and any and all 
other agreements and documents that the Director deems 
appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project 
and the Proposed IMP, all upon terms and conditions determined to 
be in the best interests of the BRA.

CHAIR STATEMENT 
January 16th, 2025 
This is a public hearing before the Boston Redevelopment Authority doing 
business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency, being held in 
conformance with Article(s) 80A-2 and 80D-5 of the Boston Zoning Code to consider 
the proposed First Amendment to the Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master 
Plan for the 101 Tremont Street Project. 
The hearing was duly advertised on December 24, 2024, in the Boston 
Herald. 
 
This is a BPDA hearing on a proposed petition by the Agency. Staff members 
will first present their case and are subject to questioning by members of the 
Agency. Thereafter, anyone who wishes to testify about the proposed project will 
be afforded an opportunity. We are taking support and opposition at the same 
time. 
If you are planning to testify via Zoom, please take the time now to verify that 
your computer microphone is active and click the hand icon on your Zoom control 
panel. This will signal to staff that you would like to speak. When your hand is 
raised, it will be blue. If you are calling in to the meeting and would like to testify, 
please dial *9 to raise your hand. When I call for all testimony, staff will announce 
your name and allow you to talk. You must unmute your microphone, your webcam 
will not be active. 
If you are planning to testify in person in the Boardroom, please line up 
behind the podium after the presentation has concluded, we will call on you. 

In an effort to accommodate all who would like to speak about this proposal, 
each person will be given up to two minutes to comment. BPDA staff will indicate 
when thirty seconds remain. At that time, please conclude your remarks so that the 
hearing may continue, and others may be heard. Finally, the proponents are 
allowed a period of five to ten minutes for rebuttal if they so desire. 
Scott, please begin the presentation.
