_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) 
authorize the Director to: 1) issue an Adequacy Determination 
approving the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form filed with the 
BPDA on August 15, 2024 (the “IMPNF”) for the proposed First 
Amendment to the Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master Plan 
(the “Proposed IMP Amendment”) in connection with the 101 Tremont 
Street Project (“Proposed Project”); (2) petition the Boston Zoning 
Commission (“BZC”) for approval of the Amendment to Suffolk IMP and 
associated map amendment (the “Zoning Map Amendment”); (3) issue 
a Scoping Determination waiving further review of the Proposed 
Project pursuant to Section 80B-5.3(d) of the Boston Zoning Code 
(“Code”); (4) issue a Certification of Compliance for the Proposed 
Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code, upon successful 
completion of the Article 80 Large Project review process; (5) issue a 
Certification of Consistency for the Proposed Project pursuant to 
Section 80D-10 of the Code in connection with the Proposed Project as 
described in the IMPNF, upon successful completion of Article 80D 
Institutional Master Plan Review process; and (6) take any and all 
actions and execute any and all documents deemed necessary and 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
20 
DOCUMENT NO. 8197 
 
2 
 
appropriate by the Director in connection with the Proposed Project 
and the Amendment to Suffolk IMP, including, without limitation, 
executing and delivering a Cooperation Agreement. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Suffolk University (the “University” or “Suffolk”) seeks to amend the 
Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master Plan (“Suffolk IMP”) to add the Proposed 
Project which involves the redevelopment of 101 Tremont Street to create 
approximately 280 units of housing for undergraduate students. 
 
The Suffolk IMP was approved by the BRA Board on May 14, 2020, adopted by the 
BZC on June 10, 2020 and approved by the Mayor on June 19, 2020, with an 
effective date of June 19, 2020. 
 
On August 15, 2024, Suffolk submitted the Institutional Master Plan Notification 
Form for Amendment to the Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master Plan. On 
October 23, 2024, Suffolk submitted the Proposed IMP Amendment. 
 
The Proposed IMP Amendment includes the 101 Tremont Street Residence Hall 
Project, a conversion of the existing approximately 88,265 square foot office 
building into approximately 67,170 square feet of student housing with a second-
floor amenities space for various student activities and student lounge. The ground-
floor level consists of approximately 8,938 square feet of publicly accessible 
retail/restaurant space which will remain (the “Proposed Project”). 
 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its 
institutional mission. In the earlier 2008 IMP, the University set a target of housing 
50 percent of FTE undergraduate student population by 2018. For the Suffolk 2020 
IMP, Suffolk renewed its commitment to the 50 percent target with the One Court 
Street Residence Hall project. The University currently houses 1,518, or 
approximately 34.3% of the FTE undergraduate student population. With the 
addition of 1 Court Street in 2020, and the Proposed Project, the University will 
have created approximately 550 on campus beds since the Suffolk 2020 IMP. As 
such, the Proposed Project represents the University’s latest effort to secure long-

 
BOARD APPROVED 
20 
DOCUMENT NO. 8197 
 
3 
 
term student housing over 10 years through 2030. The amended Suffolk 2020 IMP 
will include a total of 14 institutional projects in the City of Boston.

Suffolk University

DESCRIPTION OF AMENDMENT AND THE 101 TREMONT STREET PROJECT 
The Suffolk IMP was approved by the BRA Board on May 14, 2020, adopted by the 
BZC on June 10, 2020 and approved by the Mayor on June 19, 2020, with an 
effective date of June 19, 2020. 
 
The Proposed Project, as described in the IMPNF, proposes a mixed-use 
institutional project at 101 Tremont Street in Downtown (“Project Site”), which 
includes changes to the building and use program. The Proposed Project is a 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
20 
DOCUMENT NO. 8197 
 
4 
 
conversion of the existing approximately 88,265 square foot office building into 
approximately 67,170 square feet of student housing with a second-floor amenities 
space for various student activities and student lounge. The ground-floor level 
consists of 8,938-SF of publicly accessible retail/restaurant space which will remain. 
The Project will also include other supporting uses, including a student housing 
reception area, laundry room, student lounge space, and study rooms – all of which 
will be secure and accessible only to University students. 
 
 
The Proposed Project adds up to 280 student housing beds to the University’s 
permanent housing inventory. This helps relieve the burden on the existing 
multifamily housing stock in downtown neighborhoods and, notably, East Boston, 
which is currently the most popular off-campus housing neighborhood among the 
University’s undergraduate students. 
 
Moreover, the University continues its commitment to house 50 percent of full-time 
equivalent (“FTE”) students in University-managed housing within the ten-year term 
of the Suffolk IMP. The Proposed Project represents the next step in achieving this 
goal, which requires the University to continue identifying and securing long-term 
additional student housing capacity. This represents a significant increase from the 
current figure of FTE students housed on campus, which stands at approximately 
40 percent. The University’s goal contributes to the City’s established goal of 
reducing the number of undergraduates living off campus in Boston’s rental 
housing market by approximately 50 percent by the year 2030. 
 
 Existing trash removal equipment and containers located on Bosworth Street will 
be removed and all trash removal for the building will be handled by the utilization 
of the trash facility and compactor located at Suffolk’s neighboring building-Sargent 
Hall- at 120 Tremont Street, and Suffolk maintenance personnel will remove trash 
from the building on a daily basis. 
 
During ongoing design review with the urban design staff, the Proponent for the 
Project will study the articulation, constructability and energy impacts of 
maintaining the existing window profiles for all windows to be replaced. Where 
operable windows exist today, the Proponent will consider providing a replacement 
window with a horizontal mullion at the location of the existing meeting rail and 
offset the panes of glass to maintain the appearance of an operable window. The

design team will work with the urban design staff to ensure the design meets the 
historical nature of the building and applicable green buildings and energy 
performance requirements moving forward .

PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
 
Launched in October 2023, the Downtown Residential Conversion Incentive Pilot 
Program “Downtown Conversion Program” aims to support the adaptive reuse of 
commercial office buildings into residential use. The Pilot Program was informed by 
both 1) the City of Boston’s October 2022 Downtown Revitalization Report which 
analyzed and made recommendations for downtown economic revitalization, as 
well as 2) the PLAN: Downtown planning process which recommended a downtown 
office conversion program as a key strategy for achieving the PLAN goals. While this 
project is not utilizing the tax credit offered by the Pilot program, the Proposed 
Project helps to further the goals outlined in the plan and help to reinforce the 
residential growth of Downtown. The Proposed Project and corresponding IMP 
amendment also the further goals of the Boston Housing Strategy 2025 which 
notes, “the City will work with Boston’s many colleges and universities through their 
Institutional Master Plan processes to reduce the number of students living in off-
campus housing.”

The Project Site is located in Area 4 of the Midtown Cultural District governed by 
Article 38 of the Code. The Project Site is also located within a Restricted Parking 
Overlay District. The University is seeking a change in use of a building greater than 
50,000 GSF within a Downtown District, and such use is classified as a High Impact 
Sub-use of an Institutional Use. Therefore, the Proposed Project is subject to review 
and approval from both the BRA and the BZC. 
 
IMP AMENDMENT AND PROJECT REVIEW PROCESS 
 
The Proposed IMP Amendment is subject to review under Section 80D of the Code, 
and the Proposed Project is subject to review under Section 80B of the Code. On 
August 15, 2024, Suffolk submitted the IMPNF and the Project Notification Form 
(“PNF”) for the Proposed Project. On October 23, 2024, Suffolk submitted the 
Proposed IMP Amendment. 
 
Suffolk presented the Proposed Project to the Suffolk Task Force and public in joint 
Task Force and Public Meetings held on September 17, 2024, and November 19, 
2024. 
 
PROJECT BENEFITS AND MITIGATION 
 
TRANSPORTATION 
The University will make much-needed sidewalk and streetscape improvements to 
Bromfield and Tremont Streets. All sidewalk improvements are subject to design 
review and may require approval for a Specific Repairs Action with the Public 
Improvement Commission (“PIC”) 
● The Proposed Project will include a complete restoration of the surrounding 
sidewalks on Bromfield, Tremont and Bosworth Streets, as well as an 
extension of the sidewalk on the corner of Tremont and Bromfield Street to 
provide additional pedestrian areas, construct ADA-compliant curb ramps, 
and improved crosswalks in a heavily pedestrian area of Boston. 
● The project will also remove the trash storage for 101 Tremont from the 
Bosworth Street right-of-way, and instead provide building trash storage in a 
neighboring Suffolk University building at 120 Tremont Street. 
● Within thirty (30) days of issuance of the Building Permit, the Proponent will 
make a one-time $75,000.00 contribution to the Boston Transportation 
Department (“BTD”) to support the bike share system.

● The University shall enter into a Transportation Access Plan Agreement 
(“TAPA”) with Boston Transportation Department (“BTD”) to articulate a 
Transportation Demand Management (“TDM”) strategy following BTD’s 
Transportation Demand Management Points System; and to set forth the 
timing for the University’s implementation of these improvements. 
 
 
SUSTAINABILITY / ARTICLE 37 
 
Per Zoning Article 37, the Proposed Project will achieve LEED v4 New Construction 
Silver / 53 points and will pursue additional green building strategies and credits, if 
obtainable, to achieve LEED Gold / 60+ points. The existing building will be 
improved through a combination of exterior enclosure and mechanical system 
upgrades including all-efficient-electric space and DHW water heating systems. The 
Proposed Project has a modeled Building 2035 preliminary Carbon Emissions 
Intensity of 1.78 kg CO2e/sf-yr (Grid Elec. Emission without RPS). 
 
Within 60 days of Board approval, the Proposed Project will provide the following 
items for Interagency Green Building Committee review and approval: 
● Preliminary (updated) Building Performance Model - including annual carbon 
emissions, Building 2035 predictive Carbon Emissions Intensity, energy uses, 
and a summary of the Proposed Project building enclosure and system 
upgrades. 
● Climate Resiliency Checklist – to be completed via the Developer Portal with 
the resultant PDF submitted with these responses. 
● Embodied Carbon Life Cycle Assessment – to reduce embodied carbon 
related emissions prepare a whole building Life Cycle Assessment of building 
structure, enclosure and insulation components and materials including the 
benefits of existing building reuse. Identify and include lower embodied 
carbon solutions. 
 
SMART UTILITIES 
 
The project plan will comply with the Smart Utilities requirements found in Article 
80B of the Code. As proposed no new utilities will be needed, but any new utilities 
and/or lateral connections related to the project within any City right of way will be

further review to ensure they are not in conflict with any landscape design features 
such as tree pits and/or other green infrastructure elements. The project shall 
include city shadow conduit in accordance with sidewalk reconstruction and PIC 
review where applicable. The Proposed Project will also provide access for local 
telecom and fiber providers to ensure broadband equity and possible future 
deployment of smart technologies. 
 
The proposed scope of any in-kind work agreed to by the University shall be 
developed in consultation with staff and appropriate city agencies, departments,

incorporated into the Cooperation Agreement between the Proponent and the 
BPDA. To the greatest extent possible, the Proponent will provide the BPDA with 
evidence indicating that the above-referenced mitigation and community benefits 
have been satisfied. 
 
INCLUSIONARY DEVELOPMENT POLICY 
 
The Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”), dated December 10, 2015, exempts 
any Proposed Projects from IDP requirements if the Project is: (a) financed as one 
entity and provides 40% or more of units within the project as income-restricted, (b) 
a dormitory, or (c) an otherwise exempt site usage under the Zoning Code. As such, 
the Proposed Project, as a dormitory, is exempt from obligations under the IDP.

Suffolk University Institutional Master 
Plan Amendment 
In accordance with Article 80D-9 of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”), Suffolk University 
(“Suffolk” or the “University”) is submitting this Institutional Master Plan Amendment (“IMP 
Amendment”) to the Boston Planning and Development Agency (BPDA) to amend the 2020 Suffolk 
University Institutional Master Plan (the “2020 IMP”) to include the conversion of 101 Tremont Street, 
an existing approximately 88,265-square foot (SF) office building recently acquired by the University, 
into a residence hall for students consisting of up to 280 beds (the “Proposed Project”). The existing 
office building is located at 101 Tremont Street within the Downtown neighborhood of Boston (the 
“Project Site”). Refer to Figure 1 for the Campus Locus Map. 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its institutional mission. In the 
2020 IMP, the University renewed the 2008 Institutional Master Plan (“2008 IMP”) commitment to the 
target of housing 50 percent of the full-time equivalent (“FTE”) undergraduate student population. In 
September 2019, Suffolk University submitted an Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (the 
“2020 IMPNF”) commencing the 2020 IMP, which considers the ten years of the University’s growth 
and development through 2030. The 2020 IMP was submitted to the BPDA in January 2020, and 
approved by the BPDA Board on May 14, 2020, and was then adopted by the Boston Zoning 
Commission (BZC) on June 10, 2020 for a ten (10) year term until June 19, 2030. An Institutional 
Master Plan Notification Form (IMPNF) and Project Notification Form (PNF) were submitted on 
August 15, 2024 for the Proposed Project. 
1.1 Suffolk University Mission and Objectives 
Since its inception, Suffolk University’s fundamental mission has been to respond to the evolving 
needs of society by providing an opportunity for motivated and capable students to obtain a quality 
education in a challenging yet supportive environment at an affordable cost. 
Suffolk University welcomes and remains accessible to people from a wide variety of backgrounds. It 
is the University's tradition, and remains its practice, to provide academic services for people of 
various levels of preparation and ability, and programs of sufficient depth and academic quality 
education at a reasonable cost. To respond to the evolving needs of today's world, Suffolk furnishes 
a variety of cross-cultural and international experiences in which diversity and excellence are 
inextricably interdependent.

Suffolk University places students at the center of its efforts and emphasizes academic excellence 
through teaching based on the application of theory, research to practice, and public service. In 
keeping with its historic mission of serving a broad constituency, the University offers day and 
evening programs at both the graduate and undergraduate levels. In addition, the University is 
strongly committed to continuing education. 
Suffolk University's location near the State House, government agencies, the courts, and New 
England's legal, medical, business, and financial centers allows it to utilize neighboring institutions to 
provide internships, cooperative education assignments, and other forms of experiential learning and 
research. Throughout its history, Suffolk University has established linkages with business, public 
administration, and legal communities for the purpose of providing financial support, research 
opportunities, adjunct faculty, professional advice, and placement for graduates. 
In its most recent strategic planning effort, the University updated the Mission Statement and Vision, 
respectively, as follows: 
Mission Statement 
At Suffolk University we are driven by the power of education, inclusion, and engagement to change 
lives and positively impact communities. Committed to excellence, we provide students with 
experiential and transformational learning opportunities that begin in the center of Boston, reach 
across the globe, and lead to extraordinary outcomes for our graduates. 
Vision 
Suffolk University will be a leader in experiential learning, known nationally and internationally for 
excellence in providing students access to real-world and global learning opportunities through 
outstanding academic and co-curricular programs and partnerships that take full advantage of our 
borderless, urban campuses in Boston and Madrid. We will advance our mission by ensuring that our 
students gain the core competencies needed to build successful careers in a rapidly changing world. 
A sharp focus on preparing students and alumni for lifelong career and community success will put 
Suffolk at the forefront of career education efforts at colleges and universities nationwide. 
1.1.1 University Objectives 
Suffolk’s development of competitive undergraduate and graduate programs in the arts and 
sciences, business, and law has been the foundation of its ongoing planning process. To continue to 
be a competitive institution, Suffolk has determined that it must enhance the academic, residential, 
student life, athletic, and cultural resources available to its current and prospective students. 
In summer 2019, the University issued the Suffolk 2025 Strategic Plan, stating the University’s Mission 
Statement and Vision and identifying a strategic framework for achieving them (the “Strategic Plan”). 
The Strategic Plan outlines specific goals to be met over the six-year period (2019-2025) and 
identifies six interrelated focus areas, including integrated education, community, reputation, 
infrastructure, resources, and finance, which are described further below in Section 1.1.3.

1.1.2 Major Programs and Initiatives 
Suffolk University prides itself on being a provider of high quality, practical, and experiential 
education designed to prepare graduates for careers. The University believes that the characteristics 
that distinguish it from competing institutions are: 
› A broad range of flexible class schedules that include day, night, and weekend sessions; 
› Affordable tuition; 
› Small class sizes; and 
› A convenient downtown location that is accessible to commuters and professionals. 
The University’s academic programs are offered through three schools: College of Arts and Sciences, 
Law School, and Sawyer Business School. 
College of Art and Sciences 
The College of Arts and Sciences has as its credo that liberal learning prepares students of all ages 
and backgrounds to live more fulfilling lives, to appreciate and contribute to the communities of 
which they are members, and to reach their ethical, personal, intellectual, and financial goals. To help 
its students maximize their potential, the college emphasizes critical and analytical thinking through 
a rigorous “success skills” undergraduate core program in written and oral communication, 
computing, analyzing, and integrating. Faculty scholarship supports diversified liberal arts 
concentrations available in the humanities, the natural sciences, and the social sciences, along with 
graduate programs in several fields, most offering career-related professional program tracks and 
practical experience on or off campus. 
The College of Art and Sciences goals are as follows: 
› 
To provide students with liberal learning that emphasizes a curriculum of inquiry, expanding 
perspectives and specialization. 
› 
To offer undergraduate, graduate and professional education that provides students with the 
means to explore and adapt their career and personal goals and objectives in a changing 
economic and technological environment. 
› 
To assure that undergraduate and graduate students develop an appropriate level of core 
competencies and their capacities for critical inquiry, creativity, research and analysis. 
› 
To create a diverse community of teachers and learners where students and faculty engage in 
the free expression of ideas, fostering independent thought and mutual respect. 
› 
To provide opportunities for students to enhance their aesthetic, intellectual and moral 
capabilities, and their sense of self-worth, self-confidence, and civic responsibility. 
› 
To attract and maintain an excellent faculty with a commitment to teaching, research, and 
service to the University and the greater community. 
› 
To attract and retain an increasingly competent student body consistent with the mission of 
the University. 
› 
To provide an educational environment, which includes appropriate classrooms, technologies, 
libraries, laboratories, recreation areas, and other facilities that enhance the process of student 
learning.

Suffolk Law School 
The Law School offers Juris Doctor and Master of Laws degrees. Founded over a century ago as a 
night school with nine students and one professor, today the Law School’s expansive curriculum

1.1.3 Strategic Plan 
In June 2019, the University issued the Suffolk 2025 Strategic Plan, which states the University’s 
Mission Statement and Vision, and identifies a strategic framework for achieving them. 
The Strategic Plan presents six interrelated focus areas, as follows: 
1. Integrated Education identifies targets relating to the University’s academic programming, 
highlighting a focus on experiential learning and career readiness. This section underscores the 
University’s commitment to lifelong learning, public engagement, civil discourse and service 
learning, and transformative co-curricular opportunities. 
2. Community establishes targets for the University’s workforce (focusing on diversity, inclusion, 
safety, health, and wellness) as well as alumni engagement and communications. The University 
plans to increase the number of faculty and staff from historically underrepresented groups and 
increase programming to support students from historically underrepresented groups as well. 
3. Reputation outlines the University’s strategy for strengthening its brand and promoting greater 
visibility. This will be achieved through hosting events, enhancing communications strategy, 
focusing on improving Suffolk’s rankings, and other key initiatives. 
4. Infrastructure identifies the University’s goals for developing campus infrastructure. This 
includes optimizing space usage in existing facilities, expanding the student housing portfolio, 
identifying and utilizing dedicated performance spaces, and exploring options for acquiring 
space to support new academic programs. This section emphasizes the University’s plans to 
develop and refine sophisticated Information Technology systems and policies. 
5. Resources identifies goals for developing the University’s resources with a focus on growing 
enrollment, retaining a greater percentage of students, decreasing admission rates, and 
enhancing campus diversity. This section describes the University’s plans for increasing 
philanthropic activity, improving corporate and foundation partnerships, optimizing resources 
for more efficient operation, and supporting new programs for institutional research. 
6. Finance identifies strategies for bolstering the University’s ability to respond nimbly to a 
changing marketplace. This section also establishes goals for improving bond ratings, 
generating an annual operating surplus of 3 percent to 5 percent, and revising the approach to 
managing the University’s endowment. 
1.1.4 Campus Master Plan 
Accommodating growth on an urban campus poses unique master planning challenges. In such a 
setting, institutional master planning requires the University to be clear about preferred areas of 
expansion and to maintain a proactive approach to opportunities as they arise. The 2020 IMP for the 
Suffolk University campus will build on the existing campus resources that include the University’s 
historic core, which is located on the edges of Beacon Hill. The vision of the 2020 IMP framework

represents a trajectory located along Cambridge and Tremont Streets that extends from the existing 
core of the campus in the direction of Downtown Crossing. This framework is best described as the 
Suffolk Crescent, which was originally conceptualized during the 2008 IMP process. 
The campus planning goals of the 2020 IMP are to: 
› 
Formalize an on-going effort to create a long-term strategic plan that will establish the

›

› 
Seek opportunities for development where no one cluster must bear the burden of all of the

› 
Locate future uses near existing University assets without overwhelming any one cluster with a 
saturation of university-related uses; and 
›

1.2 Status of 2020 IMP Projects and Need for Amendment 
The most recent IMP renewal commenced in May 2018, when Suffolk filed for the renewal of the IMP 
and approval for a new student dormitory project at 1 Court Street. Approval of the 2020 IMP on 
May 14, 2020 was a continuation of the University’s institutional master planning efforts supported 
by the BPDA and BZC since 2002. 
Suffolk’s campus is integrated throughout Downtown Boston, loosely located along the spine of 
Tremont Street to Cambridge Street. The physical character of the campus is emblematic of how the 
University's students are integrated into the working environment of Boston; at a physical and 
human level, the University's campus is knitted into the urban fabric of the city. The 2020 IMP 
proposed to utilize thirteen buildings within Boston, in addition to one outdoor athletic facility in 
East Boston (Figure 1). 
The 2020 IMP aimed to build on existing campus resources, including the University's historic core 
located on the edges of Beacon Hill. Furthermore, the 2020 IMP sought to support the well-planned 
development of institutional facilities to enhance Suffolk's public service and economic development 
roles in surrounding neighborhoods. The 2020 IMP acknowledged that universities often need to 
expand and renovate their facilities more frequently than other types of establishments, and 
recognized that the cumulative impact of such expansions could be more significant than that of 
individual projects. 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its institutional mission. In the 
2008 IMP, the University set a target of housing 50 percent of FTE undergraduate student population 
by 2018. For the 2020 IMP, Suffolk renewed its commitment to the 50 percent target. Figure 2, shows 
the existing property locations and building footprints within the City of Boston. To date, the

1.3 Amended IMP Proposed Institutional Project 
The Proposed Project, as described in this IMP amendment, will include the addition of a new 
institutional project at 101 Tremont Street, Boston, MA (Figure 2). This addition will expand the 
University’s student housing, echo the 2020 IMP to establish a strong sense of campus in Downtown 
Boston and SU growth clusters and provide students with convenient access to the University’s 
academic facilities. The new addition is located in growth cluster #2, as depicted in Figure 3. 
the Proposed Project is consistent with the goals of the approved 2020 IMP, proposing to convert the 
existing approximately 88,265-SF office building into approximately 67,170-SF of student housing 
with a second-floor amenities space for various student activities and student lounge. The ground-
floor level consists of 8,938-SF of publicly accessible retail/restaurant space which will remain. 
In summary and as shown on the floor plans in Figures 4a-c, the proposed uses for the Proposed 
Project include: 
› 
Up to 280 student beds for student housing; 
› 
Approximately 8,938 sf of retail/restaurant area accessible to the public; and 
› 
Other supporting uses, including a student housing reception area, laundry room, student 
lounge space, and study rooms – all of which will be secure and accessible only to University 
students.

1.4 Consistency with 2020 IMP 
As detailed in the 2020 IMPNF, it is the University’s institutional mission to provide an opportunity for 
motivated and capable students to obtain a quality education in a challenging yet supportive 
environment at an affordable cost. Although the majority of students commute to campus, Suffolk 
has continued to transition from a strictly commuter school to a partially residential school over the 
last twenty years. Within the 2020 IMP, the University committed to continue efforts to secure long-
term additional student housing capacity. As part of this goal, the University has made every effort to 
seek additional residence halls. 
The Proposed Project will accommodate up to 280 students conveniently located near other campus 
buildings and amenities, which represents the University’s ongoing commitment to aggressively 
pursue university housing opportunities for students. Conversion of mostly vacant office buildings to 
student residences, especially in the downtown area, helps reduce student demand for private 
apartments in the surrounding area. 
Suffolk University aspires to make the neighborhood an even more vibrant and engaging downtown 
area while offering students unique and attractive amenities. The campus planning framework for the 
2020 IMP defines potential areas for Suffolk University’s growth, which are growth clusters 
mentioned above. The Proposed Project is within the growth cluster #2 and, therefore, meets the 
planning goals set in the 2020 IMP for future Suffolk expansion.

Project Coordination:

loading elements. The developer should coordinate with William Moose regarding the downtown crossing 
reconstruction project. The developer should also coordinate with BDPA and BTD regarding any potential 
mitigation.

The developer should coordinate with BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for 
pedestrians and cyclists in the area.The developer shall coordinate with PWD in regards to the construction of the 
pedestrian ramps at the corner of Tremont St and Bosworth St and Tremont St. and Bromfield St according to 
current MAAB/ADA standards. 
 
Site Plan: 
Developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb functionality on 
both sides of all streets that abut the property. 
 
Construction Within The Public vs Private Right-of- Way: 
Although the general comments below apply specifically to work associated with the project within the public 
right-of-way, it is preferred and encouraged for construction in the private right-of-way to be consistent with City 
standards for public ways, as well, to the extent possible. Should these streets ever become public ways, they must 
conform to the City standards as outlined below. 
 
All work within the public way shall conform to Boston Public Works Department (PWD) standards. Any 
non-standard materials proposed within the public way will require approval through the Public 
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification 
(LM&I) Agreement with the PIC. 
 
Sidewalks: 
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to 
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel 
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet 
current American’s with Disabilities Act (ADA)/ Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines,

Suffolk University Institutional Master 
Plan Notification Form 
In accordance with Article 80D, Institutional Master Plan Review of the City of Boston Zoning Code 
(the “Code”), Suffolk University (“Suffolk” or the “University”) is submitting this Institutional Master 
Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) to the Boston Planning and Development Agency (“BPDA”) to 
amend the 2020 Suffolk University Institutional Master Plan (the “2020 IMP”) to include the 
conversion of 101 Tremont Street, an existing approximately 88,265-square foot (SF) office building 
recently acquired by the University, into a residence hall for students consisting of up to 280 beds 
(the “Project” or “Proposed Institutional Project”). The existing office building is located at 101 
Tremont Street within the Downtown neighborhood of Boston (the “Project Site”). Refer to Figure 1 
for the Campus Locus Map. 
This chapter presents an overview of Suffolk University’s mission, vision, institutional objectives, and 
academic programming initiatives. Each of these subjects has an impact on capital spending and will 
exert influence over ten years of growth and development from 2020 to 2030. 
1.1 Suffolk University Institutional Master Plan Overview 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its institutional mission. In the 
2020 IMP, the University renewed the 2008 Institutional Master Plan (“2008 IMP”) commitment to the 
target of housing 50 percent of the full-time equivalent (“FTE”) undergraduate student population. 
Suffolk University submitted an Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (“2020 IMPNF”) 
commencing the 2020 IMP, which considers the ten years of the University’s growth and 
development through 2030. The 2020 IMP, was approved by the BPDA, on May 14, 2020, and was 
adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission on June 10, 2020, for a ten (10) year term until June 19, 
2030. 
1.1.1 Suffolk University Mission and Objectives 
Since its inception, Suffolk University’s fundamental mission has been to respond to the evolving 
needs of society by providing an opportunity for motivated and capable students to obtain a quality 
education in a challenging yet supportive environment at an affordable cost. 
Suffolk University welcomes and remains accessible to people from a wide variety of backgrounds. It 
is the University's tradition, and remains its practice, to provide academic services for people of 
various levels of preparation and ability, and programs of sufficient depth and academic quality

education at a reasonable cost. To respond to the evolving needs of today's world, Suffolk furnishes 
a variety of cross-cultural and international experiences in which diversity and excellence are 
inextricably interdependent. 
Suffolk University places students at the center of its efforts and emphasizes academic excellence 
through teaching based on the application of theory, research to practice, and public service. In 
keeping with its historic mission of serving a broad constituency, the University offers day and 
evening programs at both the graduate and undergraduate levels. In addition, the University is 
strongly committed to continuing education. 
Suffolk University's location near the State House, government agencies, the courts, and New 
England's legal, medical, business, and financial centers allows it to utilize neighboring institutions to 
provide internships, cooperative education assignments, and other forms of experiential learning and 
research. Throughout its history, Suffolk University has established linkages with business, public 
administration, and legal communities for the purpose of providing financial support, research 
opportunities, adjunct faculty, professional advice, and placement for graduates. 
In its most recent strategic planning effort, the University updated the Mission Statement and Vision, 
respectively, as follows: 
Mission Statement 
At Suffolk University we are driven by the power of education, inclusion, and engagement to change 
lives and positively impact communities. Committed to excellence, we provide students with 
experiential and transformational learning opportunities that begin in the center of Boston, reach 
across the globe, and lead to extraordinary outcomes for our graduates. 
Vision 
Suffolk University will be a leader in experiential learning, known nationally and internationally for 
excellence in providing students access to real-world and global learning opportunities through 
outstanding academic and co-curricular programs and partnerships that take full advantage of our 
borderless, urban campuses in Boston and Madrid. We will advance our mission by ensuring that our 
students gain the core competencies needed to build successful careers in a rapidly changing world. 
A sharp focus on preparing students and alumni for lifelong career and community success will put 
Suffolk at the forefront of career education efforts at colleges and universities nationwide. 
1.1.1.1 
University Objectives 
Suffolk’s development of competitive undergraduate and graduate programs in the arts and 
sciences, business, and law has been the foundation of its ongoing planning process. To continue to 
be a competitive institution, Suffolk has determined that it must enhance the academic, residential, 
student life, athletic, and cultural resources available to its current and prospective students. 
In summer 2019, the University issued the Suffolk 2025 Strategic Plan, stating the University’s Mission 
Statement and Vision and identifying a strategic framework for achieving them (the “Strategic Plan”). 
The Strategic Plan outlines specific goals to be met over the six-year period (2019-2025) and 
identifies six interrelated focus areas, including integrated education, community, reputation, 
infrastructure, resources, and finance (described in further detail in Section 1.1.3 below).

Major Programs and Initiatives 
Suffolk University prides itself on being a provider of high quality, practical, and experiential 
education designed to prepare graduates for careers. The University believes that the characteristics 
that distinguish it from competing institutions are: 
› A broad range of flexible class schedules that include day, night, and weekend sessions; 
› Affordable tuition; 
› Small class sizes; and 
› A convenient downtown location that is accessible to commuters and professionals. 
The University’s academic programs are offered through three schools: College of Arts and Sciences, 
Law School, and Sawyer Business School. 
College of Art and Sciences 
The College of Arts and Sciences has as its credo that liberal learning prepares students of all ages 
and backgrounds to live more fulfilling lives, to appreciate and contribute to the communities of 
which they are members, and to reach their ethical, personal, intellectual, and financial goals. To help 
its students maximize their potential, the college emphasizes critical and analytical thinking through 
a rigorous “success skills” undergraduate core program in written and oral communication, 
computing, analyzing, and integrating. Faculty scholarship supports diversified liberal arts 
concentrations available in the humanities, the natural sciences, and the social sciences, along with 
graduate programs in several fields, most offering career-related professional program tracks and 
practical experience on or off campus. 
The College of Art and Sciences goals are as follows: 
› 
To provide students with liberal learning that emphasizes a curriculum of inquiry, expanding 
perspectives and specialization. 
› 
To offer undergraduate, graduate and professional education that provides students with the 
means to explore and adapt their career and personal goals and objectives in a changing 
economic and technological environment. 
› 
To assure that undergraduate and graduate students develop an appropriate level of core 
competencies and their capacities for critical inquiry, creativity, research and analysis. 
› 
To create a diverse community of teachers and learners where students and faculty engage in 
the free expression of ideas, fostering independent thought and mutual respect. 
› 
To provide opportunities for students to enhance their aesthetic, intellectual and moral 
capabilities, and their sense of self-worth, self-confidence, and civic responsibility. 
› 
To attract and maintain an excellent faculty with a commitment to teaching, research, and 
service to the University and the greater community. 
› 
To attract and retain an increasingly competent student body consistent with the mission of 
the University. 
› 
To provide an educational environment, which includes appropriate classrooms, technologies, 
libraries, laboratories, recreation areas, and other facilities that enhance the process of student 
learning.

1.1.1.3 
Strategic Plan 
As mentioned in Section 1.1.1.1, the University issued the Suffolk 2025 Strategic Plan in June, 2019, 
stating the University’s Mission Statement and Vision and identifying a strategic framework for 
achieving them. 
The Strategic Plan presents six interrelated focus areas, as follows: 
1. Integrated Education identifies targets relating to the University’s academic programming, 
highlighting a focus on experiential learning and career readiness. This section underscores the 
University’s commitment to lifelong learning, public engagement, civil discourse and service 
learning, and transformative co-curricular opportunities. 
2. Community establishes targets for the University’s workforce (focusing on diversity, inclusion, 
safety, health, and wellness) as well as alumni engagement and communications. The University 
plans to increase the number of faculty and staff from historically underrepresented groups and 
increase programming to support students from historically underrepresented groups as well. 
3. Reputation outlines the University’s strategy for strengthening its brand and promoting greater 
visibility. This will be achieved through hosting events, enhancing communications strategy, 
focusing on improving Suffolk’s rankings, and other key initiatives. 
4. Infrastructure identifies the University’s goals for developing campus infrastructure. This 
includes optimizing space usage in existing facilities, expanding the student housing portfolio, 
identifying and utilizing dedicated performance spaces, and exploring options for acquiring 
space to support new academic programs. This section emphasizes the University’s plans to 
develop and refine sophisticated Information Technology systems and policies. 
5. Resources identifies goals for developing the University’s resources with a focus on growing 
enrollment, retaining a greater percentage of students, decreasing admission rates, and 
enhancing campus diversity. This section describes the University’s plans for increasing 
philanthropic activity, improving corporate and foundation partnerships, optimizing resources 
for more efficient operation, and supporting new programs for institutional research. 
6. Finance identifies strategies for bolstering the University’s ability to respond nimbly to a 
changing marketplace. This section also establishes goals for improving bond ratings, 
generating an annual operating surplus of 3 percent to 5 percent, and revising the approach to 
managing the University’s endowment.

Accommodating growth on an urban campus poses unique master planning challenges. In such a 
setting, institutional master planning requires the University to be clear about preferred areas of 
expansion and to maintain a proactive approach to opportunities as they arise. The 2020 IMP for the 
Suffolk University campus will build on the existing campus resources that include the University’s 
historic core, which is located on the edges of Beacon Hill. The vision of the 2020 IMP framework

1.2 Status of 2020 IMP Projects and Need for Amendment 
The most recent IMP renewal commenced in May 2018, when Suffolk filed for the renewal of the IMP 
and approval for a new student dormitory project at 1 Court Street. The 2020 IMP approved on May 
14, 2020 continued the institutional master planning by the University supported by the BPDA and 
the Boston Zoning Commission (“BZC”) since 2002. 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its institutional mission. In the 
2008 IMP, the University set a target of housing 50 percent of the full-time (“FTE”) undergraduate 
student population by 2018. For the 2020 IMP, Suffolk renewed its commitment to the 50 percent 
target. As shown in Figure 2, the approved 2020 IMP lists a total of 13 Proposed Institutional Projects 
within the City of Boston that the University plans to construct over a decade. To date, the University 
continues its efforts to increase its student housing portfolio in order to meet this target. The 
University currently houses 1,518, or approximately 34.3% of the FTE undergraduate student 
population. With the addition of 1 Court Street in the 2020 IMP and the Project of 101 Tremont 
Street residence hall and the termination of the temporary 1047 Commonwealth Avenue housing, 
the University will have created approximately 550 on campus beds since the 2020 IMP. As such, the 
Project represents the University’s latest effort to secure long-term student housing over 10 years 
through 2030. The amended 2020 IMP will include a total of 14 Proposed Institutional Projects in the 
City of Boston. 
Over the past years, the University has experienced a greater demand by its students for guaranteed 
residential accommodation for the first and second years of enrollment. It is believed that the Project 
could enhance the experience of its students by offering more student housing on campus. With the 
campus located in the heart of Boston, the Proposed Institutional Project will provide student 
housing in an area with convenient access to Suffolk’s academic facilities and is in keeping with the

1.5 Consistency with 2020 IMP 
As detailed in the 2020 IMPNF, it is the University’s institutional mission to provide an opportunity for 
motivated and capable students to obtain a quality education in a challenging yet supportive 
environment at an affordable cost. Although the majority of students commute to campus, Suffolk 
has continued to transition from a strictly commuter school to a partially residential school over the 
last twenty years. Within the 2020 IMP, the University committed to continue efforts to secure long-
term additional student housing capacity. As part of this goal, the University has made every effort to 
seek additional residence halls. 
The Proposed Institutional Project will accommodate up to 280 students conveniently located near 
other campus buildings and amenities, which represents the University’s ongoing commitment to 
aggressively pursue university housing opportunities for students. Conversion of mostly vacant office 
buildings to student residences, especially in the downtown area, helps reduce student demand for 
private apartments in the surrounding area. 
Suffolk University aspires to make the neighborhood an even more vibrant and engaging downtown 
area while offering students unique and attractive amenities. The campus planning framework for the 
2020 IMP defines potential areas for Suffolk University’s growth, which are growth clusters 
mentioned above. The Project, which is located at 101 Tremont Street in Downtown Boston, is within 
the growth cluster #2 and, therefore, meets the planning goals set in the 2020 IMP for future Suffolk 
expansion.

MEMORANDUM 
 NOVEMBER 16, 2023 
 
 
TO: 
 
BOSTON REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY 
 
 
D/B/A BOSTON PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT AGENCY (BPDA) 
 
 
AND JAMES ARTHUR JEMISON II, DIRECTOR 
 
FROM: 
MICHAEL CHRISTOPHER, DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
 
 
CASEY HINES, DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
 
 
NUPOOR MONANI, DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF MASTER PLANNING AND POLICY 
SCOTT GREENHALGH, PROJECT MANAGER 
 
SUBJECT: 
REQUEST AUTHORIZATION AND APPROVALS REGARDING THE 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN NOTIFICATION FORM FOR THE 
RENEWAL OF THE TUFTS UNIVERSITY HEALTH SCIENCES CAMPUS 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a the Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”): (1) 
approve the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form for renewal 
and extension of the Tufts University Health Sciences Campus 
Institutional Master Plan, dated October 13, 2023, ("IMPNF for 
Renewal") pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, and Section 
80D-8 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"); and (2) authorize the 
Director to take all actions and execute any and all documents 
deemed necessary and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Tufts University’s most recent Institutional Master Plan for their Health Sciences 
Campus, based in the Chinatown, Mission Hill, and Fenway neighborhoods of 
Boston, was approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority in December 1994, 
adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission in March 1995, updated May 3, 2004, 
amended in 2007, amended and renewed in 2009, and further amended and 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
18 
DOC No. 8087 
 
 
 
renewed in 2020. The term of the IMP expired on October 20, 2023 (collectively, the 
“Tufts IMP”). 
 
On October 13, 2023, Tufts submitted an IMPNF for Renewal to the Boston Planning 
& Development Agency (“BPDA”), signaling its intention to renew the Tufts IMP for a 
period of two years. Tufts is not proposing a new “Proposed Institutional Project”, 
as that term is understood in the Code; is not adding new land area to the Tufts 
IMP; is not proposing any changes to the Tufts IMP which would constitute a 
change in use, dimensional, parking or loading elements thereof (other than de 
minimus dimensional changes), and BPDA staff do not anticipate any greater 
impacts from the continuation of the implementation of the Tufts IMP than that 
which were originally evaluated. 
 
 
INSTITUTIONAL TEAM 
 
Proponent: 
Tufts University 
Liza Perry 
 
Legal Counsel: 
 
Krokidas & Bluestein LLP 
 
 
 
 
Kathy Cochrane Murphy 
 
Consultant: 
 
LSC Planning & Development, LLC 
 
 
 
 
Lauren Shurtleff 
 
 
 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 
The IMPNF for Renewal is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review and qualifies 
for a waiver of further review in accordance with Sections 80D-5.2(e), 80D-6, and 
80D-8 of the Code in that: (i) no new Proposed Institutional Projects are planned; (ii) 
no changes in the Institutional Master Plan are proposed that would constitute a 
change in the use, dimensional, parking or loading elements of the Institutional 
Master Plan (other than de minimus dimensional changes); and (iii) no significantly 
greater impacts would result from continued implementation of the approved 
Institutional Master Plan than were originally projected. Tufts seeks approval of the 
IMPNF for Renewal of Tufts IMP for a period of two years, until November 16, 2025. 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
18 
DOC No. 8087 
 
 
 
 
The submission of the IMPNF for Renewal on October 13, 2023, initiated a 30-day 
comment period that ended on November 15, 2023. Notice of submission was 
published in the Boston Herald on October 16, 2023. 
 
 
CONTINUED COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
All community benefits currently offered pursuant to the existing Tufts IMP will 
continue through the length of the renewed IMP. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, staff recommends that the BPDA Board: (1) approve the 
IMPNF for Renewal dated October 13, 2023, pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 
80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"); and (2) authorize 
the Director to take all actions and execute any and all documents deemed 
necessary and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That in connection with the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
for the renewal and extension of the Tufts University Health Sciences 
Campus Institutional Master Plan, dated October 13, 2023, (the “IMPNF 
for Renewal”), and after consideration of the IMPNF for Renewal, the 
Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) hereby finds that: (a) the 
Tufts University Health Sciences Campus Institutional Master Plan and 
the IMPNF for Renewal (collectively, the “Renewed IMP”), conforms to 
the provisions of Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code (“the Code”); 
(b) the Renewed IMP, conforms to the general plan for the City as a 
whole; and (c) on balance, nothing in the Renewed IMP, will be 
injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public 
welfare, weighing all the benefits and burdens; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the BRA waives further review of Tufts University Health Sciences 
Campus Institutional Master Plan and the IMPNF for Renewal pursuant 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
18 
DOC No. 8087 
 
 
 
to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6 and Section 80D-8 of the Code 
and approves the Renewed IMP as the renewed Institutional Master 
Plan for a period of two (2) years from the date of approval of this 
renewal vote by the BRA, that is November 16, 2025; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the BRA hereby authorizes the Director to take all actions and 
execute any and all documents deemed necessary and appropriate 
and in the best interest of the BRA by the Director in connection with 
the Renewed IMP.

CHAIR STATEMENT 
October 10, 2024 
This is a public hearing before the Boston Redevelopment Authority doing 
business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency, being held in 
conformance with Articles 80A-2 and 80D-5 of the Boston Zoning Code to consider 
the proposed 2024-2034 Institutional Master Plan for Wentworth Institute of 
Technology. 
The hearing was duly advertised on September 26 in the Boston Herald. 
This is a BPDA hearing on a proposed petition by the Agency. Staff members 
will first present their case and are subject to questioning by members of the 
Agency. Thereafter, anyone who wishes to testify about the proposed project will 
be afforded an opportunity. We are taking support and opposition at the same 
time. If you are planning to testify, please take the time now to verify that your 
computer microphone is active and click the hand icon on your Zoom control panel. 
This will signal to staff that you would like to speak. When your hand is raised, it will 
be blue. If you are calling in to the meeting and would like to testify, please dial *9 
to raise your hand. When I call for all testimony, staff will announce your name and 
allow you to talk. You must unmute your microphone, your webcam will not be 
active. 
In an effort to accommodate all who would like to speak about this proposal, 
each person will be given up to two minutes to comment. BPDA staff will indicate 
when thirty seconds remain. At that time, please conclude your remarks so that the 
hearing may continue, and others may be heard. Finally, the proponents are 
allowed a period of five to ten minutes for rebuttal if they so desire. 
 

Nick, please begin the presentation. 
 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
 
 
MEMORANDUM 
OCTOBER 10, 2024 
 
TO: 
BOSTON REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY 
 
D/B/A BOSTON PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT AGENCY 
 
AND DEVIN QUIRK, DIRECTOR 
FROM: 
CASEY HINES, SENIOR DEPUTY DIRECTOR FOR DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
NUPOOR MONANI, SENIOR DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT 
REVIEW 
SETH RISEMAN, DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF DESIGN REVIEW 
NICK CARTER, DEVELOPMENT PORTFOLIO MANAGER 
KRISTINA RICCO, SENIOR URBAN DESIGNER 
 
JILL ZICK, ASSISTANT DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC REALM REVIEW 
 
NICK SCHMIDT, SENIOR TRANSPORTATION PLANNER 
 
SCOTT SLARSKY, SENIOR ARCHITECT 
 
 
SUBJECT: 
PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER THE INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
FOR WENTWORTH INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 
______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”): (1) issue an 
Adequacy Determination pursuant to Section 80D-5.4(c) of the Boston 
Zoning Code ("Code") approving the Wentworth Institute of 
Technology Institutional Master Plan ("Wentworth IMP") for a term of 
10 years from the effective date; (2) authorize the Director of the BPDA 
to petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the 
Wentworth IMP and associated Map Amendment, pursuant to Section 
80D-6 of the Code; and (3) authorize the Director to execute and 
deliver any and all documents deemed necessary and appropriate in 
connection with the Wentworth IMP. 
 
 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
INTRODUCTION 
Wentworth Institute of Technology (the “Proponent” or the “University”) is seeking 
an Adequacy Determination approving its 2024-2034 Institutional Master Plan 
(“Wentworth IMP”). The Wentworth IMP describes the proposed institutional 
projects that Wentworth aims to complete over the next decade to realize strategic 
goals in both academic and community development. The Wentworth IMP includes 
six (6) proposed institutional projects totaling approximately 916,000 square feet, 
including the creation and improvement of four (4) significant open spaces. These 
proposed institutional projects include the following institutional uses: academic, 
student housing, student life, open space, parking, and accessory and support 
spaces. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
Proponent: 
Wentworth Institute of Technology 
 
David Wahlstrom 
 
Master Planning 
Perkins & Will 
Architect: 
Gautam Sundaram 
Brad Rogers 
 
Legal Counsel: 
Nixon Peabody LLP 
 
Jennifer Schultz, Esq. 
 
Transportation: 
VHB 
Sean Manning 
 
Sustainability: 
Riverstone Sustainability 
Debra Shephard 
 
Government Relations: The Strategy Group 
 
Dave Newman 
 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
 
ZONING CONTEXT 
Wentworth’s Campus (the “Site”) is in the Mission Hill Neighborhood District, at the 
crossroads of the Fenway and Mission Hill neighborhoods, and is located in the 
Institutional Master Plan Area. The northern portion of the Site is located within (i) 
the Wentworth Institute IS subdistrict under the base provisions of the Code, (ii) the 
Groundwater Conservation Overlay District, which is governed principally by Article 
32 of the Code, and (iii) the Restricted Parking Overlay District. The southern 
portion of the Site is located within (i) the Local Industrial subdistrict under the base 
provisions of the Code, and (ii) the Special Study Overlay District. The entire Site is 
subject to an Institutional Master Plan pursuant to Article 80D of the Code. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
The Wentworth Institute of Technology Institutional Master Plan (IMP) for 2024-
2034 contains six new Proposed Institutional Projects (PIPs) and identifies progress 
made since the implementation of the previous IMP. The IMP covers the university 
campus, comprising 31 acres in the Mission Hill and Longwood neighborhoods. The 
previous Institutional Master Plan was submitted in 2011, amended in 2017, and 
extended through March 2023. 
 
The previous IMP and its subsequent amendments provide the planning and zoning 
context for this IMP. The 2010 IMP included five PIPs, including the renovation and 
building addition for the Flanagan Campus Center at Beatty Hall, an addition to the 
Ira Allen Building, a new seven-story student residence hall, a new Center for 
Engineering and Innovation Sciences, and a New Sweeney Field athletic field. With 
the exception of the Field, presently under construction, all PIPs were completed as 
of the expiration of the prior IMP. 
 
The proposed IMP includes a series of Urban Design Guidelines that, in conjunction 
with the development proposals, align with existing citywide planning initiatives. 
These guidelines include the development of an open space framework, a strong 
civic identity, and an inclusive campus. The WIT campus forms an important 
connection between the Emerald Necklace park system and the Southwest 
Corridor. The proposed “front lawn” and improved connectivity from Huntington 
Avenue through the campus work toward the goal of connecting the Emerald 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
Necklace to other systems, as enumerated in the City’s 2023-2029 Open Space and 
Recreation Plan. The IMP continues to align with other citywide plans, such as 
Housing a Changing City: Boston 2030, through its intention to create a new 
residence hall netting the campus 630 additional student residential spaces, which 
feeds into the goal of creating 16,000 new undergraduate student dorm beds for 
Boston colleges and universities by 2030. 
 
Of the citywide and localized planning initiatives, most relevant to the proposed 
Institutional Master Plan is the Avenue of the Arts Design Guidelines Study, a local 
planning study intended to guide design of buildings and open space along 
Huntington Avenue between Massachusetts Avenue and Longwood Avenue. The 
Guidelines set forth goals for design along the avenue, emphasizing mobility, 
placemaking, active programming, and comfort. The proposed IMP for the WIT 
campus directly addresses each of the Study goals: 
• Mobility, creating a clear, safe, well-connected pedestrian experience, is 
improved through the proposed reinforcement of the campus “Pike,” a 
pedestrian spine from Evans Way to Annunciation Road, connecting the 
Emerald Necklace across the campus to the Southwest Corridor via the Alice 
H. Taylor Apartments. 
• Placemaking, expression of institutional identity through architecture, open 
spaces, and the creation of a cohesive, high-quality environment, is explored 
through the clustering of taller buildings along Huntington Avenue, 
suggesting that these buildings serve as landmarks within the campus and 
the surrounding neighborhood. Patterns of taller buildings and open space 
connections form the fabric of the campus along the Avenue of the Arts 
study area. 
• Programming, through the creation of an active, inclusive environment is 
pursued in the IMP through the proposed Urban Design Guidelines including 
Development Along Urban Corridors, which suggests that buildings lining 
primary urban corridors should locate active student, public and community-
oriented programs along these perimeter edges to foster a rich and active 
public realm and strengthen connections to surrounding neighborhoods and 
commercial nodes. 
• Comfort, the promotion of pedestrian comfort in the public realm, is 
addressed through care taken to reduce substantive shadows on existing 
public open spaces, and the intention to create pedestrian-scale connections 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
that facilitate safe and accessible links to surrounding neighborhoods, 
institutions, open spaces and public pedestrian pathways. 
The Wentworth Institute of Technology campus and Institutional Master Plan area are 
located in the Mission Hill Neighborhood District, within the Wentworth Institute 
Institutional subdistrict. The Institutional Master Plan zoning overlay sets forth the 
dimensional and use regulations for the campus and the subsequent development 
projects. Per the IMP, all PIPs are planned to comply with the dimensions as anticipated 
and codified in the IMP. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
The Wentworth IMP is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review pursuant to 
Section 80D of the Code. 
On March 10, 2023, the University filed an Institutional Master Plan Notification 
Form (“IMPNF”) proposing this IMP. Pursuant to Section 80D-5.3 of the Code, a 
Scoping Session was held on April 4, 2024, with the City’s public agencies to review 
and discuss the IMPNF. The Boston Planning and Development Authority (“BPDA”) 
then issued a Scoping Determination in response to staff and public comments on 
the IMPNF on December 5, 2023. On February 21, 2024, the Proponent filed the 
IMP in response to the BPDA’s Scoping Determination. 
Copies of submissions were sent to the Wentworth Institute of Technology Task 
Force. Community meetings to discuss the Wentworth IMP have been held on the 
following dates: 
• Task Force Meeting: April 3, 2024 
• Task Force Meeting: August 16, 2024 
• Public Meeting: May 13, 2024 
 
FUTURE PROJECT REVIEW 
At this time, BPDA Board approval is being sought only for approval of the 
Wentworth IMP. The future Article 80B Submissions for the PIPs will be reviewed by 
staff, be subject to all applicable regulations at the time of submission and be 
considered by BCDC before any further BPDA Board action on such submissions. 
INSTITUTIONAL PROJECTS 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
Although no 80B Institutional Projects have been proposed alongside the 80D 
Institutional Master Plan, the IMP does describe [6] PIPs that are intended for 
future review and development within the next 10 years: 
• Residential Life: 
o Pike Residence Hall (up to 400 beds, approximately 126,000 GSF, 
approximately 190’ tall) 
o Huntington Residence Hall (up to 850 beds, approximately 275,000 
GSF, approximately 250’ tall) 
o New Baker Hall (up to 550 beds, approximately 155,000 GSF, 
approximately 105-175’ tall) 
 
As set forth in detail in the IMP, Wentworth is proposing three new residential life 
dormitories to address and replace existing outdated, inaccessible dormitory 
buildings on campus, and also consistent with both Wentworth and the City’s policy 
goal of housing as many students on campus as possible. The three residential life 
projects will total approximately 1,800 beds over the three buildings. 
• Academic: 
o West Quad Academic Building (approximately 140,000 GSF, 
approximately 150’ tall) 
o New Annex Academic Complex (2 buildings, approximately 200,000 
GSF total, approximately 95’ tall) 
 
In its IMP, Wentworth is proposing two new academic additions to campus. The 
West Quad Academic Building, located in what is currently a surface parking lot, is a 
single-building replacement for the School of Architecture & Design that is currently 
located in the so-called Annex of Wentworth’s campus, inside the former, 
inaccessible and outdated, Boston Trade High School building. The New Annex 
Academic Complex, located on the current site of the Annex, will be reconfigured 
into multiple buildings with a generously sized Academic Quad open space. 
• Administration: 
o Pavilion & Wentworth Hall Renovation (approximately 20,000 GSF, 
approximately 25’ tall) 
 
On its main frontage along Ruggles Street, Wentworth has proposed a reconfigured 
and upgraded front lawn space intended to create an open and welcoming space 
for students and the general public and multimodal gateway connecting the 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31

B. Student Housing 
The PIPS in total add approximately 1,324 net new student housing beds to the 
University’s permanent housing inventory. This significant increase is intended to 
help relieve the burden on the existing multifamily housing stock in nearby 
neighborhoods such as Fenway and Mission Hill by freeing up space in the local 
rental market. As of School Year 2023-24, Wentworth housed approximately 55% of 
its students on campus; with the completion of the three Residential Life dormitory 
PIPs described in the IMP, Wentworth will be able to house approximately 80% of 
its students on campus. 
 
C. Improved Street and Multimodal Networks 
 
The PIPs intend to create clear student life and academic clusters on campus, 
fostering a vibrant campus that consolidates much of Wentworth’s surface parking 
to two underground garages, thus freeing up more open space for improved 
circulation around and through the campus by walking, biking, and taking transit. 
Enhanced landscaping will further beautify the street edge and enhance the 
pedestrian experience along Ruggles Street, Huntington Avenue, Parker Street, and 
Annunciation Road.

Improvements to the existing pedestrian Pike, framing the south edge of the 
Campus, will better facilitate east-west neighborhood access in and through the 
campus for people walking and biking. The Proponent shall ensure the Pike is open 
to the public 24 hours per day, seven days per week, and will be limited to walking, 
dismounted biking, and placemaking activities. The Pike shall not be used for motor 
vehicle access for parking, loading, or services. The Pike must be a minimum of 12 
feet in width, free and clear of obstructions and open to the sky, with a typical 
minimum width of 20 feet clear of obstructions and open to sky. It will be 
constructed of an accessible surface in coordination with the Disabilities 
Commission. The Pike enhancements will be connected with the PIPs located in the 
existing West Lot and will be completed with the final building completing the new 
West Quad. A pedestrian path will remain open through construction. 
 
Implementation of other multimodal improvements will be similarly phased in 
coordination with PIPs: 
• Improvements to the legacy Ruggles Street driveway immediately east of 
Huntington Avenue will serve as an enabling element of the first PIP of the 
West Quad PIPs to eliminate conflicts between pedestrians and left-turning 
vehicles and create an accessible, multimodal gateway for the campus. 
Anticipated changes will include, at minimum, a wider sidewalk and 
furnishing zone; a narrowed Ruggles Street driveway with a continuous, 
raised sidewalk along the Ruggles Street edge; and the prohibition of left-
turning motor vehicle movements into and out of the driveway, reinforced 
with physical changes to the street and curb cut. 
• The remainder of the enhancements to and along the Ruggles Street 
frontage will occur in coordination with the New Front Lawn PIP and will 
include a wider sidewalk furnishing zone; a continuous raised sidewalk along 
the Ruggles Street edge; and, in coordination with and as approved by the 
MBTA, a high-quality bus stop of sufficient length to serve multiple high-
frequency bus routes and passenger amenities, including a shelter. 
Wentworth will coordinate with the 500 Huntington project to design and 
implement a mid block crossing on Ruggles Street as part of this PIP. 
• In concert with New Baker Hall, the Huntington Residence Hall, and the Pike 
Residence Hall, the Proponent is committed to modifying the intersection of 
Huntington Avenue / Evans Way to serve as the western gateway for the Pike.

compliant curb ramps in coordination with City departments and the MBTA.

D. Historic Preservation 
Wentworth has committed to immediate repairs needed to stabilize designated 
landmark buildings referred to as the “Vienna Brewery Complex” located at 47 and 
133 Station Street, Boston. The objectives of the immediate repair and shoring work 
are to stabilize, replace, and/or repair deteriorated masonry at the facades of the 
two buildings and shore portions of the deteriorated framing and reduce water 
infiltration. These repairs are associated with the Certificate of Occupancy needed 
for the New Sweeney Field project. In a memo to the Boston Landmarks 
Commission on August 26, 2024, Wentworth stated that the “re-use, of the Brewery 
Complex cannot be incorporated into Wentworth’s future planning; it is therefore 
apparent that Wentworth must find another organization with a community-based 
mission that has the resources and vision to rehabilitate and transform this site in a 
manner that furthers Wentworth’s and that organization’s mission while also 
honoring its historic status.”

The PIPs have been informed by strategies to encourage development along 
important corridors and framing open spaces. Buildings along Huntington Avenue 
intend to locate active student, public, and community-oriented programs along 
these perimeter edges to foster a rich and active public realm and strengthen 
connections to surrounding neighborhoods and commercial nodes. The PIPs will 
also attractively frame existing and new campus quadrangles and provide vibrant 
new spaces that will attract both students and members of the public. The PIPs will 
also create greater usable open space by replacing many current surface parking 
lot areas with new landscaped and hardscape areas and accessible connections 
through the campus, thus providing significant aesthetic and physical 
improvements available to the surrounding neighborhood. As part of the ongoing 
Planning Department Development Review process for each PIPs and associated 
public realm improvements, the University will work closely with Planning 
Department Urban Design Staff and other stakeholders through the full design 
review process. 
F. Green Building & Environmental Planning 
The University endeavors to prioritize increasing energy performance for its PIPs, 
and intends to seek strategies that support low-carbon building operations, 
integration of renewable energy resources, embodied carbon reduction, and LEED 
points that may be achieved with each PIP without significantly adding cost to the 
PIPs. Through the increase in open spaces set forth in the Wentworth IMP, the 
University also intends to follow strategies that expand the tree canopy, mitigate 
stormwater, promote biodiversity, and enhance the resiliency of Wentworth’s 
landscape features by planting a mix of native and adaptive species, and creating 
microhabitats and other design features appropriate to the campus context.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
Wentworth Institute of Technology, Inc. (“Wentworth” or the “University”) is a technology university 
with five schools focused on engineering, computing, design, science, and management. The 
University consists of 31 acres of land between the Southwest Corridor and the Back Bay Fens. 
Wentworth previously filed its Institutional Master Plan approved by the Boston Planning and 
Development Agency (“BPDA”) in 2011, as amended in 2017 and extended in 2021 for two years 
(“Prior IMP”). Upon expiration of the Prior IMP, in March 2023, Wentworth filed its Institutional 
Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) on March 10, 2023. Wentworth is pleased to submit this 
Institutional Master Plan (“IMP”) to the BPDA to commence the review process pursuant to Section 
80D-8 and 80D-5(2) of the Boston Zoning Code, 1956 Mass. Acts c. 665 (“Code”). 
With this IMP, Wentworth seeks to modernize and evolve into an institution that educates the 
leaders of tomorrow while continuing its tradition for more than a century of contributing to the 
local community. Modernizing means creating a sustainable, resilient, and accessible campus that 
reflects the University’s values, ensuring that Wentworth continues to attract students who will 
become future industry leaders in Boston and beyond. It also means strengthening the Wentworth 
community by providing more permanent long-term housing on campus to create a cohesive on-
campus experience for our students and to help alleviate the housing affordability crisis in Boston. 
Through the goals set forth here, Wentworth is setting the stage for the continued pursuit of 
educational excellence as the University seeks to train students in industries with the most in-
demand jobs and provide them with the real-life experience that makes Wentworth students and 
alumni so effective and sought after. 
Lastly, this IMP is also about remaining consistent and stable, and ensuring that as the University 
continues to modernize and evolve, it also remains on strong footing. Therefore, while Wentworth 
is seeking to increase enrollment during the term of the IMP, its enrollment goal is to return to pre-
pandemic levels; not above and beyond that. Moreover, despite consistent increased demand for 
more parking and vehicles even after the pandemic, and despite Wentworth’s plans to bring more 
students back to campus housing, the number of parking spaces is intended to remain consistent 
with the current campus supply. And, as always, this IMP has its roots firmly in Wentworth’s long-
standing dedication to a collaborative and iterative relationship with its neighbors and fellow 
community members, who the University continues to enjoy working closely with to create a more 
vibrant and diverse community within the Mission Hill neighborhood. 
1.1 
History and Background of Wentworth 
For more than a century, Wentworth has delivered a first-rate highly relevant education to prepare 
students for rewarding careers. Along with close faculty mentorship, Wentworth has prepared 
students to work with industry-standard technology by employing one of the most effective 
practices in education: you learn best by doing it. Wentworth is a nationally recognized, private, 
coeducational university offering master’s, bachelor's, and associate degrees, in addition to 
certificate programs, to over 3,500 full-time students annually. More than 50,000 alumni—who have

government—have graduated from Wentworth since it first opened its doors in 1911. 
Wentworth has been a university committed to training the technical workforce of greater Boston 
and continues to evolve its courses, programs, and degrees, making the City a beacon of scientific 
and technical development. Employers seek out Wentworth co-op students and graduates for their 
demonstrated abilities to quickly become productive members of the workforce, technical problem-
solving skills, and educational preparation that allows them to adapt to continuously changing 
technologies. More than 58% of Wentworth students are offered post-graduate, full-time 
employment by their co-op employers. 
The University is proud of its role in the surrounding neighborhood and community. In partnership 
with Mission Main Apartments and Alice Heyward Taylor Apartments, Wentworth has worked with

Through the STRIVE Program, Wentworth has provided vocational opportunities for Boston Public
