CHAPTER 7 
SUSTAINABILITY & RESILIENCY 

Wentworth Institute of Technology 
 Institutional Master Plan 
 
7-1 
Sustainability & Resiliency 
CHAPTER 7 
SUSTAINABILITY & RESILIENCY 
This chapter describes Wentworth’s existing sustainability programs, while also setting forth future 
goals for sustainability initiatives to ensure that Wentworth continues to demonstrate its 
commitment to these important goals that has earned the University recognition as one of the 
nation’s leading environmentally responsible colleges and universities. 
7.1 
Existing Sustainability Initiatives and Programs 
Since 2010, Wentworth has continued to demonstrate its leadership in campus sustainability. 
According to the Princeton Review Green Rating, Wentworth has been recognized as one of the 
nation's most environmentally responsible colleges and universities for nine years in a row. The 
University takes an integrated approach to sustainability, embedding environmental and social 
responsibility principles in its planning, operations, and academic programs. Progress is monitored 
through regular reporting using the Association for Advancement of Sustainability in Higher 
Education's Sustainability Tracking and Rating System (“STARS”). Wentworth is also a signatory of 
the Oganakan Charter, working to promote both health and sustainability across the campus. 
7.1.1 
Sustainable Design and New Construction 
Wentworth adopted LEED Silver-certifiable new construction practices in 2005, pre-dating the City 
of Boston's Article 37 zoning amendment and exceeding its current requirement to meet LEED 
certifiability. Over this timeframe, Wentworth's new construction and major renovation projects 
have achieved the LEED Silver certifiable target, resulting in more than 25% of campus buildings 
(by gross square feet) being built or renovated to high-performance building standards. Highlights 
of major projects since the Prior IMP filing are provided below: 
• 
Flanagan Campus Center (2012) created a hub for student activities, integrating 
energy efficiency, daylighting, and views and adding spaces for flexible programming. 
 
• 
Ira Allen Building (2012) is an example of adaptive reuse, conserving resources, 
reducing embodied carbon, and avoiding urban sprawl. The "Forum" connects old and 
new buildings to provide spaces designed for today's engineering teaching and 
practice. 
 
• 
The Apartments at 525 Huntington (2014) offer student residences built with 
sustainable materials and focused on occupant comfort. Wentworth ensured that this 
site, formerly gas stations, was remediated to remove environmental contamination. It 
was also the first campus project to incorporate design features to improve climate 
resiliency, such as locating critical HVAC equipment on upper floors. 
 
• 
Schumann Library and Learning Commons (2016) was an interior renovation project 
that followed LEED ID+C standards to refresh the library and create a dynamic area for 
student collaboration, with improved acoustical performance and natural light. 
 

Wentworth Institute of Technology 
 Institutional Master Plan 
 
7-2 
Sustainability & Resiliency 
• 
Center for Engineering, Innovation and Sciences (“CEIS”) (2018) is a building 
designed for energy and water efficiency, as well as human health. It houses state-of-
the-art laboratories, classrooms, gathering spaces, and offices to foster hands-on, 
interdisciplinary learning. This project reduced operational carbon by 23% compared 
to baseline construction, reduced indoor water use by 39%, and reduced outdoor water 
use by 57%. It also hosts Wentworth's first 22kW solar panel photovoltaic array on its 
roof as a demonstration project. 
 
• 
Beatty Dining Hall (2022) is a recently completed interior renovation project of the 
University's only dining hall. Formerly a grab-and-go operation, the new all-you-care-
to-eat facility approaches zero-waste by eliminating disposable food packaging and 
sending 100% of food waste to an off-site biodigester. More than 50% of new kitchen 
equipment is Energy Star rated, and the project reduced reliance on fossil fuels by 
switching from a gas to an all-electric pizza oven. 
 
• 
600 Parker/New Sweeney Field (Opening 2024) will consist of an athletic playing field 
constructed above a single-story parking garage. This project is being constructed to 
Parksmart standards, a green rating system for parking garages. Sustainable 
transportation features include Wentworth's first installation of EV charging stations 
(45 spaces with Level 2 charging and two spaces with Level 3 fast-charge capability) 
and a secure bicycle shelter to store both bikes and motorized scooters. 
7.1.2 
Sustainable Campus Operations 
Wentworth’s operational sustainability programs focus on five core areas: 
 
•

7.1.2(a) 
Climate and Energy 
Overseen by Wentworth's Director of Energy Management and Sustainability, the University's 
climate action program includes numerous initiatives to lower energy use and reduce the campus's 
carbon footprint. Wentworth tracks campus GHG emissions annually and has partnered with 
National Grid and Eversource in a strategic energy management program since 2017. More than 35 
energy efficiency projects have been implemented, with expected annual savings of nearly nine 
million kWh of electricity, 187,000 therms of natural gas, and 3,900 metric tons of CO2 avoided. 
These included: 
• 
Energy Infrastructure Improvements such as repairs to the power plant cogeneration 
system, which produces nearly one-third of campus power and recovers waste heat to 
produce steam for heating buildings; repairs to the smaller cogeneration units at 610

• 
Integrative Energy Planning for New Construction including energy modeling,

•

contract. Wentworth has been recognized as an EPA Green Power Partner since 2018. 
7.1.2(b) 
Waste and Recycling 
Wentworth has continued its successful 35-year partnership with Boston Public Schools’ STRIVE 
program, detailed in Chapter 8, to offer career pathways and work experience for students 
receiving special education services. The STRIVE team collects and sorts recyclables from across the 
University, thereby providing a critical service of reducing recycling contamination and engaging 
daily with campus community members. In addition, Wentworth hosts annual green move-out 
campaigns to donate household items to Goodwill and regularly achieves 50-70%+ diversion of 
construction and demolition waste on large projects. Other waste diversion programs include 
recycling of mattresses, electronics, and waste vegetable oil, and yard waste composting. 
Collectively, these efforts divert approximately 30% of overall campus waste. 
7.1.2(c) 
Land Use and Water 
Wentworth recognizes the ecosystem services and community wellness benefits that the campus 
landscape provides. Existing stormwater recharge systems have an estimated capacity of over 8,800 
cubic feet of storage. Since the Prior IMP filing, several projects have led to improvements, such as 
reducing the heat island effect and increasing stormwater recharge. These include: 
• 
Apartments at 525 Huntington Avenue: Added a groundwater recharge system on 
a formerly impervious site, used native and adaptive plantings requiring no irrigation, 
and installed a cool roof to reduce heat gain. 
• 
Pike Pathway: New trees, rain gardens, permeable pavers, and bioswales were added 
to encourage rainwater infiltration, and a light-colored concrete walkway was installed 
to reduce heat gain. 
• 
CEIS: Installed smart irrigation technology and adaptive plantings to reduce water 
demand surrounding the building and selected light-colored concrete and roof 
materials, architectural shading, and shade trees to reduce the heat island effect. 
7.1.2(d) 
Purchasing 
Following higher education best practices, Wentworth uses its procurement process to minimize 
environmental impacts associated with the following products and services: electronics purchasing, 
janitorial services, and dining services.

7.1.2(e) 
Transportation 
Wentworth continues to invest in resources to minimize traffic congestion and the associated air 
quality impacts from single-occupant vehicle commuting to and from campus. With the 
construction of the Apartments at 525 Huntington Avenue, Wentworth increased student housing 
by just over 15% of its previous total. The University encourages commuters to take alternate modes 
of transportation by offering subsidized MBTA passes and preferred parking for carpools in the 
West Lot. The Longwood Collaborative CommuteWorks program provides employees with shuttle 
buses, emergency ride home, rideshare matching, and other services. More than 400 bicycle parking 
spaces are available across campus. Wentworth has expanded its support by adding secure, covered 
bike shelters adjacent to Beatty Hall and within the Apartments at 525 Huntington Avenue. There 
are numerous transit and bus stations, Bluebikes stations, and the Southwest Corridor bike path 
within walking distance from the campus. As a result of these efforts, more than 90% of students 
either live in Wentworth housing or take sustainable commute modes to campus.

contributions to a global society. Tomorrow's leaders will need multidisciplinary skills, real-world

Wentworth's academic programs include more than 20 courses that focus exclusively on 
sustainability concepts and more than 70 additional courses related to sustainability. Students can 
study topics ranging from energy systems and climate change to green infrastructure and 
environmental justice. The University offers a major in Climate Resilience, a major in Building 
Sciences, an environmental engineering minor, access to the COF minor in sustainability, and co-

7.2 
Future Goals of Sustainable Initiatives and Programs 
In 2022, Wentworth convened workshops with key stakeholders to determine future planning 
objectives for sustainability. These facilitated sessions included reviewing the University's 
sustainability performance, discussing regional policy development, and exploring opportunities 
related to the scope of changes being proposed in the Campus Master Plan. Ideas and feedback 
were gathered from the Sustainability Committee, the Campus Master Planning Steering Team and 
consultants from various disciplines, and external stakeholders such as the Boston Water and Sewer 
Commission (“BWSC”), Longwood Collective, Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, and the 
Muddy River Restoration Project Oversight Committee (“MMOC”). Based on this input, a series of 
recommendations will be incorporated into IMP Projects and future campus planning to position 
the University to meet the City of Boston’s goals for carbon neutrality by 2050.

7.2.1 
Green Buildings and GHG Reduction 
To support the City of Boston’s GHG reduction targets, the University will continue implementing 
its climate action program to address existing buildings and new construction decarbonization. 
7.2.1(a) 
Existing Buildings – Decarbonization and Electrification 
Currently, Wentworth's campus-wide carbon emissions intensity is below the BERDO 2025 and 2030 
carbon performance standards for university buildings. However, Wentworth is planning now to 
ensure its operations will comply with BERDO over the long term. To meet future GHG reduction

Wentworth's decarbonization efforts will be generally phased based on payback and incentive 
eligibility (in order of priority below):

renovations).

Infrastructure upgrades will be assessed as aspects of the decarbonization plan are implemented – 
i.e., building-level upgrades as smaller existing buildings are individually electrified, followed by 
more complex upgrades at high EUI buildings and the central plant. Wentworth will continue 
collaborating with Eversource and National Grid on electrification planning and heat pump 
conversion studies. The University also intends to continue participating in the ISO demand 
response program and anticipates peak load shaving to be an important aspect of distributed 
energy resources, such as on-campus solar PV. 
As a university that values future-focused innovation, Wentworth will explore emerging 
technologies and use the campus as a living laboratory. For example, a team of faculty and students 
are working with external collaborators to research campus electricity demand profiles, solar PV, 
and microgrid technologies to help understand what's needed to manage distributed energy 
resources and load shedding across the campus grid. Recent publications highlight these efforts.13

Low Carbon Design 
The University will prioritize LEED credits and strategies that support low-carbon building 
operations, integration of renewable energy, and embodied carbon reduction. Wentworth will 
comply with the MA Specialized Stretch Energy Code, and the BPDA's Zero Net Carbon Building 
Zoning and updated Article 37 requirements (when adopted and applicable). 
Future IMP Projects will reduce operational carbon through strategies such as: 
• 
Establishing targets for building energy use intensity (“EUI”) and carbon emissions 
intensity (“CEI”) early in the design. 
• 
Partnering with MassSave sponsors to identify, model, and incentivize energy efficiency 
measures that are at or go beyond code compliance. 
• 
Utilizing passive design, high-performance envelopes, and energy recovery ventilation 
to minimize air leakage and heat loss. 
• 
Prioritizing electrification/fossil fuel-free technology for space heating, water heating, 
and appliances where economically viable. 
• 
Prioritizing refrigerants with a low global warming potential. 
• 
Studying the feasibility of on-site renewable energy (solar and geothermal), battery 
technology, or provisions for future solar plus storage-ready design. 
• 
Geothermal applications will be assessed for locations beneath new buildings or under 
adjacent open spaces based on soil conditions and where there are no obstacles from 
buried infrastructure. 
Wentworth will reduce the embodied carbon impacts of new construction projects by evaluating 
structural designs, product selection, and materials reuse opportunities. These strategies will be 
emphasized by continuing to pursue credits within the LEED rating system, such as: 
• 
Construction and Demolition Waste Management – setting goals for total waste 
diversion (90%+) and waste intensity early in design, planning for waste diversion, and 
tracking progress throughout construction 
• 
Building Life-Cycle Impact Reduction – reusing building elements and incorporating 
salvaged and recycled content materials 
• 
Building Product Disclosure and Optimization – selecting building materials designed 
to protect human health, conserve resources, and reduce environmental impacts across 
the entire product life cycle.

7.2.1(c) 
Transportation 
Air pollution and transportation impacts are a key concern for the Wentworth community and its 
neighbors. According to EPA's EJScreen Tool, the environmental justice (“EJ”) indexes for the 
Mission Hill neighborhood indicate high vulnerability to particulate matter, ozone, air toxics risks, 
and traffic proximity. In addition, there is a higher rate of asthma. In response to these concerns, 
Wentworth will adopt an innovative approach to mitigating regional air pollution through ongoing 
transportation demand management, a significant investment in electric vehicle infrastructure, and 
more resilient land use and tree canopy strategies (see Section 7.2.2(a)). 
Thanks to Wentworth's student housing and commuter benefits programs, the majority of students 
either live on campus or travel via transit, biking, and walking. Approximately 33% of faculty and 
staff take alternative modes. Full-time drivers are only a small proportion of the overall campus 
population. Nearly half (48%) of Wentworth's faculty and staff drivers commute part-time due to 
academic or hybrid schedules. While Wentworth's contribution to peak traffic impacts is relatively 
low for these reasons, the University anticipates that demand for parking will remain stable given 
the mix of community needs (co-ops, academic schedules, family obligations, and median commute 
distances of ten miles). 
Wentworth's IMP Projects will consolidate parking from several surface lots into new underground 
garages. By following the City of Boston's EV Readiness Policy, these projects will support a future 
transition to electric vehicles. Across the three projects—600 Parker, West Lot, and the Annex—over 
180 spaces will have EV charging installed, and an additional 600+ will be EV-ready (see Table 7.1). 
Ultimately, 69% of Wentworth's total parking will have future EV charging capability. 
The benefits of this transition can be estimated using the Department of Energy's AFLEET tool. 
Compared to a baseline scenario with internal combustion engines, 789 EVs would significantly 
reduce GHGs and local air pollution (see Table 7.2). Wentworth is working with stakeholders such 
as the Boston Fire Department and Eversource to ensure a safe and well-orchestrated deployment 
of this equipment. As new technology becomes more proven in the market, future installations may 
explore options for vehicle-to-grid and passive survivability, particularly when located adjacent to 
residential buildings or emergency services. 
Multi-modal transportation will also be enhanced through the IMP (see Figure 4.4). Bicycle storage 
facilities will be added at strategic locations along the campus perimeter to enable easy connections 
to regional bicycle networks. Facilities will be designed similar to the bike storage unit at 600 Parker, 
following best practices from the City of Boston Bike Parking Guidelines and supporting 
micromobility by providing space and charging capability for scooters and e-bikes. Landscape 
design elements such as extending pedestrian paths across campus and the Front Lawn and

7.2.2 
Climate Resiliency and Urban Ecosystem 
Resiliency planning efforts centered on two hazards from the 2022 Greater Boston Research 
Advisory Group Report: extreme heat and more intense storms (including flooding and 
groundwater impacts). The Wentworth team evaluated campus vulnerabilities and risks, drawing 
from historical events and interviews with regional stakeholders such as BWSC and the MMOC. A 
series of overarching strategies were then developed. For all IMP Projects, the BPDA Resiliency 
Checklist will be employed early in the planning process to review the hazards, identify any specific 
vulnerabilities, and implement the appropriate design criteria.

Open Space Land Use Analysis 
Intentional land use changes and the addition of new open spaces will improve environmental 
quality, enhance resiliency, and promote a more walkable and activated campus community: 
• 
Consolidation of parking from surface lots to underground garages will net a 60% 
reduction in impervious surface parking area. 
 
• 
Reimagining open areas will create more than 2.5 acres of appropriately-scaled 
gathering spaces with a mixture of programmed lawns, native/adaptive landscaping, and 
tree canopy for shade and visual interest.

7.2.2(d) 
Stormwater Management 
Wentworth is constructed on land originally functioning as a tidal basin and bisected by the Stony 
Brook. While the Stony Brook was culverted down Parker Street in the 1800s, the main campus still 
depends on this infrastructure and the surrounding Muddy River/Fens drainage. In addition, the 
campus is part of the Groundwater Conservation Overlay District, designed to preserve wood pile 
foundations and other historic structures in the region through groundwater restoration. Given this 
history and the vulnerabilities of citywide drainage systems, the University has proposed the 
following strategies to reduce runoff, enhance groundwater levels, and mitigate potential 
stormwater and flood impacts: 
 
• 
Adding a significant amount of stormwater infiltration over time as new construction 
projects (with retention systems), landscaping, and green infrastructure are added (see 
Figure 7.5). 
• 
Targeting specific areas prone to stormwater flooding for green infrastructure projects 
that serve a dual purpose of activating open space for recreation and increasing 
stormwater retention. 
• 
Exploring opportunities for additional rainwater harvesting systems for irrigation, such as 
blue roofs. 
• 
For new construction in relatively low-lying areas, the first floor of buildings can be raised, 
and critical mechanical equipment can be placed on upper levels. 
• 
Implementing a preventive maintenance program to ensure building backflow 
prevention systems remain functional. 
• 
Honoring the historic route of the Stony Brook when planning the placement of 
stormwater management features and sharing the story of the watershed and its civil 
engineering systems with students through educational signage.

Employment & Job Training Analysis 
 
CHAPTER 8 
EMPLOYMENT & JOB TRAINING ANALYSIS 
This chapter describes Wentworth’s current employment and projected employment needs, and 
also describes current programs Wentworth has with Boston Public Schools (“BPS”) aimed to train 
and employ students from Boston, particularly within the vicinity of the University. 
8.1 
Current Workforce 
In total, Wentworth employs a total of 881 personnel—comprised of employees and contractors—
of which 38% are Boston residents. As of December 1, 2023, Wentworth employed a total of 771 
full-time and part-time employees, approximately 32% (249) of whom are Boston residents. In 
addition to employees, Wentworth also funds 110 full-time and part-time positions provided 
through private contractors who provide operational services in the areas of cleaning, food service, 
health services, and copy and mail center. Approximately 77% (85) of the individuals employed by 
these service contractors are Boston residents. 
Wentworth’s payroll and benefits for Fiscal Year 2023 totaled approximately $74,800,000. 
8.2 
Projected Employment Needs 
Wentworth estimates that the PIPs proposed in this IMP term will generate approximately 1,000 
construction jobs. Wentworth does not expect a significant increase in faculty and staff employment 
over the term of this IMP and plans to maintain existing faculty and staff employment levels. 
8.3 
Workforce Development and Programs with Boston Public Schools 
Wentworth is proud of its over 35-year partnership with BPS, during which time it has helped 
provide opportunities for students to gain work skills and practical work experience. Since 1988, 
Wentworth’s workforce development programs have served over 6,000 Boston students. Two of 
the most significant programs to train and employ students include the Supported Training to 
Reach Independence through Vocational Experiences (“STRIVE”) and Industry Corps: 
STRIVE 
This Wentworth training program is a school-to-work transition program for BPS students with a 
variety of special needs, including physical, cognitive, and emotional disabilities. This award-
winning vocational training program leads to internships, externships, employment, and 
postgraduate opportunities in a myriad of fields, including facilities management, hospitality, 
customer service, business management, and public works. Participants come from all over Boston 
and go on to a 100% job or internship placement rate after matriculation. Wentworth spends over 
$500,000 annually on this one-of-a-kind successful program and serves over 150 non-diploma 
bound BPS students. 
As of Spring 2024, 63 students are working at Wentworth at the University’s Recycling Training 
Center of STRIVE, which is a 2,054 sf facility that supports student learning and the recycling

program operations. Another STRIVE program, the Facilities Maintenance Program, focuses on 
custodial training in a 1,600 sf facility located in the 610 Huntington Avenue Residence Hall. This 
program supports student training and work operations responsible for caring for 20,550 sf of area 
throughout the residence hall. 
Industry Corps 
In 2022, Wentworth created Industry Corps which helped expand its impactful and effective Boston 
Pipeline to high school graduates from the last ten years interested in joining the skilled labor 
workforce by providing educational credentials, career exposure, and individualized support, 
resulting in gainful employment and a family-sustaining wage. Nationally, and further highlighted 
locally, there are significant challenges facing the skilled labor workforce. With the demographics 
shifting to a majority non-white population by 2045, the lack of diversity (racial, gender, and age) 
in the current skilled labor workforce has never been more important to address. Despite local 
policies that were created to positively influence the industry, the number of diverse residents in 
the local workforce has improved only slightly. To close the workforce gap, significant opportunities 
exist for local schools, higher education institutions, industry, and government to come together 
and develop solutions that grow and diversify the future skilled workforce. 
Built as a “community school” concept, Industry Corps aims to eliminate perceived and actual 
barriers that limit post-secondary success for underrepresented populations who do not pursue a 
traditional four-year degree pathway. By providing a tuition-free scholarship to nearly every 
applicant and educational stipends for all participants, Wentworth seeks to remove barriers—like 
high-cost tuition and burdensome student loan debt—that typically limit post-secondary success 
for students. Additionally, Industry Corps offers a tiered educational credentialing system with the 
goal of awarding certificates in various education-to-career pathways. The program is designed as 
a four-semester training program with Construction Management, specifically Field Leadership, as 
the initial focus, and an expansion in year two into the tech industry with a pathway in Data Analytics 
and Information Technology. 
Industry Corps provides an expansion of credit-bearing certificates for students interested in a 
fulfilling career in skilled trades. All pathways include coursework in management and 
entrepreneurship, with the aim of not only training participants through on-the-job, hands-on 
opportunities, but of providing them with the foundational knowledge to manage projects, crews, 
and establish their own businesses in the future. Students also learn essential traits and professional 
skills to be work-ready, confident, career-minded employees. At the end of the program, our aim 
is that students will have achieved competencies that enable them to work full-time on a job site. 
Students may also elect to continue their education at Wentworth and earn a bachelor’s degree or 
other credentials to further their career. 
Graduates from BPS or other local public high schools are encouraged to apply to this 4-semester 
program that prepares students to compete for jobs in skilled labor industries.

Community Benefits Plan 
CHAPTER 9 
COMMUNITY BENEFITS PLAN 
Building and maintaining a thriving relationship with the neighborhood has remained a primary 
objective of Wentworth’s central mission. Wentworth prides itself on being part of the very fabric 
of the local community. See Figure 9.1 for a map of neighboring entities. Its community relations 
approach is unique as Wentworth does not seek transactional, project-based support. Rather, its 
community relationships are based on ongoing relationships that keep Wentworth engaged in 
public life. 
9.1 
Community Benefit Programs 
Wentworth’s community benefits have two primary aims. The first is to enhance educational 
opportunities for the young people of Boston. The second is to contribute to and support the 
surrounding neighborhoods. These objectives are realized through continuing partnerships with 
Wentworth’s neighbors, community-based organizations, and the City of Boston. These 
partnerships create a strong foundation of community-focused programs. With this IMP, 
Wentworth will build upon this foundation with new resources and a renewed commitment to 
partnerships that will achieve an even greater impact. 
Overall, in Fiscal Year 2023, Wentworth contributed over $7,000,000 of community benefits in cash 
and in-kind value. 
Specifically, the University channels resources into five key initiative areas: (1) college access and 
success, (2) workforce development (see Chapter 8), (3) youth outreach, (4) investment in 
neighborhood development, and (5) community-campus relationships. 
9.1.1 
College Access and Success 
Wentworth understands that improved access to higher education is necessary to support 
historically disadvantaged groups in the community. The University has therefore implemented 
multiple scholarship opportunities for students to help mitigate the financial burden that college 
can place on families, including the following: 
Jimmie Beverly Scholarship 
Named after a beloved community activist and longtime Wentworth Task Force Member, this 
scholarship has allowed residents of Mission Hill and Fenway to attend Wentworth free of cost. In 
2023, Wentworth contributed $228,014 to this scholarship fund. 
Boston Residents Scholarship 
This scholarship is an agreement with Boston Public Schools (“BPS”) that allows selected high school 
graduates from any Boston public school to attend Wentworth tuition-free. Ten scholarships are 
provided per academic year, but Wentworth expands that number by covering any gap between

government aid and tuition for additional BPS students. In 2023, this scholarship covered around 
$480,703 in tuition for students from Boston. 
Merit Scholarships 
Wentworth also offers a variety of merit-based scholarships for motivated students to decrease the 
cost of higher education. In 2023, Wentworth provided more than $4 million in merit-based aid to 
Boston residents. 
Boston Pipeline 
Wentworth understands that financial support is only one component necessary to improve access 
to and success in higher education. Through the Center for Community and Learning Partnerships, 
the University is committed to increasing matriculation and retention of local youth by growing a 
new cohort of youth interested in design, engineering, computer science, and management; 
helping students persist in college, and supporting them through graduation. The Boston Pipeline 
Initiative offers several programs for youths in Boston to advance these goals: 
• 
Beacon Pathways: As Wentworth’s rendition of Dual Enrollment, Beacon Pathways is 
the University’s Early College Pathways Program a collaboration with BPS that aims to 
increase the attendance, retention, and graduation rates of youth from Boston who are 
pursuing degrees that reflect the local economy with pathways in computer science, 
engineering, and entrepreneurship. Wentworth is proud to be the only private 
university in Boston to receive Early College designation from the state’s Executive 
Office of Education with three separate BPS high schools. 
• 
RAMP Summer Bridge: RAMP assists first-time college students with navigating the 
transition from high school to college, providing them with project-based hands-on 
learning, individualized case management, and a diverse network of support. Students 
who participate in RAMP receive a stipend—so they do not have to choose between 
RAMP or needing a summer job—and have a higher first-to-second year retention rate 
and higher six-year graduation rate than Wentworth’s population who do not attend 
RAMP, especially compared to Boston residents who do not decide to participate in 
the program. 
9.1.2 
Youth Outreach 
An important part of community engagement is connecting with youth of all ages. Wentworth has 
served as a gathering space and community hub for Boston children by providing free space for 
the Mission Hill Summer Program—operated by the Phillips Brooks House Association—for over 
30 years. This program serves residents of Mission Hill, especially from the Alice Taylor and Mission 
Main Apartments, and aims to curb youth violence early on and provide resources to the parents 
of Mission Hill. Wentworth is proud to serve as a meeting place for youths from various housing 
developments across Boston, where they may establish long-lasting relationships and connections 
with their peers and the community-at-large.

Furthermore, Wentworth actively supports the youth of the community through its Boston Pipeline 
programs mentioned above. 
9.1.3 
Investment in Neighborhood Development 
One of the University’s primary objectives is providing its students with tools and resources for 
success in life, and the same can be said of Wentworth’s commitment to its surrounding 
neighborhood. An integral element to advancing this objective is investment in the planning of 
community-oriented spaces and amenities that serve the surrounding community, as well as 
investment in mitigation efforts to alleviate some of the issues it faces. These investments include 
the following: 
Transportation 
Wentworth employees can ride the MBTA for free with the local bus and train combination pass, a 
unique benefit not offered by many colleges or hospitals. This incentivizes staff to rely on public 
transportation, thereby decreasing traffic congestion and reducing vehicle emissions in the area. 
The benefit highlights the University’s commitment to environmental sustainability, environmental 
justice, and its concern regarding the impact of climate change for future generations. 
Parks 
Publicly accessible open spaces are necessary to create a vibrant, pleasant community. Wentworth 
maintains Boston’s Evans Way Park, which is a portion of Boston’s “Emerald Necklace” and the 
State’s Kitty Dukakis Park (a pocket park at the corner of Evans Way and Huntington Avenue). Costs 
associated with care and preservation of these important public spaces costs approximately $50,000 
per year. Wentworth is committed to continuing its role in making these spaces accessible. 
Facilities Usage 
Wentworth allows partnering neighborhood groups to use space on campus, free of charge, from 
small groups of residents needing meeting spaces to large-scale events operated by BPS, Boston 
Centers for Youth and Families, and more. For example, in 2023, large-scale events included a two-
day staff retreat for the staff of Boston Centers for Youth and Families. Wentworth is committed to 
continuing to make its facilities available to partnership neighborhood groups and the City of 
Boston departments. 
Land Donations 
Wentworth has on multiple occasions throughout its history donated land to the City of Boston or 
to other organizations to enhance the neighborhood. The creation of the Maria Sanchez Senior 
Building, which provides affordable housing to seniors in the community, was made possible by 
Wentworth’s contribution of land to the Mission Hill Neighborhood Housing Services. Wentworth 
also provided 34 parking spaces to the Mission Hill Neighborhood Housing Services for a period of 
3.5 years, which allowed for construction of its Phase II affordable housing development.

Additionally, the University also donated portions of its sidewalk along 525 and 610 Huntington 
Avenue, and along the New Sweeney Field at Ruggles Street and Huntington Avenue to the City, 
helping to double the width of the sidewalk, creating more disability-friendly sidewalks in Boston. 
More recently, the University has committed to donating portions of its sidewalks along Halleck 
Street and Prentiss Street to the City as part of the New Sweeney Field Project. 
9.1.4 
Community Campus Relationships 
Wentworth’s commitment to its surrounding neighborhoods and community is a continuous and 
ever-evolving partnership. Its relationship with its neighbors and the broader Boston community is 
ongoing, and not just one-off or project based. The University considers itself an active member, 
and, as such, works with community groups to coordinate and provide services like the ones listed 
below: 
Laptop Donations 
In an ever-advancing technological world, Wentworth makes it a priority to donate laptops to the 
greater Boston community. Access to laptops in both schools and at home gives the students the 
opportunity to access information, improve their financial literacy, seek help with homework and 
assignments, and more. Recently, Wentworth donated new laptops to residents of the Alice Taylor 
and Mission Main Housing Developments. 
Community Work Study Program 
Wentworth students are encouraged to be engaged members of their community. The University 
partners with local nonprofit organizations and places students in those offices to perform their 
work-study hours to gain real-world work experience. Wentworth students serve as volunteers, 
tutors, and mentors throughout the community, teaching classes at computer labs to improve 
digital proficiency, helping with income tax filing, and more. 
Community Public Safety 
Yearly contributions to weekend Boston Police details for the Mission Hill ride-around accompanied 
by Wentworth campus police in the Mission Hill community. The goal is to monitor and ensure our 
neighbors’ positive quality of life. 
Cash Contributions 
Wentworth spends approximately $40,000 annually on cash contributions to community 
organizations, projects, and individuals. 
Community Partnerships 
Being part of the fabric of the community means going above and beyond planned projects or 
recurring events. Neighbors count on Wentworth for an array of support. In addition to those listed

9.2 
Taxes, PILOT Program, and Linkage 
Wentworth is currently paying property taxes on certain land parcels it owns. In Fiscal Year 2023 
(July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2023), Wentworth paid $86,066 in property taxes to the City of 
Boston.

Wentworth also participates in Boston’s PILOT program. Due to its existing community benefits and 
other exceptional credits it provides to the City, as well as annual budget impacts due to COVID, 
and drop in student enrollment, Wentworth has not made a voluntary PILOT contribution in the 
last few years. 
Housing Linkage contributions to the Neighborhood Housing Trust and jobs linkage contributions 
to the Neighborhood Jobs Trust will be made for all projects that are deemed to be Development 
Impact Projects in accordance with Article 80B-7 of Boston Zoning Code. 
It is to be noted that with the private development of 500 Huntington Avenue (a 3-acre parcel 
previously used as Wentworth’s athletic field), the parcel will transition from nonprofit status and 
be subject to both yearly real estate tax and one-time linkage payments.

Re: Wentworth IMP
Dear Chair Rojas and Members of the Board,
We write to express our support for Wentworth Institute of Technology’s Institutional Master
Plan (IMP). It’s been encouraging to witness the evolution of this project over the past year, and
we recognize the significant changes it has undergone even before our tenure as councilors.
Wentworth has been a great institutional partner, and over conversations with their president
Mark Thompson, it’s clear that the college’s bold vision for the future provides opportunities for
City of Boston residents and aligns with many City goals and initiatives.
This IMP meets the moment for a primary concern we hear from residents of Boston: that is the
pressing issue of housing affordability and availability in our city. Institutions like Wentworth
play a critical role in addressing this challenge. We are pleased to see the focus on retaining
students on campus, which not only supports the student body but also alleviates some of the
housing pressure in the community.
The Wentworth Institute of Technology’s Institutional Master Plan includes several
transformative projects designed to enhance campus life and address community needs. Central
to this plan is a new eight-story, 111,000-square-foot integrated athletics field house, along with
a 217-bed residence hall, which will enrich the student experience. Additionally, a prominent
267,000-square-foot residence hall featuring 672 beds will front Huntington Avenue, offering
study and event spaces, a dining hall, and an expanded fitness center. The reconfigured 13-story
residence hall at 630 Huntington Avenue, set to replace Baker Hall, will also include a café and
additional study and event spaces, further supporting student engagement. These
improvements enhance the student experience, which is one of the most important objectives
of the IMP.
In addition to residential developments, the plan includes a five-story West Quad Academic
Building to accommodate the School of Architecture and Design, as well as new North and
South Halls to replace the outdated Annex complex, providing modern facilities for the Schools
of Engineering and Management. Renovations to Wentworth Hall will introduce a new

District 8 Councilor Sharon Durkan
Councilor At-Large Henry Santana
20,000-square-foot Welcome Center and an outdoor plaza, creating inviting spaces for both
students and community members. Complementing these developments are two new outdoor
green public spaces, designed to foster community interaction and enhance the overall campus
environment.
Additionally, the thoughtful approach to opening the campus to local residents is
commendable. By creating accessible pathways and enhancing open spaces, the project fosters
a sense of belonging for community members, making them feel like integral parts of the
campus rather than mere visitors.
We respectfully urge the board to approve this project and appreciate your consideration of its
positive impact on both the institution and the community.
